title: Dolores Huerta, activist and labor leader, dies at 96
text:
Dolores Huerta, activist and labor leader, dies at 96
Dolores Huerta, a civil rights activist, feminist and labor leader who co-founded the United Farm Workers labor union, has died. She was 96.
"We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96," a post from her family and the Dolores Huerta Foundation read. "As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family. We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy."
Huerta co-founded the National Farmworkers Association, which later became the United Farm Workers, alongside the late César Chávez, who had multiple allegations of sexual abuse surface earlier this year.
Soon after the allegations surfaced, Huerta revealed that she had secret children after she said Chávez raped her and sexually abused her.
Huerta is credited with coming up with the farmworker rallying cry “Sí, se puede.”
She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women’s rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.
Huerta’s resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to “Yes, it can be done” — was grounded in the belief that people could effect change.
Homegrown activism
Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who went on to win a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.
Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.
Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students’ poor living conditions.
“I couldn’t stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes,” she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. “I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children.”
Huerta’s early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.
She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year “Delano Grape Strike.” With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers.
Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.
Fueled by courage
Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores’ 13 children, once pointed to his mom’s courage during an interview, saying it was one of the most significant drivers of her life’s work.
“To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farmworkers, to take on agriculture, which to this today is still a powerhouse. ... That took a lot of guts,” he had said.
Huerta learned the art of lobbying politicians. She secured financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farmworkers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and fought federal guest worker programs.
By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass what would be the first state law recognizing farmworkers’ right to collective bargaining.
Her work earned her many accolades. She was the first Latina to be inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame and she’s received nine honorary doctorates from U.S. universities.
Schools are named in her honor in California, Texas and Colorado. Her image graces many murals, and streets bear her name, but she didn’t always win favor with more liberal activists.
In 2016 when she endorsed Hillary Clinton instead of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont in the presidential Democratic primary, actor Rosario Dawson — a Sanders supporter who played Huerta in a 2014 movie about César Chavez — said Huerta had become “an instrument of the establishment.”
Dawson and Huerta eventually reconciled.
It was her work as a leader within the labor movement that reverberated through the U.S. and beyond, making her name synonymous with civil rights. In the 2025 documentary “Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta,” she recounted her decades-long journey in activism and talked about the inspiration she drew from the women’s movement during the 1970s, saying it provided validation that she too could stand on the stage with other labor leaders.
“I hope that my legacy will be one of an organizer that organized to fight injustice,” she said in the film. “We want to give our children an inheritance of justice, right, not jewels or property or money because they’ll just fight over it. So the main thing to do is to give them this love for justice — and that is the greatest gift I think that any of us can have.”
The Associated Press contributed to this story.

title: Class D Divisional Volleyball Championship Recap
text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - Brewer High School hosted the Class D Divisional Volleyball Championships on Tuesday night.
No. 1 George Stevens Academy defeated No. 4 North Yarmouth-Freeport in three sets (25-23, 25-20, 25-10) in the first matchup.
No. 3 Woodland beat No. 2 Narraguagus, 3-1 (17-25, 25-18, 25-18, 25-20).
The Dragons dethroned the Knights’ Class D state title defense and ended Narraguagus’s three-year run as state champs across Classes C and D.
Narraguagus won the Class D state title in 2025 and won the Class C crown in 2023 and 2024.
The state championship is set for Friday at 7 p.m. at Husson’s Newman Gymnasium.

title: How the Iran war is raising mortgage costs for US homebuyers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How the Iran war is raising mortgage costs for US homebuyers
The Federal Reserve decided to keep interest rates unchanged, leaving mortgage rates above 7% and homebuyers facing higher monthly costs.
How the Iran war is raising mortgage costs for US homebuyers
The Federal Reserve decided to keep interest rates unchanged, leaving mortgage rates above 7% and homebuyers facing higher monthly costs.
The war in Iran has driven up the cost of buying a home in America, according to experts, as the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday.
Just two days before the war began, the average 30-year mortgage rate fell to 5.98%. By Oct. 22, it had climbed to 7.32%, according to Freddie Mac.
"The Fed really hasn't been the main character for mortgage rates this year. The Iran war has been a much more significant influence," said Kate Wood, a lending expert at NerdWallet.
Wood said the connection is indirect. The war has pushed up energy costs and raised concerns that inflation could remain elevated.
"A lot of what we're seeing is actually investor concerns about inflation being translated through the bond market," Wood said.
Those concerns matter because mortgage rates are closely tied to longer-term Treasury yields, which are influenced by inflation expectations and other economic forces. When those yields rise, mortgage rates often follow.
The increased rates and the effects of the Iran war conflict with a major campaign promise from President Donald Trump.
"I will end the devastating inflation crisis immediately, bring down interest rates, and lower the cost of energy," Trump said during his nomination acceptance speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention.
What higher mortgage rates mean for homebuyers
The difference can add hundreds of dollars to the cost of financing a home.
Hearst Television's Get the Facts Data Team built an interactive calculator showing how mortgage interest charges have changed.
On a $400,000 mortgage loan, the interest charged in the first month would be approximately $2,440 at a 7.32% rate.
At the 5.98% rate recorded just before the Iran war, that same first month's interest would have been approximately $1,993.
The calculator measures the initial interest charge on a new loan, not the total monthly mortgage payment. That payment also includes principal, while property taxes and insurance can add to the overall cost.
What is the White House doing?
The Trump administration has announced several measures aimed at reducing housing costs, although much of the relief has yet to take effect.
On Oct. 22, Trump signed an executive order seeking to reduce certain refinancing expenses, create a conditional pilot program that would automatically cancel mortgage insurance for qualifying borrowers on future loans, and lower interest rates on certain USDA and VA direct home loans.
The order also established a task force to examine ways to expand manufactured and factory-built housing.
Wood said manufactured housing could offer one of the more meaningful opportunities to improve affordability because those homes can be built relatively quickly and at lower cost.
But she cautioned that much of the executive order involves developing programs and recommendations rather than delivering immediate savings.
She also questioned how much lower refinancing costs would help homeowners in the current market.
"Virtually no homeowners are in the money on a rate and term refinance," Wood said.
And while the administration's measures could reduce some housing expenses, they do not directly lower interest rates on most conventional mortgages.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has also acknowledged that geopolitical tensions are affecting longer-term borrowing costs. In September, he identified global conflicts as one of several factors pushing up bond yields.
According to The Associated Press, Wall Street investors are anticipating another rate hike in December. But the Fed has not committed to that move.
Wood cautioned that even if the Fed raises its benchmark interest rate, mortgage rates won't necessarily move by the same amount. They respond to a broader range of economic forces.
For prospective buyers considering waiting for rates to fall, she offered some advice.
"If you are thinking, 'Oh, I'm going to sit around, I'm going to wait for mortgage rates to go down.' You can do that, but you do not know how long that wait is going to be," Wood said. "The right time to buy a home is always when it is the right time for you and your finances, not necessarily when you think it is the right market."

title: Alvin K. Hellerstein, a federal judge who handled Trump, Maduro and 9/11 cases, dies at 92
text:
Alvin K. Hellerstein, a federal judge who handled Trump, Maduro and 9/11 cases, dies at 92
Alvin K. Hellerstein, a Manhattan federal judge who presided over cases involving President Donald Trump, former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and the 9/11 attacks during nearly three decades on the bench, has died. He was 92.
Hellerstein died Wednesday morning while surrounded by his family, Chief Judge Laura Taylor Swain said in a statement. His funeral is scheduled for Thursday at Riverside Memorial Chapel in Manhattan.
Related video above: Americans are wary of US involvement in Venezuela after Maduro's removal, according to new poll
Swain remembered Hellerstein as a “distinguished jurist” and praised his “energetic and dedicated service” to the court, which continued until his death.
“He is greatly appreciated and will be sorely missed,” she said.
Just two weeks ago, Hellerstein presided over the arraignment of Maduro and Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores, on torture charges that were added to their ongoing narco-terrorism conspiracy case.
Maduro, who was captured alongside his wife in January in a surprise U.S. military raid in Caracas, twice defied Hellerstein’s request to enter a plea. Irked, Hellerstein took matters into his own hands, interjecting that “a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro.”
At Flores’ Oct. 8 bail hearing, Hellerstein coughed and struggled to speak at times, telling lawyers: “I have a voice problem. As long as you can understand — hear me, I’ll keep going.” Nevertheless, he was resolute that he’d preside over Maduro and Flores’ trial, which he’d scheduled for next June.
“We were saddened to learn of Judge Hellerstein’s passing and offer our condolences to his family,” Maduro's lawyer, Barry Pollack, said.
Analisa Torres, the judge taking over the case, was part of an international monitoring delegation for Venezuela’s 2006 presidential election, won by Maduro’s late mentor and predecessor Hugo Chávez. A federal judge since 2013, she previously served on the state bench in Manhattan.
A New York native and Columbia Law School graduate, Hellerstein served in the U.S. Army Judge Advocate General’s Corps and worked as a Manhattan litigator before President Bill Clinton appointed him to the federal bench in 1998. He kept a robust docket even after moving to senior status in 2011.
Rulings left Trump’s conviction in place
In August, in one of his last significant rulings, Hellerstein again spurned Trump’s effort to erase his hush money conviction, rejecting the president’s bid to move the case to federal court and have it dismissed on presidential immunity grounds.
“Paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity,” Hellerstein wrote, referring to the $130,000 payoff to adult film actor Stormy Daniels at the heart of Trump’s case.
It was the third time Hellerstein had denied Trump’s requests to move the case. The first time was after Trump’s March 2023 indictment; the second followed Trump’s May 2024 conviction and a subsequent U.S. Supreme Court ruling that presidents and former presidents cannot be prosecuted for official acts.
Hellerstein revisited the matter after the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that he erred by failing to consider “important issues relevant” to Trump’s request. The panel expressed “no view” on how Hellerstein should rule.
In 2020, Hellerstein sprang Trump’s estranged former lawyer and fixer Michael Cohen from prison after the Justice Department revoked his home confinement to thwart his efforts to publish a book or talk to the media. The government’s action, he ruled, was retaliatory and a First Amendment violation.
‘This is different. This is 9/11.’
In the aftermath of the 2001 attack on the World Trade Center, Hellerstein presided over dozens of wrongful death, injury and property damage lawsuits — a two-decade-long effort that shaped his legacy on the bench.
Some of the judge’s former clients died in the attack and, lawyers say, he showed great empathy to victims and their families, meeting with them for hours in his chambers and rejecting what he felt were low-ball settlement offers.
In March 2010, Hellerstein rejected a proposed settlement that would have paid at least $575 million to thousands of people who fell ill working in the toxic ash of the trade center. He acknowledged he was breaking with tradition by getting so involved.
“Most settlements are private. A plaintiff and defendant come together, shake hands, and it’s done with,” he explained. The judge usually has no part in saying yes or no.
“This is different,” Hellerstein said. “This is 9/11.”
Others were dismayed when, in 2008, Hellerstein ended an effort to force New York City government to keep searching for human remains in debris moved from ground zero to a Staten Island landfill.
High-profile cases until the end
Hellerstein's other notable cases included the criminal trials of Charlie Javice, who was convicted last year of defrauding JPMorgan Chase out of $175 million by exaggerating the customer base for her financial aid startup, and hedge fund founder Bill Hwang, who was convicted in 2024 of securities and market manipulation fraud in a scheme that cost banks billions of dollars.
He also presided over a 2025 civil trial at which a jury ordered French bank BNP Paribas to pay nearly $21 million for giving the Sudanese government access to the U.S. financial system as it engaged in atrocities two decades ago. In 2015, Hellerstein ordered a New York City cable company to pay a Texas woman $229,500 for flooding her phone with 153 robocalls.
Hellerstein, known for a quirky independent streak and strict discipline in his courtroom, insisted spectators wear pandemic-era masks for years after other judges stopped the practice.
He “lived a life of commitment to public service and devotion to his community,” the court said in a statement. “His example and work ethic will continue to be a model for this court.”

title: New York enacts ban on 'unsafe' chatbot behavior with kids as states push AI regulation boundaries
text:
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — New York is enacting farther-reaching restrictions on companion chatbot behavior, as states increasingly move to protect children who use artificial intelligence, regulate how employers deploy AI systems and push developers to prevent an AI-caused catastrophe.
Legislation signed Wednesday by Gov. Kathy Hochul outlines a dozen definitions of “unsafe AI companion features” that will be prohibited when a companion chatbot interacts with a child under 18.
A violation could expose a chatbot developer to a lawsuit by the state attorney general’s office. Penalties could include monetary damages, shutting down the chatbot and destroying data. The law takes effect Jan. 1.
Hochul, in the thick of her reelection campaign, signed the bill amid growing warnings about the existential risks posed by the rapid development of AI technology and calls for bold action by a reluctant Washington.
With Congress doing little to regulate AI, state legislatures are packed with efforts to wield state consumer protection laws to make AI use more transparent and rein in chatbots and rogue AI frontier models.
New York and California are at the vanguard of such laws that also are targeting social media platforms.
In September, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation requiring chatbot developers to assess a model’s risk to children, show how they tried to eliminate those risks and submit to an independent audit to determine whether they are complying with the law.
He also signed legislation to prohibit social media platforms from deploying addictive features for users under 16.
Meanwhile, eight states sued AI giant OpenAI earlier this month, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what one activist called “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”
However, governors acknowledge that Congress and the federal government have farther-reaching abilities to clamp down on AI-posed threats, even as President Donald Trump has brushed off concerns and warned states not to regulate AI.
Under New York’s law, outlawed chatbot behavior with children under 18 includes suggestions that the chatbot is a real person that has emotions, opinions or an actual relationship with the child. It also outlaws chatbot messages that use flattery, involve sexually explicit material or encourage secrecy or unhealthy behavior.
Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of watchdog group Common Sense Media, called New York’s law “the strongest kids’ AI safety bill in the country.”
Justine Gluck, policy analyst at the Future of Privacy Forum, a nonprofit focused on data protection and AI governance, said the different regulatory approaches by California and New York could be models other states adopt after legislatures reconvene next year.
New York’s law, she said, underscores how quickly chatbot regulation is evolving, as states move beyond basic disclosures and crisis-response protocols to regulating the underlying design and operation of chatbots.
Still, several categories in New York’s law are broadly worded or undefined, Gluck said.
That raises questions, she said, about “where ordinary conversational responsiveness ends and prohibited behavior begins,” and could complicate how it is enforced.
___
Follow Marc Levy at http://twitter.com/timelywriter

title: Knox County commissioners send 10% spending hike to Budget Committee
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — Commissioners got a first look Tuesday afternoon on the preliminary draft of the 2027 Knox County budget that increases spending by more than 10%.
The amount of property taxes and communication fees to be assessed to the communities under this first draft would increase by more than 10%.
County officials stressed after the meeting that the numbers were very preliminary. The proposed budget will be sent to the Budget Committee and municipal officials next week. The commissioners and Budget Committee are scheduled to meet 5 p.m. on Feb. 5.
The first review of the 2027 budget comes five months after the 2026 budget was approved following a lengthy saga that delayed enactment for five months because of a lack of Budget Committee members.
The preliminary draft of the Knox County budget is nearly $18 million, up 7% from the approved 2026 budget of $16.8 million.
And the communications budget is proposed at $2.5 million, a 16% increase. The fees are divided among the communities, not by property valuations as the general budget is funded, but by the populations of the communities.
There are also nearly $6 million in airport projects proposed for 2027.
The largest expenditure in the draft budget is corrections at nearly $6.9 million. The department operates the holding facility in Rockland. Inmates sentenced to jail or held after their initial appearance are held at the Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
The corrections budget is an increase of about $100,000 from the 2026 budget. The largest expense is $3.4 million paid to Two Bridges.
The sheriff patrol budget is proposed at $4.7 million for 2027, up from $4.4 million in 2026.
The preliminary draft called for no staffing changes for the department, but commissioners asked that money be included for two more deputy positions. The added cost of that would be $509,000, which covers salaries, benefits, cruisers and other equipment needed for additional officers, such as firearms.
The patrol budget also includes money for new firearms, the first change in 10 years, Chief Deputy Curt Andrick told commissioners during Tuesday’s meeting.
Commissioner Marc Ratner noted that Camden pays the most in county taxes and that some people point out that the town has its own department. But, he said, towns chose to have their own departments, but the sheriff’s department is the legislative police department in the county.
He said communities with their own department, such as Camden, Rockland and Thomaston, do not deserve breaks in their county tax bills because the county is the legislatively approved department.
Budget Committee member Doug Erickson of Thomaston was in attendance at the meeting and said towns can no longer go down the road of higher costs and said there is a need for one county department.
Andrick said any move in that direction would need to come from the towns.
Ratner believes towns will see they can save money from such a move.
The overall county budget increase is due to wage increases, some that are still being negotiated with employee unions, health insurance increases of 9% and fuel cost hikes.
The airport budget is proposed at $1.3 million, up from $1.1 million.
The building maintenance budget is proposed at nearly $1.2 million, up from $900,000.
The administration budget is proposed at $679,000, up from $614,000.
The district attorney budget is proposed at $589,000, down from $592,000. The costs for the attorneys in the department are not in the county budget in the state budget.
The probate budget is proposed at $442,000, up from $412,000. The department is budgeted to bring in $193,000 in revenues.
The Registry of Deeds budget is proposed at $321,000 but will be more than offset with $573,000 in projected revenues.
The information technology budget is proposed at $576,000, up from $521,000.
The Finance Department Budget is proposed at $576,000, up from $521,000.
And the Emergency Management Agency budget is proposed at $294,000, up from $271,000 with revenues estimated at $72,000.
If the budget is approved as proposed in the preliminary draft:
— Camden would pay $3 million, an increase of $300,000
— Rockland would pay $2.1 million, an increase of $219,000
— Rockport would pay $2.1 million, an increase of $209,000
— St. George would pay $1.9 million, an increase of $192,000
— Warren would pay $1 million, an increase of $109,000
— Vinalhaven would pay $955,000, an increase of $95,000
— Thomaston would pay $920,000, an increase of $96,000
— Owls Head would pay $879,000, an increase of $88,000
— South Thomaston would pay $678,000, an increase of $69,000
— Union would pay $712,000, an increase of $75,000
— Cushing would pay $704,000, an increase of $71,000
— North Haven would pay $699,000, an increase of $68,000
— Friendship would pay $664,000, an increase of $66,000
— Hope will pay $586,000, an increase of $60,000
— Washington would pay $430,000, an increase of $45,000
— Appleton would pay $360,000, an increase of $38,000
— Isle au Haut would pay $109,000, an increase of $11,000
— Matinicus Island would pay $46,000, an increase of $4,000
The county tax is based on the state property valuation of each municipality with the higher valued towns paying more.

title: James O'Keefe charged after Minnesota polling station stunt
text:
Influencer James O’Keefe charged after Minnesota polling station stunt
A Minnesota county attorney is charging right-wing influencers James O’Keefe and Cameron Higby with felony counts of unlawful voting and identity theft, alleging that the two claimed other voters’ identities while visiting polling places with concealed cameras during the state’s August primary.
Video above: Are electronic voting machines "flipping" votes? Experts say no.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said O’Keefe and Higby attempted to register to vote on the day of the primary by claiming the names of real voters — some alive and some deceased. They stopped when told they would have to sign oaths to vouch for someone else’s residence and did not actually cast votes.
The influencers had been attempting to test the state’s “vouching” process, which allows a registered voter in a precinct to vouch that another person lives where they say they live. Moriarty said the system is often used by senior citizens who haven’t updated their driver’s licenses after moving into nursing homes.
“You cannot give somebody else’s name and misrepresent yourself,” Moriarty said. “Whether or not they intended to vote is irrelevant.”
The charges against the influencers come days before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
It also comes as President Donald Trump’s administration has sent multiple states lists of what it alleges are noncitizens on the voter rolls, intensifying its controversial efforts to stop those people from voting in the election. Trump has for years made false and disproven claims about widespread voting fraud.
The two influencers did not immediately respond to email messages seeking comment on the charges.
According to the criminal complaints, the two men disguised themselves in what O’Keefe described on X as “traditional Muslim attire.”
“We wanted to put the process to an extreme real-world test and document what election workers would tell us when confronted with the scenario firsthand,” the conservative provocateur said in a social media post in August.
O’Keefe, 42, was the founder of Project Veritas, a right-wing activist group that targeted journalists in sting videos that were often deceptively edited. He was fired by the Project Veritas board in 2023, and has since founded O’Keefe Media Group, where he has continued to produce videos that he claims take aim at corruption.
Moriarty added that the videos posted online of their efforts were deceptively edited.
She said election judges who were on hand raised concerns about what she described as their “strange behavior,” and flagged it to police. She said the living voters whose names O’Keefe and Higby attempted to use said they had no knowledge of their efforts.
“There’s no such thing as ‘undercover’ investigation in the polling place,” she said. “You have to identify yourself as a journalist in the polling place, which they did not.”
The two have not yet been arrested, but will be sent copies of the criminal complaint with the date of their first court appearances by the county clerk.
“This is not meant to send a message. It’s meant for these particular people to understand that what they did was unlawful,” Moriarty said.
“Minnesota’s enduring tradition of high voter turnout and excellence in elections administration is due in part to the work we all do to keep polling places as ‘islands of calm,’” Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon said in a statement following Moriarty’s announcement.
“These locations — our communities’ schools, churches, and senior centers – are the heart of our democracy and as such should be places of safety and peace. Any attempt to disrupt or deceive our election workers will not be tolerated.”

title: Maine supreme court will decide whether to order damages in Belfast salmon farm lawsuit
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Oral arguments are set to begin on Nov. 5 in the damages appeal by Jeffrey Mabee, Judith Grace and the Friends of Harriet L. Hartley Conservation Area in their long-running slander of title lawsuit against Nordic Aquafarms.
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court, sitting as the Law Court, has scheduled oral arguments to begin at 11 a.m. in the Cumberland County Courthouse in Portland. Mabee, Grace and the Friends are appealing Judge Michael Duddy’s lower court ruling that rejected their claim for damages, reimbursement of litigation expenses and attorney fees.
In its effort to develop a $500 million land-based salmon farm in Belfast, Nordic claimed an ownership interest in a strip of intertidal mudflats the Norwegian company needed to lay its industrial intake and effluent pipes to Penobscot Bay. Nordic, which left town in January 2025, used release deeds it secured from third parties to support its ownership claims.
In February 2023, the Law Court ruled unanimously that Mabee and Grace are the true, exclusive owners of the intertidal land, and that the Friends of Harriet L. Hartley hold a valid, enforceable conservation easement protecting the flats from industrial development.
Mabee, Grace and the Friends sought roughly $884,000 in damages, surveyor and other costs, plus legal fees, arguing that Nordic slandered their title by recording invalid deeds and clouding their property rights, which severely devalued their home and blocked its sale. The invalid deeds remain in the Waldo County land records, continuing to cloud their title to the historic (circa 1796) Belfast property they acquired in 1991 and gradually restored over the years. Planning to retire, they listed their home for sale in January 2017. A year later, Nordic and the city announced the company’s plans for the salmon farm.
In January 2024, Business and Consumer Court Judge Michael Duddy ruled that while Nordic’s deeds ultimately were found to be invalid, Nordic had acted in “good faith” rather than with malice or reckless disregard. Because proving malice and specific financial damages are absolute requirements for slander of title under Maine law, the court denied the damages claim, prompting this final appeal.
Mabee, Grace and the Friends also have a second appeal pending before the state’s high court.
When Nordic’s efforts failed to establish their ownership interest in the mudflats the salmon farm project needed, the Belfast City Council took the Mabee/Grace intertidal property by eminent domain for the company’s pipes, including intertidal land that lies outside Belfast’s boundary. After the Law Court ruled in Mabee/Grace’s favor in February 2023, Waldo County Superior Court remanded the eminent domain decision to the City Council for reconsideration based on the high court’s findings.
On May 7, 2024, the city vacated its eminent domain claim and restored the title to Mabee and Grace two weeks later. Deciding to take a close look at Belfast’s municipal boundary in that area, the city then hired an independent surveyor to establish the boundary line set by an 1813 statute. The surveyor found that part of the mudflats taken in August 2021 actually lay outside the municipal boundary, and the City Council adopted and recorded that survey in November 2024.
Mabee, Grace and the Friends subsequently sued Nordic Aquafarms and the city of Belfast, challenging the city’s use of eminent domain to benefit Nordic and transfer the use of Mabee and Grace’s intertidal land to the company. Duddy issued a final judgment in that case on July 16, finding in Nordic’s and the city of Belfast’s favor on all eight counts. The court’s judgment found no liability on the city’s part and did not award any penalties, attorney fees or costs to the plaintiffs.

‘She was screaming for her life’: Terrifying attempted kidnapping caught on video
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) — A terrifying kidnapping attempt in the middle of the afternoon on the Diamond Head Gold Coast in Honolulu was caught on video.
Authorities said they were called to Kainalu condominiums on Coconut Avenue around noon on Monday about the reported kidnapping.
Surveillance video from the area showed a truck parked outside the condominium complex that afternoon before a man was seen going inside the garage, appearing to confront two women and chasing one of them.
A 77-year-old condo resident, who asked not to be identified, said the man picked up her 24-year-old friend.
Police said the suspect elbowed the 77-year-old woman in the face.
“He shoved me away from my friend and he picked her up,” she said. “He looked like a monster. He just had so much hatred and craziness in his eyes.”
The woman added, “I was yelling, ‘Help! Help!’ and she was yelling, too. She was saying, ‘You don’t want to do this. Don’t do this.’”
The 77-year-old said her friend was trying to fend off the kidnapper while she was hoping others would hear their screams for help.
Neighbor and witness Beverly Louis said she could see the man bear-hugging the woman and dragging her to the back of his truck.
“I just started screaming, ‘Drop her! Drop her! Drop her!’” Louis said. “She was screaming for her life. She was terrified.”
Neighbor and fellow witness Mike Finkelstein said he also yelled at the man to let the woman go.
“Let her go. I’ve called the police. I’m coming down there after you,” Finkelstein recalled yelling.
Several neighbors then intervened after seeing and hearing the commotion, helping the 24-year-old break free.
Witnesses said the man in question got into his truck and sped off. Police were able to take him into custody a few hours later after police said a suspicious man matching his description was seen running naked in a nearby neighborhood.
The 77-year-old woman thanked her fellow residents for their help but said she and her friend were continuing to have nightmares as the neighborhood remained on edge.

title: Man loses more than $4,000 after scammers spoof father’s number, claim parents are at gunpoint
text:
SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) - A man lost thousands of dollars after getting a call that appeared to come from his father’s phone number, with a stranger claiming his parents were being held at gunpoint.
Curtis Indyke was asleep around 11:30 p.m. on Oct. 21 when he got a call that appeared to be from his dad, who lives in Virginia. Indyke lives in Arizona.
“I answer the phone and it’s not my dad. It’s some other male saying he has my parents basically at gunpoint,” Indyke said.
The caller told him to pay or his parents would be shot.
While still on the phone, Indyke said he texted 911 to report his parents were being held hostage in Virginia. The person who claimed to be holding Indyke’s parents hostage continued making threats. In a panic, Indyke sent more than $4,000 through Apple Pay to two separate phone numbers.
“And they also wanted $1,000 worth of crypto gift cards, which I’ve never even heard of. I’m in IT and I’ve never even heard of them,” Indyke said.
Indyke said his bank blocked that purchase.
After the call ended, Indyke called his dad’s number back, but no one answered.
“But then I got scared because, what if the guy had his phone still?” Indyke said.
Police in Virginia later went to Indyke’s parents’ home for a welfare check and they were safe.
“I mean, everybody was just shocked about it,” Indyke said.
Dawn Alexander, a network specialist for AARP Arizona, said the scammers followed a known playbook.
“It feels like there’s an uptick,” Alexander said. “What they’re trying to do is get you in a heightened state for you to react. Spoofing is a very dangerous game right now because it could be anyone from a scammer saying they’re with Medicare, with your hospital, you name it.”
Indyke said Nancy Guthrie’s disappearance immediately came to mind. She is the mother of “Today” show host Savannah Guthrie.
“Especially in Arizona, we know unfortunately about Nancy, the terrible case of Nancy Guthrie. You know, that was my first thought, is, ‘Oh my God, is this happening to me now?’” Indyke said.
Indyke has advice to anyone who might be a victim of a similar scam.
“You need to take a second, pause before you react. You need to think about it, and the safest thing to do is to hang up and call whoever they say that they have,” Indyke said.
Indyke said the $4,000 payment is still pending and that he plans to file a fraud claim once it clears in hopes of getting his money back.
Alexander said these scams used to target primarily older adults, but with artificial intelligence, anyone can become a victim.

(Gray News) - A voluntary recall over lead concerns has been issued for cans of Walmart fruit cocktail distributed to stores in at least seven states.
The Food and Drug Administration said the recall applies to 15-ounce containers of Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate.
Where the product was distributed
More than 1,830 cases, or approximately 44,000 individual cans, were distributed to Walmart locations in Alabama, Arizona, Louisiana, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wyoming, the FDA said.
How to identify the product
The product is marked with lot number “6FCB 04 C2263” and a best if used by date of Sept. 1, 2027.
Recall details
The FDA initiated the recall for “potential contamination with elevated levels of lead” on Oct. 1. It was reclassified as a Class II recall on Oct. 20.
According to the FDA, Class II recalls are issued when a product can cause temporary health effects with a remote possibility of serious issues.
What customers should do
Customers should throw the item away or return it to Walmart.

title: Obituary: Mark L. Pennell Jr.
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND – Mark L. Pennell Jr., 55, passed away peacefully on Oct. 20, 2026, in Portland, with his family by his side. Mark was born on Oct. 5, 1971, in Portland, the son of Catherine (Papineau) Pennell and Mark Pennell Sr.
Mark grew up in South Portland, where he spent most of his life and later raised a family of his own in the same community. He attended schools within the South Portland School District and graduated from South Portland High School in 1990. Growing up in the Anthoine Street neighborhood, he formed lifelong friendships that carried well into adulthood. Known from a young age for his strong work ethic and independent nature, Mark carried these qualities with him throughout his life. He was a devoted family man who took great pride in his wife, Norita, his two children, Leanne and Wyatt, and the life they built together. Of all the things Mark took pride in throughout his life, being a father to Leanne and Wyatt was among the greatest.
Mark met Norita while the two were working at the South Portland Nursing Home. What began there grew into a life and family they built together over the course of more than three decades. Mark and Norita celebrated their 31st wedding anniversary this past July.
A true Mainer through and through, Mark had a deep and lifelong love for the outdoors. He was an avid hunter, trapper, fly fisherman, ice fisherman, and snowmobiler who felt most at home in the woods and on the waters of Maine. Some of his most cherished places were the remote waterways, ponds, lakes, and forests throughout the Moosehead Lake region, where he spent countless days exploring, hunting, fishing, snowmobiling, and camping.
That love began early in life through time spent outdoors with his father, Mark, brother, Michael, and mother, Cathy, and it became a tradition Mark proudly carried into his own family. Their camp in The Forks became the setting for countless hunting trips, adventures, stories, and memories shared with family and close friends. Those fortunate enough to spend time with Mark at camp rarely left without a story of their own to tell.
Mark was known by those who loved him as one of the toughest, most stubborn, and hard-headed men they had ever met — qualities matched only by his honesty, loyalty, generosity, strong work ethic, and genuine nature. Beneath that tough exterior was a mischievous spirit and an infectious laugh that those closest to him knew well. He believed strongly in doing things the right way, standing behind his word, working hard for what you had, and remaining true to who you were whether anyone was watching or not.
A third-generation oil industry worker, Mark devoted more than 30 years of his career to Gulf Oil, where he worked as a Lead Terminal Operator. His dedication to his work was unwavering. Even while undergoing treatments, Mark continued working more than 50 hours a week until July of this year. He refused to allow his illness to define him and faced it the same way he approached everything else in life — with determination, grit, and remarkable strength.
Mark was predeceased by his father, Mark Pennell Sr., and his brother, Michael Pennell.
He is survived by his wife of 31 years, Norita Pennell; his mother, Catherine Pennell; his children, Leanne Pennell and Wyatt Pennell; Wyatt’s fiancée, McKenzie Brackett; his mother-in-law, Joyce Macomber; his sister-in-law, Cindy McNinch; his brother-in-law, Floyd “Jocko” McNinch; his beloved black Lab, Sadie Mae; and many extended family members, friends, and coworkers who were fortunate enough to know him.
Mark’s family would like to extend their sincerest gratitude and appreciation to the countless nurses, healthcare providers, and staff throughout MaineHealth who cared for and supported Mark and his family throughout his illness. Their compassion, kindness, and support throughout this journey were invaluable and will never be forgotten.
Burial services will be held privately for family and close friends. A Celebration of Life will be held on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, at 2 p.m. at Willow’s, 740 Broadway, South Portland, Maine 04106. All friends, family, and coworkers are warmly welcomed to attend and celebrate Mark’s life.
To view Mark’s memorial page or leave an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.

title: South Portland passes emergency ICE ordinance
text:
South Portland employees are prohibited from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement.
The City Council voted unanimously on Tuesday to enact an emergency ordinance restricting staff — including school employees — from cooperating with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It bypasses the typical ordinance process, which typically takes several weeks (including two readings and a waiting period) because many councilors wanted it in place in time for Election Day. It took effect immediately.
South Portland has officially opposed cooperating with federal immigration enforcement since 2017, and it expanded upon its commitment by passing a symbolic resolution in early February following the surge of immigration enforcement in Maine. On Tuesday, it joined other cities like Portland, Lewiston, Rockland, Waterville and Biddeford in enacting similar measures.
The school board voted unanimously on Monday to recommend that school employees should be included in this ordinance.
The ordinance won’t prevent detainments or control ICE activity in the area, but it’s more specific than previous resolutions.
No city employee will be able to voluntarily work with immigration enforcement, nor will any municipal funds or resources be used to facilitate enforcement, per the draft ordinance’s language.
City employees will not be able to allow ICE officers to use city-owned properties for staging or processing, nor will they be allowed to provide those federal agents with special access to nonpublic areas.
The ordinance stipulates that city employees, including police officers, are not permitted to participate in stops, arrests or detentions on behalf of ICE, or share addresses, contact information or immigration status beyond what is required by law.
All city staff will be trained about the specifics of the policies, and any suspicious activity will be directed to the city manager’s office, which will then report aggregate information to the council and through an annual report.

title: VETERANS CORNER: What is and isn’t inside the abandoned community center
text:
Well, it is with a heavy heart that for no reason other than I like to take pictures of our neglected and abandoned “Community Living Center” and what is, or should I say, what isn’t inside of those already paid for six years ago buildings, that some of our vets here already died trying to receive the comfort that was promised not only through conversation but by the signage that was displayed, so proudly stating, the home of the “Community Living Center”.
Then came the first contractor leaving because of conflict with the administration and resigning; taking with them their trailers and supplies. This was followed by a second contractor, or so I am told. Was it because of a monetary dispute? What else could it be? So down came the sign, “Community Living Center” and was replaced with a board fence.
The building went through the winter with the elements coming through the unfinished open windows. Then came a breath of spring, or so we thought and that fence came down and the administration ordered the finish to be applied to the outside, thus glamorizing the buildings. The landscaping was still in shambles but at least it appeared that the work was either finished or was at least near completion.
I decided to keep you all informed with the good news of the possibility of the soon to come “Community Living center” which has been six years in coming, but the future looked better, brighter for we older veterans. So, being a reporter of many years, I decided to show you more pictures of the interior beauty of what appeared to be a finished product. To my surprise there was nothing inside the buildings except what appeared as junk aluminum, like angle iron. It turned out what I saw was pretty representations of nothing. What happened, where did the money go? Knowing of my picture taking and reporting, a multi-thousand dollar steel fence has been erected. There is no danger there, just secrets. More needed money wasted.
As I said last week I have sent letters to the president of the USA, Trump and to our Veterans Secretary Douglas Collins. I sent everything certified with return receipts. I have received notification that my correspondence has been received. Let’s see what will become of this. Ms. Davis and Mr. Lilly, friends have some answering to do to we, the veterans and taxpayers of the state of Maine. My anger began with their decision of the poor placement of our Fisher House. They were warned and the state was informed of the dangers involved of the placement of a guest house earmarked for veteran’s families, who needed a place to stay while waiting for their beloved veteran to be treated and hopefully released. Since Mr. Lilly wouldn’t speak with me I handed my paperwork to the person who dismissed me. He was supposedly on a conference call, although I could hear laughter before I left. We immediately went to the State of Maine, another waste of time, with the same dissent on the location of the proposed “Fisher House”. It was on the edge of a pond, historically used for healing purposes, I am told. The pond is spring fed and that indicates that the soil is most likely unstable for any structure of weight. Also, it’s a Canada Goose habitat now for hundreds of ducks for breeding annually. Last but not least the location, in and of itsself and was dangerous to traffic pedestrians and emergency room that affords ambulances. (Poor planning).
The state of Maine gave us an audience and listened to our presentation in a private cubical. They promised to look into it and get back to us. This never happened. The rest is history. The house which I am told cost millions and housed many families, became a hazard and had to be condemned. All this could have been avoided. It only needed to be relocated a hundred feet to avoid this disaster.
In my opinion that team had been very good at making poor decisions and causing pain, anger and descent with their inability to make proper decisions, listen to the advice of others and respectfully investigate what is being offered. Currently, we have too many people on the administrative side and bare bones on the medical side. We have even paid people from other medical facilities to cover such areas as X-ray. I believe that has improved by some new graduates training in X-ray. Now the place to go if you are sick and a veteran is to emergency. The wait may be long but they do a good job for the most part. I do disagree with some of the medical coverage but all in all it is the place to go.
I have been here for 47 years and have to go out of state for care. The doctors I use to call friends are all gone; orthopedics is a good example, because of my many years as a patient I was always able to be seen. Now, just recently, they are booked up until next February. What does that tell you? I have some serious medical conditions and had hoped to have someone give me a clean bill of health. A five-month wait is unacceptable and outright disgraceful, to all vets. To get that I have to go to Boston, Connecticut or New Hampshire. I live next door and I leave the country to help with the thousands of veterans we have in South Pacific islands.
The E.N.T. department was shut down by the Director of Togus, Tracye Davis. She tells people that she has advertised but no takers. Why do you think that is? Why is everyone leaving the medical side? Most specialties are down to one doctor and you can tell they aren’t happy. Rheumatology and Geriatrics has been merged under one doctor. If something isn’t done soon to turn this around, there will be no Togus as we have known it. (A much needed department).
This is the week to vote and I can’t tell you who to vote for, however, I can tell you this, irrespective of which political party you belong to, if you have a veteran in your life then you must look at the candidates and if you find one that is anti-military or doesn’t vote in the best interest of veterans, you can be assured that he/she has limited feelings about social security as most of our elderly are either veterans or was married to one who passed away and relies on D.I.C. (Dependency and Indemnity Compensation).
There are those who would like to shoot some of that down for other purposes. Don’t let it happen. Ask the hard questions and insist on a straight answer. We have thousands of veterans on the way and they need all the support you can give. Always remember why we are still free and who and what harms that freedom. Love your U.S. Constitution and those with the brilliance to put it together and to last forever. Remember also the rule of law and know those who violate it. Maine is known for its hard workers and good God fearing people. Let’s keep it that way. God bless and have a safe beautiful fall weekend.

title: Group behind Maine transgender sports referendum will submit for 2027 ballot
text:
After failing to qualify for the upcoming November ballot, the group behind a proposed referendum to limit transgender students’ rights in sports says it has enough signatures qualify for the 2027 election.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows initially certified the 2026 citizens’ initiative, filed by the group Protect Girls Sports, but later met a legal challenge over the validity of its signatures.
Bellows agreed with the lawsuit — which claimed that out-of-state signature collectors broke several state rules during the name collection process — and rejected thousands of signatures during a review, leaving the group 500 short of qualification.
The case worked its way up the state court system until the Maine Supreme Judicial Court determined in July that Bellows had been right to invalidate the signatures. That decision meant the referendum would not appear on this year’s ballot.
However, the tens of thousands of lawful signatures collected by the group were still valid for a year after the petition was filed with the secretary’s office. Protect Girls Sports pledged to collect at least 5,000 additional names before Nov. 3, the date those signatures would expire.
The group announced Wednesday that it will officially resubmit its citizen initiative and signatures on Monday morning, a day before the deadline. It also said it would hold a news conference with two female student athletes who the group says had their Title IX rights violated.
If it passes, the referendum will require participation in school sports and use of facilities including bathrooms and locker rooms to be based on a student’s sex assigned at birth, rather than their gender identity.
Since 2021, Maine’s antidiscrimination law, the Maine Human Rights Act, has required schools to allow students to participate in extracurricular activities without discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The Maine Principal’s Association, the organization that oversees high school sports, changed its rules in 2024 to allow transgender athletes to participate in school sports consistent with their gender identities, which it had previously allowed for more than a decade by waiver.
Leyland Streiff, of Brunswick, the lead petitioner, said in a statement that more than 100 volunteers helped collect thousands more signatures over the past month from, “motivated Mainers that believe our schools should offer access to single-sex sports and private spaces.”
Streiff also said the group plans to file a Title IX complaint against the state, the Maine Principal’s Association and the school districts on behalf of the two female high school athletes who he said have had their rights violated. The students are soccer players from Windham and Fryeburg, according to the statement.
The students will be represented by the Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative legal advocacy group that has filed similar complaints in other states.

title: ‘I miss her like crazy’: Loved ones remembering post office worker hit and killed by car
text:
FORT THOMAS, Ky. (WXIX/Gray News) - Loved ones and a Kentucky community are mourning a post office worker who was hit and killed by a car while walking earlier this month.
Marchelle Bertram worked at the front desk of the Fort Thomas Post Office for years, helping people who came in. Sadly, she lost her life in a collision in Bellevue on Oct. 15.
Her daughter, Whitney Bertram, said she is remembering her mother while seeing a large amount of support from the community following her death.
“There are so many people I don’t know whose lives she’s touched and affected,” Whitney Bertram said.
The crash occurred while Marchelle Bertram was walking on Memorial Parkway near her home. Her daughter said she rushed to the hospital after learning her mother had been hit by a vehicle.
“Given the grave amount of injuries she sustained, there was no way she was going to survive,” she said.
Marchelle Bertram died at the hospital. Whitney Bertram said the driver stayed at the scene and believes the crash was an accident.
“I miss her like crazy; I try not to think about it too hard because I’ll break down,” she said.
According to Whitney Bertram, there has been an outpouring of support telling her that her mother was kind and well-known in the area.
Additionally, a woman at the post office began crying when she learned of Marchelle Bertram’s death.
“If she could come back for a moment just to see what a reaction has come about because she’s no longer with us, I think she’d be stunned,” Whitney said.
Whitney Bertram said those who would visit the post office would call her mother “the nice lady at the post office,” and knowing the good she put into the world is helping her get through the loss.
“You’re never truly gone until you’re forgotten about. It’s good to hear other people reaching out and expressing how much they miss her, too,” Whitney Bertram said.

title: Special master could evaluate DOJ claim of 20,000 noncitizens on California voter rolls
text:
Los Angeles (AP) — A federal judge on Tuesday said he was considering appointing a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that California has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls and to determine whether counties would be able to separate any ballots belonging to ineligible voters.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was overseeing a hearing in a lawsuit filed by the Justice Department, which is seeking to prevent California from counting ballots from thousands of people it alleges are noncitizens.
Carter said it would be too rushed to make a decision without an independent special master who could evaluate the substance of both sides’ claims. He said that could be completed before the state’s Dec. 11 deadline to certify the election results.
It is not clear what would happen if a special master did find a substantial number of noncitizen voters on the federal government’s list or whether it would affect the certification of California’s election results. The 20,000 people on the DOJ’s list constitute only a small fraction of California’s 23 million voters.
The judge said he wanted to vet the federal government’s list. He emphasized his concerns that siding with the federal government at this stage could mean illegally making substantial changes to election procedure while voting is underway.
But he said the special master also could investigate California’s claims that it could not logistically separate the ballots in time for the election certification deadline in December, an assertion the federal government has contested.
Voting has been well underway for weeks in California in the midterm election that concludes next Tuesday. Alleged voting by noncitizens has been a key focus of President Donald Trump’s administration with control of Congress at stake, though available data indicates occurrences are exceedingly rare.
The Republican administration sued election officials in California in mid-October, accusing them of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review its list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.
The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn’t win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the nation’s Capitol.
Judge issues warning not to threaten election workers
Although Carter said he was open to appointing a special master, he said he will not issue an official order until Wednesday.
The judge rarely spoke throughout the hearing, but he did express skepticism about why the federal government was suing California rather than seeking to address alleged noncitizen voting through criminal prosecutions. He referenced the federal government’s recent arrest in October of 28 people across California accused of illegally registering to vote.
“You got a remedy for goodness sakes — go out and indict,” Carter said from the bench.
Prosecutors with the federal government argued that the U.S. had an interest in preventing noncitizens from voting in the first place.
“Our goal is not to prosecute tens of thousands of people. It’s to safeguard the election,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.
Carter also seemed to respond to warnings that local county clerks who don’t heed the federal government’s demands could be criminally prosecuted.
“This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately,” Carter said before abruptly leaving the courtroom.
Federal prosecutor says US government seeks to ‘safeguard’ the election
Essayli argued Tuesday that the Justice Department’s demands would not significantly disrupt the ongoing election.
“We have not asked to void any ballots,” he said. Instead, the government was seeking to “work with” California officials to “safeguard” the election.
He said testimony would explain how the government’s list of 20,000 names was compiled.
“The case rises and falls on the credibility” of the flagged names, he told the judge, arguing the state has an obligation to investigate before counting those voters’ ballots.
California officials previously argued that once a completed mail ballot is returned, it is separated from the envelope that contains voters’ identification. That would make it impossible to separate ballots that have already been submitted, the state said. More than 3 million ballots have already been returned.
Lawyers for California warn of delays and disruptions
Lawyers for California and Los Angeles County said the federal government has not specified how or when it obtained the voter file, leaving open the possibility the list was inaccurate or outdated. They specifically questioned the government’s reliance on a private, third-party service to determine Social Security numbers used in their effort.
M. Patrick Moore, a lawyer for the Los Angeles County registrar’s office, also argued that the county would cooperate if the federal government wanted to criminally prosecute noncitizens who illegally voted.
“If an individual who is a noncitizen votes, there will be record of that, and the county will provide that record” to the federal courts, Moore said in court Tuesday.
He added that if the federal government believes the election was compromised, there are legal processes for contesting the outcome.
Tuesday’s hearing largely revolved around the reliability of the federal government’s list. Los Angeles County officials found that a small sample of people on it were indeed citizens.
The federal agent who conducted the investigation — which required roughly 800 federal employees who manually checked each name — said in an affidavit that the county’s findings were false. The filing did concede that some names could have been mistakenly included.

title: Federal judge rules top US prosecutor in Los Angeles isn't legally serving
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Republican Bill Essayli is not legally serving as the top U.S. prosecutor in Los Angeles.
The ruling is the latest roadblock to the Trump administration’s effort to extend handpicked acting U.S. attorneys beyond the 120-day limit set by federal law. The strategy was designed to bypass confirmation by the U.S. Senate — something that generally requires a degree of bipartisan support.
Essayli “is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney,” U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright wrote.
The order won’t take effect until the court rules on the government’s motion for a stay pending appeal. Essayli said he doesn’t agree with the court’s order. He said the president and Attorney General “have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department.”
“Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court, and I look forward to serving in my current role until then,” he said in a statement.
The former state lawmaker was appointed by the Trump administration last year to serve as Acting U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, which includes Los Angeles. Just before the 120-day mark, then-U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi appointed him as First Assistant U.S. Attorney.
But in October 2025, Seabright disqualified Essayli from overseeing several criminal cases, concluding he had stayed in the temporary job longer than allowed by law. He was allowed to continue to serve as a First Assistant U.S. attorney.
The administration never appointed another acting U.S. attorney, effectively making Essayli the top prosecutor. He’s been a face of the administration’s sparring with California on everything from alleged health care fraud to recent claims of widespread noncitizen voting. California has pushed back on federal efforts to prevent election officials from counting ballots of up to 20,000 people the Trump administration suspects are not U.S. citizens.
On Tuesday, Seabright wrote that Essayli’s status faced new questions following an August appeals court ruling in a similar case. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that Sigal Chattah, the Trump administration’s initial pick for U.S. attorney in Nevada, was unlawfully appointed to lead federal prosecutions in the state.
Seabright wrote that Bondi’s appointment of Essayli as a special attorney and designation of him as the FAUSA “is identical” to her appointment of Chattah in the same roles.
Despite a new designation by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche that cut a few of Essayli’s duties, the judge said that “nothing in the revised designation order materially distinguishes it from the Chattah designation order deemed improper in” the appeals court ruling.
Judges have found a number of interim U.S. attorneys installed by the administration are unlawfully serving in their positions.
A judge in New Jersey last year disqualified acting U.S. attorney Alina Habba and in January a judge ruled that John Sarcone was not lawfully serving as acting U.S. attorney for the Northern District of New York.
Essayli is a former federal prosecutor and Republican state lawmaker. In the Legislature, he took up conservative causes and criticized the state’s COVID-19 restrictions. He has been outspoken against California policies to protect immigrants living in the country illegally, and he has aggressively prosecuted people who protest Trump’s ramped up immigration enforcement across Southern California.

title: 8-month-old dies after left alone in running bathtub, police say
text:
STERLING, Va. (Gray News) - A Virginia woman was arrested after her 8-month-old died after being left unattended in a bathtub, according to authorities.
Rosellena Pisani, 30, was arrested and charged with homicide, two counts of child abuse and three counts of child endangerment, a press release said.
On Sept. 12, emergency medical personnel and sheriff’s deputies responded to the residence after receiving a call about an unresponsive infant. Investigators determined the baby had been left unsupervised in a bathtub with the water running.
Three children, ranging in age from 8 months to 8 years old, were at home during the incident, according to police.
Loudoun County Sheriff Mike Chapman called the baby’s death heartbreaking, saying caregivers have a fundamental duty to protect children. He added investigators remain committed to seeking justice in the case.

title: Wendy's, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
text:
Wendy's, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
Wendy’s shares jumped more than 14% Wednesday after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores.
Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday, in a deal that would take the company private. The offer values Wendy's at $1.4 billion.
Wendy's, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, confirmed receipt of the unsolicited proposal in a statement Wednesday and said its board has formed an independent committee to evaluate it. At the end of last year, Wendy's had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries.
Related content above: Wendy's offers $100,000 job to be its 'Chief Tasting Officer'
Wendy's, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald's and Burger King, Wendy's launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where's the beef?” ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy's fell behind. Wendy's share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.
In recent years, inflation has also hurt Wendy's and other U.S. fast-food chains, which have seen traffic from lower-income consumers fall as they raised prices to combat rising labor, food and packaging costs.
Wendy’s said Wednesday it is moving “with urgency” to rebuild its menu with a focus on quality and improve marketing and store operations. Wendy’s hired Bob Wright, who formerly led Potbelly, as its president and CEO in May. He’s the fourth CEO to lead the company since 2024.
Wendy's has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.
Then, last month, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
In a letter to the company’s board of directors, Peltz said going private “will deliver the best outcome for the broader stakeholder base.”
“Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture," Peltz wrote. "The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer, economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly within the QSR (quick service restaurant) burger category."
Peltz has invested in companies from Procter & Gamble and Disney to DuPont. According to a regulatory document filed Wednesday, Trian’s stake in Wendy’s totals 16.3%.
Peltz considered a take-private bid for Wendy's in 2022 but told the company in January 2023 that he had decided against it, citing its improved business momentum, according to TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles.
Charles said an independent special committee is expected to evaluate the proposal and both parties have entered into a confidentiality arrangement.
“In our view, a take-private makes sense as Wendy’s turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower-income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category,” Charles wrote Wednesday in a note to investors.
Wendy's is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results next week. Analysts expect the company to post earnings of 9 cents per share on sales of $531 million, according to FactSet.
Shares rose 93 cents to $7.07 Wednesday. They have fallen 26% since the start of this year.

title: This Maine man dresses ‘The Masked Singer’
text:
Luke D’Alessandro first became fascinated with the art and magic of creating a live show while acting in youth theater and school plays in Biddeford.
His passion and curiosity led him to a performing arts high school in Michigan, college in Australia, summer theater jobs in Italy and TV sets in Hollywood. The Biddeford native is now working on the Fox reality show “The Masked Singer.” He won his first Emmy this fall, for his work on the show’s outrageous costumes.
“I hope that young people in Maine see that there are opportunities everywhere, you just gotta go for it and follow your dreams,” said D’Alessandro, 30. “That’s kind of what I did.”
D’Alessandro shares the Emmy with five others who help create costumes for “The Masked Singer.” The show is focused on celebrity guests who sing for a panel of judges while wearing disguises that have some elements of props or set pieces. Some of last season’s costumes included singer/actor Jack Wagner as a giant purple eggplant, actor Taraji P. Henson in a glittering costume inspired by a scarab, and former Boston Red Sox slugger David Ortiz as a fuzzy red monster with googly eyes.
Ideas for the characters come from the producers, sometimes inspired by the real identity of the person the costume is meant to disguise, D’Alessandro said. Then the costumes are built, head to toe. As head designer, D’Alessandro is involved in all the costumes. The work is more like that of a production designer, he says.
“These aren’t just garments, jeans and T-shirts, they have some elements that are soft and sculptural and some that are hard plastics or weird material,” D’Alessandro said. “They have to blend somewhere in the middle.”
D’Alessandro and five other people won the Emmy for “The Masked Singer” costumes in early September. The category was outstanding costumes for a variety, nonfiction or reality program. In a video posted after the award was presented, D’Alessandro can be seen holding the Emmy, standing on stage in the middle of the group. He thanked the Television Academy, Fox studios, a few specific people and “the entire team that makes our costumes come to life.”
The show’s most recent season ended in April. It has been renewed for another season but no specific dates have yet been announced. The show had been filmed in Hollywood but is now being filmed in New Jersey, close to New York City.
Maine stages
Performing arts run deep in D’Alessandro’s family. His grandfather, Eugene D’Alessandro Sr., founded the legendary Geno’s Rock Club in Portland in the 1980s. D’Alessandro’s father also ran the club. He remembers spending time there on mornings when his father had errands to run, with his twin brother, Dominic. They played songs on the jukebox, danced around and drank Shirley Temples.
As a kid, he was always diving into the costume box at home. By the time he was in Biddeford Middle School, he was acting in plays and involved in various theater programs, including theater camps. He was particularly inspired by his experience at the Academy of Developing Artists of Maine (ADAM), run by Ronda Verges in Biddeford. It was then he started to explore some of the other jobs and skills needed to put on a show, besides acting.
“I remember Ronda saying ‘OK, if you’re going to be an actor you need to have some other skills. You need to learn something about costumes, lighting, sound,” said D’Alessandro. “That sort of opened up my eyes to the backstage part of it. “
By high school he realized he had a knack for design, for helping to created characters and worlds, and wanted to focus on that rather than acting. He applied to a performing arts high school in Michigan, Interlochen Arts Academy, without telling his parents. He was accepted, and his parents were immediately supportive.
At first, the family wasn’t sure how they’d pay the tuition. But then D’Alessandro got financial aid that covered most of it, and he packed his bags and headed for Michigan. After his junior year at Interlochen, he got the opportunity to travel to Italy with some of the teachers who had summer jobs working on operas. He worked as a prop master, making hand props and painting scenery, among other things.
An Interlochen graduate who was working as a set designer on Broadway suggested to D’Alessandro that he consider attending college at the National Institute of Dramatic Art in Sydney, Australia. He applied there and to a school in London. He ended up going to NIDA, where he earned a bachelor’s degree in Properties and Objects in 2018 and a master’s degree in Design for Performance in 2020.
He began working professionally in Australia, including on Australian versions of “The Masked Singer” and “Dancing with the Stars.” He started in the workroom, sewing, dying fabric, putting on rhinestones, before working his way to costume design.
After working a couple seasons on the Australian version of “The Masked Singer,” he got a chance to work on the American version, in Hollywood. He’s been head designer for the past four seasons of the show.
When not working on “The Masked Singer,” D’Alessandro lives in Utrecht, in the Netherlands, after nearly a dozen years of living in Australia. When he talks, a slight Aussie accent can be detected.
In between seasons of “The Masked Singer,” D’Alessandro has done freelance theater design, working on sets and costumes, and as a freelance prop maker and painter. He’s also done costume work for films, including a couple of Marvel superhero films: “Thor: Love and Thunder,” starring Chris Hemsworth; and “Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings,” starring Simu Liu and Awkwafina.
D’Alessandro says what he likes most about his work is collaborating with performers to tell a larger story. He likes the challenge of creating a stretched-out sweater for a character who is portrayed as nervous or an outfit that allows an active performer to do splits or cartwheels.
“When the singer or performer joins the process, they bring to life the piece you designed on paper,” he said. “The minute the actor or performer gets involved, it really elevates the ideas.”
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Ray Routhier can be reached at rrouthier@pressherald.com.
