title: John W. Goodman
text:
John W. Goodman passed away peacefully on Aug. 30, 2026, in Saratoga, Wyoming.
John was born in Sheridan, Wyoming 1948. In 1962 the family moved to Boothbay Harbor, Maine where he spent his teenage years. John then graduated high school in Maine. He then attended Maine Maritime Academy. At the age of 21, John proudly joined the United States Navy, serving from 1969 to 1972. His time in the Navy was an important part of his life and something he carried with him throughout the years.
After leaving the Navy, John met Cathy Dighton, and together they had three children. In 1990 John and his son Kevin moved back to Wyoming where he spend the remainder of his life. Throughout his life, John worked in the oil field, a career he was passionate about and took great pride in. His work ethic and dedication were a reflection of the man he was—strong, hardworking, and committed to providing for those he loved.
John’s greatest joy, however, was his family. He spent countless hours supporting his nieces and nephews at their various sporting events, always showing up to cheer them on and be part of their lives. Family gatherings, time with friends, and simply being surrounded by the people he loved were some of his favorite moments.
After retiring, John enjoyed having more time to spend with family and friends and was able to take trips and make memories that he cherished. One of his special adventures was traveling back to Maine and to Alaska with his brother, Chuck.
John had many things he enjoyed throughout his life. He loved playing cards, fishing, golfing, poker, and cribbage. He enjoyed watching football and baseball, spending time with friends and family, and traveling. Above all, John loved his family, his friends, and his country.
John was preceded in death by his father, George E. Goodman; his mother, Guyla M. Taylor; his sister, Patricia A. Arnold; his brother, Marvin D. Goodman; his daughter, Ciji Goodman; his brother-in-law, Rob Loftice; his sister-in-law Donna Goodman and Aunt, Virginia Scanlond
He leaves behind his son, Kevin Goodman; his brother, Chuck Goodman; and his sister, Vicki Loftice.
John is also survived by his grandchildren, Ciji Goodman, Orion Goodman, and Grayson Goodman; his nephew, Robert Loftice; nieces Robin Loftice (Ken O’Leary) and Kim Loftice; Nephew Jed Goodman (Tonya Goodman); niece Jenny Goodman; great-niece Sierra Martinez; great-great-nephew Kodah Martinez; great-nephews Galloway O’Leary and Sloan O’Leary; great-niece Ashley Loftice; great-great-nephew Rhett Cruickshank; and great-nephew Charles Watts, along with extended family and many friends who will forever cherish his memory.
John will be remembered for his love of family, his hardworking spirit, his sense of adventure, and the countless memories he created with the people he loved. His presence, stories, laughter, and friendship will be missed.
Though he is no longer with us, the memories John made and the love he shared will live on in the hearts of his family and friends.
Rest peacefully, John. You will be deeply missed and forever remembered.

title: InvestigateTV+: Bringing the hospital to neighborhoods
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ explores a pilot program bringing the hospital to people’s homes, delivering more than preventative care while working to expand nationwide.
Plus, we take an in-depth look at a federal initiative to recruit and retain foster homes and whether states can meet the goal of a home for every child.
Then, a story of sweet success: we go behind the scenes with a Vermont sugar maker keeping nearly century-old traditions alive.
Nurses in the neighborhood
A pilot program called Neighborhood Nursing is providing basic primary care outside the traditional clinic setting in East Baltimore, setting up in a church and visiting apartment complexes and homes to reach residents.
The program’s services are open to anyone who lives in the area. Those services are free and funded for now largely through philanthropic donations.
A home for every child
Kids sleeping in shelters, bussed between hotels, and overnights in office buildings. That’s the reality for many foster children in America.
For every 100 children in foster care, federal data shows that only 57 licenses homes are available.
Traveling for hand surgery
A family traveled from Turkey to St. Louis for their daughter’s surgery to treat a rare condition affecting fewer than 100 people worldwide.
Elisa, an 18-month-old, was born with eight fingers on her left hand. She was diagnosed with Ulnar Dimelia, also known as Mirror Hand Syndrome.
The science of sugar making
During the season of sugar making at Walker’s Pure Vermont Maple Syrup in Underhill, they steam ahead with batch after batch of the sweet stuff.
The guys in the sugarhouse will be working 10 hours or more each day. Craig Walker, who’s 86, spent a lifetime making maple syrup. Now, much of his day is on the road. “That’s my job, I’ve been promoted to truck driver,” he said. “We have to have the sap first to make the syrup.”

title: New study suggests 3 in 4 former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 had CTE
text:
New study suggests 3 in 4 former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 had CTE
A new study estimates about 3 in 4 former National Football League players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy — an even higher level than identified in another recent study of former players.
The new study, published Wednesday in the journal JAMA Network Open, aimed to provide a clearer view of how many former football players have the progressive neurodegenerative disease.
CTE has been linked to repetitive head impacts that often occur during contact sports such as football, soccer and hockey. CTE has also been detected in the brains of people who were in the military and exposed to traumatic explosions as well as victims of domestic violence. The brain trauma causes an abnormal buildup of the protein tau, and changes in the brain can begin years before symptoms are detected.
CTE can be definitively diagnosed only after death, but it has been associated with symptoms that overlap with dementia such as depression, anxiety, memory loss and lack of impulse control.
Previous studies detected the disease in as many as 99% of former NFL players whose brains had been donated for research. However, a significant limitation of these studies was in their potential bias: They were done in a group of people whose brains had been donated by family members who may have noticed symptoms while the person was still alive.
A study published in August found that at least 1 in 4 former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE. The study compared data from death certificates to determine the number of former professional players who had died against the number of brain donors confirmed to have CTE.
For this new study, Dr. Yorghos Tripodis and other researchers from Boston University’s CTE Center wanted to estimate the prevalence of CTE cases among an even broader group of former professional football players, including those who may not have noticed symptoms or donated their brains for research.
The researchers used data from the Understanding Neurologic Injury and Traumatic Encephalopathy brain bank combined with National Death Index records from former NFL players. They included brain donor and nondonor NFL players who died between January 2008 and December 2023.
Of 2,362 players who died during that time, 396 had donated their brains for research. Among those, 362 — 93.5% — had been diagnosed with CTE. Almost 70% of the players studied died at the age 70 years or older.
The researchers then looked at death certificates for the 2,362 people who died during the time period, finding that former players who had cognitive symptoms related to dementia were five times more likely to have their brains donated. Donations were more likely to come from families of players who had more symptoms or who died at a younger age.
The researchers adjusted the rate of disease among those who donated their brains to consider who was most likely to donate and applied that to the broader population of former players.
When asked about this newest study, the NFL referred to a statement sent in response to the August study: “The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.
“The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust – and expanding – set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well being. We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health.”
Tripodis said there are limitations to the new research — no study can remove all selection bias and researchers cannot expand the number to populations other than former NFL players. Evidence of CTE in the brain doesn’t mean all players have symptoms.
“Our numbers suggest that the prevalence of dementia, which is the most severe type of cognitive symptoms, is four times higher than the general population among the NFL players,” he said. “The symptoms are high, but doesn’t mean that everybody will have symptoms, doesn’t even mean that everybody with symptoms will have the most severe symptoms at the end of their lives.”
Dr. Rachel Grashow, a senior research scientist at Harvard University who was not involved in the new research, said the one “tricky” part of the study is understanding why someone donates their brain. She said that if researchers didn’t account for other factors for brain donation, the math “may not be accurate.”
It’s important to separate CTE from dementia, she said. CTE refers to the presence of the protein tau in specific regions in the brain and is measured in stages I through IV. Researchers have found higher rates of dementia among those with stages III and IV CTE only.
“We want to be careful to say that while there are no diagnostic symptoms linked to all of those found to have CTE at all stages, the ones with relatively the most tau protein aggregation show cognitive symptoms — issues with memory, concentration. Cognitive symptoms are different from mood symptoms — depression and anxiety,” Grashow said in an email.
Dr. Julie Stamm, a clinical assistant professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, said she was surprised by the high number of presumed CTE cases found in the study after researchers adjusted for who was most likely to donate their brain.
“We talk a lot about the bias of brain banks and how you don’t tend to donate unless you think something’s wrong, and I think that’s been a critique of some of the papers that have come out,” said Stamm, who was not involved with the new research.
Stamm said the NFL can go “a lot farther” in regard to safety to encourage earlier levels of the game to do more, such as not tackling in practices.
“If the NFL says that, the youth levels, the younger levels, they’ll listen, and that will go a long way in decreasing the overall number of impacts over a lifetime that these individuals sustain, which is what we’ve seen increases the risk for CTE,” Stamm said.
Tripodis said that when researchers have a precise estimate of CTE cases from deceased football players, it will motivate them to invest more into research on the disease.
“We’re having significant progress of identifying diagnostic criteria for living patients, designing the clinical trials that will find a cure for the disease,” he said.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil through Argentina and is expected to land in Miami
text:
SAO PAULO (AP) — Flávio Bolsonaro, the defeated Brazilian presidential candidate, fled his country to Argentina and then Ecuador alongside his wife and two daughters, Argentina’s migration authority said on Wednesday. The 45-year-old senator and his family were granted United States visas the day before by the Trump administration.
The move is almost certain to cause a big diplomatic rift between Brazil’s newly reelected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his Argentine counterpart Javier Milei, who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro’s campaign.
Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. The court had ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.
Argentina’s migration authority said on X that Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. It added they entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina’s northeastern province of Misiones.
“Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country,” the Argentine migration authority said.
The authority said that at 11:30 p.m. local time, shortly after clearing immigration control, the four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador.
Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro’s landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami’s Opa Locka executive airport. It was not clear whether the defeated candidate was on board.
Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told several dozen supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia that he did not have precise information about Bolsonaro’s whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil.
“I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true,” Lula said. “This act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”
Representatives of Brazil’s government and Bolsonaro did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press.
U.S. President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling him and his family “fine people.”
“The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from campaigning in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate but stressed that he didn’t endorse the election results.
Leaders all over the world and the Organization of American States (OAS) endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round.
Argentinian lawmaker Marcela Pagano said on X she filed a suit at a federal court in the city of Puerto Iguazu late Tuesday to request an investigation into her country’s government for people smuggling and abuse of authority regarding Bolsonaro.
“Our government says ‘he never entered’ Argentina. If he did, someone let him in. If they wanted to take him out through a federal airport, someone looked to the other side,” Pagano said. “Argentina’s border is not a VIP runway for anyone. Sovereignty is neither negotiated nor lent.”
On Tuesday, Milei’s administration spokesman Adrián Ravier said “there is no asylum request (from Bolsonaro) and there is nothing more to add.”
The defeated candidate was served with a Supreme Court order to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.
After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.
Flávio Bolsonaro said on Monday in a video that he was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country’s Supreme Court.
Brazil’s Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker.
___
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Farnsworth’s Joel Babb exhibit yields new perspectives with each viewing
text:
The first Joel Babb painting I ever saw was at the Bates College Museum of Art, many years ago now. The same qualities that mesmerized me then are alive and present in the paintings he makes today: The incredible precision of his technique (one Babb balances with his signature affective blend of realism and painterliness); his beguiling way with light; the invitation to enter the canvas through a street or a stream and wander through cityscapes and forests.
All of this is resplendently on view at “Shifting Visions: Joel Babb’s Painted Universe” (through Jan. 31) at the Farnsworth Art Museum, which features a dozen works spanning his long career. But the delight of this exhibition for me is the way that no matter how much you think you’ve gleaned from this artist’s work in the past, each fresh viewing — even of a painting you’ve seen before — yields new realizations that veritably spill forth from his complexly built surfaces.
The bulk of Babb’s large-scale works are preoccupied with two subjects: dizzying aerial views of Boston and depictions of the Maine woods and coastline. He has also painted the city of Rome and, I discovered on a visit to his studio last year, hospital room scenes. All of these have in common a staggering abundance of observational detail. Save for the operating room scenes, where the light is harsh and artificial (though of course, accurately so), we can sense the varied and infinite qualities of natural light.
In the Rome scenes, it can almost appear as it does in paintings of the 19th-century Barbizon school, specifically those of Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot’s less lyrical oeuvre of misty gray waterside scenes; the light in those is palpably drier, quite warm and golden. Babb’s forest scenes portray an entirely different quality of light, mostly one that comes dappling through the trees. At times, when the sun is high in the sky, it can also radiate an almost glaring prismatic halo all around it. And in the Boston scenes, light can appear mostly bright and even, its source behind us casting shadows through clouds that move overhead.
This bespeaks a breathtaking aptitude for both observation and for translating that observation precisely and fastidiously to canvas. But it is the presence that light’s qualities manifest that startled me in new ways in this exhibition.
I have always preferred the forest scenes to the Boston panoramas. Which is not to say that there aren’t things I very much admire about the latter. In “Church and State” (2018) for instance, I appreciate the wit expressed in Babb’s sense of composition. He views the city and the Charles River as expanding outward from our vantage point. But central to the composition is the pairing of the gold-domed Massachusetts State House and the white steeple of Park Street Church. The positioning of these two landmarks as the focal point of the composition is sly and playful. Though it is clearly geographically accurate, one senses that it was Babb’s trenchant humor that led him to single out this particular perspective from so many he might have chosen.
But I had never realized how, in the Boston paintings, the light brings a poignancy to all the hard surfaces of the city. We may be dazzled by the specificity of the reflections in the glass towers, which are as photographically rendered as in a Richard Estes painting. But Babb actually translates the phenomenon of light shifting rapidly as clouds scurry by, interrupting the sun’s rays from consistently illuminating the city below. That is what takes our breath away. Why? Because no matter how astonishing the details, in the end, detail without physical sensation is simply simulacra. Nature and its ever-morphing conditions are what inject the sensations that move us.
Something similar happens with “Copley Plunge” (1990), a vertiginous overhead shot that makes our heads spin because of the way it conveys the phenomenon of gravity. We feel as if we are literally hurtling through the air, about to crash into the rooftops. Sensation and emotion (in this particular instance, a rush of danger) are what transcend mere observation, no matter how microscopically impressive.
This, in turn, changed the way I looked at the scenes of Maine woods. Interestingly, again, it is not the presence of detail that ensures their effectiveness as transporting images. Quite the opposite. Yes, we can discern the stratification of rocks, that golden Barbizon light and the sliminess of seaweed in “Eggemoggin Reach” (2002). But with a scene like this, so organically awe-inspiring in its very essence, pictorial verisimilitude is almost beside the point. So, Babb takes liberties with the understory and the wispy cirrus clouds overhead. They are painterly and inexact in a way that better transmits the sense of movement propelled by wind.
In “A Sunlit Brook, Wight Brook, Grafton Notch, Maine” (2022), Babb paints the water loosely. Up close we see that the effect we perceive from afar as water rushing over rocks is essentially a collection of hundreds of splotches of color he has dabbed onto canvas, rather than obsessively rendered details. This contributes to the liquid quality of the scene. Water, after all, is not static, its surface reflections affected by its constant movement, the changing light, the breezeless steadiness of the surrounding foliage or the way that same foliage is blurred with each whisper of wind. To approach it definitively as a single image would also arrest its natural movement, so Babb chooses to be less precise for the sake of more accurately capturing the magical mutability of water’s natural state.
One can get lost in each of these paintings for hours. That seems a small thing to ask of a viewer, considering the many days and even months each requires to complete. Take your time and look deeply.
Jorge S. Arango has written about art, design and architecture for over 35 years. He lives in Portland and can be reached at [email protected]. This column is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.
‘Shifting Vision: Joel Babb’s Painted Universe,’ Farnsworth Art Museum, 16 Museum St., Rockland. Through Jan. 31. Seven days a week, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. After Dec. 31, 10 a.m.-4 p.m. Wednesday through Monday (closed Tuesday). For more, 207-596-6457 or farnsworthmuseum.org

title: A ceasefire in a devastated Ukrainian city holds for its first 30 hours, officials say
text:
A ceasefire in a devastated Ukrainian city holds for its first 30 hours, officials say
A six-day ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine held for its first day and night, officials said Wednesday, but Moscow and Kyiv continued to batter each other elsewhere.
The localized truce in the devastated southern city of Oleshky began Tuesday and is due to last through Sunday as a planned humanitarian operation races to get its about 2,000 remaining residents urgently needed food and medicine, as well as evacuate those who want to leave.
If the ceasefire holds, it will be the first time since Russia’s invasion of its neighbor more than 4 ½ years ago that the two sides have observed a significant truce. Previous attempts to stop the fighting have either failed to take hold or quickly unraveled.
Related video: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
The development coincided with U.S.-led plans to bring Moscow and Kyiv officials back to the table next month for technical talks on how to move forward on ending the war, even though neither side shows signs of backing down from their key demands.
Russia’s ombudsperson Yana Lantratova and Ukraine’s human rights ombudsperson Dmytro Lubinets both said Wednesday there had been no ceasefire violations in Oleshky for 30 hours.
The plight of the city in Ukraine's southern Kherson region caught the attention of U.S. first lady Melania Trump, and the White House said she brokered the humanitarian mission.
Pope Leo XIV also spoke this month with presidents Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine and Vladimir Putin of Russia, urging them to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky and the safe evacuation of civilians, the Vatican said.
Zelenskyy said he was grateful to Melania Trump for her role in halting the fighting in and around Oleshky, where she says humanitarian corridors are being established to take people out.
“We are grateful that they are organizing this possibility to evacuate people,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine was ready to receive evacuees from the town.
“Her personal involvement is of great importance to the entire process,” Russia’s Lantratova said.
Both sides are eager to win U.S. President Donald Trump’s approval as he pushes for an elusive peace settlement.
Elsewhere, the war rages on
A Russian drone strike on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight wounded five people, including a four-year-old child, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said.
The jet-powered drone attack started a major fire that set alight an apartment building, private house and an industrial building, the emergency services said.
In Russia, meanwhile, the Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 531 Ukrainian drones from late Tuesday through early Wednesday.
Officials said apartment buildings and industrial infrastructure in two regions were targeted, injuring five people.

title: FOR YOUR HEALTH: Leaf raking injuries are more common than you think
text:
Leaf raking injuries are more common than you think. An estimated 7,700 people landed in the emergency room in 2025 with leaf raking injuries. They’re also largely preventable.
LawnStarter analyzed ER data from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) and recommendations from Johns Hopkins Medicine and a chiropractor to help you safely rake, blow, or otherwise remove your leaves this fall.
“The leaves don’t care if they’re picked up today or tomorrow. Your spine does,” says chiropractor Kevin O’Hara, in Arlington Heights, Illinois. Pace yourself and listen to your body, he adds.
Rake like you’re doing a workout. Raking counts as moderate-intensity exercise, closer to doubles tennis and power yoga than sweeping the porch. Raking is a repetitive-motion activity, and repetitive motion with poor technique and no warm-up or recovery time is what causes overuse injuries. Every pull of the rake stresses the same spots in your lower back, shoulders, neck, and forearms and can cause strains and sprains.
Back injuries lead the list. About one in five raking-activity ER visits are back injuries, according to the CPSC.
Treating raking like it’s not exercise is one of the biggest mistakes people make, says O’Hara, So is trying to finish the whole yard in one day and working for several hours without a break. “Just as you wouldn’t go to the gym and deadlift for three straight hours, you shouldn’t rake continuously,” he says.
For some people, a few hours of leaf raking is the most strenuous activity they do all week. Sports medicine calls it the “weekend warrior” pattern, described by Mayo Clinic as sitting all week, then taking on a sudden strenuous activity your body isn’t ready for.
For an unprepared body, that sudden exertion can strain the heart. Roughly one in five raking injuries treated in the ER is described as a cardiac or systemic event, such as chest pain or fainting. Chest pain is an emergency. If you feel chest pain or become lightheaded, call 911.
About 7,700 people landed in the emergency room in 2025 with leaf raking injuries, according to a LawnStarter analysis of U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) injury data. O’Hara estimates that 60 percent to 80 percent of the patients who show up after a weekend of raking could have “either avoided the injury entirely or significantly reduced its severity.”
Start by treating raking as a workout:
Put on supportive shoes with real tread.
Dress in light layers you can shed as you warm up. Warm up with a five-minute walk, then stretch your neck, shoulders, hips, and hamstrings.
The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons recommends stretching slowly and gently, holding a stretch for 10 to 30 seconds. No bouncing, and it shouldn’t hurt.
According to Johns Hopkins Medicine, most raking injuries come from bad form. Here’s how to avoid them:
Bend at the knees, not the waist, whenever you pick up a pile or a bag. Keep the motion in your arms and shoulders, not your torso. Drive the pull toward you with a step back, not a wrist yank. Switch your lead hand every few minutes. Take a break every 20 to 30 minutes, even if you feel fine, and drink water.
According to O’Hara, the biggest mistake people make is trying to “push through” increasing pain to finish the yard. “By the time they stop, they’ve often turned a mild muscle strain into an injury that takes weeks to heal.”
Pain in your muscles, back, or joints signals it’s time to take a break. Most of the time, it’s temporary and will resolve with rest.
O’Hara says he grows more concerned when the pain: Feels sharp instead of achy; Travels into an arm or leg; Brings numbness, tingling, or weakness; Keeps worsening after 48 to 72 hours.
“Pain that makes it difficult to stand upright, walk normally, or sleep comfortably deserves to be evaluated,” he says.
Chest pain, shortness of breath, a cold sweat, or lightheadedness is a different matter. The American Heart Association considers these symptoms an emergency. Stop and call 911.
How to Recover After a Long Raking Day
Everyone responds to exertion differently.
“Some muscle soreness for a day or two is perfectly normal, especially if you haven’t been active recently,” O’Hara says.
That delay is normal and has a name: delayed onset muscle soreness. It sets in one to three days after the activity, not during it, and usually fades within a few days. It rarely lasts more than five days, according to Cleveland Clinic.
O’Hara recommends light activity over total rest. “Go for a short walk, do some gentle stretching, and avoid collapsing into a chair for the rest of the evening,” he says.
Cold helps while a spot still feels tender; heat helps a back that’s stiff rather than sore.

title: Police department closes its investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - The Greenville Police Department said it has officially closed its investigation into the death of Hayden Panettiere.
Police said Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental based on the medical examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation.
Panettiere, 36, died from an accidental overdose involving multiple prescription medications and fentanyl, according to findings previously released by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office.
Toxicology testing determined the cause of death to be the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. An autopsy showed no signs of contributing trauma.
On Aug. 16, Panettiere was found unresponsive inside an apartment in Greenville, where she had been temporarily staying. Dispatchers received a 911 call reporting a woman in cardiac arrest at approximately 1:51 p.m. She was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m.
Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the apartment where she died.
The coroner’s office had previously closed its case after the cause and manner were established. Police said at the time their independent investigation remained open while detectives continued to follow leads.
Panettiere was best known for her roles in the TV shows “Heroes” and “Nashville” as well as films such as “Ice Princess” and the “Scream” franchise.
Panettiere published a memoir in May called “This Is Me: A Reckoning.” In the book, she detailed her childhood, time in the limelight and struggles with alcohol, opioids and postpartum depression.

title: Brewer City Council bans needle exchange programs
text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - The Brewer City Council voted unanimously Tuesday to prohibit needle exchange programs at both fixed and mobile sites in the city.
The council made the change through an amendment to the land use ordinance.
The vote followed public comments from Brewer residents who spoke against syringe service programs. Many said allowing the programs could lead to negative results.
Many residents pointed across the river to Bangor as an example of what they do not want their community to become.
“I think a service location could attract increased foot traffic, loitering, and public drug use. We’ve seen it all in Bangor. Bangor is having huge problems,” one resident said.
Brewer Mayor Jenn Morin said the council considered input from the police chief and residents.
“I think listening to our Chief of Police and then also having conversations with constituents enabled this council body to feel comfortable that we were making a decision that our community endorses,” Morin said.
A six-month ban was proposed in Bangor earlier this year. Brewer is the first neighboring community to pass a ban like this.

title: Swing state Sen. Mark Kelly rallies with Troy Jackson, Maine Democrats one week before Election Day
text:
Swing state Sen. Mark Kelly rallies with Troy Jackson, Maine Democrats one week before Election Day
Kelly flipped a seat from Republican to Democrat in 2020, and believes Jackson can do the same on Tuesday.
Swing state Sen. Mark Kelly rallies with Troy Jackson, Maine Democrats one week before Election Day
Kelly flipped a seat from Republican to Democrat in 2020, and believes Jackson can do the same on Tuesday.
With just one week to go until Election Day, notable national figures have made their way to Maine to stump for candidates. On Tuesday, Arizona Democrat Sen. Mark Kelly made a stop in Freeport to support Troy Jackson, Hannah Pingree, and Rep. Chellie Pingree.
"I actually think the odds are on our side," said Kelly.
Kelly is no stranger to tight races. In 2020, the Navy veteran and former astronaut flipped a Republican seat in Arizona in a special election and went on to hold his seat, winning re-election in 2022. Arizona is considered a swing state, voting for Joe Biden in 2020 and Donald Trump in 2024. Kelly outlined his priorities he said will be much easier with a Democratic majority on the Hill.
"Together we can lower costs, we can build more homes instead of support hedge funds. We can make corporations pay their fair share, and we can make sure we get a say in how AI changes this economy," said Kelly.
Kelly did not call out Sen. Susan Collins by name at all on Tuesday. He did call on Democrats to lower the cost of living and to ban congressional stock trading, and went after billionaires for "writing the rules" in the Trump administration.
"To have a federal government that works with the state so that we can put forward policies that help people, people are really inspired right now, and they want it too. They want change," said Jackson.
Rep. Chellie Pingree, who has called numerous times to reign rein in ICE, said Democrats need to take back the majority to pass Medicare for All, increase the minimum wage and action on climate change. Her daughter, Hannah Pingree who is vying for the Blaine House, said she will use her power as governor to fight back against Donald Trump.
"The next governor is going to have to stand up to this reckless president. The way he is overriding our rights if it is immigrant rights, reproductive rights or LGBT rights we are going to have to hold things together," said Hannah Pingree.
There was a moment in which a supporter yelled to Mark Kelly to run for president in 2028 to which Kelly responded with "we'll see." That reaction drew an applause.
Other notable Democrats who have appeared with Jackson have been progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

title: Ashland Sawmill to Nearly Double Production
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ASHLAND, Maine (WAGM) - One county sawmill has plans to expand and will bring over 200 new jobs to the area. The Ashland sawmill, Irving Forest Products, is set to expand. With the combined funding from federal and state tax credits, TD Bank, and Irving, the sawmill will nearly double its annual lumber production from 130 million to 250 million board feet.
Will Richter, Senior Relationship Manager for TD Community Development Corporation said: “The project’s expected to create and retain around 220 full-time equivalent jobs and beyond that you have construction jobs. You have loggers, truckers, railroad workers. All of the surrounding inputs that go into making a sawmill in production. They are moving very quickly in getting equipment ordered and starting the construction process. So, just overall they’re looking to nearly double production there which is going to have a huge impact for the state of Maine as well as the county in general.”
TD Bank provided a $10 million funding allocation and backed $49 million in other investments for the project. “We really enjoy partnering with rural communities in particular and supporting the economies that are driving rural America. One job makes a big difference for that community and when we are looking at impact and looking at investing in new markets tax credit transactions. We like to look at the surrounding area and how will a particular project benefit that economy, benefit the communities around it, and JD Irving seemed like a fantastic partner to work with. Our goal with any investment is to see that the families, the community members, those that are in and around a project that we’re investing in benefit. Whether that’s from jobs, community services, education, healthcare, etc. Our goal is to see that the local community is thriving because those are our neighbors,” Richter continued.
Richter says TD Bank is continuing to look for other rural businesses in the county to invest in. Irving has not been available for an interview but in a press release, Irving and TD Bank say the Ashland sawmill expansion is an investment in Aroostook County’s economic resilience and Maine’s forest products industry. They are unsure how long the expansion will take but look forward to providing more jobs and a stronger forest products industry in the area.

title: Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — At the height of the Los Angeles fires in 2025, millions of residents were exposed in a 24-hour period to toxic lead levels from smoke that were 80 times higher than the typical background level, according to a new study.
Researchers from the California Institute of Technology compared the chemical composition of smoke from the Eaton Fire with that of a wildfire and found that the urban plume had more lead, arsenic and halogens (which include chlorine and bromine) linked to burning vehicles, building materials and electronics.
“The main, key finding is really that wildfire smoke is very different fundamentally from the urban smoke,” said Nga Lee “Sally” Ng, an author of the study published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances. With the new technology they used to measure what was in the smoke, they were able to “actually see the very detailed component of these particles that we are breathing.”
Co-author Haroula Baliaka said understanding the different chemical compositions of smoke from an urban versus a wildland fire helps bridge a missing gap in research. Wildfires are growing larger, more intense, faster-moving and more frequent largely because of drier and warmer weather associated with human-caused climate change. As urban growth and climate change push more fires into cities, researchers said monitoring and emergency response will have to adapt.
Ed Avol, professor emeritus in the Keck School of Medicine at the University of Southern California who has researched the health effects of air pollution for decades, said significant exposure to heavy metals is consistent with what he’d expect, “but certainly surprising because we haven’t been able to document this sort of thing.”
“One of the real advantages of this study is that it had the opportunity to make measurements sort of hour-by-hour across the sampling network. And typically we make measurements of airborne particulates and so forth a couple of times a week, at best,” said Avol, who wasn’t involved in the study.
Thousands of structures burned, releasing toxic chemicals
The two wind-whipped infernos in Altadena and the Pacific Palisades that ignited on Jan. 7, 2025, killed at least 31 people and destroyed more than 16,000 structures, mostly homes, and everything in them — cars, paint, furniture, chemicals under sinks and more. Millions of people were exposed to smoke, which across the entire United States has been linked to tens of thousands of deaths annually. A recent study found that metal mixtures in the leftover smoke, ash and debris from the deadly 2023 Maui wildfires were harmful to the lung health of people living nearby long after the burning ended.
During the fires, researchers measured trace elements of fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, every hour reported by instruments in the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork ( ASCENT ), a relatively new network of air quality monitors across the U.S. that measures the size and chemical composition of these particulates in real time. Ng said ASCENT is the U.S.’s first measurement network able to measure the chemical composition of airborne particles in real time.
Researchers were able to see what chemicals were in the smoke, track how its composition changed over the fire’s course, and distinguish emissions coming from burning structures. From there, they estimated how many people across Los Angeles were exposed to the heavy metals, particularly lead, during the fire’s first days.
They compared the typical value of lead before the fires and the chemical makeup of smoke from a 2024 fire in Riverside County that burned mostly vegetation with data from the Eaton Fire plume. Contrasted with the wildfire smoke, the plume from the LA fire contained 50 times more lead, three times more arsenic, and seven times more halogens. At the peak of burning, about 7 million people were exposed for 24 hours to lead levels more than 80 times what’s typical.
Lead is a neurotoxin that can stunt children’s development, lower IQ scores and increase blood pressure in adults. Scientists still don’t know how short-term, high exposure to lead impacts human health. Arsenic exposure is associated with various cancers.
Yaguang Wei, assistant professor in the department of environmental medicine at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai who researches the health impacts of air pollution, wildfire smoke and severe weather, said their findings reinforced some conclusions of a recent study he co-authored that found, in part, that PM2.5 from wildfire smoke was more toxic than particulates from other sources.
“I think their findings are not surprising,” said Wei, who was not involved in the study. When fires burn properties, they’re also burning “a lot of lead on your wall paint and the plastics and electronics and those are very toxic” when they burn, he said.
Monitoring, policies and emergency response need to adapt, experts say
Wei said the study has “important policy implications.” He thinks governments should take stronger actions to protect public health during these fires by investing in more wildfire monitoring and public alerts, and having more prescribed fires.
For Avol, the study is a reminder of our “strange and increasingly dangerous new world” where urban and wildland intersect — and increasingly catch fire.
“It reminds us to be cautious and be concerned and, you know, think about what we can do to minimize this. We’re not going to stop using all these materials containing metals and halogens and so forth in our homes,” he said. “How do we protect people from being exposed to that?”

title: Rumford police probe gunshot damage to clock tower: ‘Enough is enough’
text:
RUMFORD — The Rumford Police Department used a large crane to inspect apparent gunshot damage to the Municipal Building clock tower Wednesday as part of an investigation into the reports of gunfire earlier this month.
Police said repairs are needed to prevent water and other damage to the historic building due to holes in the walls.
In a news release, Police Chief Tony Milligan said that on Oct. 10 about 8:42 p.m., officers working at the police department on River Street heard multiple gunshots, along with what sounded like a projectile striking the Municipal Building on Congress Street. As officers began investigating, calls came in from residents reporting gunfire in the area of Waldo Street near its intersection with Rumford Avenue.
Police conducted an extensive search of the surrounding area, but no suspects were located at that time. Additional reports of gunfire in the same neighborhood followed during the early morning hours of Oct. 11 and again on Oct. 14, prompting a shelter-in-place advisory.
As the investigation developed, police identified suspects and served a search warrant at 209 Waldo St. early the morning of Oct. 14. Rumford police were assisted by the Maine State Police Tactical Team, but the suspects had fled before they arrived.
On Oct. 20, the U.S. Marshals Service arrested Blake Lachance, 21, of Lewiston, in Westbrook on multiple felony counts, including aggravated assault, reckless conduct and criminal mischief. Lachance was captured after attempting to flee on foot, the Marshals Service said.
Investigators discovered damage consistent with a bullet strike to an elevated section of the Municipal Building’s clock tower facing Waldo Street. Due to the height and location of the damage, investigators were unable to immediately access the area for a closer examination.
“These recent acts of violence are serious, and I fully understand the concerns and frustrations of our residents,” Milligan said. “They deserve to feel safe in their homes, on their streets, and throughout their community. We share those concerns and take them very seriously.”
Meanwhile, at the same address where police served the search warrant, a teen and an adult were arrested in connection with a stabbing Sunday that left two people injured. After a foot pursuit, police arrested Jazya D. Swan, 19, of Lewiston, after discovering him on the porch of a Cumberland Street home. Deputies also arrested a 15-year-old girl from Lisbon, who was not named, after finding her at another home on Waldo Street.
“It is frustrating to see our community unfairly characterized by the criminal actions of a relatively small number of individuals,” Milligan said. “Like every community, we have people who engage in dangerous criminal activity and sometimes prey upon others. But those individuals do not define Rumford, and their actions are not a reflection of the overwhelming majority of the good people who live here.”
Milligan said his department is working to make sure the quality of life of residents is not undermined by “reckless and dangerous” acts.
“Let me be clear: Enough is enough,” he said. “…Rumford is a good community filled with good people, and we intend to do everything within our lawful authority to keep it that way.”
Anyone with information concerning the recent gunfire or related violent criminal activity in the Waldo Street area is encouraged to call the Rumford Police Department at 207-364-4551.

title: Centuries-old Gouldsboro building with a harbor-view apartment is selling for $335K
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
Nestled in Prospect Harbor, a $335,000 Gouldsboro building offers buyers a chance to own both a ground-floor shop space and a one-bedroom apartment above.
This property has more than 2,700 square feet of living space and a full bathroom on both the first and second floors, according to Tacy Ridlon of Better Homes & Gardens Real Estate The Masiello Group, the listing agent for the property.
Located on West Bay Road and across the bay from Mount Desert Island, the property is a less than 10-minute drive to Winter Harbor and roughly 35 minutes to Ellsworth.
The building dates back to 1800 and once served as the town’s post office. It later became a real estate office, then a clothing boutique, until the sellers bought it in 2018 and transformed it into an antique store. At the time, the building still had the post office boxes left over from its prior use, Ridlon said.
“They’re a very interesting couple who have dealt in antiques for many years, first in New York, and then in Maine,” Ridlon said.
The sellers considered registering it as a historic building given its age and significance to the community, but ultimately decided against it, as the certification would’ve limited how the building could be changed and updated later.
The sellers also updated the living space upstairs to transform it into a “darling” apartment with views of the harbor from the bedroom and plenty of sunlight, Ridlon said.
“They’ve redone the bathroom and kitchen but it still has all the period details of the building,” she said. “The sellers made it what it is. It’s a great space.”
Since listing the property, the owners have sold off some of the antique store’s merchandise. However, if a buyer wants to continue operating the business, the remaining antiques — and the apartment’s furniture — could be included in the sale.
While the building’s lower level has served as a commercial space for years, Ridlon said it could easily serve as a studio, gallery, cafe or other use. The owner could live on the second floor or rent out the unit for additional income.
“It would make a great artist’s studio, whether they’re a painter, potter or even a woodworker,” she said. “There’s quite a bit of space and multiple rooms.”
The less than half-acre plot also includes a gravel parking area with a stone patio and gardens in the backyard.
The property was initially listed over a year ago for more than $480,000, according to Zillow records. The asking price was knocked down to $335,000 earlier this year.
While Ridlon said plenty of prospective buyers have toured the property and imagined how they would use the space, no one has submitted an offer yet. She credited this to the building’s unique layout and the slowdown of Maine’s housing market in the years since the pandemic.
“The pandemic frenzy could never sustain itself,” she said. “We need to find just the right person who has a business for themselves and can live upstairs.”

title: Lily Robbins Comes Home To Searsmont After Months Of Burn Treatment Following The Robbins Lumber Fire
text:
Waldo County EMT, Whose Father Died From Burns He Received During Mill Explosion, Is Finally Coming Home After Her Hospital Stay
It's been an incredibly trying year for Waldo County community, especially first responders, their families, and those connected to the family business, Robbins Lumber.
Lily Robbins checks both those boxes; the young woman was a local EMT, and her family owned and managed the mill.
After a massive fire and explosion took place at the Robbins Lumber mill this past May, a dozen firefighters and personnel were injured, among them Lily, her father, 51-year-old Alden J. Robbins who was the co-owner and Vice President of Sales at the mill, and her uncle Jim Robbins, the other co-owner. Alden Robbins eventually succumbed to his injuries and passed away in July, after battling for months on a specialized burn unit at Mass General.
The incident also claimed the lives of 2 firefighters, 27-year-old Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross, 76-year-old Wayne Woodbury who was the Assistant Fire Chief in Searsmont.
Read More: NIOSH Report On Robbins Lumber Fire
Local and Federal investigators spent weeks looking into the incident, which was ultimately classified as an accident. The mill was able to reopen about a month later.
Read More: Robbins Lumber Company: Recovery After A Devastating Fire In Maine
Some of the injured still remain in burn units across New England as they fight to recover from their wounds. Others have recovered enough to be released, like Belmont Firefighter Katherine Paige who was released in July.
This week, the Town of Searsmont announced that yet another one of the injured, Lily Robbins, is finally ready to come home. Like her father and uncle, Lily was taken to Mass General in May, and has been receiving treatment for wounds she sustained while trying to help at the scene of the blaze. Lily was volunteering as an EMT at the time of the explosion.
This will be the first time Lily has been home since the fire and her father's death, and the town is rallying the community to give her a warm welcome.
"After a long road to recovery, we are looking forward to welcoming Lily home and celebrating this special day with our community! We would love your help making her homecoming extra special! Friday, October 30, 2026. Anyone wishing to drop off desserts, snack foods, or a handmade Welcome Home sign is welcome to bring them to the station from 9:00 am to noon, so things can be all set up for that afternoon."
They say the plan to share an updated timeline of Lily's travel route once those details are finalized.
Read More: Community Unites To Support Injured EMT Lily Robbins
The young woman responded to the online post with great appreciation.
"Thank you everyone! I’m so grateful for this community."
A Gofundme campaign was set up, right after the explosion occurred, to help Lily with medical bills and lost income she's sustained as a result of her injuries.
You can contribute to that effort by clicking here.
We wish Lily, her entire family, the folks at Robbins Lumber and the community of residents and EMTs from Waldo County the best as they welcome this local hero back home. And we hope for everyone's continued healing and recovery.

title: ‘The Exorcist’ Curse: The Real-Life Horror Behind the Legendary Film
text:
‘The Exorcist’ Curse Is Almost as Disturbing as the Movie Itself
The Exorcist terrified audiences on screen, but the trouble surrounding the 1973 horror classic began long before it hit theaters.
A fire destroyed much of the set. Several people connected to the production died, and cast members suffered serious injuries. The string of tragedies fueled rumors that the movie was cursed.
Even director William Friedkin admitted the production was unlike anything he had experienced before.
What Happened During ‘The Exorcist’ Filming?
Before filming got underway, a fire destroyed the set of the MacNeil family home. According to the documentary Fear of God: 25 Years of The Exorcist, the only room left untouched was Regan's bedroom. Rebuilding took six weeks.
READ MORE: 10 Bad-on-Purpose Movies That Are Actually Great
"We were plagued by strange and sinister things from the beginning; it is simply the hardest thing I have ever done in my life," Friedkin said in 1974.
The bad news continued. Max von Sydow, who played Father Merrin, lost his brother during his first week of filming, while young star Linda Blair lost her grandfather.
Ellen Burstyn later said nine people died during production, including an assistant cameraman's newborn baby and a night watchman. Actor Jack MacGowran, who played Burke Dennings, also died from flu complications shortly after filming.
READ MORE: The 10 Best Horror Movie Practical Effects, and How They Did It
The string of unsettling events prompted Friedkin to seek reassurance for his cast and crew. He approached Father Thomas Bermingham, a technical advisor on the film, to perform an exorcism on the set. Bermingham couldn't conduct an exorcism, but he did give a solemn blessing in a ceremony attended by the cast and crew.
Were Actors Injured on ‘The Exorcist’ Set?
The production's injuries were real and sometimes severe. Blair fractured her lower back while filming Regan's violent convulsions, an injury she said contributed to lifelong scoliosis.
In Fear of God, Blair recalled crying out in pain during a take, but the crew mistook her screams for part of the performance. The footage was ultimately used in the movie.
Burstyn also injured her back when a crew member pulled too hard on her harness during a scene.
READ MORE: The Most Overrated Horror Movies Of All Time
According to Castle of Frankenstein, other accidents included a crew member losing a toe and a carpenter chopping off his thumb.
Did Director William Friedkin Believe in the Curse?
In a 1974 interview with Castle of Frankenstein, Friedkin said the production had changed his views on demonic possession.
"I'm not a convert to the occult, but after all I've seen on this film, I definitely believe in demonic possession," he said. "There are things that cannot be treated by medical or psychiatric means."
Friedkin's comments helped fuel the film's sinister reputation, but there's no evidence that supernatural forces caused the production's accidents or deaths.
More than 50 years later, the curse of The Exorcist remains one of Hollywood's most chilling legends — even if the documented tragedies are disturbing enough on their own.

title: After surviving near-fatal crash, Falmouth man can’t get next care he needs in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Richard Day has been on life support at Maine Medical Center in Portland for more than two months following a car crash in Gorham that left him with critical neck and spinal cord injuries. His father, Greg Day, sleeps in a cot in Richard’s hospital room most nights, talking to his paralyzed son, reading his lips for responses and changing the television channel when he asks.
The crash upended the duo’s life. They live together in Falmouth and are the sole employees of Greg’s masonry business, Greg Day Family Masonry. Richard, whose family and friends call him Rich or Richie, turns 23 on Thursday.
Though Greg said Rich feels hopeful and “lucky to be alive,” his uphill battle is getting steeper. Doctors say Rich likely will need a ventilator for the rest of his life, and his possible next treatment — at a Long-Term Acute Care Hospital (LTACH) or a specialized rehabilitation facility — are not found in Maine. Greg said the family’s ultimate goal is to bring Rich home, but he would have to go much farther away first.
Maine Health Acute Care Surgery and Trauma Medical Director Bryan Morse said his organization’s largest hospital can save the lives of patients with critical spinal cord injuries, but cannot meet their needs long-term. That reality places tremendous logistical, financial and emotional stress on families faced with moving their loved one out of state.
Morse said it is common for patients who need high levels of long-term care and physical therapy to remain in Portland’s Maine Medical Center for months without the full treatment they need. The patients can weaken, struggling with cognitive, physical and psychiatric decline without frequent stimulation. Rich should have moved on to a higher level of treatment weeks ago, Morse said.
“There’s a major gap in healthcare in Maine at the moment,” Morse said.
Morse said Rich should move to an LTACH, likely in Massachusetts or New Jersey, where trained professionals could gradually reduce the settings on his ventilator to help him breathe more independently. Greg said he and Rich would rather he qualify to settle in a specialized rehabilitation care for spinal cord injuries — Shepherd Center in Atlanta, for example — where he would be surrounded by people with similar injuries and receive rigorous physical therapy to move him toward recovery.
“He doesn’t want to sit here and get flipped back and forth in a bed for the rest of his life. We’d both just rather die right now than have that be the final sentence,” Greg said. “He wants to sit up in a wheelchair, he wants to be able to go outside, he wants to be able to be mobile, he wants to go to the ocean.”
Greg and Rich are lifelong Mainers. If Rich moves to an LTACH in another state, Greg said he would go with him, but the medical bills are already mounting while Greg is out of work to care for his son. If Rich went to a rehabilitation center, temporary housing for patients’ family would be provided, Greg said.
Maine Medical Center sees about 12 patients with spinal cord injuries like Rich’s a year, Morse said. The hospital sent about 107 patients with various critical injures to out-of-state facilities in 2025 and 2026 due to a lack of in-state recourses, according to Richard Marino, senior medical director of post-acute care at MaineHealth.
Marino said the problem comes down to a lack of funding in Maine for LTACHs and long-term care facilities. Ventilator units require staff that know how to operate them, units designed to accommodate them, and consistent power and oxygen to keep them running. Springbrook Center in Westbrook had a ventilator unit about 10 years ago, Marino said, but closed it because it wasn’t profitable.
In a rural state like Maine, the number of people in need of ventilators at a given time is inconsistent, Marino said. That doesn’t make the consequences for those who do less dire, and he said the situation for people who need long-term care for conditions beyond spinal cord injures has worsened since more facilities closed following the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.
“People have to leave their homes, they have to leave their families, they have to potentially go to places where they actually have no social support,” Marino said.
Marino is on a committee with the Maine Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, a nonprofit that advocates for for long-term care consumers. It is lobbying the Maine Legislature for funding that would bring more long-term care infrastructure to Maine.
Greg said he has now heard repeatedly how challenging injuries like Rich’s become when they happen in Maine. He said he saw Rich laughing and smiling for the first time in a while this week after a physical therapy session, something he needs much more of.
“He just needs a different atmosphere — mentally, psychosocially, spiritually, holistically… That’s the urgency I feel every day,” Greg said. “We’re just stuck here.”
Greg’s childhood friend has raised more than $16,505 through an online fund for him and Rich to help their family while they are unable to work.

title: Federal Reserve keeps rates unchanged despite elevated inflation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Federal Reserve keeps rates unchanged despite elevated inflation, gives little signal of next move
The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9% despite elevated inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves.
Video coverage from last month above: Fed raises rates for first time since 2023 to fight inflation
“Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2% inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2% target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases.
The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets. Whether the Fed is still leaning toward another hike will likely be a key issue in the news conference held by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh this afternoon.
The Fed’s decision comes just six days before a midterm election that has focused heavily on concerns around the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Yet Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.
Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied.
President Trump has also slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank's rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed.
Other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans' sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.
And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed's 2% target.
A separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, comes out Thursday and is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month.
The Fed's policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3%, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter.
Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren't particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

title: Beth A. Barter
text:
Beth Ann York Barter, Boothbay, passed away Sept. 27, 2026 at the age of 57.
Beth was born on Sept. 24, 1969. She grew up in Bristol, Maine, and graduated from Lincoln Academy. In 1995, Beth began her nursing career, starting a lifelong journey dedicated to caring for others.
Beth was a wholehearted, compassionate, and generous woman who gave love freely to everyone around her. She had a natural desire to help others and a kindness that reached far beyond her own family. Throughout her life, she dedicated herself to taking care of those in need, working in Home Health care and spending many years serving her community as an EMT in Boothbay, Maine. Beth loved her work, but more importantly, she loved the people she cared for. Helping others was more than a job to her; it was a reflection of who she was. She touched many lives through her compassion, generosity, and willingness to be there for anyone who needed her.
Above all, Beth cherished her family. She loved spending time with those closest to her. Throughout Brogan and Madison’s childhood, Beth traveled to countless sports games and practices, cherishing every moment she shared with them and supporting them in all they did. These memories, along with the time she shared with her family, were among the many things that brought her joy. Beth most especially enjoyed watching women’s basketball with her daughter, Madison; and always cooking enough dinner for an army. She was an amazing cook. Beth’s love extended to her friends and her community, where she was loved by many and will be remembered for her big heart, caring nature, and the difference she made in the lives of others.
Beth is survived by her husband, Samuel Barter; her daughter, Madison Barter; her son, Brogan Barter; her aunt Joan Smyrski; and her mother, Colleen Leonard. She also leaves behind many beloved family members and friends whose lives were made better by knowing her.
She was predeceased by her father, Clifton York; her brother, Shawn York; her grandmother, Elaine Trask; and her aunt, Janet Grondin.
Beth’s life was one of love, kindness, and selflessness toward others. She had a heart that always made room for one more person, a willingness to help without hesitation, and a gift for making others feel cared for. Though she will be deeply missed by her family, friends, and community, the love she gave and the lives she touched will remain a lasting part of her legacy. The family wishes to thank the people who donated to the Go Fund Me for us.

title: Maine lawmakers weigh in on federal fraud charges
text:
State lawmakers weigh in on federal fraud charges
For the majority of the last legislative session, Republican lawmakers held press conferences talking about what they said was a major fraud problem in Maine.
State lawmakers weigh in on federal fraud charges
For the majority of the last legislative session, Republican lawmakers held press conferences talking about what they said was a major fraud problem in Maine.
Last legislative session, just about every week, Republican lawmakers held press conferences at the State House raising concerns about healthcare fraud in Maine.
Now, six people from a South Portland personal care agency have been indicted on federal charges alleging they defrauded MaineCare.
"This is a huge vindication for the Republican caucus," Rep. Billy Bob Faulkingham, R-Winter Harbor, said. "Because we've been talking about this for almost two years now, at least a year, that we've been calling for some action to be taken on this."
Faulkingham said fraud would not happen if Republicans were in control in Augusta, and he's looking ahead to Tuesday.
"If we can get all three, the governor's office, the Senate and the House, we will completely overhaul the way DHHS is working. They are clearly not doing their job. And the federal government expects states to manage that money properly," he said.
This summer, Vice President JD Vance visited Maine to highlight what he said is a fraud problem here in the state.
Faulkingham said the vice president coming to Maine highlighted the issue.
"When you have the vice president, giving attention to an issue, then you know that you have basically the attention of the federal government finally. And he specifically came to the state of Maine to focus on this. So we knew that some action was being taken," Faulkingham said.

title: Boothbay Harbor Rotary Club
text:
Last week our program speakers were Kay Wilder and Connie Hartley of the Boothbay Region Historical Society (BRHS). Kay reviewed that the mission of the BRHS is to collect, preserve, and promote interest in the history of the Boothbay region through research, exhibits, and programs. The society is a non-profit membership 501(c)(3) organization.
The BRHS was founded in 1967 by local interested residents and then in 1984, it moved to its present location at the Elizabeth F. Reed house and its grounds, Fullerton Park. Originally it was called the “Monday Club” and had multiple programs, speakers, poets and even covered political issues for a while. In 1984 the society was given and moved into the Reed House.
BRHS has traditionally represented the towns of Boothbay, Boothbay Harbor, and to some extent Southport. Today, Southport is also well represented with its own museum. In addition to ongoing exhibits and collections of artifacts, photographs, and historical and genealogical documents, the society offers programs of local interest throughout the year. The society maintains an extensive archive of primary and secondary materials to help visitors and researchers explore their fields of interest. In addition, the society is a museum with a large collection of artifacts of local historical importance.
The BRHS is governed by a volunteer board of trustees assisted by administrative staff and other volunteers. The society’s mission is financially supported by membership dues, donations, and fundraising events. Barbara Rumsey, a volunteer from the 1980s, became a talented curator and director creating catalogue systems and the beginnings of the current system.
Connie then reviewed the outreach aspects of the BRHS. She reminded us that if you have not ever visited the society it needs to be high on your list of must do’s and admission is free! They will be celebrating their 60th anniversary next year. Currently they have an exhibit that connects our nation’s 250-year celebration looking at Boothbay Harbor and US Navy history. Their “Footbridge” celebration is upcoming as well as the “Holiday Open House” with decorations, raffles and much energizing fun!
President Jim Herbold led our meeting in which Laurie Zimmeli and Barb Thornton once again provided an update on Rotary Barn donations and sales. As fall donations have been especially generous we invited Habitat for Humanity’s ReStore to share in the bounty of furniture & building supplies.
This Thursday we look forward to a spellbinding program about Boothbay Harbor ghosts by Cheryl Reif from American Ghost Walks. Some members of the Interact Club will be joining us too. Come one and come all! It's going to be a fun, spooky evening. We’ll need to set up a few more tables. Come early, around 4:30 to do a bit of decorating and table wrangling.
Then, on Saturday the 31st, Halloween, we're meeting living, breathing ghosts and goblins at the Boothbay Railway Village Spooktacular from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. We're setting up a table, greeting our neighbors and bribing the ghosts and goblins with candy. Contact Conxa if you can help. It will be a fun time. Then, Irene is meeting more ghosts and goblins at the Trunk or Treat at the Opera House – the final stop on the annual Halloween Parade. Let Irene know if you want to be amazed and spooked by all the costumes and Halloween spirit.
The Rotary Barn is still open every Saturday from 8:30 to 11 a.m. The official closing for the season is Dec. 12, barring a big storm or power outage.
Interested in the work and fun of Rotary? Join us every Thursday at our clubhouse, 66 Montgomery Road, Boothbay Harbor at 6 p.m. for dinner and a program. You'll be glad you did.

title: N.H. man charged in Maine construction zone hit-and-run
text:
New Hampshire man charged in Maine hit-and-run in I-95 construction zone
A worker was seriously injured in the Oct. 14 crash on Interstate 95 north in Pittsfield
New Hampshire man charged in Maine hit-and-run in I-95 construction zone
A worker was seriously injured in the Oct. 14 crash on Interstate 95 north in Pittsfield
Maine State Police officials announced Wednesday that a New Hampshire man has been charged in connection with a hit-and-run crash that happened in a construction zone on Interstate 95 in Pittsfield two weeks ago and left a worker seriously injured.
Jonathan McDonald, 22, of Laconia, was issued a summons to appear in court on the following charges, according to state police:
- Accidents involving death or personal injury (Class D)
- Driving to endanger (Class E)
- Accident reports (Class E)
The crash happened at about 8:17 a.m. on Oct. 14, near mile marker 150 on I-95 northbound.
Investigators said a light-colored pickup truck, which was towing a black dump trailer, struck a concrete Jersey barrier on the right side of the roadway, causing an orange construction barrel to hit a Northeast Construction worker in the construction zone.
Richard Smart, 56, of Westfield, was identified as the injured worker. He was transported to Northern Light Sebasticook Valley Hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. State police said Smart has since been released from the hospital.
Officials said the pickup truck did not stop and continued driving north on the interstate. Investigators believe the driver of the truck, later identified as McDonald, was aware of the crash, as witnesses reported seeing him turn around in his vehicle as the crash occurred before speeding away.
State police shared a photo of the suspect vehicle on Oct. 21 and two days later, announced that they had identified the driver involved in the crash. Authorities did not, however, publicly share McDonald's name at the time of the Oct. 23 announcement.
Maine State Police officials said they would like to thank the members of the public who came forward with information and shared tips that helped investigators identify the suspect.
