title: Presque Isle elementary unveils attendance-based book vending machine
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Elementary students in Presque Isle can earn free books through new book vending machines that reward good attendance.
Pine Street Elementary held an assembly Tuesday to unveil their machine and explain to students how they can earn books.
Attendance at Pine Street
Bill Guerrette, the Principal of Pine Street Elementary, said the school has an issue with attendance.
“We have an issue at Pine Street with truancy, and truancy are kids who miss 10% of the school year and it could be for any reason. It could be a family vacation, could be sickness, could be whatever but it’s 10%. So, in 181 days it’s about 18 days of school and we were about at 33% of our kids were missing at least that much school. So, we were looking at a way that we could kind of promote attendance, promote literacy, and doing things as a family. And so, we thought the book vending machine would be a good way to do that,” Guerrette said.
The hope is that a free book will give students one more reason to come to school every day.
How students earn books
Students who meet the attendance criteria each month earn a token to spend on a book.
“I think it will make an impact. I think they’re excited about it and it will just be our job as adults to kind of sustain that excitement,” said Guerrette. “Each month we are going to check with attendance records to see who’s been here at least 90% of the time and all of those kids will get a token for the month that they’ll get a chance to spend. So, we could be spending up to close to 200 tokens a month if attendance is really good. So, we’ve got to be prepared for that and have books ready to go.”
Donations fund machines and books
School officials reached out for donations toward the project. Presque Isle’s Kiwanis Club purchased the machines, and other businesses and organizations donated money and books to fill them.
Skyway Elementary also received donations toward a machine.
Students pick first books
Several students at Pine Street Elementary picked out books from the machine during the unveiling.
Walter Martinez Sanchez, a first grader at Pine Street Elementary, said the experience felt “good.”
Mary Stevens, another first grader, said: “It was cool. It’s about a lot of books.”

title: The science behind Jalen Hurts’ blood clot diagnosis is more complicated than it sounds
text:
The science behind Jalen Hurts’ controversial blood clot diagnosis is more complicated than it sounds
The Philadelphia Eagles quarterback played with a “superficial” blood clot that turned into something much more serious. Where did things go wrong?
The science behind Jalen Hurts’ controversial blood clot diagnosis is more complicated than it sounds
The Philadelphia Eagles quarterback played with a “superficial” blood clot that turned into something much more serious. Where did things go wrong?
Ever since it was announced that Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts’ season was over due to a blood clot diagnosis, everybody has developed an opinion on how the situation could have been handled better. It turns out that it’s more complex than fans might jump to believe.
Over the weekend, it was announced that the NFL and the NFL Players Association would be launching a review of how the diagnosis was handled, after the NFLPA made a call for an investigation last week.
Hurts was sidelined after a blood clot in his left calf traveled to his lungs. The Eagles announced that Hurts had “deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli,” a condition that required blood thinners as part of the treatment. Hurts cannot participate in any “football activities” until he is no longer on them.
The issue at hand is the timeline of the diagnosis. Initially, after Hurts suffered a “cleating” injury in his calf on Oct. 4 in a game against the Los Angeles Rams, doctors in London — where the Eagles were set to play the Jacksonville Jaguars on Oct. 11 — performed an ultrasound and diagnosed Hurts with “superficial vein thrombosis.” Despite the clotting, he went on to play against the Jaguars, completing 21 of 40 passes for 220 yards and one touchdown.
It was only after he returned home to the United States that the clot’s movement was discovered, and he was re-diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis.
The distinction is important. Superficial vein thrombosis involves clots in veins close to the skin surface that pose minimal risk of traveling to the lungs, but deep vein thrombosis poses a far greater risk of a pulmonary embolism, which could be life-threatening.
The question at the core of this uproar is whether doctors in London missed some key signs from the ultrasound in making the initial diagnosis, allowing Hurts to play in a game he wouldn’t have played in if there had been a DVT diagnosis, or whether his condition simply worsened after that initial ultrasound.
Dr. Chuck Dinerstein, a vascular surgeon, published a piece for the American Council on Science and Health before the NFL and NFLPA made their decision to review the diagnosis. In it, he addressed the diagnosis question and the blame game that immediately followed, stressing that “as a vascular surgeon, I know a bad outcome doesn't necessarily mean someone made a bad call."
“Taking all the opinions into account,” Dinerstein says, “the NFL and the Eagles left one question unanswered: what the exact findings were at the time of the initial venous ultrasound.”
“Our description of the leg veins contains an oddity,” he notes. “The superficial femoral vein is, in fact, deep and a source of pulmonary emboli. For the most part, we have changed the language used to describe these veins as the femoral vein, but I am not sure whether the British report used that language, nor do I know whether the treating physician reviewed the ultrasound with the radiologist.”
To date, we do not have this sensitive medical information. Hurts’ medical records, Dinerstein notes, are “his to disclose, not ours to demand.” The forthcoming NFL and NFLPA review may, however, provide greater clarity on that front.
It may also answer another question, namely if those initially identified superficial clots “went on to propagate deeper clots that ultimately were the source of his pulmonary embolisms.”
Dinerstein cites the CALISTO study, an abbreviation for Comparison of Arixtra in Lower Limb Superficial Vein Thrombosis With Placebo, which examined the efficacy of anticoagulants vs. placebos in cases of superficial venous clots. Comparing the effects of anticoagulants vs. placebos, the study found “pulmonary embolism in 0% versus 0.3%” and “deep-vein thrombosis in 0.2% versus 1.2%.”
“With these facts in hand,” Dinerstein notes, “physicians presumably counseled Mr. Hurts.”
No one, he argues, would have let Hurts play football while on an anticoagulant, due to the risk of a “serious bleed.” So, he suggests, a decision was made regarding whether Hurts could continue to play in spite of the “small risk” of developing DVT or a pulmonary embolism. “That is a judgment call, and only Mr. Hurts and his physicians can tell us about that conversation.”
Dinerstein concluded by noting the importance of differentiating between accountability and blame. When a complication like Hurts’ arises, “it is both tempting and necessary to work backward from the outcome to identify the moment someone might have made a mistake. But that is not how medical decisions are made.”
“Shared medical decision-making does not guarantee a good outcome,” he argued. "It provides a framework for choosing among imperfect options.”
Accountability, he suggests, “requires knowing what those decisions were and the circumstances in which they were made.” Perhaps this new review may shed light on just how those decisions were made.

title: Alvin K. Hellerstein, a federal judge who handled Trump, Maduro and 9/11 cases, dies at 92
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Alvin K. Hellerstein, a Manhattan federal judge who presided over matters involving President Donald Trump, former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and the 9/11 attacks during nearly three decades on the bench, has died. He was 92.
Hellerstein died Wednesday, according to Edward Friedland, district executive for the Southern District of New York federal courts. No cause of death was immediately provided.
Only two weeks ago, Hellerstein presided over a Manhattan hearing in the ongoing narco-terrorism conspiracy prosecution of Maduro, who was captured earlier this year in a surprise raid.
President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, appointed Hellerstein to the federal bench in 1998. He was a district judge until he moved to senior status in 2011. Before that, Hellerstein served in the U.S. Army Judge Advocate General’s Corps and was a Manhattan litigator.
In the aftermath of the 2001 terror attack on the World Trade Center, Hellerstein presided over dozens of wrongful death, injury and property damage lawsuits — a two-decade-long effort that shaped his legacy on the bench.
Some of the judge’s former clients died in the attack and, lawyers say, he showed great empathy to victims and their families, meeting with them for hours in his chambers and rejecting what he felt were low-ball settlement offers.
Others were dismayed when, in 2008, Hellerstein ended an effort to force New York City government to keep searching for human remains in debris moved from ground zero to a Staten Island landfill.
Hellerstein, known for a quirky independent streak and strict discipline in his courtroom, insisted spectators wear pandemic-era masks for more than two years after other judges stopped the practice.
In August, in one of his last significant rulings, Hellerstein again spurned Trump’s effort to erase his hush money conviction, rejecting the president’s bid to move the state court case to federal court and have it dismissed on presidential immunity grounds.
It was the third time Hellerstein denied Trump’s requests to move the case. The first time was after Trump’s March 2023 indictment; the second followed Trump’s May 2024 conviction and a subsequent U.S. Supreme Court ruling that presidents and former presidents cannot be prosecuted for official acts.
Hellerstein’s latest ruling against Trump came after an appeals court ordered him to reconsider his prior decision. The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Hellerstein erred by failing to consider “important issues relevant” to the president’s request. However, the appeals court judges said they “express no view” on how Hellerstein should rule.
In 2020, Hellerstein ordered Trump’s estranged former lawyer and fixer Michael Cohen released from prison after the Justice Department revoked his home confinement to thwart his efforts to publish a book or talk to the media. The government’s action, he ruled, was retaliatory and a First Amendment violation.
In 2015, Hellerstein made headlines when he ordered a New York City cable company to pay a Texas woman $229,500 for flooding her phone with 153 robocalls.

Related video above: 'CPR in progress': Dispatch audio in Hayden Panettiere's death
Panettiere, 36, died Aug. 16, 2026, in an apartment at Judson Mill Lofts in Greenville, according to the coroner's office and police.
Greenville Police Department said Wednesday that based on the coroner's determination and the investigation, Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental.
The department said it has concluded its investigation with no charges filed.
The Greenville County Coroner's Office released the final report on her death last month.
It said, "The cause of death has been ruled as toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol, and Quetiapine. The manner of death has been ruled an accident."
It also said, "No signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to the death."
What's next?
As previously reported by sister station WYFF, the Drug Enforcement Administration is also assisting in the investigation.
In our previous reporting from Sept. 22, the DEA provided the following statement:
"When requested by state or local authorities, and when appropriate based on the circumstances, DEA may provide investigative or technical assistance in drug-related death investigations. These cases are complex and take time to develop. To protect the integrity of ongoing investigative work, DEA does not comment on specific investigations."
WYFF reached out to the DEA on Wednesday after the Greenville Police Department announced its case was closed. We will update this story when they come back.

title: Disinformation videos, likely from Russia, are exploiting real people to malign Senate candidates
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Social media videos believed to be produced with artificial intelligence and linked to Russia are misusing real people’s names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in the final stretch of midterm voting.
One of the targets is Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio. The video, which appears to include some AI manipulation, depicts a newscast and includes pictures of Haya Akbik, who interned for Brown several years ago, and other former staff members.
It was appalling to Akbik, who told The Associated Press that any claims attributed to her in the clip are “completely made up.”
“It’s my name, it’s my reputation, making this allegation, and it’s just completely false,” she said. “And it harms the senator, someone else, in the process. So, it’s just messed up.”
The videos demonstrate how foreign adversaries continue to use a familiar playbook to try to influence American voters who are deciding which party controls Congress next year. The threat could be magnified with AI, a powerful tool for fabricating damaging information that can sometimes appear very real.
Another target is James Talarico, who is running against Republican Ken Paxton for a Senate seat in Texas. The video, also believed to include some AI manipulation, is framed as a direct-to-camera confessional from a former student of Talarico.
“The most powerful people in the world know they can’t beat James Talarico with the truth, so they’re slandering him with AI deepfakes, foreign bots, and conspiracy theories to protect their broken, corrupt political system,” Talarico spokesperson JT Ennis said in a statement.
The social media company X has taken down the initial posts that shared the videos and suspended the users for violating the platform’s rules. However, copies could still be found online Tuesday — some with hundreds of shares — demonstrating how difficult it can be to contain disinformation that can proliferate in the final days of an election.
Experts see a resemblance to Russian clips from 2024
The videos resemble clips from a Russian network known as Storm-1516 that targeted former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris and her running mate, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, two years ago.
The new ones bear similar hallmarks and are likely products of the same network, according to Clemson University professor and media forensics expert Darren Linvill. He found that the accounts that shared recent material had also shared former content from Storm-1516.
The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the past, it has denied interfering in U.S. elections.
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has publicly identified some videos as Russian disinformation in past election cycles, also didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Hany Farid, a Dartmouth College professor who studies artificial intelligence deepfakes, said his analyses showed that videos targeting Brown and Talarico were likely either generated or manipulated using the technology.
He noted the video targeting Brown is a “fairly low-tech fake.” The other one, targeting Talarico, is likely generated by AI and “it is consistent with previous disinformation campaigns released close to Election Day,” Farid said.
Akbik said the video featuring her shows the importance of Congress regulating “AI slop on the internet.”
“This is so damaging,” she said.

title: Watch: Winthrop cross country is Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches, fans and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Take some veteran talent that’s been there and done that, add a top-tier coach, then throw in a freshman phenom and other solid youngsters, and you have a recipe for success.
The Winthrop boys cross country team has successfully defended its Mountain Valley Conference and Class C South titles. For that, the Ramblers are the Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week.
Winthrop was expected to be in the championship mix again this fall. Alfie Cognata, the MVC and C South runner-up in 2025, was returning for coach Ed Van Tassel’s squad. So were Sam St. Germain, Michael Van Tassel and Gianni Haefele, the Ramblers’ 3-5 runners from last season.
As if those returners weren’t enough, the Ramblers added a top freshman, Sawyer Wess. He has jockeyed with Cognata for Winthrop’s top-runner status throughout the year, starting with winning the season-opening race at Maranacook. He placed third on Saturday at the South regional.
“Just being on a championship team as a freshman means a lot to me,” Wess said. “I think this is the best boys team that Winthrop cross country has ever had, and I think that us all being together the same year is just something we have to cherish. We’ve taken all the small moments (and not taken them) for granted.”
At MVCs two weeks ago, Winthrop claimed five of the top-10 spots, scoring 30 points to finish 42 clear of runner-up Maranacook. Van Tassel was named MVC Boys Coach of the Year at the meet. A larger regional field over the weekend didn’t hinder the Ramblers, who placed five in the top 14 to beat the Black Bears by 62 points.
A state title this Saturday at Cony High School would be the second in program history (2007). The Ramblers’ biggest challenger appears to be Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian Academy, which took the North title in Belfast and topped Winthrop for the state crown a year ago.
“They’re looking at us in the results, we’re looking at them in the results, and we’re kind of figuring things out,” Van Tassel said. “Really, our focus is on the process. … We’re going to frame things in a way that, when we leave Cony, we know we did what we wanted to do, and the results will certainly stand by themselves.”

title: Supporting the reelection of Sally Cluchey in House District 52
text:
Whenever I travel around our amazing state – but especially now when the forests are ablaze with color — I am reminded of how important Maine’s wild lands and waters are to our quality of life, our economy, our well-being and our future.
That is one of the several reasons I am voting to re-elect Sally Cluchey as state representative for House District 52 (Bowdoin, Bowdoinham, Richmond).
Sally shares my conservation values. She knows how important it is to protect our wild places and wild species. And she understands what is required to do so. Earlier this year, she was even recognized as a “wildlife champion” by Maine Audubon.

title: Seahawks move on with 4-0 win over Waynflete
text:
Junior Moriah Smith scored one goal and had two assists as the Boothbay Region Seahawks defeated the visiting Waynflete Flyers, 4-0, in the Class C South quarterfinal on Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Smith’s assists were to sophomore Lilly Cowing, who scored goals in the first quarter at the 12:30 mark and one in the third quarter at 8:40. Smith scored her goal in the third quarter off an assist from freshman Meabh Hennessey at 6:52.
Boothbay’s second goal came early in the second quarter. After a corner entry, junior Arabella Hodgdon took a pass from junior Izzy Andreasen and sent the ball into the goal at the 13:32 mark.
The Seahawks, now 11-4, controlled the game most of the time, as Wayflete only managed a steady offense in the first quarter with two shots on goal. Boothbay had seven corners to Waynflete’s one in the game. Waynflete, seeded #5, finishes its season at 10-5. The shutout win was Boothbay's seventh of the season.
With the win, the #4 Seahawks will face the Winthrop/Maranacook Ramblers in the semifinal – Update: BRHS Athletic Director Allan Crocker has announced that the semifinal will be played in Winthrop on their turf field (at the former high school) on Saturday, Oct. 31 at 1 p.m. The #1 Ramblers defeated #8 Oak Hill, 3-0, on Tuesday. It will be the third straight year the Seahawks and Ramblers face off in the playoffs, with the Ramblers winning 1-0 at BRHS last year in the semifinal and 7-1 in a quarterfinal game at Winthrop in 2024.
On Sept. 30, the teams battled for 60 minutes at Perkins Field before the Ramblers got a goal off a corner entry with no time remaining and won, 2-1.

title: TV personality Ernie Johnson says this will be final season on 'Inside the NBA'
text:
Longtime TV personality Ernie Johnson says this will be final season on 'Inside the NBA'
Ernie Johnson, a longtime television personality and sportscaster, announced Wednesday that this will be his final season hosting "Inside the NBA."
Related video above | Broadcaster Ernie Johnson returns to hometown Milwaukee
Johnson has hosted the popular basketball program since 1990, one year after it premiered. In a social media video, Johnson said it was his decision to step away.
"It's just time," he said.
Johnson explained that long hours prepping for the show, along with some recent health complications, including recovering from a heart bypass surgery 14 months ago, contributed to his decision. He added that he wants to spend more time with family.
"Going through (heart surgery) has made me treasure even more every second with my amazing wife of 44 years, Cheryl Ann, and being poppy to our five grandchildren," Johnson said. "So I just want to slow down a bit. Spend more time enjoying that."
Johnson made clear that he wasn't retiring entirely. He said he plans to keep covering "March Madness and other projects" and focus more on his new production company.
Several former players have appeared on "Inside the NBA" alongside Johnson over the years. However, Johnson, Shaquille O'Neal, Charles Barkley, and Kenny Smith have become the show's iconic panel.

title: Rockport gets another funding boost for harbor upgrades
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Rockport Harbor improvement project has secured another $698,750 to shore up its working waterfront against coastal storms and strengthen its safety and long-term sustainability.
The latest funding, from the U.S. Department of Transportation Maritime Administration’s Port Infrastructure Development Program, will support the town’s East Side Working Waterfront Resilience Project, according to a news release. The project was previously awarded $4 million.
The project stems from harbor flooding during major storm events over the past couple of years, necessitating repeated repairs to keep the harbor safe and accessible for commercial and public use, the town said.
Rockport’s working waterfront includes fisheries, commercial marine services and boat builders. Public uses include the Rockport Boat Club and public facilities at Marine Park, including picnic and event areas, a boat ramp and historical exhibits.
Previous awards
In 2024, Rockport secured a $2 million state resilience grant through a one-time funding opportunity aimed at helping coastal communities protect vulnerable properties from storm damage. The award covered a significant portion of construction costs but required the town to identify additional funding sources for remaining project expenses.
Since receiving the initial award, town staff have pursued numerous grant opportunities to close the funding gap. That resulted in an additional $2 million grant, through the Maine Department of Transportation’s Working Waterfront Infrastructure Fund, to cover remaining project costs, including design, engineering and construction activities.
“By securing these grant dollars, the town can advance a critical infrastructure project without relying on local taxpayers to fund the full cost,” Jon Duke, town manager, said in a social media post earlier this year. “The project will strengthen the harbor’s resilience, support commercial marine activity and preserve this important community asset for generations to come.”
Raising and reinforcing
Sea wall improvements include raising site elevations by around two feet to reduce flooding impacts. Repairs and structural reinforcements will be made to the existing bulkhead and seawall. Sub-grade soils will be stabilized and damaged pavement restored.
To mitigate further environmental risk, the Main Street sewer pump station will be improved to match the final site elevation, an emergency generator will be installed at the Main Street pump station to reduce the risk of overboard discharge and secondary containment for the harbor diesel fuel tank will be built.
Earthwork will be built to prepare for a new fisherman’s pier and site lighting will be upgraded to improve operational safety. A new pedestrian pathway with landscaping improvements is planned.
Design and engineering services have been awarded through a competitive request for proposals process to Woodard & Curran, a Portland-based engineering firm.
The town will next solicit construction bids and select a contractor.

title: Lincoln County Historical Association’s forum series highlights local art history and more
text:
The Lincoln County Historical Association announced its fall 2026 series of online talks for members, featuring presentations on local art history, colonial land claims, and Maine’s musical traditions.
LCHA Members Forums connect members with presenters who have ties to the organization or whose topics explore subjects close to home. While the forums are designed as a special benefit of membership, the public is welcome to join LCHA and participate. Individual memberships begin at $25.
The this year’s series features three presentations, each offering a fresh perspective on a distinctive aspect of Maine’s history and cultural heritage.
The series began on Oct. 29 covering historical association founder Mildred G. Burrage’s historical maps.
It continues on Thursday, Nov. 5, at 5:30 p.m. with forester, economist and writer Lloyd Irland turning the focus back to the Colonial era to examine Sir Ferdinando Gorges, the Kennebec Proprietors, and the history of Colonial land grant claims.
The series concludes on Thursday, Nov. 12, at 6 p.m. with musician and educator Kelley Doore, who will explore the question “What are Maine’s musical traditions?” The presentation will examine the regional music traditions that have helped shape Maine’s cultural identity.
Each presentation brings an expert perspective to a distinctive facet of local history, offering members an opportunity to learn more about the people, events, and traditions that have shaped the region.
Participation is free, but registration is required. For more information and to register, visit lincolncountyhistory.org/events.
Those who are not yet members can learn more about membership and join LCHA at lincolncountyhistory.org/get-involved.

title: Enjoy Sunshine Today, Then Warm Up Big Time Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A warm front approaching from the Great Lakes Region will bring us a bit more cloudiness today. We’ll still see a good deal of sunshine too with partly to mostly sunny skies expected. Temperatures will warm to seasonable levels this afternoon with highs in the mid-40s to low 50s. Skies will be clear to partly cloudy tonight. It’ll be chilly tonight but not as cold as last night with lows in the 30s thanks to warmer air moving into the mid-levels of the atmosphere.
High pressure will slide to our south for Thursday... setting us up with a warmer west/southwest flow which will push temperatures well above average Thursday afternoon. Thursday looks awesome with partly to mostly sunny skies and high temperatures in the upper 50s to around 60° along the coast and low to mid-60s elsewhere. A cold front will cross the state Thursday night into Friday. This front will also be lacking any decent moisture and therefore shower chances will be minimal at best. All locales will have a chance for a few showers Thursday night followed by isolated shower chances... mainly across the north on Friday. Otherwise expect a mix of sun and clouds on Friday with high temperatures in the mid-50s to low 60s. Cooler air will move in behind the cold front later in the day Friday... setting us up with cooler weather for the weekend. High pressure will bring us lots of sunshine Saturday with highs in the 40s to around 50°. Sunday looks great too with mostly sunny skies and slightly warmer temperatures with highs in the upper 40s to low 50s. At this point... it looks like our mainly dry and storm-free weather pattern continues through much of next week. We may see some showers around on Wednesday otherwise much of the week looks dry with the potential for a larger storm as we approach next weekend. Stay tuned for updates on that.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly sunny. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s. Light and variable wind.
Tonight: Clear to partly cloudy. Lows mainly in the 30s. A few upper 20s possible across the north. Light southwest wind.
Thursday: Partly to mostly sunny and warmer. Highs in the upper 50s to mid-60s. West/southwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Friday: Mix of sun and clouds. Isolated showers possible... mainly across the north. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s.
Saturday: Mostly sunny and cooler. Highs in the 40s to around 50°.
Sunday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the upper 40s to low 50s.

title: Election candidates should take a look at USPS
text:
During this election season, everyone has concerns: healthcare, Social Security benefits, the economy and ICE activity. Those are important topics and concerns for everyone in the state and country. I would like to add the concern of the United States Postal Service.
The prices keep going up for the standard first-class stamp, while the delivery of first-class mail service continues to go down.
I can’t believe that a first-class piece of mail would take 13 days to be delivered from New York. In this case, there were two pieces of mail that were sent at the same time, from the same place. The other piece was delivered within four days. Where was the other piece for the extra nine days?
Instead of these candidates spitting in each other’s eye every five minutes on TV with campaign ads, how about them telling us what they are going to do about this mess we have, now, with the Postal Service? The complaints are overwhelming and no one seems to want to take care of the problem.
How about first going back to the way things use to be done? If the mail was handled the old way, I’m sure people wouldn’t be so upset when the price of postage increases.
Cleon M. Nelson Jr.
Scarborough

title: Officials working to expand foster care for children in America, here’s how
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Kids sleeping in shelters, bussed between hotels, and overnights in office buildings. That’s the reality for many foster children in America.
For every 100 children in foster care, federal data shows that only 57 licenses homes are available.
In an effort to close that gap, the federal government launched a campaign in November 2025 called “A Home for Every Child.”
“When we launched this, we offered states the choice: if they joined the Home for Every Child campaign, they would get administrative relief,” said Alex Adams, assistant secretary for the administration for children and families. “We would get them out of mountains of paperwork so that they could spend more time focused on things that actually improve child welfare outcomes. They would have more time working with kids, more time working with families.
Since then, the idea to reinvent systems that recruit and retain foster families has gained nationwide momentum.
Millions of dollars in cash rewards are available to the state, territory, or tribal agency with the greatest improvement of its ratio of children to foster homes.
All 50 states, along with Washington D.C. and Puerto Rico, have signed up for the challenge. It will run until September 2027.
One of the first states to jump in was Tennessee. In total, the state would need more than 3,000 foster families to meet the goal set forth by the federal government.
But state leaders say a new approach is already working to encourage families to say yes to fostering.
Finding families in Tennessee
Kenni and Blake Cavalier are one family that opened up their home and their hearts, helping twin toddlers learn what it means to feel loved and feel safe.
“We have a home. We have stability and that right there is what these kids need,” said Blake. “So, I think that kind of flipped a switch where we’re like, we have to do it.”
After lots of prayer and conversation with other foster parents, the Cavaliers said they knew they had to step up and be part of the solution to Tennessee’s critical need for foster families.
“Something that I think really hit us was just like, we may have these excuses or these fears even, but that fear doesn’t compare to like the fear this child is probably in right now,” explained Kenni.
The state’s latest numbers show Tennessee needs an additional 3,081 foster families to meet the new federal initiative. The program seeks to establish a one-to-one ratio — one foster home for every child in foster care.
Lindsay Coleman, executive director of statewide specialized support services, said doing that “will be a challenge.”
“I think it’ll take some time. It’ll take some adjustments,” Coleman said. “But I think with the things we have in place, with continued prevention, with our new permanency team that’s looking at children trying to exit kids out of custody who don’t need to be in foster care any longer, and then with our recruitment and support efforts, I think we can get there.”
The state has developed a four-pronged plan to increase the number of foster care homes and support families:
- Prevention
  - Keeping families together and providing support services so children don’t enter foster care
- Recruitment
  - Using technology to determine where the biggest needs are for children, then heavily recruit in those areas
- Retention
  - Supporting foster families with teams that provide hands-on community support
- Transition
  - Support for youth aging out of foster care.
Coleman said the state’s plan is working, with this year’s recent quarter showing a 7% increase in foster families.
“What’s your talent? What’s your skill? What do you have to offer? What do you enjoy doing, hobbies, interests, and we can connect that to foster care,” said Tennessee Kids Belong Child Welfare Director Tiffany Kelly.
Kelly said the question for all Tennesseans right now is, “What’s your yes?”
She explained that not everyone can foster, but everyone can help, and everyone’s yes may look different — from mowing lawns to babysitting, helping with meals, laundry and more.
“All those yeses matter, and all those yeses mean that a family can really take the next step of pouring into the kids and take that time to build attachment and healing and carry the journey a little lighter,” said Kelly.
“Seeing them develop, start walking, start smiling, start talking, running around. And being able to look at them and be like, we’re giving them a safe place,” said Blake. “We’re seeing them have fun and be loved. And I think that’s really rewarding.”
Coleman said that “the community needs to know the need.”
“I think that there are lots of folks out there who are interested and willing to care for children. I just don’t think they understand or know what the need is,” said Coleman. “And so this story, hopefully, will help viewers know that we have this need for foster families and we would love for families to sign up. ...I’ve never met a foster parent who’s regretted their decision.”
Tennessee Kids Belong has a Foster-Friendly app that helps support foster families.
Businesses can sign up to give foster families discounts.
“It’s very easy for a business to sign up to be featured on the app. Our registration form takes less than five minutes for a business to sign up,” said Emily Barnes, Tennessee Kids Belong Foster Friendly Business Manager.
How to help
You don’t need to commit to being a foster parent to help children in need. State agencies and nonprofits often have volunteer opportunities available.
You can also advocate for foster children in the judicial system by becoming a court-appointed special advocate volunteer.
CASA volunteers are appointed by judges to act in the best interest of a child during the legal process of foster care.
Volunteers work with child welfare professionals, educators, and social service providers to ensure judges have all the information they need to make the most well-informed decision for each child.

title: ‘Pretty low individual’: Man scammed by fake life insurance agent shortly after sister’s death
text:
CORINTH, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) — A Mississippi man says he was scammed shortly after the death of his sister.
According to Tim Williams, he was called by a woman who identified herself as the life insurance agent for his sister, Stephanie Jeanine Williams Machado.
The woman gave him account numbers and policy numbers, and requested $1,375 for the insurance company to release payment to the Corinthian Funeral Home.
Williams said he entered a three-way phone call with the woman and the funeral home, and that it all seemed to be legitimate.
All the money he had available at the time was $620, and the woman told him to send it.
When Williams asked how the woman would like the funds sent, she said to get it to her however was easiest, either by going to the insurance office or via the Cash App.
Williams said he sent the money to his nephew, who then sent it through the app.
However, Williams said the funeral home told him it never received payment, so he looked up the number and found that it belonged to a man who lived in Alabama.
The number did not belong to the woman who spoke to him or match the name on the Cash App account.
“When you’re already in a bad time in your life ... losing your loved one. Then for somebody to do this on top of that takes a pretty low individual to go to that extent,” Williams said.
Williams said that anyone who suddenly loses a loved one should make sure to double-check and triple-check that everything is real.

title: Augusta’s Gretchen Livingston is Teacher of the Year
text:
The Maine Department of Education (DOE) is excited to announce Augusta School Department Spanish teacher Gretchen Livingston as the 2027 Maine Teacher of the Year. On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Livingston celebrated this award with fellow Augusta educators and students during a surprise ceremony in the Viles Auditorium, at Cony Middle and High School.
“As the daughter of a longtime English teacher and as someone who raised five Maine public school students, I know firsthand the impact a teacher can have on a child’s future. Throughout her 25 years teaching middle and high school students in Maine, Gretchen Livingston has helped prepare countless students for bright futures. I congratulate Gretchen on the tremendous honor of being named Maine’s 2027 Teacher of the Year and thank her for her unwavering dedication to Maine’s students,” said Governor Janet Mills.
Hundreds of educators across the state were nominated for the 2027 Maine Teacher of the Year process. In May, Livingston was selected as the 2026 Kennebec County Teacher of the Year, alongside 15 other County Teachers of the Year. In August, Livingston became one of four state finalists before she was ultimately named 2027 Maine Teacher of the Year.
“Language is a superpower. Language is communication. Language is identity and culture. Multilingualism is already part of our classrooms, our communities, and our state. The future I imagine for Maine is one where every student hears their language respected, every child learns the history of the first peoples of this land, multilingual students are recognized for the gifts they bring, and every graduate leaves school prepared to communicate across cultures. Language is not a barrier – it is an asset and a bridge. It builds empathy, opens doors, and helps us see how our differences make our schools, communities, and world stronger,” said Gretchen Livingston, 2027 Maine Teacher of the Year.
With 25 years of experience teaching Spanish at the middle and high school levels in Maine, Gretchen Livingston is dedicated to helping students develop language proficiency, intercultural understanding, and a deeper connection to the world around them.
She teaches Spanish Levels 1 – 6 for students in grades 8 – 12 at Cony Middle and High School, in Augusta, where she has served as World Language Department chairman since 2014 and coordinates the district’s Seal of Biliteracy program.
Livingston is recognized for her student-centered, culturally responsive approach to teaching, which incorporates authentic communication, project-based learning, and service-learning experiences.
Beyond the classroom, she is a leader in curriculum innovation and student engagement, having led eight service-learning trips to Guatemala in partnership with Safe Passage and Niños de Guatemala, with a ninth trip in the planning stages. She also founded the Cony girls lacrosse team in 2006 and continues to coach, reflecting her commitment to empowering students as confident communicators, compassionate global citizens, and engaged members of their communities.
“Gretchen Livingston is an inspiration to students,” Pender Makin, Commissioner of the Maine Department of Education, said. “We are proud to be able to elevate and share the incredible work she has done not only with language development but also with creating a community of sharing and connectedness.”
The Maine Teacher of the Year Program is a year-long process that involves educator portfolio and resume submissions, interviews, oral presentations, and classroom visits made by a selection panel comprised of Maine State Board of Education members, school administrators, Maine DOE staff, legacy Maine Teachers of the Year, and Maine business partners.
As 2026 Maine Teacher of the Year, Livingston will spend her year of service advocating for students and teachers and speaking about the importance of education in preparing Maine’s next generation of leaders for the future. She will also represent Maine in the National Teacher of the Year program.
“Gretchen isn’t just a Teacher of the Year. Her influence has been felt across her entire career,” said Mike Tracy, superintendent of the Augusta School Department. “I taught alongside her 20 years ago, and she was this good then, so the honor comes as no surprise to those of us here in Augusta. Her positive impact on students and the whole school community has been evident for decades. We couldn’t be prouder of her!”

title: ‘She is forever my hero’: 5th-grader’s quick thinking helps save bus driver
text:
CEDAR RAPIDS, Iowa (KGAN) - An Iowa fifth grader’s quick thinking helped save a bus driver who was struggling to breathe.
And it was all caught on camera.
It started as a routine ride home from Viola Gibson Elementary School, until bus driver Christine Houston said a strong cologne scent set off a coughing fit, and her breathing kept getting worse.
“It just kept progressively getting worse, and I kept going to at least two to three stops before I realized I can’t go anymore,” Houston said.
Fifth grader Bella Scott says she knew something was wrong and decided she had to do something.
“She was wheezing. She was struggling to breathe, and obviously she needed help. You can’t just watch something like that happen,” Bella Scott said.
She jumped into action and called the one person she knew could help — her dad.
Nick Scott was nearby, and at first he thought Bella just wanted more time on her phone, until he heard the fear in her voice.
“And the third time that she called, I could hear the terror in her voice, and I knew something was wrong,” Nick Scott said.
Nick Scott got on the bus and saw Houston was struggling to breathe. He called 911, then helped the students call their families and stay calm.
“She wanted to get the kids home, which I understand, but with 20 kids or so left on the bus, we couldn’t risk something happening. So I basically told her, too bad, we’re calling 911, and then you could kind of see the relief on her face,” he said.
Houston says Bella Scott did what students learned during bus safety training: call a trusted adult.
“She called the one that she knew would answer, and that was her dad,” Houston said.
Emergency responders arrived, and the bus driver got the help she needed. Cedar Rapids Schools later recognized Bella Scott for her quick actions.
“She is forever my hero, and I’ve said this from the beginning,” Houston said. “Not all heroes wear a cape. She had a cell phone with a backpack. She called her dad. And I don’t know, I, I just, I’m totally grateful for her.”
Houston says she’s always cared deeply about the students on her route, and Bella Scott’s actions showed that care goes both ways.

title: LETTERS: 99-year-old urges you to vote
text:
To the editor:
As a 99-year-old voter from Bangor, I’ve learned that one of the most important rights we have is the right to vote. Throughout my lifetime, I’ve seen how elections shape our communities, our state and our future.
That’s why I encourage every Mainer to make their voice heard this November. Whether you’re concerned about Social Security, rising costs, health care or the future you want for your family, voting is how we make those priorities known.
The good news is that older voters are engaged. A recent AARP Maine poll found that 87 percent of Mainers age 50 and older are motivated to vote this year.
No matter your age or political views, your vote matters. I’ve been voting for almost 80 years. Democracy works best when all of us participate.
Margie Higgins
Bangor

title: MaineHealth offers free CNA apprenticeship training
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MaineHealth is offering a certified nursing assistant (CNA) apprenticeship training program, providing a paid pathway for individuals interested in beginning a health care career.
The upcoming session of the six-week program begins Jan. 11, 2027 and will be held at the MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital Education Center in Damariscotta. Training takes place four to five days per week and includes classroom instruction, hands-on skills labs and clinical experience at local hospitals and long-term care facilities.
The CNA apprenticeship program is a collaborative effort between Maine Adult Education and MaineHealth. Participants are hired as CNA apprentices at either MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital or MaineHealth Pen Bay Hospital and paid during training. They are also eligible for benefits, provided they agree to a one-year work commitment following successful completion of the program.
To be considered, applicants must attend a required virtual information session via Microsoft Teams. Sessions will be held:
• Oct. 29, 6-7 p.m.
• Nov. 12, 10-11 a.m.
• Dec. 10, 10-11 a.m.
During the information sessions, attendees will learn about the application process, program requirements and next steps. They can also complete their registration for the program.
Following the session, candidates will be contacted to schedule the Comprehensive Adult Student Assessment Systems (CASAS) exam, which must be passed at a 9th-grade reading level.
To apply, candidates should visit careersatmainehealth.org and search for “CNA Apprentice” and the Damariscotta location.
For more information, contact cna@mainehealth.org or visit mainehealth.org

title: Ernie Johnson announces this will be his final season on ‘Inside The NBA’
text:
(Gray News) - Ernie Johnson announced he will be stepping down as host of “Inside the NBA” at the end of the season.
The Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer took to social media on Wednesday to explain his decision to step away, saying, “It’s just time.”
Johnson, 70, stated that he would not be retiring, but cutting back.
“This is by no means the end. It’s just a turning of the page,” Johnson said. “And I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with ‘Inside the NBA.’”
Johnson said he plans to continue to work, including covering the NCAA men’s basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports.
The six-time Sports Emmy Award winner acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years, but that isn’t the reason he’s stepping away from the show.
“I just want to slow down a bit,” he added in his social media post.
Johnson joined Turner Sports in 1989 and has hosted “Inside the NBA” since 1990. He thanked his TNT Sports and ESPN crews for their support over the years, as well as the viewers.
“I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support. And on this day, for your understanding,” Johnson said.

title: Indiana governor is urged to let death sentence proceed against man who killed 2 kids in fire
text:
A death sentence for an Indiana man who killed his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire should remain in place, the state parole board recommended Wednesday, just days before a Nov. 5 execution by lethal injection.
Jeffrey Weisheit has a right under Indiana law to seek clemency and ask for a life sentence for his murder and arson convictions. The final decision rests with Gov. Mike Braun.
“We unanimously recommend that you deny Jeffrey Weisheit’s request,” parole board chairperson Gwendolyn Horth wrote to Braun.
The board heard two days of testimony from Weisheit, lawyers, the children’s parents and first responders who were at an Evansville home in 2010 when the bodies of 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and 5-year-old Caleb Lynch were recovered from the ruins of the fire.
Alyssa’s body was in a closet. Caleb’s body was on a mattress, restrained with duct tape. A railroad flare was in his underwear and another was under his body.
“There is no excuse or explanation for what I did,” Weisheit, 50, said on Oct. 16, adding that he wants to live and improve the lives of other people in prison.
The children’s mother, Lisa Lynch, was in a relationship with him when the fire was set 16 years ago while she was at work.
Before the fire, Weisheit had his eye on an engagement ring, but the relationship with Lynch was breaking down. He quit his job, withdrew money from the bank and canceled the ring order, telling the jeweler that he would soon leave the country, said lawyer Tyler Banks of the Indiana attorney general’s office.
“Clemency is meant for those who show genuine remorse and hold true value for human life,” Lynch told the board by video. “Nothing about the murder of my children showed mercy, humanity or remorse.”
Their father, Steven Lynch, said he would accept a life sentence.
Weisheit’s lawyer, Joseph Perkovich, said Wednesday that the governor is considering a request to have him transported from prison for brain scans.
Perkovich acknowledged the “unspeakable” crimes when he spoke to the parole board on Oct. 19 but said Weisheit has a history of head injuries and mental health problems that didn’t get enough attention at his 2013 trial.
“We remain grateful for the governor’s deliberative approach to the exercise of his constitutional responsibility and unfettered authority to determine whether a reprieve or commutation should be granted here,” Perkovich said.
In its recommendation against clemency, the parole board said it considered information about Weisheit’s mental health but found it “does not greatly distinguish his situation from a vast majority of incarcerated individuals.”

title: Enter if you dare: Trails of Terror returns for another fright-filled weekend of haunted fun
text:
WATERVILLE – The scares are back and more terrifying than ever as the Alfond Youth & Community Center invites brave souls to experience the annual Trails of Terror, a spine-chilling Halloween attraction that transforms the organization’s outdoor camp trails into a horrifying journey through darkness, suspense and unexpected encounters.
Trails of Terror has become a favorite seasonal tradition for thrill-seekers from across Central Maine. Participants will venture into the woods where eerie scenes, frightening characters, and surprises around every turn create an unforgettable Halloween experience.
While Trails of Terror delivers heart-pounding thrills for those who love a good scare, the AYCC also recognizes that Halloween fun looks different for everyone. Families with younger children can enjoy Halloween Village, a festive, not-so-spooky celebration featuring candy, themed activities and family-friendly fun led by our childcare staff. Together, the two events create Halloween experiences for community members of all ages and comfort levels.
“This event is all about bringing our community together for a fun, immersive Halloween experience,” Patrick Kearns, Camp and Trails of Terror director, said. “Whether you’re a fan of the super scary or the cuter side of Halloween, we’re excited to deliver a night full of thrills, screams, smiles, giggles, and memories.”
Guests can expect:
- A haunted trail experience in the woods at McGrath Pond
- Live scare actors and themed scenes on the trails
- Surprises around every corner
- Family-friendly Halloween fun for all ages
In addition to welcoming visitors, the AYCC is also seeking volunteers to serve as scare actors and support staff. Community members who enjoy Halloween, theater, or simply making people scream with laughter are encouraged to get involved.
“Trails of Terror wouldn’t be possible without our incredible volunteers. We welcome anyone who wants to help create a memorable experience for hundreds of guests while having a great time themselves.”
Event proceeds support scholarships that help youth attend summer camp opportunities at Camp Tracy Day Camp, Specialty Camps and New England Sports Camps.
Details:
Event: Trails of Terror
Dates & Times: Oct. 30 & 31 and Nov. 1 from 6 to 9 p.m.
Location: Camp Tracy’s Lodge at McGrath Pond, 152 Camp Tracy Meadows, Oakland
Admission: Sold at the event & includes both the Trail & Halloween Village
Groups of four $40 | Adult (13+) $15 | Youth (under 12) $10 | Children under age 3 $0
Concessions: available for purchase
Volunteers needed: https://bit.ly/3TGTROd
Event details: https://bit.ly/4B0tmUQ
The Alfond Youth & Community Center is a leading nonprofit community center in Waterville, Maine, dedicated to strengthening youth, families and the greater community through impactful programs in youth development, health and wellness, education and recreation. As the only fully merged Boys & Girls Clubs and YMCA in the world, the AYCC uniquely combines the missions and resources of both movements to deliver innovative programs that empower young people, support families, and foster lifelong well-being. Serving thousands of individuals each year, the AYCC provides a welcoming, inclusive hub where children, teens and adults can learn, grow, stay active and build meaningful community connections.

title: Greely volleyball advances to first Class B state final in a decade
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
LEWISTON — Greely hasn’t advanced to a volleyball state final since 2016, so Anabelle Talley was excited when her team finally secured its return.
“This is an amazing feeling,” said Talley, a senior outside hitter. “It’s been three years now and we’ve gotten kicked out either in quarters or semis, and so I’ve never gotten to this point yet, no one on the team has, and it’s been 10 years since we’ve even gotten in states. So it’s really cool for us to be able to make an appearance now and hopefully win it.”
The Rangers defeated Messalonskee 3-1 in the Class B semifinals on Wednesday at Lewiston High School.
Talley finished with a team-high 22 kills and eight aces to pace top-seeded Greely (15-1), which faces second-seeded Washington Academy (15-1) – a 3-1 winner over York – in the Class B state final on Saturday.
HOW IT HAPPENED
Messalonskee (9-7) may have been the lower-seeded team at No. 4, but it certainly didn’t play like it.
The Eagles eked out an opening-set win, 26-24, getting the jump on a Rangers team that claimed a 3-0 head-to-head win on Oct. 3. Greely, however, rebounded to win the second set, 25-14.
In sets three and four, the Rangers had to dig out of deficits. Messalonskee held an early 7-2 lead in the third set and a 20-13 lead in the fourth. Both times, Greely chipped away and closed it out when the sets could’ve swung either way. The Rangers took set three, 25-20, and set four, 26-24.
“Espeically in a playoff game, it’s hard to get out of those ruts and it’s hard to kind of pick yourself up,” Talley said. “And so we really just needed to count on every point and we needed to push, and that’s kind of the same thing that we kept saying, was just, ‘push, push, push and find the spots.’”
UNSUNG HERO
With her team down 24-22 in the fourth set, Greely’s Reagan Dailey recorded a timely kill to keep the Rangers alive. They went on to score the next three points to clinch a trip to the state final. Dailey, a sophomore, finished with eight kills.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “It’s one game at a time, which we’ve been saying the whole season, and it’s just another match. Yeah, it’s states, but it’s just another match. We’re just going to go for it. Leave it all on the court.” — Greely coach Autumn Vargo
• “Class B, I think, is the toughest division in the state. It’s so hard to make it to this point, and we did. And I told the girls, ‘what are we, one of 16 teams left at this point in the year? And out of how many other teams?’ And if I had told them that at the beginning of the season, I think they would have been really happy to be here.” — Messalonskee coach Dan Juilli
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Greely: Anabelle Talley (22 kills, eight digs, eight aces), Alena Tierney (23 assists, eight digs), Avery Enos (17 assists, six digs)
• Messalonskee: Alanna Voter (27 digs, three aces), Lauryn Swails (23 digs), Leah Adams (21 kills)

title: Meet the volunteers who bring flowers from weddings and funerals to hospice patients
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (Aging Untold) — Inside Crescent Hill Baptist Church in Louisville, a group of volunteers gathers each week surrounded by color, creativity and collaboration.
They call themselves the Flower Buds.
From events to those in need
The Flower Buds take donated flowers from weddings, funerals, wholesalers, supermarkets, florists, galas, banquets and other community events. They cut, clean and arrange the blooms into vases, then deliver them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities and shelters.
“Amazingly gifted with so many flowers from places like Kroger who have overbought and can’t sell them, and they allow us to pick them up and then bring them here, and then we cut them, clean them and vase them. Then we take them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities,” Jodie Raible, a Flower Buds volunteer, said.
The group sends out about 100 vases every week.
“I take flowers to Up for Women and Children, it’s a day homeless shelter for women,” Stephanie Mullins, a Flower Buds volunteer, said.
Delivering to the VA
Volunteer Clem Russell is a veteran and takes particular pride in delivering flowers to the VA hospital.
“We deliver to the hospice unit there at the VA and they love seeing them come in. The families are so happy to see the flowers,” Russell said.
“When you are in the end stages of your life you want to be cheered up,” Raible said.
A growing group with a big milestone
The Flower Buds started with six to eight volunteers. The group now has 40.
Mullins has been doing it for 18 years.
“I love flowers and this is what I wanted to do when I retired, so, I’ve been doing this for 18 years now,” she said.
“All these flowers would be thrown in the garbage, so we put them to good use,” Mullins said.

title: Elizabeth F. Klein
text:
Elizabeth Flynt “Betsy” Klein, 82, of Wiscasset, Maine, passed away on Oct. 25, 2026, after navigating a period of declining health.
Born in Augusta, Maine, on July 17, 1944, to Barbara (Burr) and Horton Flynt, she was the youngest of three sisters. Betsy moved to Falmouth, Maine, during her elementary school years. Her social personality flourished in high school, where she was class secretary, played basketball, and graduated as salutatorian from Falmouth High School. Her love of travel blossomed during her time in Falmouth with two trips to Europe, once with the People-to-People organization and once to stay with her sister Pat and brother-in-law John for a summer.
She met her best friend and the love of her life, Earl “Skip” Klein, at the University of Connecticut. They eloped on Nov. 6, 1965, after coordinating family dynamics proved to be too much of a hassle for a wedding. After welcoming a daughter, they made their longtime home in West Hartford, Connecticut, where they lived until retirement. They celebrated 60 loving years of marriage before her passing.
When her children were in elementary school, Betsy returned to the workforce as secretary of the West Hartford United Methodist Church and then returned to her medical assistant training during her children’s high school years. She was incredibly proud of her time as the administrative assistant to the Head of the Infectious Disease Department at the University of Connecticut Medical School.
Betsy spent time growing up with her family in Ocean Point, Maine. She and Skip were able to purchase a small cottage there early in their marriage, and it became a foundation for Betsy’s social and active lifestyle. She made best friends, played tennis, kayaked, and raised her children on the rocky shore of Maine. From the day school ended in the spring until it started in the fall, Betsy and the children spent their summers at Ocean Point, with Skip joining them on weekends.
Betsy and Skip spent 12 years after retirement “snow birding” in Tucson, Arizona. As a highly social butterfly who invented Fear of Missing Out before it became “FOMO,” she made loads of friends. She was a highly active volunteer for the Humane Society and had several “foster fail” rescues who enjoyed being spoiled by her in their senior years.
Her four grandchildren were a particularly bright spot in her life. She loved having them around as individuals and as an unruly group, often instigating shenanigans that occasionally led to tears. Sometimes hers. They all enjoyed trips without parents to Tucson or Ocean Point to enjoy “kid time” with Mammy and Grumpy.
She was predeceased by her sisters, Margaret “Peg” Haskell and Patricia “Pat” Waldman. She is survived by her husband, Skip Klein; daughter Jennifer Klein; son Peter Klein and his wife Barbara (Foote); grandchildren Jo Klein, Madeline Mazjanis and her wife Alison Murray, Jessica (Klein) Reynolds and her husband Ryan, and Peter Mazjanis; and great-grandchildren Nicholas (Nico) and James Reynolds. She loved her extended family and friends with as much fervor as she did her immediate family and had deep relationships with her brothers-in-law, nieces, nephews, many cousins and life-long friends.
Betsy lived life big and did everything with joy, energy, and presence. She loved and was loved. She will be deeply missed and long remembered.
Services will be private and at the discretion of the family.
In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to an animal rescue organization of your choice.
Hall’s of Boothbay has care of the arrangements. To leave the family condolences please visit hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Former Islander publisher honored at groundbreaking for boat launch bearing family name
text:
ORRINGTON — Former Mount Desert Islander owner and publisher Alan Baker was honored last week in his hometown of Orrington at a groundbreaking ceremony for a boat launch facility that will bear his family’s name.
Located about a mile and a half north of his home on the Penobscot River, as the sturgeon swims, Baker Landing will provide all-tides access to the river to recreational boaters, fishing enthusiasts and first responders alike.
A decades-long dream of community leaders, the new boat launch is expected to open to the public by next summer.
“I was thinking about the Penobscot River,” said U.S. Senator Susan Collins, speaking at the event. “It is historic, inspiring and it covers a lot of territory, much like the remarkable individual and dear friend, Alan Baker, whom we are honoring today.”
The site was very much still in a raw state. But between now and mid-2027, crews from Sargent Corporation will transform it from a grown-over gravel pit to a boat launch with plenty of parking, picnic tables, a pavilion and a play area.
“This will be a facility for everybody, not just boaters,” said Orrington Town Manager Chris Backman, noting that plans also call for the creation of hiking trails on the property. “You can spend a whole day here without even going in the water.”
Collins is in the midst of a closely contested reelection campaign, and although that drew a large media presence (including C-SPAN), the senator did not address any political matters. Instead, she spoke about Baker, recounting the service he and his family have given to Orrington over the years.
As a teenager during World War II, Collins said, Baker spent 250 four-hour shifts in a tower above the Orrington town office, scanning the skies to help keep nearby Dow Army Airfield in Bangor safe from possible attack.
In more recent years, Baker has been involved in historic preservation efforts in Orrington, the Dean Hill Cemetery Association and the committee that worked to make the boat launch a reality. He served a term in the Maine House of Representatives in the mid-1980s, following in the footsteps of his mother, Ethel, who served seven terms in the House.
Ethel Baker was Orrington’s town clerk in the 1930s and 40s, and her home doubled as the clerk’s office. When she was away from the home, young Alan would step in to issue hunting, fishing or dog licenses (though never marriage licenses).
“I was in effect the pro tem town clerk,” Baker said on a previous occasion. “I would make out the license and sign my mother’s name and then sign a capital ‘A’ underneath it to indicate that I had issued it and collected the $1.15.”
It would have taken a lot of 1940s license sales to fund the boat launch project, which carries a price tag of $2.5 million. Rather than coming from residents, however, 100% of the funding is coming from the Penobscot Estuary Beneficial Environmental Projects Trust.
That $20-million trust was established as part of a larger, $187-million settlement with Mallinckrodt for “cleanup of mercury contamination in the Penobscot River Estuary,” as described by Greenfield Environmental Trust Group, Inc., the court-appointed firm administering the settlement.
Though the contamination stretches along miles of the river in dozens of communities, it originated at a facility in Orrington once operated by Mallinckrodt (as well as others, including HoltraChem Manufacturing Company). It was just one type of pollution that used to foul the waters of the Penobscot River, as noted by State Senator David Haggan, R-Hampden, in his remarks.
“The river was quite smelly when I moved to the Bangor area; it was quite polluted,” said Haggan, who grew up in East Millinocket. “Ask me what a bald eagle looked like, or an osprey, and I couldn’t tell you because they did not exist here.”
But now, Haggan said, thanks to the efforts of many groups, including the Penobscot Nation, as well as the remediation efforts being overseen by Greenfield, the river is clean and everything from eagles to sturgeon can be seen there.
“What a wonderful project this is,” said Baker, speaking on location after the event. “And all you need to do is to look at that river and see how right it was that we should have access to it here in our community.”
Keith Bowden, former chair of the town’s select board and a member of the boat launch committee, credited Baker with the idea of adding amenities such as the picnic tables and restroom.
“Alan said down in Ellsworth, the folks come and sit at the marina, and they just have their lunch, and we wanted to have a site up here where they could do that,” said Bowden.

title: Addiction treatment facility opens in Westbrook
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WESTBROOK — Guardian Recovery Pine Tree opened a new addiction treatment facility in Westbrook on Tuesday, consolidating and expanding its services to provide a wide range of care for clients with substance use and mental health disorders.
“We hope and believe that with this change comes improved continuity, quality and access,” Kerry MacDonald, executive director of Guardian Recovery Pine Tree, said.
Pine Tree — a member of the national behavioral health network Guardian Recovery — began in Portland in 2018 as a standalone substance withdrawal management program. Since then, it has added an inpatient residential program, a partial hospitalization program and an in-person and virtual intensive outpatient program.
For eight years, Pine Tree has been working toward providing levels of care as clients work through the recovery process, from detoxification with around-the-clock medical monitoring to structured treatment that works around clients’ day-to-day lives.
Relocating to Westbrook allows Pine Tree to provide all these services under one roof, while adding 35 more beds.
Pine Tree, which serves clients across Maine and the country, also offers a monthly alumni meeting to celebrate former clients’ sobriety and a weekly virtual family meeting for people who had a loved one in Pine Tree’s care.
At the grand opening Tuesday, dozens of people walked through the maze of rooms in the new facility. Many said it’s unusual that Pine Tree will be able take people through so many steps of recovery in one place.
For the Westbrook community, Pine Tree’s move to 40 Park Road is a full-circle moment.
That location was the site of Mercy Hospital’s substance abuse recovery center, before it closed in 2015.
Hospital officials said at the time that the Mercy Recovery Center had been losing money for years. Most of the 250 patients impacted then were being treated for opioid addiction, and the closure created a void that the recovery community scrambled to fill.
The closure came after 208 people in Maine died of overdoses in 2014 — a record at the time. In 2020, that number was 504. And in the post-COVID lockdown era, the issue has gotten more acute and complex, MacDonald said, as Pine Tree is seeing more people who haven’t received care for a long time.
It was a sad day when the Mercy Recovery Center closed, Gordon Smith, director of the Maine Opioid Response, said at the opening Tuesday, and it’s only right that the location serves the addiction treatment community once more.
Tyler Hanson, who is now the executive director of Zysk Recovery Partners, said he spent a couple of years at the Mercy Recovery Center. At 17, he had started using alcohol and prescription medications, including opiates and other pain medicines, after he fell off a roof when working construction. At 18, he was addicted.
“Back then, they never gave you any warning when they prescribed you medications,” Hanson said.
On Tuesday, he stood in Pine Tree’s new facility, moved by the experience of coming back years later. He remembered the nurse who grabbed his hand and said, “You don’t need the pills.”
“The doctor and nurse who helped me here are still in my heart,” he said.
In the room where people now gathered to enjoy snacks and refreshments for the new facility’s opening, he remembered attending his first Narcotics Anonymous meeting in a hospital gown.
“It’s amazing to be able to see the bones of the place that’s helped thousands of people,” Hanson said.
For Mayor David Morse, this is also a personal issue. His mother died eight years ago from substance abuse.
“This location that we’re in has a long history of being a place of healing and recovery,” Morse said.
Press Herald reporter Rachel Estabrook contributed to this report.

title: We can all agree: Political ads need to be curtailed
text:
I feel very strongly that we need change to curtail political advertising over (publicly owned) airwaves. In Britain, the licensed TV companies must make available public airwaves for public political debate at election time for no cost.
Here in the U.S., candidates with wealthy donors generally dominate the public discourse with misleading advertising. I believe that just about everyone wants this to end.
Candidates can send us flyers and we can decide to read them, or not. Newspapers can accept political advertising, but presumably won’t publish lies, etc. It’s time for change in political advertising.
Donna Williams
Portland

title: Madawaska Coach Hits 100 Wins as Four County Boys Teams Advance
text:
The County Scoreboard: Madawaska’s Gagnon Reaches 100 Wins as Four County Boys Soccer Teams Advance to Semifinals
Tuesday brought another big afternoon of tournament soccer across Northern Maine, with four Aroostook County boys teams moving into the regional semifinals, a coaching milestone in Madawaska and a near-upset for Caribou.
Fort Kent, Madawaska, Fort Fairfield and Wisdom all picked up shutout victories to keep their seasons going.
And while Caribou couldn't quite pull off the upset against top-seeded John Bapst, the Vikings gave the Crusaders everything they could handle.
Here's how Tuesday's boys quarterfinal games played out.
Class B North: Caribou Nearly Knocks Off Top-Seeded John Bapst
(1) John Bapst 2, (8) Caribou 1
Caribou came close to delivering one of the biggest surprises of the Class B North tournament Tuesday.
The eighth-seeded Vikings went on the road against top-seeded John Bapst and battled to a 2-1 finish before their postseason run came to an end.
Declan Miller scored Caribou's lone goal in the contest.
It was a strong effort against the top team in the bracket, and while the Vikings fell just short, they certainly didn't make it easy for the Crusaders.
Class C North: Fort Kent Shuts Out Washington Academy
(3) Fort Kent 2, (6) Washington Academy 0
Fort Kent is headed to the Class C North semifinals after a 2-0 victory over Washington Academy.
Dom Cyr and Finn Marquis provided the offense for the third-seeded Warriors, each finding the back of the net.
The shutout sends Fort Kent into a semifinal matchup against second-seeded George Stevens Academy.
The Warriors are now one win away from playing for a regional championship.
Class D North: Madawaska Advances as Coach Ben Gagnon Reaches 100 Wins
(1) Madawaska 5, (8) MSSM 0
It was a big afternoon for Madawaska, and not just because the Owls are moving on.
Top-seeded Madawaska rolled to a 5-0 victory over the Maine School of Science and Mathematics, giving head coach Ben Gagnon his 100th career coaching victory.
Josh Querze scored twice and added an assist, while Aiden Gagnon finished with two goals and two assists.
Quinn Pelletier also found the back of the net for the Owls.
Madawaska's five-goal performance secured another postseason victory, but the coaching milestone made Tuesday an especially memorable day for the program.
The Owls move on to the Class D North semifinals.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield Blanks Washburn
(3) Fort Fairfield 3, (6) Washburn 0
Fort Fairfield is also headed to the Class D North semifinals after shutting out Washburn, 3-0.
Asher Winters led the Tigers with two goals, while Dax Milton added the insurance goal.
Levi Cole recorded the shutout in net.
The third-seeded Tigers will now wait for the winner of Wednesday's matchup between second-seeded Central Aroostook and seventh-seeded Penobscot Valley.
That semifinal will determine which team gets an opportunity to play for the Class D North championship.
Eight-Person Boys: Calais Ends Van Buren's Tournament Run
(2) Calais 3, (7) Van Buren 0
Van Buren's postseason run came to an end Tuesday with a 3-0 loss on the road against second-seeded Calais.
The seventh-seeded Crusaders had advanced through the preliminary round but couldn't get past Calais in the quarterfinals.
Calais moves on to face Wisdom in Friday's regional semifinal.
Eight-Person Boys: Wisdom Rolls Past Lee Academy
(3) Wisdom 5, (11) Lee Academy 0
Wisdom put together an impressive performance Tuesday, shutting out Lee Academy 5-0 to advance to the eight-person boys regional semifinals.
Cayden Hartgrove led the Pioneers with two goals and two assists.
Zeek Cyr added a goal and an assist, while Preston Lavoie and Sam Paradis each scored once to complete Wisdom's five-goal afternoon.
Bentley Nadeau recorded the shutout in goal.
The third-seeded Pioneers will now travel to face second-seeded Calais on Friday, with a trip to the regional championship on the line.
