title: Temperatures warm up tomorrow
text:
Temperatures warm up tomorrow
Temperatures warm up tomorrow
Wednesday morning was off to a freezing start, and temperatures this afternoon will be on the cooler side as well. Cloud cover will increase later today, and temperatures will peak in the low 50s and 40s.
High pressure overhead will begin to move offshore this evening. This will cause the winds to start blowing out of the south, which will bring in warmer air to enjoy at the end of the week. The warmer air will kick in after a night of temperatures in the 30s, bringing high temperatures in the upper 60s for Thursday and Friday.
Thursday night, a cold front will pass over Maine, bringing light showers to mountain regions and a few spot showers to the coast. The rain won't make a dent in the drought conditions, and many areas will stay dry on Friday morning.
Halloween weekend is looking dry and cool, with temperatures on Saturday peaking in the low 50s. Trick-or-treaters can expect conditions to be mostly clear with temperatures in the low 40s once the sun starts to set.

title: Maine students hand Susan Collins' Senate seat to Troy Jackson in mock election
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Maine students handed U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ seat to Troy Jackson in this week’s mock election.
More than 12,000 students across 115 schools participated in Tuesday’s mock election.
In Maine’s highly contested U.S. Senate race, Democrat Jackson won narrowly with 50.8% of the vote over Republican Collins’ 45.1%, according to results that the Maine secretary of state’s office released Wednesday.
Students handed Democrat Hannah Pingree a plurality victory in the race for governor. She secured 41.8% of the vote, compared with 30.4% for Republican Bobby Charles and 24.4% for independent Rick Bennett.
In the 1st Congressional District race, Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree kept her seat with a comfortable margin over her Republican opponent, Ron Russell, who garnered 39.7% of the vote.
But the Democratic sweep stopped in the 2nd Congressional District, where 52% of students supported Republican former Gov. Paul LePage over 43.2% for Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap.
“The Maine Student Mock Election is an engaging way for students across the state to learn about elections and have their voices heard even before they can cast a real ballot,” Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said in a statement. “We always say that voting is not a test, but we know that practicing voting before students turn 18 can help them feel prepared to participate in our democracy when the day comes. Mock election creates a fun environment for civic participation and civil discourse about the upcoming election.”
In recent years, the results of the mock election have mirrored the results of the general election. Students rejected voter ID and backed a red-flag law referendum last year, much like eligible voters did that November. In presidential elections, the favorite among Maine students went on to win in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
But the prognosticating powers of Maine’s teens haven’t always borne fruit.
In 2016, they backed Donald Trump for president but also backed a gun background check referendum that failed. Then in 2020 they backed Democrat Sara Gideon in her bid to unseat Collins, but considering who’s on the ballot this year, you know how that race turned out.
This year’s race between Collins and Jackson is very tight, with poll after poll after poll giving the former Maine Senate president just a narrow edge over Collins, who has led in at least one public poll, also by a single digit, this fall.
Both Republicans and Democrats have brought out heavy hitters to boost their candidates here, including Vice President JD Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson for Republicans, and U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for Democrats. Former President Barack Obama also gave a prominent endorsement to Jackson this month, and former Democratic U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia stumped for Collins last week.
It will be an uphill battle for Democrats to unseat Collins, who officially announced her historic bid for a sixth term in February. The Republican has handily beaten back challengers, including in 2020 when she defied polls and expectations to secure a fifth term in the Senate. But Collins, who has been ranked the country’s most bipartisan senator and relied on cross-party appeal to carry her to victory, has seen her popularity slump since Trump’s first term in the White House.
If Collins is successful in winning a sixth term, she would be Maine’s longest-serving U.S. senator.

title: Portland woman settles with state police after allegations of body-slamming, excessive force
text:
A Maine woman has reached a settlement in her lawsuit against a Maine State Police trooper she accused of body-slamming her without cause during a 2024 incident in Chelsea.
Marie Searles, of Portland, agreed to an award of $54,000 on Oct. 13, according to the settlement agreement provided by the Office of the Maine Attorney General. The payment for her alleged physical injuries and emotional distress was first reported by the Bangor Daily News.
Searles filed the complaint in U.S. District Court against both Trooper Hunter Belanger and his supervisor, Lt. Aaron Turcotte. Neither man immediately responded to requests for comment about the allegations Wednesday, but both denied the allegations in court paperwork.
Searles’ lawsuit also came weeks after a Limerick man sued another Maine State Police trooper for repeatedly punching him in the face while he was handcuffed on the ground, as reported in an investigation by The Maine Monitor and Bangor Daily News.
The parties agreed to dismiss Searles’ claims on Wednesday, according to court documents.
In the October 2025 complaint, Searles claimed that Belanger assaulted her in Chelsea after she refused to speak with him. Searles had walked near Belanger’s cruiser, where he was drafting a search warrant for a nearby camper. He asked her to come speak with him, and she walked away, according to court documents.
Then, Searles alleged, Belanger grabbed her, “flipped her body up into the air” and slammed her against the ground. According to the complaint, Searles also accused Belanger of pinning her the ground with his knee and slamming her against his car.
Searles also alleged that Turcotte let Belanger commit similar conduct during a man’s January 2024 arrest in Readfield.
Belanger and Turcotte denied the allegations in November 2025 court filings, which state that Belanger “secured Searles and took her to the ground,” as well as “put Searles on the hood of his cruiser.”
They said any injury to Searles “was the result of her own fault,” according to court documents.

title: Canned fruit sold at Walmart recalled in several states
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - A voluntary recall over lead concerns has been issued for cans of Walmart fruit cocktail distributed to stores in at least seven states.
The Food and Drug Administration said the recall applies to 15-ounce containers of Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate.
Where the product was distributed
More than 1,830 cases, or approximately 44,000 individual cans, were distributed to Walmart locations in Alabama, Arizona, Louisiana, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wyoming, the FDA said.
How to identify the product
The product is marked with lot number “6FCB 04 C2263” and a best if used by date of Sept. 1, 2027.
Recall details
The FDA initiated the recall for “potential contamination with elevated levels of lead” on Oct. 1. It was reclassified as a Class II recall on Oct. 20.
According to the FDA, Class II recalls are issued when a product can cause temporary health effects with a remote possibility of serious issues.
What customers should do
Customers should throw the item away or return it to Walmart.

title: Maine man arrested on 12 counts of gross sexual assault and sexual abuse of minors
text:
Man wanted on 12 counts of gross sexual assault found in a car in Buckfield
A South Portland man is facing a dozen counts of gross sexual assault after he was found in a car in Buckfield.
At about 7:10 a.m. on Tuesday, someone called 911 to report a possibly unresponsive man in a vehicle at the intersection of Darnit Road and Brock School Road in Buckfield.
When a deputy from the Oxford County Sheriff's Office arrived, they found Diego Ramirez, 29, in the car and said he was not in crisis or having any medical emergency.
Deputies determined he was wanted on an outstanding warrant charging him with 12 counts of gross sexual assault, sexual abuse of minors, unlawful sexual contact and other drug and alcohol-related offenses.
Ramirez was taken to the Oxford County Jail and held on $25,000 cash bail.
Police told Maine's Total Coverage the initial warrant was issued by the Rumford Police Department.

title: Bangor Fire adds fourth ambulance to tackle rising call volume
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - For the first time in over two decades, the Bangor Fire Department is expanding its ambulance fleet to keep up with record call volumes.
Following a four-month pilot program, the department officially put a fourth staffed ambulance into full-time rotation on Sunday. City funding also added eight new personnel dedicated exclusively to EMS.
Officials say medical calls now make up nearly 90% of all Bangor Fire calls, with crews on track to handle roughly 9,000 medical calls this year alone.
“What we’ve already noticed in the three days that it’s been up and running is that call volumes are already starting to even out. So, it’s already showing that being able to spread that workload out is vital,” said Jeremy Ogden, EMS Division Chief for Bangor Fire Department.
Since going in service Sunday morning, the new unit has already responded to 27 medical calls.

title: Federal judge releases six defendants in MaineCare fraud case with conditions; all plead not guilty
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WMTW) - A judge released all six people charged in a federal MaineCare fraud case with conditions after they pleaded not guilty in a Bangor courtroom, according to court filings.
Prosecutors had filed motions asking the court to detain the defendants, citing “serious risks” of obstruction and the defendants fleeing before trial.
A judge disagreed and released all six on Tuesday “on conditions.” The court docket does not include a full release order or specify what those conditions are.
The defendants are 37-year-old Noora Abd, 51-year-old Faysal Kalayaf Manahe, 47-year-old Adel Al Rashid, 47-year-old Sura Almohammed, 46-year-old Ethar Alyaseen and 41-year-old Mohammed Alkhalaf.
Abd is cited as the owner and operator of Community Home Health Care in South Portland, which was also named in the now unsealed federal grand jury indictment. It alleges that she and her five employees conspired to defraud MaineCare by submitting electronic visit-verification records for personal care services that were not provided. According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Community Home Health Care and Abd allegedly submitted more than $600,000 in claims since 2020 for services purportedly provided to one client.
Abd and her husband Manahe are also charged with obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation; prosecutors allege they pressured someone who knew about the alleged fraud scheme not to speak to investigators. Alkhalaf is charged with making false statements.
According to a filing opposing detention, Abd’s attorneys argued that the government’s motion sought detention based on flight risk, did not claim Abd was a danger to anyone and did not qualify for a statutory presumption of detention.
Abd’s attorneys also pointed to the government’s timeline. They said the indictment was returned Oct. 22, but Abd was not arrested until Oct. 27, and that the conduct attributed to her in the indictment ended in August. Attorneys argued those delays undercut the government’s claims that she posed a serious flight or obstruction risk. In the filing, attorneys wrote that Abd knew she was the subject of a federal fraud investigation since June, but in the four months since, she did not leave her home in Maine.
“A defendant who presents a serious risk of flight is not left in her home for five days after a grand jury returns a sealed indictment against her,” wrote attorney Michael J. Conley in submitted court documents. “A defendant who presents a serious risk of obstruction is not left alone for two months after the government says her conduct stopped.”
Abd’s attorneys also argued that prosecutors had not shown that release conditions could not address there concerns. They said that Abd would accept any conditions that the court deems necessary, including the surrender of her passport, travel restrictions, living at an approved address, location monitoring and no-contact provisions.
Community Home Health Care was previously cited by Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services over more than $49,000 in alleged overpayments for services billed between 2016 and 2019. The company repaid the amount in August.
If the defendants are convicted of healthcare fraud conspiracy, they face up to 10 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000 or twice the total loss due to fraudulent claims, and up to three years of supervised release. The charges of obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation and making false statements each carry a maximum of five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release.

title: Southport Column: Busy days ahead
text:
Sunday mornings are always lovely, quiet with the sounds of lobster boats at work and the rustle among the trees in the woods, a perfect beginning. It has been the week of the oaks, glowing as fall continues to envelop us with brilliant sunny days. Bird feeders have needed constant refilling as feathered companions flit in and out to grab a seed, song and wing beats hang in the air. A bit further from home the water beckons, crystal clear, calm and chilly, being in it clears away aches, brain clutter and fatigue. Kitten Island is ringed by a crimson crown, rafts of mergansers circle schools of fish for easier eating, black ducks, geese, gulls a pair of grebes and a lone loon dive, float and paddle with ease creating an idyllic scene that is once again still and virtually empty. Empty is not for everyone, for those of you looking for community events, we have quite a few this week and in the near future.
At the Library, 1032 Hendricks Hill Road this week there is the Coffee Table on Tuesday and Thursday beginning at 10 a.m., hot beverage, baked treat and lively conversation. Thursday, from 2-4, you can join the Mah Jongg group, whether you are a beginner, or a proficient player, all are welcome. Thursday evening, Oct. 29, beginning promptly at 6 p.m., there will be screening of the “Texas Chainsaw Massacre,” followed by discussion facilitated by James M. Kopf who will provide background on production, some common interpretations, and guide and answer questions from the audience. Dr. Kopf is a scholar, author, and translator currently based on Southport. His work pertains to the interactions between media technology, literature, and philosophy from the 19th century to today. Come to the Southport Island debut of a horror classic for thrills, chills, and cinema history! Light refreshments will be served.
Join consultant Kari Smith Thursday, Nov. 5 at 6 p.m., at the library, for a Digital Legacy Readiness talk. Everyone’s life is kept in two places. Some of it is online: email, photos, social media, bank logins and subscriptions. The rest is on paper: vital records, insurance policies, property papers, medical information and wishes that were never written down. When someone dies or can no longer manage, their family has to search for both, at one of the hardest times of their lives. Accounts get locked, documents go missing, photos are lost, and subscriptions keep charging. Most estate plans cover only one of these halves, and most people don’t have a plan at all. Kari will present what you can do now to avoid this outcome. During the talk she will give you information about how to navigate decision-making and will suggest some methods for organizing your paper and digital files. There will be time for Q&A after the presentation.
Friday, Oct. 30, 4:30-7 and 7:30-9 join the Southport Community at the Southport Central School Field for Spooktober Storytime and Movie Night. There will be storytime, crafts, pumpkin painting, pizza, popcorn and a screening of the “Boxtrolls,” followed by “Beetlejuice” at 7:30. Wear a costume, though not necessary, bring a chair and blankets and enjoy a double feature on a big outdoor screen. This free community event is brought to you by the Southport Memorial Library, SIA, and Friends of Southport School. In case of bad weather all events move to the library.
Remember to enroll for the Fused Glass Workshop held at the Barn on Saturday, Nov. 7 from 10-Noon. It will give you an opportunity to make three Christmas ornaments in shapes, sizes, and designs of your choice. For more information visit southportgeneralstore.com click on Barn and then workshops.
Another fun community opportunity for Friday, Oct. 30, 5-8, is listening to the School Street Band at Robinson’s Wharf and enjoying some of their delicious specials, or an expertly made or poured beverage, or both. The Crew is still with us 7 days a week from 11-8, so show them some appreciation.
There will be a new art exhibit at the library in a week or so, I am looking into more details regarding the Mid Coast Fiber Arts Group and will let you all know in the next column. In the meanwhile enjoy the “spooky” time of year, there are some great decorations out and about, and if there are young children in your life soak in the excitement of dressing up, the parades and get a lot of pictures, have fun, and May Peace Be With You All.

title: Man accused of threatening girl with a gun to get in his car later determined to have .292 BAC, deputies say
text:
Salem, Ind. (WDRB/WAVE/Gray News) — The sister of a man accused of threatening a girl with a gun to get in his car said that the whole thing was a “huge misunderstanding.”
The incident happened on Friday in an Amish community in Salem, Indiana.
Probable cause documents said 53-year-old Jeffrey Mauck went up to a girl outside her home and asked if her family sold any eggs. The girl told police that she said no and walked away.
The Washington County Sheriff’s Department said Mauck then grabbed her and threatened her with a gun, telling her to get in his car. Officials said the girl’s family heard her screaming and came to the rescue.
Court documents said that the girl’s father and his sons were able to restrain Mauck while waiting for the police to arrive.
One of the responding officers said he found a pair of black handcuffs lying on the ground underneath Mauck and could smell what he believed to be the odor of alcohol coming from Mauck.
Court documents said Mauck admitted to having been drinking. A chemical test determined that Mauck had a blood alcohol content of .292.
Mauck is facing six charges, including attempted kidnapping and driving while intoxicated.
But Mauck’s family said he’s been wrongfully charged.
“Just a huge misunderstanding of events,” Mauck’s sister Anna Hall said.
“Everything that is being stated right now is very out of character for what me and my family know,” she continued.
Mauck’s sister said the brother she knows would not do what he is accused of.
“He has a tattoo of a blue, the blue bear, because that’s what he is,” she said. “He is, you know, just not aggressive.”
But the Washington County Sheriff’s Department called the incident “extremely disturbing” in a statement. The department also said it is “thankful this young girl was able to get away and that her family acted quickly.”
“I do believe that it will be very hard to believe that that is what occurred when the truth comes out,” Hall said.
The sheriff’s department’s statement also said that anybody “who attempts to harm or abduct a child in Washington County” will be met with serious consequences, including the “full force of law enforcement.”
Hall is hoping the judge doesn’t make her brother face those serious consequences for a crime she claims he didn’t do.

title: Maine’s housing shortage will be the focus of upcoming Portland conference
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Affordable Housing Coalition will bring together housing industry leaders, researchers, advocates, policymakers, philanthropists and community members on Nov. 9 for its annual conference.
“Housing is the single biggest burden facing Maine’s families and working people today,” said Laura Mitchell, executive director of the coalition. “As rents soar and homeownership slips further out of reach, the ripple effects are felt across every corner of our state: young workers are forced to leave, parents face impossible choices between housing and basic needs, fixed-income seniors struggle to age in place and local business owners can’t recruit or retain the staff needed to keep their doors open.”
A host of speakers will discuss housing policy, the need for more middle-income and senior housing and the effects of the Buy America Build America legislation, which was enacted in November 2021, as part of the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
Alex Horowitz with the PEW Charitable Trust will moderate a panel on the role of philanthropy in housing development.
Jennifer Schwartz, with the National Council of State Housing Agencies, will share a federal perspective.
Maine State Economist Amanda Rector will focus on Maine’s housing outlook.
The program will be held at the Holiday Inn by the Bay, 88 Spring St. in Portland, and will be Monday, Nov. 9, from 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. More details and registration information are available on the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition website. Registration is required to attend and closes at noon Oct. 30.

title: Maine can’t afford Troy Jackson in Washington
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Laurel Libby represents Auburn and Minot in the Maine House of Representatives and is the founder of Lead Maine.
By the time Troy Jackson finished his run as Maine Senate president, the state government was spending about $2,800 more per year for every household in Maine than when he took over.
What would your family do with an extra $2,800 a year? For a lot of Mainers, the answer is simple: keep up with the basics. Four in 10 Maine households can’t cover housing, child care, food, transportation, health care and a phone plan, according to 2024 United Way ALICE data.
Now the bill is coming due. Gov. Janet Mills’ own budget office projects a gap of about $1.3 billion in the 2028-2029 budget: $1.085 billion in the General Fund and $257 million in the highway fund. Rising MaineCare costs alone account for $345 million.
That hole didn’t appear overnight. The two-year General Fund budget was $7.2 billion when Jackson got the gavel. The budget for 2024 and 2025, the last one written on his watch, was $10.6 billion. That’s an increase of nearly 47%, and that budget alone was 24% bigger than the one before it.
That’s $3.4 billion more for the two-year budget cycle, or about $2,800 per taxpaying household per year.
Gov. Mills may be the face of the shortfall, but she didn’t build those budgets alone. In 2021 and again in 2023, Democrats unilaterally passed two-year budgets, without any Republican support. Both times, Troy Jackson was presiding over the Senate. The spending commitments made on his watch didn’t leave the State House when he did.
Maine families feel it on their power bills, too. Since 2019, the price Maine households pay for electricity has climbed more than 70%, from about 18 cents to 32 cents per kilowatt-hour. Nationally, prices rose 40% over the same stretch. Maine now has the fourth-highest residential rates in the country.
I believe that is a direct effect of choices made in the State House, crafted by Troy Jackson and Augusta Democrats. Maine’s renewable energy mandates require every power supplier to buy credits from subsidized solar and wind, power that flows when the sun shines or the wind blows, instead of investing in the reliable power generation families count on during a January cold snap. Ratepayers paid $110 million in 2024 just to comply with the mandate, on top of the solar subsidies now billed separately.
Troy Jackson helped build that system. In 2019, he voted to raise Maine’s renewable mandate to 80% by 2030 and cosponsored the law that created the solar subsidy program. When the costs started landing on family bills, Republicans pushed to rein them in. In 2023, a bill to end the solar program cleared the House, then died in Jackson’s Senate.
This is all just a small taste of the agenda I believe Troy Jackson would bring to Washington if elected. He has already made clear one of his top priorities is to pass Medicare for All — a program one study found could cost $34 trillion in federal spending over the next decade.
Someone has to pay for that. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, whose 2016 Maine campaign Jackson ran, proposed a new 4% premium on household income, with only families of four earning less than $29,000 exempt. That would reach straight into the paychecks of working Maine families.
Sen. Susan Collins has worked the other direction, bringing federal dollars home to Maine. Since 2021, she has secured nearly $1.5 billion for 672 community projects across all 16 counties.
Maine families can’t spend money they don’t have and send the bill to someone else. The people they send to Washington shouldn’t either.
Troy Jackson has shown us how he budgets. Before you vote on Nov. 3, look closely at his record, and remember who’s paying for it.

title: Man accused of threatening girl with a gun to get in his car later determined to have .292 BAC, deputies say
text:
Salem, Ind. (WDRB/WAVE/Gray News) — The sister of a man accused of threatening a girl with a gun to get in his car said that the whole thing was a “huge misunderstanding.”
The incident happened on Friday in an Amish community in Salem, Indiana.
Probable cause documents said 53-year-old Jeffrey Mauck went up to a girl outside her home and asked if her family sold any eggs. The girl told police that she said no and walked away.
The Washington County Sheriff’s Department said Mauck then grabbed her and threatened her with a gun, telling her to get in his car. Officials said the girl’s family heard her screaming and came to the rescue.
Court documents said that the girl’s father and his sons were able to restrain Mauck while waiting for the police to arrive.
One of the responding officers said he found a pair of black handcuffs lying on the ground underneath Mauck and could smell what he believed to be the odor of alcohol coming from Mauck.
Court documents said Mauck admitted to having been drinking. A chemical test determined that Mauck had a blood alcohol content of .292.
Mauck is facing six charges, including attempted kidnapping and driving while intoxicated.
But Mauck’s family said he’s been wrongfully charged.
“Just a huge misunderstanding of events,” Mauck’s sister Anna Hall said.
“Everything that is being stated right now is very out of character for what me and my family know,” she continued.
Mauck’s sister said the brother she knows would not do what he is accused of.
“He has a tattoo of a blue, the blue bear, because that’s what he is,” she said. “He is, you know, just not aggressive.”
But the Washington County Sheriff’s Department called the incident “extremely disturbing” in a statement. The department also said it is “thankful this young girl was able to get away and that her family acted quickly.”
“I do believe that it will be very hard to believe that that is what occurred when the truth comes out,” Hall said.
The sheriff’s department’s statement also said that anybody “who attempts to harm or abduct a child in Washington County” will be met with serious consequences, including the “full force of law enforcement.”
Hall is hoping the judge doesn’t make her brother face those serious consequences for a crime she claims he didn’t do.
Mauck was in court Monday afternoon and had his bond set at $2 million, full cash.

The review team will assess whether all alternatives considered by Lincoln Hospital management, including those identified in the White Paper and those provided by external entities, were reasonable, feasible and sustainable. title: Couple charged after 4 children removed from ‘deplorable conditions’, police say
text:
MIDDLETOWN, Ohio (WXIX/Gray News) - A couple is facing multiple charges of child endangerment and animal cruelty following a welfare check at their home in September, authorities said.
Melanie and Christopher Todd were arrested after officers responded to their home on Cardinal Court to check on their children and animals, according to the criminal complaint.
Police described the living conditions as “deplorable and unlivable.”
Officers conducted the welfare check Sept. 29 after Middletown City Schools reported that two 10-year-old children appeared dirty and said they had no food to eat, police said.
The children also said two cats were dead inside their home, the complaint said.
During the check, officers found holes large enough to see outside in the walls and floors. One of the couple’s four children said the holes were caused by punching when Melanie and Christopher would get angry, the complaint said.
The home also had little to no edible food inside, officers said.
According to the complaint, the floors were covered in dirty clothes, trash, animal feces, and debris. The house was also infested with bedbugs and cockroaches.
Police removed all four children from the home and placed them with other family members. Officers also removed four cats, pet fish, mice, gerbils and pet tarantulas.
The couple is facing four counts of child endangerment and several counts of animal cruelty.
Both are in custody at the Butler County Jail. They will be arraigned Thursday.

title: QUINN QUESTIONS: What did the ancient humans eat?
text:
Sometimes I wonder how our ancient ancestors survived without foods like breakfast cereal and ice cream. But maybe they didn’t realize what they were missing, because pre-historic television commercials got such poor reception.
Seriously, consider the paleolithic period, which covers about 2.5 million years. Up until 12,000 years ago, these folks were hunters and gatherers. They just kind of wandered around, searching for fruit, vegetables, and slow animals that looked tasty.
Their housing was basic. They lived in huts, teepees, or caves. However, without pest exterminators, you can guess the size of cave bugs that crawled over them. Yuck!
Anyway, about this time some genius found a way to start a fire. He – or she – heated some meat over it.
Wow, that tasted lots better than raw gristle. And it didn’t make them quite as sick.
Nobody knows who first invented fire, or how. There’s speculation that some cave dude rubbed two sticks together, or created sparks with flint stones.
Today, I can simply rub two sticks together. I call them “matches.”
Soon, people realized that flames could keep them warm, improve food flavor, and illuminate the evening hours. They sat around those fires, and invented chants they later called “songs for summer camp.”
These people were possibly humankind’s first artists. They created paints from things like animal fats, tree sap, and bone meal. Then, they drew humans, animals, and strange designs on cave walls.
Some of this cave art is still around. Because it’s on the walls, it can’t be displayed in museums.
But back then, it probably improved a cave’s resale value.

Searsmont EMS volunteer injured in mill explosion expected to return home Friday
More than five months after she was seriously injured in an explosion and fire at the Robbins Lumber Mill in Searsmont, emergency medical services volunteer Lily Robbins is preparing to come home.
Searsmont EMS volunteer injured in mill explosion expected to return home Friday
More than five months after she was seriously injured in an explosion and fire at the Robbins Lumber Mill in Searsmont, emergency medical services volunteer Lily Robbins is preparing to come home.
Town officials announced on Facebook that Robbins is expected to return home Friday, following months of recovery at the burn center at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston.
Commenting below the post Wednesday morning, Robbins thanked the community and expressed her gratitude for the support.
The town of Searsmont has a celebration planned for Robbins and invited community members to bring desserts, snacks and handmade "welcome home" signs to the station between 9 a.m. and noon on Friday.
The welcome-home procession for Robbins is scheduled to leave the Augusta Civic Center at 2 p.m. and take Route 3 toward Searsmont, ending at the Searsmont Fire/EMS station.
Fire trucks and ambulances will also gather at Cox Machine on Route 3 to join the procession.
Mosaic, a restaurant in Camden where Robbins worked, has raised more than $78,000 to support Robbins' recovery and medical expenses.
"She has served our community not only here, but also as an EMT, showing up for people on some of their hardest days with compassion, courage, and grace," wrote Hannah Scott, who created a GoFundMe to support Robbins. "She gives so much of herself to others, often with a joke ready at exactly the right moment."
Robbins was among 12 people left badly hurt after a silo at the mill exploded and flames rapidly spread around the surrounding area. Her uncle and president of the mill, James A. Robbins, was also injured and is recovering at Mass General.
Robbins' father, Alden Robbins, who was co-owner of the mill, was also injured in the fire and died from his injuries at the same hospital in June.
Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross died at the scene and was laid to rest in May.

title: Dolores Huerta, pioneering labor organizer and civil rights icon, dies at 96
text:
(AP) - Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation’s fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase “Sí, se puede!” that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta’s family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.
Huerta was born in New Mexico and raised by a single mother in California’s San Joaquin Valley, where she worked as a school teacher and then helped found a local chapter of a grassroots organization that fought segregation and police brutality.
She quickly turned her interests to farm laborers and co-founded with César Chavez what eventually became the United Farm Workers of America.
Huerta’s resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to “Yes, it can be done” — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.
Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.
This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community and activist circles when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died.
Huerta said she stayed silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life’s work and unravel all the progress made for workers.
In the wake of the revelation, she urged people to stand firm in fighting for their rights.
Even into her mid-90s, Huerta marched and spoke in cities nationwide on race, poverty and women’s rights on behalf of her California-based Dolores Huerta Foundation.

title: Finding Our Voices provides $540,000 in aid to Maine domestic abuse survivors
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Finding Our Voices, the grassroots nonprofit supporting Maine women survivors of domestic abuse and their children, has distributed $540,000 in direct financial assistance to more than 1,000 low-income survivors across all 16 Maine counties through its Get Out Stay Out Fund.
Launched in 2021, shortly after the group became a nonprofit, the fund provides low-barrier microgrants for essential needs that can make the difference between remaining in danger, constraint, and misery, and building a safe, independent life. Assistance includes security deposits, car repairs, gas and grocery cards, overdue utility bills, legal expenses, and other critical costs.
According to Finding Our Voices CEO+Founder Patrisha McLean, financial abuse with the resulting lack of available funds is the number one factor trapping women in domestic abuse.
The program began with a $50,000 grant from Doris Buffett’s Sunshine Lady Foundation. Finding Our Voices is entirely donor-funded and does not accept government funding, a model that allows the organization to respond quickly and flexibly to survivors’ urgent needs, according to McLean.
“Finding Our Voices kept my electricity on and gas in my car," one funding recipient said, after I had been physically, emotionally, & financially abused by my ex-boyfriend and isolated 2000 miles away from my family and friends. They helped me when nobody else could, or would.”
Demand for emergency assistance is growing
Finding Our Voices is experiencing a surge in requests for help that they attribute to rising costs of housing, fuel, and groceries and cutbacks to the social safety net. McLean said the survivor-led nonprofit, working out of a home office in Camden and with a staff of three plus a brigade of volunteers spanning the state, now receives an average of eight reach-outs a day from referral partners and survivors, increasingly involving women who are homeless or living in cars with their children.
“We are immensely grateful to our donors for allowing us to provide lifelines to the most vulnerable women and children in our communities,” McLean said.
The assistance is often immediate and practical: a security deposit that makes a hard-to-find apartment accessible; a gas card that allows a survivor to flee the state when a dangerous former partner is released early from prison; a car repair that enables a woman to keep her job; or storage fees that preserve treasured belongings, including children’s artwork and, in one case, a mother’s ashes.
McLean described a growing gap between survivors’ urgent needs and the help available through other systems. One woman reported spending more than eight hours on hold with social service agencies. Another single mother was told she needed to take a day off from her new job to apply for assistance in person. In early October, a woman was told the next available appointment to apply for heating assistance was in January.
Helping survivors stay out and rebuild their lives
The “Stay Out” component of the fund recognizes that leaving an abusive relationship is only the beginning of a survivor’s journey. Rebuilding financial stability, navigating legal proceedings, addressing trauma, and supporting children can create significant challenges long after a woman has gotten herself and her children physically safe.
“I left my abuser 17 months ago,” one recipient wrote to Finding Our Voices. “But no one ever tells you how hard the next part is. I felt like I was drowning—in legal fees, in the ongoing divorce being weaponized against me, mounting therapy fees for PTSD, and still trying to earn an income without a car to drive.”
The survivor described the support she received from Finding Our Voices as more than financial: “I felt like I was hanging off a cliff by my fingernails. The help I received from you guys was not only a lifeline, but a tsunami of relief that gave me the strength to keep going.”
The fund’s impact is reflected in its recent growth. According to McLean, assistance has doubled since 2024. In the first 10 months of 2026 alone, Finding Our Voices distributed $120,000 to 245 survivors and their 95 children. That amount represents more than one-third of the organization’s annual budget.
The fund has also established separate Children’s and Pet Funds, recognizing the impact of domestic abuse on children and the importance of pets in the healing journey. Recent Children’s Fund payments have included $350 for art camp, an $80 weighted stuffed animal, and $750 for driving lessons for a teenager who had just finished testifying in a domestic violence trial involving her father.
Pet Fund assistance has included a muzzle and flea treatment needed for a dog to accompany its owner into emergency shelter, as well as $750 for a life-saving operation for a beloved furbaby named Daisy.
A network of community support
Finding Our Voices works with an expanding network of referral partners throughout Maine, including health care and social service agency caseworkers, therapists, and state workers and officials who connect survivors with assistance through Finding Our Voices that they cannot find anywhere else.
After Finding Our Voices paid a client’s $1,000 overdue electric bill, Nancy Cormier, a caseworker with the mental health clinic Spurwink, praised the nonprofit.
“I had a response by email and phone within an hour of submitting the contact form,” Cormier said. “This is a life-changing organization. The amount of kindness shown has blown me away.”
Finding Our Voices provided another survivor with a $500 grocery card after her food assistance benefits were suspended, and a $500 gas card to allow her to escape terrifying stalking of her ex by staying with family in Texas.
“Finding our Voices was a light in the middle of a lot of darkness for my client,” her caseworker said. “They were genuinely interested in my client’s needs, and were quick to respond and provide tangible and practical help.”
“They are actually helping victims of domestic violence. They are active and proactive. They are using their funds well and wisely and helping survivors break through.”
Funding comes from a mix of grants, individual donations, and creative community fundraising campaigns. Grants this year include $20,000 from the John T. Gorman Foundation exclusively for security deposits.
Finding Our Voices’ largest fundraising initiative is its annual Into the Light! Yellow Festival, with 100 percent of proceeds going to the Get Out Stay Out Fund. During July, businesses promote, and donate proceeds from, yellow-themed menu or retail items, with participation this year from 126 businesses from Damariscotta to Stonington. Proceeds are significantly boosted with corporate sponsorships including lead sponsors Camden National Bank and First National Bank.
Additional fundraising efforts include register round-ups this year at Aubuchon Hardware locations in Buxton and Belfast, both locations of Morning Glory Natural Foods in Brunswick, and Lois’ Natural Marketplace in Scarborough. Christine Buckley has raised a total of $7,000 for the Get Out Stay Out Fund through art sales at Christine’s Framing Gallery and “yellow dot” sales at her second business, Camden Curated.
Beyond financial assistance
Finding Our Voices also supports survivors through Finding Our Smiles, which connects women with donated dental care from 40 volunteer dental providers across Maine; Healing Together workshops and retreats; and a weekly online support group.
The nonprofit’s public education efforts include its Teen Healthy Relationship program, with classroom visits in 2026 to 18 schools from Sanford to Baileyville.
For the domestic abuse survivors running Finding Our Voices including McLean, the group's COO Mary Kamradt, and dozens of devoted volunteers, these services and the financial assistance are part of a broader effort to empower their sisters to cross over to the bright side of safety and freedom, as they managed to do.
A recent donation captured that journey in the donor’s own words:
“I’m on the other side of a rough 15 years. I’ll always be grateful for your work. It wasn’t until I read one of your posters in Belfast that it truly hit me how mentally abusive my ex was. My life now is peaceful, purposeful & full of good friends. Thank you for helping others get through the dark and into the light.”
As requests for assistance continues to rise, Finding Our Voices invites donations from the public, which can be designated for the Get Out Stay Out Fund, its children or pet offshoots, or any other of its programs.
About Finding Our Voices
Finding Our Voices is the Maine-based, grassroots nonprofit and sisterhood supporting women survivors of domestic abuse and their children. Its programs include the Get Out Stay Out Fund, Children’s Fund, Pet Fund, Finding Our Smiles donated dental care initiative, Healing Togetherworkshops and retreats, a weekly online support group, and public education campaigns promoting awareness of domestic abuse and teen dating abuse.
The group is hosting a free Financial Health workshop in Camden on Tuesday November 10 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
For more information about Finding Our Voices, its programs, or ways to support its work, visit the organization’s official website https://findingourvoices.net or contact McLean directly at hello@findingourvoices.net

title: Vassalboro cemetery committee hears about trees, stones and green burials
text:
According to the minutes of the Vassalboro Cemetery Committee’s Oct. 19 meeting, committee members discussed work completed and still to be done and ideas about green burials, presented by resident Gillian Lalime.
Committee and other volunteers had repaired most stones in Maple Grove Cemetery. A few needing expert work were postponed to the summer of 2027, when the committee plans to contract again with Gravestone Matters, in Hoosick Falls, New York.
Symmetree Arborist, of Vassalboro, had finished contracted tree work in Union Cemetery, and the town public works crew had taken away most of the logs left behind. Committee member David Jenney had watched some of Symmetree’s work and approved.
Committee members Jody Kundreskas and Jenney walked Union Cemetery and found almost three-quarters of the stones there need attention. Union was added to the 2027 work schedule.
The Symmetree crew had not started in Weeks Cemetery because of the poison ivy. That cemetery and Maple Grove were sprayed to kill the weed.
The select board had awarded another tree removal contract, to Pro Tree Service of Vassalboro (see the Oct. 22 issue of The Town Line, p. 2), for Union and Oak Grove cemeteries.
Committee members discussed three dead trees in front of Webber Pond Cemetery Annex. Removal might be a job for the public works crew. Committee Chairman Savannah Clark said the town crew still plans to cut back brush that is intruding into several cemeteries before winter.
Lalime brought two topics to the committee. She asked about the status of the Bog Road Cemetery; committee members said select board members agreed to allow private maintenance with town oversight of veterans’ graves.
Lalime explained two types of green burials, methods of putting dead bodies without embalming directly into the ground. Committee members will explore the subject.
The next Vassalboro Cemetery Committee meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m., Monday, Nov. 16, in the Vassalboro town office. The 2026-27 budget will be one agenda item.

title: Damariscotta art gallery features paintings by Mainer Martha Bracy
text:
River Arts in Damariscotta announces a new River Room exhibition featuring the paintings of Martha Bracy, on view through Nov. 18.
Meet the artist at an opening reception on Friday, Oct. 30, from 5 to 7 p.m.
After earning a BFA from the University of Southern Maine in 1995, Bracy spent the following years working intermittently as an illustrator and mother while continuing to develop her own painting practice. Three years ago, she began painting full time, allowing her long-standing commitment to painting to take center stage.
Bracy’s work explores the quiet mysteries of familiar landscapes and domestic spaces, revealing stories hidden in plain sight. Through layered color, shifting shadows, and the rich textures of oil paint, she explores the space between observation, fantasy, and memory, finding unexpected depth and atmosphere in ordinary surroundings. With a keen eye for visual detail and a fascination with the fleeting secrets of everyday moments, her paintings invite viewers to look beyond the familiar and discover the possibilities held within even the smallest details.
Bracy describes her approach to painting in a prepared release: “My paintings begin with the sense of familiarity you feel when you walk down a side street in your home town, get lost in the wallpaper of your aunt’s kitchen, or catch a glimpse of an old country store as you drive by. Something about the changing light slows the eye and invites a different kind of attention. Stories form, histories suggest themselves, shadows open into space and ordinary details take on an unexpected weight.
“I paint from this sense of discovery, and the search for the expansive possibility inside one fleeting moment. The commonplace becomes quietly mysterious, causing me to imagine that magic might exist here after all.”
River Arts is located at 36 Elm St. in Damariscotta and is open Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. For more information, visit riverartsme.org or call 207-563-6868.

title: OBITUARIES for Thursday, October 29, 2026
text:
JOHN L. JONES
PALERMO – John L. Jones, 85 of Palermo, passed away at his home on Saturday October 3, 2026. John was the son of the late Dana Jones and Dorothy Sabins, of Fairfield Center.
John grew up in Fairfield Center and attended Fairfield schools. He worked at Pratt & Whitney Aircraft, in Connecticut, for several years before marrying Bernice in 1966 and afterward worked 20 years at Ethan Allen Furniture, in Burnham. Lastly, he worked at Wal-Mart, in Augusta, for more than 20 years.
Many remember John as the friendly greeter, working at the entrance doors during his time with Wal-Mart. John enjoyed visiting coastal Maine areas and walking and picnicking in the parks with his wife. He also enjoyed going to church, Bible study, listening to gospel music, and his favorite past time was doing search a word puzzles and playing games on his iPad.
John and Bernice were truly honored and forever grateful for the love and support they received as they recently celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary back in August.
He is survived by his wife Bernice; his son Gary and his wife Virginia Jones, of Palermo; his daughters Kelly Jones, of Waterville, and Leanne and her husband Andrew Pellerin, of Fairfield; his grandchildren Joseph Pellerin, Kaylah and her husband Jeremy Blazon, of Oakland, Abigail and her husband Chris Corey, of China, Isaac and his partner Hailey Ruest, of Fairfield; and great-granddaughter Charlotte Pellerin; his stepbrother Richard Dyer and his partner Kerry, of Searsport; and his sister Mary and her husband Jerry Sylvester, of Fairfield.
John was predeceased by his brother Dana and David Jones and sister Althea Nutt.
A private memorial and celebration of life will be held by the family.
BERTRAND J. GAUVIN
WATERVILLE – Bertrand J. Gauvin passed away peacefully on Sunday, October 18, 2026, in Augusta. Bertrand was born on February 1, 1937 to Damase and Alma Gauvin.
He was preceded in death by his parents, Damase and Alma; sisters Juliet, Dorothy, and Bertha, and his brother Ray.

RICHARD CLOUTIER
WINSLOW – Richard Cloutier, 83, of Winslow, passed away peacefully on Monday, October 19, 2026. He was born on January 26, 1943, in St. Zacharie, Province of Québec, Canada, to Romeo and Julia Cloutier.
Richard was educated in schools in St. Zacharie. He was married January 14, 1972, in St. Joseph, Québec to Gertrude Cloutier.
He was a resident of the Waterville/Winslow area for 54 years and previously lived in St. Zacharie where he grew up. He started drywalling at the age of 14, in Connecticut. He then moved to Maine to continue his drywalling career, along with building homes. Then, became a long-time business owner of a construction company and apartment rentals.
He enjoyed seeing his grandchildren. He also enjoyed working on his equipment and around the home.
He was predeceased by his wife, Gertrude Cloutier; sister, Suzanne Roy, sister, Lize Lachance, and brother, Renald Cloutier.
He is survived by his longtime companion, Evelyn Willett; a son, Rodney Cloutier and his wife Jackie, of Winslow; a daughter, Lynn Andrews and her husband Travis, of Madison; grandchildren, Aimee and Nicole Cloutier, Brandon Davis, and Jaynna Andrews; great-grandchildren, Aubree Cloutier, Emilee Cooper, Jordan Weatherspoon, Johnathan Owens, Connor Green, Madyson Whitlock; brothers Paul and Michael Cloutier; sisters Claudette Cyr and Francois Dulac; many nieces and nephews.

MARY BESS

title: Officials working to expand foster care for children in America, here’s how
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Kids sleeping in shelters, bussed between hotels, and overnights in office buildings. That’s the reality for many foster children in America.
For every 100 children in foster care, federal data shows that only 57 licenses homes are available.
In an effort to close that gap, the federal government launched a campaign in November 2025 called “A Home for Every Child.”
“When we launched this, we offered states the choice: if they joined the Home for Every Child campaign, they would get administrative relief,” said Alex Adams, assistant secretary for the administration for children and families. “We would get them out of mountains of paperwork so that they could spend more time focused on things that actually improve child welfare outcomes. They would have more time working with kids, more time working with families.
Since then, the idea to reinvent systems that recruit and retain foster families has gained nationwide momentum.
Millions of dollars in cash rewards are available to the state, territory, or tribal agency with the greatest improvement of its ratio of children to foster homes.
All 50 states, along with Washington D.C. and Puerto Rico, have signed up for the challenge. It will run until September 2027.
One of the first states to jump in was Tennessee. In total, the state would need more than 3,000 foster families to meet the goal set forth by the federal government.
But state leaders say a new approach is already working to encourage families to say yes to fostering.
Finding families in Tennessee
Kenni and Blake Cavalier are one family that opened up their home and their hearts, helping twin toddlers learn what it means to feel loved and feel safe.
“We have a home. We have stability and that right there is what these kids need,” said Blake. “So, I think that kind of flipped a switch where we’re like, we have to do it.”
After lots of prayer and conversation with other foster parents, the Cavaliers said they knew they had to step up and be part of the solution to Tennessee’s critical need for foster families.
“Something that I think really hit us was just like, we may have these excuses or these fears even, but that fear doesn’t compare to like the fear this child is probably in right now,” explained Kenni.
The state’s latest numbers show Tennessee needs an additional 3,081 foster families to meet the new federal initiative. The program seeks to establish a one-to-one ratio — one foster home for every child in foster care.
Lindsay Coleman, executive director of statewide specialized support services, said doing that “will be a challenge.”
“I think it’ll take some time. It’ll take some adjustments,” Coleman said. “But I think with the things we have in place, with continued prevention, with our new permanency team that’s looking at children trying to exit kids out of custody who don’t need to be in foster care any longer, and then with our recruitment and support efforts, I think we can get there.”
The state has developed a four-pronged plan to increase the number of foster care homes and support families:
- Prevention
  - Keeping families together and providing support services so children don’t enter foster care
- Recruitment
  - Using technology to determine where the biggest needs are for children, then heavily recruit in those areas
- Retention
  - Supporting foster families with teams that provide hands-on community support
- Transition
  - Support for youth aging out of foster care.
Coleman said the state’s plan is working, with this year’s recent quarter showing a 7% increase in foster families.
“What’s your talent? What’s your skill? What do you have to offer? What do you enjoy doing, hobbies, interests, and we can connect that to foster care,” said Tennessee Kids Belong Child Welfare Director Tiffany Kelly.
Kelly said the question for all Tennesseans right now is, “What’s your yes?”
She explained that not everyone can foster, but everyone can help, and everyone’s yes may look different — from mowing lawns to babysitting, helping with meals, laundry and more.
“All those yeses matter, and all those yeses mean that a family can really take the next step of pouring into the kids and take that time to build attachment and healing and carry the journey a little lighter,” said Kelly.
“Seeing them develop, start walking, start smiling, start talking, running around. And being able to look at them and be like, we’re giving them a safe place,” said Blake. “We’re seeing them have fun and be loved. And I think that’s really rewarding.”
Coleman said that “the community needs to know the need.”
“I think that there are lots of folks out there who are interested and willing to care for children. I just don’t think they understand or know what the need is,” said Coleman. “And so this story, hopefully, will help viewers know that we have this need for foster families and we would love for families to sign up. ...I’ve never met a foster parent who’s regretted their decision.”
Tennessee Kids Belong has a Foster-Friendly app that helps support foster families.
Businesses can sign up to give foster families discounts.
“It’s very easy for a business to sign up to be featured on the app. Our registration form takes less than five minutes for a business to sign up,” said Emily Barnes, Tennessee Kids Belong Foster Friendly Business Manager.
How to help
You don’t need to commit to being a foster parent to help children in need. State agencies and nonprofits often have volunteer opportunities available.
You can also advocate for foster children in the judicial system by becoming a court-appointed special advocate volunteer.
CASA volunteers are appointed by judges to act in the best interest of a child during the legal process of foster care.
Volunteers work with child welfare professionals, educators, and social service providers to ensure judges have all the information they need to make the most well-informed decision for each child.

title: Experts debunk claim that voting machines in Cook County, Illinois, are 'rigged'
text:
Experts debunk claim that voting machines in Cook County, Illinois, are 'rigged'
In Cook County, Illinois, a woman in a viral video said a voting machine displayed a message about her chosen candidate’s popularity.
“One of the questions was about the judges, and I picked the Republican judges,” the woman said in a TikTok post that is no longer public but is still visible on other posts that reshared it. “And once I selected one of the judges, I got a notification on the bar that said, ‘People are not typically choosing this person!’”
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
She said when she made three selections in that race, the message disappeared: “Why is my ballot telling me that who I’m picking isn’t the more popular choice? I have a problem with that.”
Popular X accounts such as Wall Street Apes and Catturd reshared her video and garnered more than a million views. The accounts reposting it said it’s evidence of election fraud.
“According to the Illinois State Board of Elections’ Voting Systems Equipment Log, Dominion is listed as both the equipment vendor and support vendor for their voting machines and has their contract,” read the caption of the Wall Street Apes’ X post with 1.4 million views. “It’s RIGGED.”
A Cook County election official responded to fraud claims, saying voting machines don’t give information about a candidate’s popularity with voters. Instead, voting machines give alerts when people don’t make all available selections in a race, known as an undervote.
Machines notify voters when they don’t make all available selections
The woman in the video said she lives in Streamwood and that she voted early in Cook County.
Although she said she “picked the Republican judges,” Sally Daly, deputy clerk of communications at the Cook County Clerk’s Office, told PolitiFact in an email that there are no Republican judicial candidates on the ballot.
The woman in the video appeared to concede that and later uploaded another video saying she initially and unintentionally mentioned the wrong race. But she maintained she had received the notification she had described.
Cook County Clerk Monica Gordon, a Democrat, disputed the woman’s account about the message, calling it “false and misleading.”
“Voting equipment does not tell voters which candidates are more popular, nor does it discourage voters from selecting any particular candidate,” she wrote. “The equipment may display a notification if a voter leaves a contest blank or does not make all available selections (an undervote).”
The clerk’s office shared an image showing such a notification, which reads, “This contest is undervoted!” when a voter makes fewer selections than those available.
Gordon said the feature allows voters to review their ballots and voters are free to leave any contest blank.
“This is the only report of this type that has been brought to the Clerk’s Office attention in a jurisdiction with nearly 1.8 million registered voters,” Daly said.
Aris Garcia, Streamwood Village Clerk and a Republican, addressed the claim in a statement posted on Facebook: “We have attempted to recreate the reported message and were unable to reproduce the experience described.”
‘Undervoting’ notifications are required by federal certification standards
Cook County uses the ballot marking device ImageCast X made by Dominion Voting Systems, which was acquired by Liberty Vote, a company founded by Scott Leiendecker, a former Republican election official. President Donald Trump and his supporters have long targeted Dominion with baseless claims about election fraud.
Liberty Vote referred PolitiFact to Gordon’s statement.
When a voter selects fewer or more candidates than allowed, voting equipment gives undervote or overvote warnings.
“This is generally referred to as ‘second chance voting’ because it provides a voter a second chance to correct a potential mistake before casting and counting the ballot,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who held federal government roles in both Trump administrations and the Biden and Obama administrations.
The 2002 Help America Vote Act mandated that voting systems used in federal elections allow voters to correct any errors before casting their ballots, and notify voters if they selected more than one candidate for a single office, known as an overvote.
The U.S. Election Assistance Commission’s voluntary guidelines for testing and certifying voting systems issued in 2005 required certain systems to “indicate to the voter when no selection, or an insufficient number of selections, has been made for a contest (e.g., undervotes)” and to “notify the voter if he or she has made more than the allowable number of selections for any contest (e.g., overvotes).”
Macias said the requirements apply to devices such as the ImageCast X.
Dozens of states and the District of Columbia use aspects of the Election Assistance Commission’s guidelines, so election technology vendors typically follow those standards.
The bottom line
Viral social media posts said a woman’s account of a message displayed on a Cook County, Illinois, voting machine proves the election is “rigged.”
A Cook County election official disputed the woman’s account of a voting machine notification about a candidate’s popularity. But machines are programmed to alert voters when they don’t make all available selections in a race, known as an undervote. Federal law requires voting systems allow voters to correct any potential errors on a ballot before voting.
The account is not evidence of rigging. This claim is untrue.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Holden-area voters to decide whether to close school or risk $670K fee
text:
Voters in Holden, Clifton and Eddington will be faced with the decision to close one of the area school district’s schools at the ballot box next Tuesday.
A referendum vote in the three Regional School Unit 63 communities asks voters to approve closing the Eddington Elementary School. The elementary school is one of three school buildings in the district.
The closure would save the district $669,950 by cutting eight positions and eliminating maintenance and operating costs, according to reports from the school district. It’s unclear how the closure would change local taxes.
School districts across Maine have been proposing or approving school closures in recent years due to declining enrollment and rising costs. The proposed closure of the Eddington Elementary School is no different, but it would require all three towns to agree to consolidate. Any towns that vote against the consolidation could be faced with a $669,950 fee.
The referendum to close the school will be voted on by the three communities. If all the towns agree and the school closes at the end of this academic year, Superintendent Sheila Caldwell said students would have shorter bus rides and the chance for more collaboration.
“There are a lot of things that will be positive about it. The kids will be in closer proximity to one another, in closer proximity with all the teachers, and then the buildings are more bustling and full because all the classrooms are being utilized,” Caldwell said.
Students will be consolidated in the Holden Elementary School and Holbrook Middle School, according to the district’s plans. Bus routes will be shorter because the stop at the Eddington Elementary School won’t be necessary, Caldwell said.
The lost positions, which include two and a half full-time teachers, will not affect student education, Caldwell said.
If the closure is approved, it’s unknown what will happen with the school and surrounding land. The school board can decide what will be done with it within the parameters of state law, but those discussions haven’t happened yet, Caldwell said.
Because a majority of “yes” votes is needed in all three communities, the school would remain open if voters in just one of the three communities decide against the closure. The process to bring the referendum back to voters, which took years, could be restarted by the school board, Caldwell said.
But a “no” vote comes with a price.
If one of the three towns votes against the consolidation, that community would be assessed a $669,950 fee, the cost to keep the school open, under state law. If two communities vote against the proposal, the cost would be split between them.
Even without the fee, it’s unclear whether approving the proposal would lower taxes.
In a letter shared on social media last week, the Eddington Select Board said residents should not expect lower local taxes if the town’s school is closed.
“If school-related costs continue at their current level or are shifted elsewhere, the anticipated savings from closing the school will not materialize for local taxpayers,” the letter reads.
Eddington Town Manager Shawna Hinkley did not respond to a request for comment. The letter encourages Eddington residents to ask the district questions and review documents before voting.
Although she could not speak to how local taxes would change, Caldwell said it made sense for the school board to send the proposal to residents because the district is basically “paying double” to offer the same education that could be consolidated into fewer buildings.
“The number of students continues to decline, and the need for an additional building is really no longer necessary for us to be able to provide the quality academic and learning resources and opportunities and programs that we provide our students,” Caldwell said.

title: These Cities Have the Most Ghost Sightings in Maine
text:
These Cities Have the Most Ghost Sightings in Maine
Okay, Maine friends, I have a question. Have you ever been sitting in your house, minding your own business, when you hear a noise upstairs and suddenly decide you absolutely do NOT need to know what that was? Yeah. Same.
Well, just in time for Halloween, we've got another reason to keep the lights on.
A new ranking from search-data company Answer Socrates puts Maine at the sixth most haunted state in America per person, with a spooky score of 73 out of 100.
Maine Ranks Among the Most Haunted States in America
And apparently, we're not just making this stuff up in our heads. Maine reportedly has the most ghost sightings per person in the country, with 811 reader-submitted sightings.
We also have 2,998 cemeteries, ranking fourth per person. So, there's that.
My thoughts are that basically, we're surrounded by places where ghosts could hang out. How wonderful! And get this, do you want to know where Maine's ghost activity is supposedly happening?
Well, Sanford takes the top spot, with 27 reported sightings, followed by Auburn and Bangor.
And here's my favorite part: Maine ranks second in the country for Googling cryptids, those mysterious creatures like Bigfoot.
Even Google seems to think we're a little spooky, with searches about why Maine is so haunted pointing people toward Portland, Bangor, and Derry and yes, that the fictional town made famous by Stephen King.

The ranking is based on reported sightings, cemeteries, spooky locations, and search trends. It doesn't prove ghosts are real, obviously… but it certainly gives us something to think about.

title: CSD school committee seeks answers on bus removal, survey
text:
Questions abounded at the Community School District (CSD) school committee's Oct. 13 meeting. As reported in the Register, the board was concerned that CSD schools lacked heat or hot water for five weeks and questioned how the situation escalated. However, that wasn't the only issue brought forth.
During public comment, Michelle Bryer of Timber's Tire and Auto asked why Bus #3 was removed from her property without permission, alleging the decision was illegal.
"Whoever removed the bus did not know if that bus was safe to drive. They did not know if that (bus') work had been done, and they did not know if it was safe to put children on," she said. Additionally, Bryer said multiple bills to the school have gone unpaid.
In a post-meeting interview, Alternative Organizational Structure (AOS) 98 Superintendent Robert Kahler said the bus was removed because it required additional repairs, and the school needed it back on the road as soon as possible. Work was completed by O'Connor Auto Park in Augusta. As for the unpaid bills, the school is confirming what work was done at Timber's and what at O'Connor's to avoid double payment.
Relaying information she was given from a parent, member Stephanie Hawke had concerns about a 12-year-old student on an Individualized Education Program (IEP) who participated in a survey that allegedly went out to BRES students with questions about sexuality and pronouns.
"Why are kids being asked to fill that out when they should be talking about other things? ... That's not what we're here for," she said.
Kahler told the Register he is compiling more in-depth information for the board. However, in sum, these were anonymous surveys related to participating in and using grant funds. Students are not required to take the surveys and, if they do, they don't have to answer all the questions. The school also doesn't get individual responses, only a summary.
During discussion on the Sept. 8 minutes, board member Tom Perkins asked if his prior "yes" vote allowing Kahler to accept donations for the BRES renovations on behalf of the board could be changed, explaining he felt "coerced" into making the decision unanimous. Otherwise, he'd vote "no" on accepting the minutes.
The CSD is taking donations to meet the about $7 million funding gap caused by the lawsuit delay and rising material/labor costs. If a naming request is attached to the donation, the matter will go to the board for approval.
While fairly certain the deadline to change a vote had passed, Kahler said he'd double-check. The board tabled the minutes.
On Election Day, there will be a survey for voters regarding Boothbay Region High School's future, and what options residents want to see explored. The board discussed providing as much additional information as possible, so people can make an informed decision based on cost comparisons and other factors.
The CSD received $19,760 from the state, since reported data shows that more than 40% of students were found to be economically disadvantaged. Chair Jenn Whitney highlighted this reimbursement as one benefit of families filling out the Economic Status Form sent out in early September.
BRES recently received a $5,000 grant from Education Boothbay for PreK-first grade curriculum materials to support the new “4ME” curriculum that focuses on theme-based, hands-on, community-based learning. The Mildred H. McEvoy Foundation gave a $150,000 grant to continue developing creative play opportunities for the PreK to second grade playground.
BRES Principal Shawna Kurr clarified that the McEvoy grant's purpose is to address urgent needs in the lower playground, such as making it Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliant. Meanwhile, the upper playground for older students will be moved and rebuilt due to renovations.
The board did a second read of several policies: IEPs, Child Abuse or Neglect Reporting, Prevention and Education, Procedure for Reporting Child Abuse, and Use of Physical Restraint. Temperature Standards for Schools was moved back to first read. Policies on public comment at board meetings and automated external defibrillators also went through a first read.

title: Widow searches for lost wedding ring when husband dies 3 days after getting married in Las Vegas
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) — A South Dakota woman is asking for help finding the wedding ring her husband lost in Las Vegas the night they married.
Tammy Bishop and Will Mulroy were married Oct. 20 at the Viva Las Vegas Chapel.
Bishop said they celebrated on a party bus and toured the Strip. At a bar, though, she says Mulroy looked down and realized his ring was gone.
“We got to a bar. He looked down and his band was gone. He lost it. He started crying,” Bishop said.
According to Bishop, he told her the ring was two sizes too big because he had lost weight.
She said the ring may have slid off on the bus or while he moved into his wheelchair. It may also have come off while he rolled down the Strip.
“We backtracked our steps. We told the bus driver. We had everyone looking. We couldn’t find it,” she said.
The next day, she joked with him: “You didn’t even have your ring on for 24 hours and you lost it.”
Everyone laughed, she said.
“I said it’s not a big deal; we will buy you a new one, but now that he is gone it is a big deal to me,” Bishop said.
Sadly, Bishop said Mulroy died just three days after their wedding.
She said he was in a lot of pain on the way home and mentioned going to the ER as soon as they returned to South Dakota.
The next morning, he was so congested that she told him not to go to work.
Bishop said she couldn’t wake him and called 911. She said doctors declared him brain dead at the hospital. He was on life support for 24 hours. His heart stopped three times in the ER.
“It just doesn’t make sense. When we started dating, that’s when the accident happened, then we got married, and it’s hard,” Bishop said.
Bishop and Mulroy met in July 2023 and began officially dating in March 2024.
However, a week later, Mulroy was in a motorcycle accident and became paralyzed.
“There was a lot of anger at first,” Bishop said.
Mulroy kept asking her to marry him. And this summer, she said yes.
On her Oct. 4 birthday, Bishop said he told her he had planned a Vegas wedding, everything was booked, and her friends were going.
“It was a perfect day,” Bishop said. “He was on cloud nine,” she said.
The groom’s party and bride’s party got ready separately. Mulroy first saw Bishop in her dress when she walked out to the party bus.
“It was pretty cool,” she said.
Bishop remembers Mulroy as a hands-on guy.
“He was very savvy, very mechanically inclined, could fix things, just that guy,” she said. “He didn’t have to call other guys to get stuff done.”
He worked at Fleet Farm and had worked with party buses in the past. The couple had decided to start their own party bus business.
Now, Bishop hopes a stranger finds the ring.
“It would mean a lot. The rings were blessed, and that was our wedding ring, and that was him and how much it meant to him. That’s why it means so much to me,” she said.
