title: For politics, what is an October surprise?
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - An October surprise is an event that could shake up an election, but does it often make the difference?
Matt Dallek, a professor of political management at George Washington University, described it as “an event that, at least in theory, has the potential to shake up an election, something that people did not foresee coming that upends the debate.”
He said the term dates back to around the 1980 election, when President Jimmy Carter failed to secure the release of American hostages being held in Iran before November 4, 1980, election day. Carter lost to Republican rival Ronald Reagan.
Several surprises have occurred in the years since.
Surprises can be driven by a campaign or by news events. Examples include Iran-Contra-related indictments in 1992 and the global financial collapse in 2008.
Dallek said those surprises likely did not change the outcome of the election that November.
“There’s no evidence that they flip a dynamic that was already in place,” Dallek said. “What’s more typical is that an event occurs, it dominates the news cycle and the trend line starts to move further toward the candidate who was already doing well, who was already likely to prevail.”
One exception was the Comey letter. In 2016, less than two weeks before the election, then-FBI Director James Comey wrote a letter informing Congress the FBI had received new information concerning the email investigation into Hillary Clinton.
Days before Election Day, Comey wrote another letter saying the new information did not change previous conclusions in the investigation.
“It became a big news story,” Dallek said. “And it rekindled the impression, at least for some voters, it cemented this idea that she was corrupt. She was hiding something. It reminded people of her email scandal.”
Dallek said the closest thing to an October surprise this year may be the much-talked-about ad in the Ohio governor’s race. Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy tracked down his rival’s estranged mother. The ad uses the mother of his opponent, Amy Acton (D), to attack her.
The full impact of that ad will not be known until the votes are counted.

title: 100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County Maine selects CHiP as major donation recipient
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Oct. 6, more than 200 local women gathered at Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens to socialize, network and share joy. During the meeting, names for three nominated nonprofits were drawn at random: CHiP, Mainely Memory Foundation, and Healthy Lincoln County. After hearing brief presentations about each organization, members voted to award the quarterly “Impact Donation” to CHiP (Community Housing Improvement Project), an organization dedicated to “neighbors helping neighbors stay safe, warm and dry” by assisting with seasonal fuel and firewood assistance, urgent home repairs, wheelchair and accessibility ramps—all while lifting spirits and giving neighbors hope.
The meeting netted an initial contribution to CHiP of $18,011, and the total will grow until the next quarterly meeting in January. Project Manager Brittany Gill of CHiP stated, “This is coming just in time for heating season and I already have 40 people who are really eager to get help so it’s really nice to get finances to help us go into this season confidently. We really appreciate the women who come out and want to support their community because this is such a community-based effort. We can’t do this alone; we have to do this together.”
Mainely Memory Foundation and Healthy Lincoln County went home with just over $1,000 each thanks to funds raised from the raffle. The meeting also provided an opportunity to present Lincoln County Dental with a check for $18,294 resulting from the July meeting. Director of Development Holly Stover addressed the crowd regarding the impact the donation will make toward sustaining and improving oral health for so many in our community.
The local chapter of 100+ Women Who Care operates exclusively on a donation basis led by the volunteer leadership team comprised of Leah Bauer, Kate Elmes, Shannon Parker, Alyssa Allen, Ali Stevenson and Jessica Tindal. Together, the team gathers support from local businesses to host quarterly meetings, food and raffles. October’s meeting would not have been possible without the donation of space from Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens (CMBG), with special thanks to Gretchen Ostherr, president and CEO of the gardens for her imaginative and eager support. After one year in existence, membership in 100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County stands strong with over 400 women.
Financial support for “100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County Maine” has arrived from local businesses including Tindal & Callahan Real Estate; Bangor Savings Bank; Jordan Construction; Damariscotta Region Chamber of Commerce; The Cheney Financial Group; First National Wealth Management; Mid-Maine Millwork; Social Graze Charcuterie, Coastal Maine Popcorn and a handful of anonymous donors. Raffle items have raised over $6,000 for local non-profits and include donations by Fiction Bookshop in Wiscasset; Veggies to Table in Nobleboro; The Tipsy Butler Inn in Newcastle; Moose Crossing in Waldoboro; Frances Perkins Center in Newcastle; The Waldo Theatre in Waldoboro; Creative art by Deb Arter, Shannon Parker, Felicity Myers and Alistair McCallum; Skidhompha Public Library; Du Jardin, and Waterstruck Wellness in Newcastle; Adrienne Zahner with Sotheby's; Local Batch Kitchen in Damariscotta; Ocean Blue Fitness in Damariscotta, and Morning Dew Farm in Newcastle.
Lincoln County’s 100+ Women chapter has set a target of raising $100,000 by the end of 2026 and are currently within a few thousand of reaching that benchmark. Readers are encouraged to inquire about how to contribute to help our community reach this impactful goal.
Want to participate in “100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County Maine”? Membership forms and nomination forms are available on the organization’s website at WomenWhoCareLincolnCountyMaine.org.
The next quarterly meeting is scheduled for Tuesday, Jan. 5 from 5 to 7 p.m. at Bigelow Laboratory in East Boothbay. As with all meetings, attendees can expect light bites, refreshing drinks and inspiring company. The organization hopes you’ll join “100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County Maine” for vibrant and diverse gatherings that prove there’s strength in numbers. Because together we are a wave of change.

title: MaineDOT grant won't save transit services for low-income riders in Cumberland County
text:
Transportation services for low-income riders in Cumberland County still being cut despite new grant
The Regional Transportation Program (RTP), a service based in Westbrook that provides services to people throughout Cumberland County, says a grant from the Maine Department of Transportation will not prevent previously-announced cuts to services for low-income riders.
In early October, RTP said the Maine Department of Health and Human Services cut its 2027 funding for low-income transportation in half.
RTP said its funding from the state went from $296,220 in 2026 to $147,739 in 2027. RTP said that money pays directly for rides, especially for income-eligible residents throughout Cumberland County who have no other means of transportation.
In 2025–2026, RTP provided more than 14,000 low-income trips under this program.
In early October, Maine DHHS told Maine's Total Coverage it was restructuring the Social Services Block Grant (SSBG) and Community Services Block Grant (CSBG) into one contract to align all low-income programming and that funding was allocated based on federal poverty data.
Don Libby, Executive Director of RTP, said RTP expected to make several changes to low-income transportation services starting on Jan. 1, 2027. Those changes include reducing the number of shopper shuttles, capping the number of rides available for medical appointments, capping the number of low-income rides each person can get, and reducing service hours.
On Monday, Oct. 25, the Maine Department of Transportation (MaineDOT) announced grants to eight different agencies across Maine, including RTP, to support transit operators.
The grant to RTP is $180,000 for microtransit service. Libby said that grant is specifically to run a regional microtransit in the rural Lakes Region.
"It will help RTP but the funding is not going to help the low-income riders of Cumberland County," Libby told Maine's Total Coverage. "The low-income riders, especially dialysis patients, need funding for service to mostly Portland for medical appointments and this new funding is targeted outside Portland."
MaineDOT awarded grants totaling $1 million to agencies across the state as well as $500,000 for priority public transportation projects in the Midcoast Region and the Lewiston-Auburn to Portland commuter bus service.
In previous years, MaineDOT had $2 million to award, but that amount was reduced this year due to department-wide budget constraints.
MaineDOT also awarded grants to:
- Aroostook Regional Transportation System: $174,230 to support workforce transportation
- Bangor Community Connector: $75,000 to support driver training
- Biddeford Saco Old Orchard Beach Transit: $80,165 to support microtransit service
- Greater Portland Metro: $93,000 for equipment to remove snow at transit stops
- Kennebec Valley Community Action Program: $140,000 for trip planning technology and $5,000 for automated fare payment
- Waldo Community Action Program: $100,000 for a hybrid or electric vehicle and charging infrastructure
- Western Maine Transportation Services: $75,000 to support workforce transportation and $14,000 for vehicle location software
- York County Community Action Corporation: $63,605 to support workforce transportation

title: Whistleblower claims Brewer defense company wanted to illegally sell goods to UAE-based firm
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Brewer defense technology company accused of trying to illegally sell ballistic armor to a Middle Eastern firm allegedly retaliated against a whistleblower, a lawsuit filed this year said.
Compotech, Inc., which manufactures items like transportable military shelters for both the United States military and foreign entities, is accused of retaliating against Adrian Horn, who worked for the company in 2024, in part as an export compliance officer.
Horn sued the company in January, saying he was fired after raising concerns about Compotech not following required due diligence when selling ballistic armor panels to a company based in the United Arab Emirates. He alleges retaliation under the Maine Human Rights Act, the False Claims Act and the National Defense Authorization Act.
The relatively unknown Brewer company has made headlines this year as it is a finalist in the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Freedom 250 Patriot Pitch Competition. It also recently hosted Vice President JD Vance for a midterm election rally and has received nearly $8 million from the Department of Defense in the last decade.
Horn was fired from Compotech on Nov. 21, 2024, the day after he emailed a brief to all employees explaining export compliance regulations. Compotech said he was not a good fit for the company, according to the lawsuit, but Horn alleges that explanation was to cover up the real reason he was terminated.
The parties are discussing a settlement, according to records in the U.S. District Court of Maine in Bangor. A conference was held Tuesday, but discussions will continue as no decision was reached.
Horn wants a federal judge to say Compotech violated his rights, as well as give him double back pay and any other unspecified damages.
Compotech declined to comment on pending litigation through attorney Melinda Caterine. Horn’s attorney, Martin Tartre, did not respond to a request for comment.
Compotech was planning to sell ballistic armor panels to International Golden Group, according to the lawsuit. The company provides support services for the United Arab Emirates defense ministry and other governmental agencies, according to its website.
The United Arab Emirates was rated second highest for corruption risk through the Transparency International’s Government Defense Integrity Index, the lawsuit said.
Horn alleges that Jacques Nader, then Compotech’s chief financial officer, told Horn to stop asking the required due diligence questions about the sale.
Nader, now the CEO, allegedly told Horn that sale would be very lucrative and it needed to happen, the lawsuit said.
Court records do not say if the sale was completed.
Compotech disputes Horn’s allegations, according to court records. The due diligence questions were not required by law, and failing to follow what Horn thought was the “prudent, compliant course” doesn’t violate the law, the company said in a motion to dismiss.
The motion goes on to deny the allegations raised by Horn, saying he did not have a plausible argument to believe the company violated the law, which means the company couldn’t retaliate.
Nader didn’t tell Horn to stop due diligence, according to Compotech’s response. It said Horn was not doing his job and did not have the work ethics and experience necessary.
The motion to dismiss is pending.

title: Woman gets 30 days in jail after fake pregnancy claims involving 'Bachelor' star
text:
Woman gets 30 days in jail after fake pregnancy claims involving 'Bachelor' star
Laura Owens, an Arizona woman at the center of multiple fake pregnancy schemes involving former "Bachelor" star Clayton Echard, has been sentenced to 30 days in jail and 11 years of probation.
Owens was sentenced Friday following a roughly two-hour hearing in Maricopa County Superior Court.
Prosecutors, victims Clayton Echard and Greg Gillespie, and presentence investigators had asked Judge Jeffrey Rueter to sentence Owens to a year or more in jail.
Instead, Rueter said he did not believe Owens’ actions were part of a calculated scheme. The judge said he believed Owens was suffering from untreated mental health issues.
Owens also received 12 months of deferred jail time. If she violates probation and it is revoked, she could be ordered to serve that additional year in jail.
Owens pleaded guilty to four felonies
Owens was indicted earlier this year on 14 felony charges related to the allegations.
She ultimately pleaded guilty to four charges, including fraudulent schemes, perjury and taking the identity of another person.
The case stems from Owens’ relationships with Echard and Gillespie, whom she met in Scottsdale.
According to court proceedings, Gillespie and Owens had protected sex, while Echard said he had only oral sex with Owens during their brief relationship.
Owens later claimed she was pregnant with twins by Gillespie. She also used an ultrasound image found online and represented it as her own, according to the case.
Both men were involved in family and paternity court proceedings with Owens. Echard and Gillespie have said her actions caused them significant emotional and financial harm.
The case has been ongoing for roughly five years.
During Friday’s sentencing hearing, Owens became emotional and apologized to both men. She pleaded with the judge to keep her out of jail.
The judge ultimately ordered Owens to begin serving her 30-day sentence immediately at the Maricopa County Jail. She is expected to be released two days before Thanksgiving.
After the hearing, Echard spoke about the sentence and expressed disappointment with the judge’s decision. He said he believed the sentence did not adequately reflect the impact Owens’ actions had on him.
Gillespie was also named as a victim in the case.
The case has drawn national attention because of Echard’s previous appearance on "The Bachelor."

title: Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family land in Miami
text:
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family land in Miami
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family arrived in Miami on Wednesday after he refused to concede the election to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and fled the country.
In a circuitous journey, Bolsonaro left for Argentina on Tuesday with his wife and two daughters, then traveled to Ecuador, according to Argentine officials and flight data. The 45-year-old senator, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, visited the White House in May, and the Trump administration approved U.S. visas for him and his family this week.
Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later.
Video above: UCLA expert Bryan Pitts analyzes Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's historic runoff victory over Flávio Bolsonaro
Flávio Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court, accused of corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. The court ordered him to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.
On Wednesday, Bolsonaro issued his first comments on his flight in a statement on X, in which he called himself the victim of electoral fraud and political persecution, and again asked for the annulment of the Lula–Alckmin ticket.
“I want to tell not only my 60 million voters but also the Brazilian people as a whole that I am the president-elect, and that the criminals who stole Brazil’s election are part of a criminal organization that has established a tyranny,” he said. In a later version of the letter, Bolsonaro swapped the term “president-elect” for “leader.”
Bolsonaro lands in Miami
Dressed casually in a dark polo shirt and flanked by his wife and two daughters, Bolsonaro stepped out of the plane shortly after it landed in Miami at about 9:30 a.m. EDT. Florida is home to the largest population of Brazilians in the U.S.
The family fled Brazil late Tuesday, entered Argentina via a border checkpoint and quickly boarded a private charter plane, Argentine immigration officials said.
Flightradar24 showed the plane believed to be carrying Bolsonaro landed in Guayaquil, Ecuador, about 4 a.m. local time, then took off minutes later for Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport.
Before the family landed in Florida, Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, spoke to dozens of supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia.
“I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true,” Lula said. “This act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”
Bolsonaro’s route through Argentina could deepen diplomatic tensions between Lula’s government and Argentine President Javier Milei, another Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to assist in Bolsonaro’s campaign.
Milei has not commented directly about Bolsonaro's defeat, but Juan Pablo Carreira, a presidential spokesperson, said on social media that Milei's administration rescued Bolsonaro “from the claws of communism, which seeks to imprison all opposition figures.”
Representatives of Brazil's government have not responded to requests for comment.
Trump questions Brazilian election results
Trump has said Bolsonaro is welcome in the U.S., calling him and his family “fine people.”
“The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on Tuesday. Earlier, Trump also said, without evidence, that the election was “rigged.”
When asked about Bolsonaro’s assertion on Wednesday that he was the “rightful president-elect of Brazil” — a term the defeated candidate later softened to “leader of Brazil” — the U.S. president said he would not comment. Instead, Trump said he has given Bolsonaro a “pass” to come into the country.
“I won’t get involved,” Trump said, before repeating his claim that the election was “very strange."
Leaders around the world and the Organization of American States have endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round.
The U.S. has imposed double-digit sanctions on Brazil, which boasts Latin America’s largest economy. Lula has championed Brazil’s long tradition of nonalignment, cultivating ties with competing powers. His government has deepened trade ties with China and sought greater global influence through BRICS, a group of emerging economies.
Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving Brazil
Brazil's Supreme Court ordered the defeated candidate to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received the order outside the home where his father is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for his attempted coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.
A Brazilian diplomat, who was not authorized to speak about the matter publicly, told The Associated Press that Bolsonaro used an Italian passport to enter Argentina and that Brazilians leaving the country via a land border are not scrutinized by Brazilian authorities.
The diplomat said Brazil’s federal police were not monitoring Bolsonaro when he left his home in Brasilia because the Supreme Court had not issued a warrant for his arrest.
Flávio Bolsonaro said in a video Monday that he was attempting to organize opposition to the election results among his congressional colleagues. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027. His Liberal Party released a statement saying it accepted the election results.
Brazil's Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker. Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing.

title: 200 passengers stranded after US cruise ship suspends yearslong global voyage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia (AP) — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said.
Those on the ship had hoped to sail for years to come
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said. “We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement.”
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
For some, the venture was a risk worth taking
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn’t outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
“I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it’s a dream to live on the ship and I don’t want it to end,” Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn’t need to use a cane to walk anymore. “You come to this ship to live … it’s just sad that it’s all over.”
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship’s woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn’t regret her investment.
“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.
The cruise began in Northern Ireland in 2024
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship’s operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia’s then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.
——-
Associated Press writers Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Grant Peck in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: New Italian restaurant coming to Wells
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Veteran Maine restaurateurs plan to open an Italian restaurant in Wells this November.
Posta is slated to open by mid-November at 60 Mile Road, according to co-owner Ian Miller. The space had briefly hosted Battery Steele Kitchen + Bar, and was also the longtime home of Varano’s Ristorante Italiano.
“We haven’t had an iteration of an Italian restaurant in Wells since Varano’s closed (about four years ago),” said Miller. “We felt it fitting to revive that in that building to fit the need of the area.”
Miller and his partner, Morey Highbarger, own and operate seven other Maine restaurants, including Cape Neddick Lobster Pound, three locations of Pepper’s Landing, and Signal in Kennebunk. Miller said Posta is named for a hotel in Livorno, Italy, that Highbarger’s family used to run.
Posta will be a traditional American red sauce-style Italian restaurant, with a menu featuring items like chicken parmesan, chicken piccata, salmon puttanesca, meatballs, T-bone steak, cacio e pepe pasta, lasagna, linguine and clams and build-your-own pasta dishes. Downstairs, in a section they refer to as The Grotto, the restaurant will offer subs, salads and Neapolitan-style pizzas with toppings like pepperoni cups with hot honey, and Hawaiian-style with spicy capicola.
Posta will have a full bar serving cocktails, 10 draft beers and an Italian-leaning wine list. Posta has seating for about 100, with another 40 seats on the downstairs Grotto level.
The restaurant will be open seven days. The Grotto will be open from 11:30 a.m. until 9 p.m., while Posta will open 4-9 p.m.

title: Death toll from train collision in central Spain rises to 64, authorities say
text:
High-speed train collision kills at least 68 in Spain’s 2nd deadly rail crash this year
A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks in Spain Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January.
“Today all of Spain is grieving,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the central province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.
A train operated by the state-owned RENFE company struck the rear of another train operated by private company IRYO that had stopped. The collision derailed two cars in a rural area between two villages.
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
“People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought,” until emergency services arrived, he said. “As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg.”
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Before this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992.
Transport minister says crash was due to ‘inexplicable’ decision
Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a “stop signal” active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
“I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts,” Puente said.
Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers focused on rescuing survivors and bodies from the most damaged train cars.
“It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy,” García said.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
“We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact,” he said. “The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.”
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
Authorities said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has “activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities.”
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, said civil protection authorities asked his officials to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers.
A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.
Spain’s King Felipe VI also visited the crash site. He and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were closely following the news.
“We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected," the royals said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “My heart goes out to the victims’ families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you.”
Spain's soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.
Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when an IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
The January incident had already shaken confidence in the country's extensive high-speed rail service. Rail officials responded by promising more maintenance and reducing the maximum speed of the high-speed trains.
Spain is a leader in high-speed rail
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country’s railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.
Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”
___
Wilson reported from Barcelona, Spain. Teresa Medrano contributed from Madrid.

title: Read the poem ‘First Frost along the Sebasticook’ by Dana Holley Maloney
text:
In this week’s poem, “First Frost along the Sebasticook,” Dana Holley Maloney shares a transcendent moment under the morning sky, then meditates on the euphoria and larger wholeness of the encounter. I love this poem’s luminous imagery of light through mist, and its quiet conclusion with an image of frost on vines — another incarnation of the mist, and of the wholeness.
Maloney teaches English at Montclair State University in New Jersey. Her poems have previously appeared in Lips, North Dakota Quarterly, Killing the Angel, English Journal, and Journal of New Jersey Poets. At Duke University, she received the Anne Flexner Award for Poetry. When not in New Jersey, she lives in Freeport.
Poets, please note that submissions to Deep Water are open now and through the end of the year. Deep Water is especially eager to share poems by Black writers, writers of color, indigenous writers, LGBTQ+ writers, and other underrepresented voices. Submit your credits at mainewriters.org/deep-water
First Frost along the Sebasticook
Benton, Maine
Because I turned east toward it, I was on
the bridge when swallowed into spectacle. Light
exploded white in fog that rose above the river.
Refracted, splintered even, by what was wholly
hidden behind mist. Pure shards—a monochromatic
composition—seemed sent by some diamond
in the sky. Words spilled out of me, addressed to
whomever might hear me struck by The Sublime
that mid-September morning while en route
to the Common Ground Country Fair. But by
“my god” what did I mean? Some marriage of earth
and ether? Nothing strictly masculine.
That same day in Unity, ice crystals wilted
tender vines, leaving green gourds far from orphaned.
– Dana Holley Maloney
Megan Grumbling is a poet and writer who lives in Portland. title: 'GOURD TIMES': Watch as sea otters go 'Pumpkin Dunkin' in a zoo's adorable Halloween tradition
text:
'Otterly' adorable video: Sea otters go 'Pumpkin Dunkin' in a zoo's adorable Halloween tradition
Trick or treat? These otters chose "Pumpkin Dunkin'."
An "otterly" adorable video shared by The Oregon Zoo shows sea otters getting into the Halloween spirit, one tiny pumpkin at a time.
As part of a fall-themed enrichment activity, the otters slam-dunk miniature pumpkins through a rock formation resembling a basketball hoop.
With fall in the air, the leaves changing and spooky season in full swing, the "Pumpkin Dunkin" activity was worked into the otters' regular training to stay healthy and active, the zoo, which is located in Portland, Oregon, said.
And animal lovers and zoo patrons love the activity so much that it's become an annual Halloweentime event.
And the otters aren't the only ones getting in on the autumn fun.
The zoo shared videos of a polar bear, elephants, ring-tailed lemurs and a beaver enjoying their own gourd-filled enrichment, from gnawing and smashing pumpkins to swimming with them.

Three more Aroostook County girls soccer teams are moving on after convincing victories in Tuesday's regional quarterfinals.
Houlton scored seven goals against Central, Fort Fairfield shut out Washburn, and Wisdom put six goals on the board against George Stevens Academy.

title: NH man charged in Maine interstate hit-and-run that injured road worker
text:
A driver who allegedly injured a road worker in a construction zone on Interstate 95 in Pittsfield earlier this month has been identified and charged, Maine State Police said Wednesday.
Jonathan McDonald, 22, of Laconia, New Hampshire, has been issued a summons with charges in three categories: accidents involving death or personal injury, driving to endanger, and accident reports.
The incident happened on the morning of Oct. 14 in a single-lane construction zone in Pittsfield.
A silver pickup truck hauling a black dump trailer hit a concrete Jersey barrier. The truck then hit an orange construction barrel on the right side of the road that was knocked into 56-year-old Richard Smart of Westfield, who was working for Northeast Construction unloading Jersey barriers.
Smart was taken to Northern Light Sebasticook Valley Hospital with serious injuries and later released.
The male driver of the pickup, later identified as McDonald, continued north without stopping, according to police, who said witnesses reported seeing him turn around inside the truck as the crash occurred then speed away.

title: Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader, feminist and civil rights icon, dies at 96
text:
Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation’s fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase “Sí, se puede!” that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta’s family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.
She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women’s rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.
Huerta’s resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to “Yes, it can be done” — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.
Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.
This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement’s co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died.
From the early 1970s on, Huerta’s life partner was Richard Chavez, César’s brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.
Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life’s work and unravel all the progress made for workers.
When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: “It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I’ll say it that way.”
Homegrown activism
Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who went on to win a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.
Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.
Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students’ poor living conditions.
“I couldn’t stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes,” she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. “I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children.”
Huerta’s early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.
She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year “Delano Grape Strike.” With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers.
Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.
On the campaign trail
She met U.S. Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and became a volunteer on his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her moments before he was shot.
The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing for farmworkers’ rights.
Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating. In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush’s opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco.
Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer’s baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims.
After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus and hit the road to campaign for women’s rights and encourage Latinas to run for office.
She also campaigned for Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden. California Gov. Gavin Newsom considered her a close friend.
Fueled by courage
Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores’ 13 children, once pointed to his mom’s courage during an interview, saying it was one of the most significant drivers of her life’s work.
“To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farmworkers, to take on agriculture, which to this today is still a powerhouse. … That took a lot of guts,” he had said.
Huerta learned the art of lobbying politicians. She secured financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farmworkers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and fought federal guest worker programs.
By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass what would be the first state law recognizing farmworkers’ right to collective bargaining.
Her work earned her many accolades. She was the first Latina to be inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame and she’s received nine honorary doctorates from U.S. universities.
Schools are named in her honor in California, Texas and Colorado. Her image graces many murals, and streets bear her name, but she didn’t always win favor with more liberal activists.
In 2016 when she endorsed Hillary Clinton instead of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont in the presidential Democratic primary, actor Rosario Dawson — a Sanders supporter who played Huerta in a 2014 movie about César Chavez — said Huerta had become “an instrument of the establishment.”
Dawson and Huerta eventually reconciled.
Guitarist Carlos Santana later oversaw a documentary based on Huerta’s life after the pair had a late-night conversation about music while in Hawaii. Santana, a Miles Davis fan, discovered Huerta was a huge fan of bebop legend Charlie Parker.
“I even met Charlie Parker. That’s my claim to fame,” Huerta joked during an interview with The Associated Press when she was 87.
It was her work as a leader within the labor movement that reverberated through the U.S. and beyond, making her name synonymous with civil rights. In the 2025 documentary “Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta,” she recounted her decades-long journey in activism and talked about the inspiration she drew from the women’s movement during the 1970s, saying it provided validation that she too could stand on the stage with other labor leaders.
“I hope that my legacy will be one of an organizer that organized to fight injustice,” she said in the film. “We want to give our children an inheritance of justice, right, not jewels or property or money because they’ll just fight over it. So the main thing to do is to give them this love for justice — and that is the greatest gift I think that any of us can have.”
___
Associated Press journalist Brian Melley contributed to this report. Former AP journalist Russell Contreras also contributed reporting previously for this story.

title: New Mexico man risks life to save families from floodwaters: 'I jumped in'
text:
New Mexico man risks life to save families from floodwaters: 'I jumped in'
As floodwaters swept through a New Mexico neighborhood, a homeless man risked his life to warn families and help others escape the danger.
Joseph Barrela, who has been homeless for about three years and living beneath a bridge for months in New Mexico's Bloomfield neighborhood, went door to door waking up families and warning them about the rising water.
"We were actually sleeping inside, and then Joseph Barrela, he came and knocked on the door, pounded, made sure he waited here till we were awake," Lonnie Campbell said.
Campbell said Barrela’s warning made all the difference.
"We were able to save vehicles. Our dogs, our dogs would have been underwater. My grandparents got out in time, I was able to get them out," Campbell said.
Barrela had been observing the rising water levels days prior to the extreme flooding.
"The water was already coming up over the bank, many people didn’t notice that but I did," Barrela said.
Even after neighbors evacuated, Barrela continued checking on homes.
"Across the street where your neighbors are, the water is already in their backyard, and when it rains it climbs fast," Barrela said.
Barrela’s efforts didn’t stop there. He spotted a semi-truck surrounded by floodwaters with its lights flashing and believed someone was inside.
"After I evacuated the neighborhood, I jumped in and tried to help that truck, and I got swept away and almost died," Barrela said.
Caught in the current, Barrela called out for rescue before finding something to hold onto. He turned to prayer in the moment.
"At that time, it was time to ask, ‘Holy Heavenly Father, please forgive me for anything I did at this moment,’" Barrela said. "I know that you can forgive me eternally and save my eternal soul. But tonight, can you please save my flesh?"
His prayers were answered when help arrived.
"I got rescued, and from there I was able to come over here and help more and help around a little bit more," Barrela said.
Now, Barrela is volunteering at First Baptist Church in Bloomfield, assisting other flood victims. While his neighbors call him a hero, Barrela credits someone else.
"No, God’s the hero. I don’t like to hear it because God is the hero. He’s the one that gives us strength," Barrela said.
For San Juan County, New Mexico residents still recovering from the flooding, information on resources and recovery assistance can be found through the county’s Office of Emergency Management.

title: Tom Jones postpones tour dates to recover from illness
text:
'I look forward to seeing you all soon': Tom Jones postpones tour dates over health issues
Singer Sir Tom Jones has announced that he's postponed multiple upcoming shows in California due to an ongoing illness.

"I've had a great time these last few weeks, completing 20 shows and singing for wonderful audiences across the USA," the 86-year-old Welsh crooner said in a post on his Instagram account on Monday. "I've been hit with a bad case of the flu. Following doctor's advice, I unfortunately have to reschedule tonight's show in Los Angeles and tomorrow's show in San Diego."

title: Special master could evaluate DOJ claim of 20,000 noncitizens on California voter rolls
text:
Los Angeles (AP) — A federal judge on Tuesday said he was considering appointing a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that California has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls and to determine whether counties would be able to separate any ballots belonging to ineligible voters.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was overseeing a hearing in a lawsuit filed by the Justice Department, which is seeking to prevent California from counting ballots from thousands of people it alleges are noncitizens.
Carter said it would be too rushed to make a decision without an independent special master who could evaluate the substance of both sides’ claims. He said that could be completed before the state’s Dec. 11 deadline to certify the election results.
It is not clear what would happen if a special master did find a substantial number of noncitizen voters on the federal government’s list or whether it would affect the certification of California’s election results. The 20,000 people on the DOJ’s list constitute only a small fraction of California’s 23 million voters.
The judge said he wanted to vet the federal government’s list. He emphasized his concerns that siding with the federal government at this stage could mean illegally making substantial changes to election procedure while voting is underway.
But he said the special master also could investigate California’s claims that it could not logistically separate the ballots in time for the election certification deadline in December, an assertion the federal government has contested.
Voting has been well underway for weeks in California in the midterm election that concludes next Tuesday. Alleged voting by noncitizens has been a key focus of President Donald Trump’s administration with control of Congress at stake, though available data indicates occurrences are exceedingly rare.
The Republican administration sued election officials in California in mid-October, accusing them of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review its list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.
The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn’t win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the nation’s Capitol.
Judge issues warning not to threaten election workers
Although Carter said he was open to appointing a special master, he said he will not issue an official order until Wednesday.
The judge rarely spoke throughout the hearing, but he did express skepticism about why the federal government was suing California rather than seeking to address alleged noncitizen voting through criminal prosecutions. He referenced the federal government’s recent arrest in October of 28 people across California accused of illegally registering to vote.
“You got a remedy for goodness sakes — go out and indict,” Carter said from the bench.
Prosecutors with the federal government argued that the U.S. had an interest in preventing noncitizens from voting in the first place.
“Our goal is not to prosecute tens of thousands of people. It’s to safeguard the election,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.
Carter also seemed to respond to warnings that local county clerks who don’t heed the federal government’s demands could be criminally prosecuted.
“This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately,” Carter said before abruptly leaving the courtroom.
Federal prosecutor says US government seeks to ‘safeguard’ the election
Essayli argued Tuesday that the Justice Department’s demands would not significantly disrupt the ongoing election.
“We have not asked to void any ballots,” he said. Instead, the government was seeking to “work with” California officials to “safeguard” the election.
He said testimony would explain how the government’s list of 20,000 names was compiled.
“The case rises and falls on the credibility” of the flagged names, he told the judge, arguing the state has an obligation to investigate before counting those voters’ ballots.
California officials previously argued that once a completed mail ballot is returned, it is separated from the envelope that contains voters’ identification. That would make it impossible to separate ballots that have already been submitted, the state said. More than 3 million ballots have already been returned.
Lawyers for California warn of delays and disruptions
Lawyers for California and Los Angeles County said the federal government has not specified how or when it obtained the voter file, leaving open the possibility the list was inaccurate or outdated. They specifically questioned the government’s reliance on a private, third-party service to determine Social Security numbers used in their effort.
M. Patrick Moore, a lawyer for the Los Angeles County registrar’s office, also argued that the county would cooperate if the federal government wanted to criminally prosecute noncitizens who illegally voted.
“If an individual who is a noncitizen votes, there will be record of that, and the county will provide that record” to the federal courts, Moore said in court Tuesday.
He added that if the federal government believes the election was compromised, there are legal processes for contesting the outcome.
Tuesday’s hearing largely revolved around the reliability of the federal government’s list. Los Angeles County officials found that a small sample of people on it were indeed citizens.
The federal agent who conducted the investigation — which required roughly 800 federal employees who manually checked each name — said in an affidavit that the county’s findings were false. The filing did concede that some names could have been mistakenly included.

title: Beth A. Barter
text:
Beth Ann York Barter, Boothbay, passed away Sept. 27, 2026 at the age of 57.
Beth was born on Sept. 24, 1969. She grew up in Bristol, Maine, and graduated from Lincoln Academy. In 1995, Beth began her nursing career, starting a lifelong journey dedicated to caring for others.
Beth was a wholehearted, compassionate, and generous woman who gave love freely to everyone around her. She had a natural desire to help others and a kindness that reached far beyond her own family. Throughout her life, she dedicated herself to taking care of those in need, working in Home Health care and spending many years serving her community as an EMT in Boothbay, Maine. Beth loved her work, but more importantly, she loved the people she cared for. Helping others was more than a job to her; it was a reflection of who she was. She touched many lives through her compassion, generosity, and willingness to be there for anyone who needed her.
Above all, Beth cherished her family. She loved spending time with those closest to her. Throughout Brogan and Madison’s childhood, Beth traveled to countless sports games and practices, cherishing every moment she shared with them and supporting them in all they did. These memories, along with the time she shared with her family, were among the many things that brought her joy. Beth most especially enjoyed watching women’s basketball with her daughter, Madison; and always cooking enough dinner for an army. She was an amazing cook. Beth’s love extended to her friends and her community, where she was loved by many and will be remembered for her big heart, caring nature, and the difference she made in the lives of others.
Beth is survived by her husband, Samuel Barter; her daughter, Madison Barter; her son, Brogan Barter; her aunt Joan Smyrski; and her mother, Colleen Leonard. She also leaves behind many beloved family members and friends whose lives were made better by knowing her.
She was predeceased by her father, Clifton York; her brother, Shawn York; her grandmother, Elaine Trask; and her aunt, Janet Grondin.
Beth’s life was one of love, kindness, and selflessness toward others. She had a heart that always made room for one more person, a willingness to help without hesitation, and a gift for making others feel cared for. Though she will be deeply missed by her family, friends, and community, the love she gave and the lives she touched will remain a lasting part of her legacy. The family wishes to thank the people who donated to the Go Fund Me for us.

title: Lily Robbins Comes Home To Searsmont After Months Of Burn Treatment Following The Robbins Lumber Fire
text:
Waldo County EMT, Whose Father Died From Burns He Received During Mill Explosion, Is Finally Coming Home After Her Hospital Stay
It's been an incredibly trying year for Waldo County community, especially first responders, their families, and those connected to the family business, Robbins Lumber.
Lily Robbins checks both those boxes; the young woman was a local EMT, and her family owned and managed the mill.
After a massive fire and explosion took place at the Robbins Lumber mill this past May, a dozen firefighters and personnel were injured, among them Lily, her father, 51-year-old Alden J. Robbins who was the co-owner and Vice President of Sales at the mill, and her uncle Jim Robbins, the other co-owner. Alden Robbins eventually succumbed to his injuries and passed away in July, after battling for months on a specialized burn unit at Mass General.
The incident also claimed the lives of 2 firefighters, 27-year-old Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross, 76-year-old Wayne Woodbury who was the Assistant Fire Chief in Searsmont.
Read More: NIOSH Report On Robbins Lumber Fire
Local and Federal investigators spent weeks looking into the incident, which was ultimately classified as an accident. The mill was able to reopen about a month later.
Read More: Robbins Lumber Company: Recovery After A Devastating Fire In Maine
Some of the injured still remain in burn units across New England as they fight to recover from their wounds. Others have recovered enough to be released, like Belmont Firefighter Katherine Paige who was released in July.
This week, the Town of Searsmont announced that yet another one of the injured, Lily Robbins, is finally ready to come home. Like her father and uncle, Lily was taken to Mass General in May, and has been receiving treatment for wounds she sustained while trying to help at the scene of the blaze. Lily was volunteering as an EMT at the time of the explosion.
This will be the first time Lily has been home since the fire and her father's death, and the town is rallying the community to give her a warm welcome.
"After a long road to recovery, we are looking forward to welcoming Lily home and celebrating this special day with our community! We would love your help making her homecoming extra special! Friday, October 30, 2026. Anyone wishing to drop off desserts, snack foods, or a handmade Welcome Home sign is welcome to bring them to the station from 9:00 am to noon, so things can be all set up for that afternoon."
They say the plan to share an updated timeline of Lily's travel route once those details are finalized.

The young woman responded to the online post with great appreciation.
"Thank you everyone! I’m so grateful for this community."
A Gofundme campaign was set up, right after the explosion occurred, to help Lily with medical bills and lost income she's sustained as a result of her injuries.
You can contribute to that effort by clicking here.
We wish Lily, her entire family, the folks at Robbins Lumber and the community of residents and EMTs from Waldo County the best as they welcome this local hero back home. And we hope for everyone's continued healing and recovery.

title: Supporting Midcoast communities on Small Business Saturday
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Next month, on Saturday, Nov. 28, Maine — along with the rest of the nation — will celebrate our locally owned shops and storefronts with Small Business Saturday.
Small Business Saturday began as an American Express initiative in 2010, and was cosponsored by the United States Small Business Administration just a year later. The day was deliberately planned around Black Friday and Cyber Monday as a way to support small, locally owned businesses and help them attract holiday customers during a time when many head to larger corporate retail stores to take advantage of deals and discounts that most family-owned businesses cannot afford to offer.
The initiative has been a huge success across the country, with people celebrating their communities by turning out to support the businesses owned by their friends and neighbors.
This event is always quite special in our district. The vibrant small businesses throughout our part of the Midcoast are the perfect places to find goods for your holiday preparations. Locations like Downtown Bath are packed with family-owned shops selling wares, services and experiences that are hard to find anywhere else. You can also find breakfast, lunch and dinner at the local cafes, delis and restaurants to keep yourself nourished throughout the day and to give yourself a chance to relax and spend time with your family and friends.
This year’s Small Business Saturday is especially exciting, as our community has a number of businesses that are either new to the area or have new ownership. Pink Parlor Studios is a dance studio that offers a variety of dance classes for adults. They are new to the Bath area and have set up their studio at 92 Oak St.
In Topsham, Knead & Nosh recently upgraded their pop-up restaurant to a brick-and-mortar location. Their storefront is located at 4 Bowdoin Mill Island (the former location of Blueberries). Their bagels have won several awards. Stop by to see what specialty pastries are available that day! Their new neighbor, Morning Moose, similarly moved from a food truck to a permanent location just around the corner at 11 Main St. There you can enjoy specialty coffee and mini donuts.
A relative newcomer to Lincoln County is the Dresden Coffee & Gallery, located at 769 Gardiner Road. They are a Polish cafe featuring coffee and baked goods that are made using locally sourced ingredients, while also utilizing their space as a gallery for local artists. It is wonderfully cozy — a perfect place to stop on your way to shop for holiday goods.
Little City Vintage is another new business that recently joined the many local businesses in Downtown Bath. Located at 4 Centre St., customers can find clothing, artwork, furniture and much more. This is a great place to find holiday gifts for friends and family while welcoming a new business to the city.
Finally, Bay Bowls of Bath is yet another restaurant that was recently purchased by new owners. They will continue serving the same delicious fruit bowls and smoothies year-round. I would like to wish them and the rest of these new businesses and owners a warm welcome to the district. I hope to visit them all very soon.
This Small Business Saturday and throughout the rest of the year, I hope you will join me in supporting our local businesses — both new and old. These shops, restaurants and studios make up the backbone of our communities. The owners and employees are our fellow community members. Helping them means they can help us in turn.
If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me for assistance. I can always be reached by email at [email protected], or you can call my office at 207-287-1515.
Sen. Denise Tepler represents Maine Senate District 24, which includes all of Sagadahoc County, plus Dresden in Lincoln County.

title: Iran War's cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
text:
Iran War's cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
The cost of the Iran War to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to a new estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. The fallout from the conflict has become a key issue in the midterm elections and could increase as President Donald Trump leaves open the possibility of renewed hostilities.
The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion.
The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week's midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump's last two years in office.
The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks. As the war's costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll.
The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal. The White House also is asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities.
Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress.
"Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. "Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House."
In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war's costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army's Patriot and THAAD systems, with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars.
The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force's costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army's are more than $2 billion. The Navy's costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September.
When asked why the Navy's cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates.
The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The Pentagon's official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or disposal of Iranian drones.
While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or "finish them off," a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. The Trump administration also has reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel.

title: Elizabeth F. Klein
text:
Elizabeth Flynt “Betsy” Klein, 82, of Wiscasset, Maine, passed away on Oct. 25, 2026, after navigating a period of declining health.
Born in Augusta, Maine, on July 17, 1944, to Barbara (Burr) and Horton Flynt, she was the youngest of three sisters. Betsy moved to Falmouth, Maine, during her elementary school years. Her social personality flourished in high school, where she was class secretary, played basketball, and graduated as salutatorian from Falmouth High School. Her love of travel blossomed during her time in Falmouth with two trips to Europe, once with the People-to-People organization and once to stay with her sister Pat and brother-in-law John for a summer.
She met her best friend and the love of her life, Earl “Skip” Klein, at the University of Connecticut. They eloped on Nov. 6, 1965, after coordinating family dynamics proved to be too much of a hassle for a wedding. After welcoming a daughter, they made their longtime home in West Hartford, Connecticut, where they lived until retirement. They celebrated 60 loving years of marriage before her passing.
When her children were in elementary school, Betsy returned to the workforce as secretary of the West Hartford United Methodist Church and then returned to her medical assistant training during her children’s high school years. She was incredibly proud of her time as the administrative assistant to the Head of the Infectious Disease Department at the University of Connecticut Medical School.
Betsy spent time growing up with her family in Ocean Point, Maine. She and Skip were able to purchase a small cottage there early in their marriage, and it became a foundation for Betsy’s social and active lifestyle. She made best friends, played tennis, kayaked, and raised her children on the rocky shore of Maine. From the day school ended in the spring until it started in the fall, Betsy and the children spent their summers at Ocean Point, with Skip joining them on weekends.
Betsy and Skip spent 12 years after retirement “snow birding” in Tucson, Arizona. As a highly social butterfly who invented Fear of Missing Out before it became “FOMO,” she made loads of friends. She was a highly active volunteer for the Humane Society and had several “foster fail” rescues who enjoyed being spoiled by her in their senior years.
Her four grandchildren were a particularly bright spot in her life. She loved having them around as individuals and as an unruly group, often instigating shenanigans that occasionally led to tears. Sometimes hers. They all enjoyed trips without parents to Tucson or Ocean Point to enjoy “kid time” with Mammy and Grumpy.
She was predeceased by her sisters, Margaret “Peg” Haskell and Patricia “Pat” Waldman. She is survived by her husband, Skip Klein; daughter Jennifer Klein; son Peter Klein and his wife Barbara (Foote); grandchildren Jo Klein, Madeline Mazjanis and her wife Alison Murray, Jessica (Klein) Reynolds and her husband Ryan, and Peter Mazjanis; and great-grandchildren Nicholas (Nico) and James Reynolds. She loved her extended family and friends with as much fervor as she did her immediate family and had deep relationships with her brothers-in-law, nieces, nephews, many cousins and life-long friends.
Betsy lived life big and did everything with joy, energy, and presence. She loved and was loved. She will be deeply missed and long remembered.
Services will be private and at the discretion of the family.
In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to an animal rescue organization of your choice.
Hall’s of Boothbay has care of the arrangements. To leave the family condolences please visit hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Couple charged after 4 children removed from ‘deplorable conditions’, police say
text:
MIDDLETOWN, Ohio (WXIX/Gray News) - A couple is facing multiple charges of child endangerment and animal cruelty following a welfare check at their home in September, authorities said.
Melanie and Christopher Todd were arrested after officers responded to their home on Cardinal Court to check on their children and animals, according to the criminal complaint.
Police described the living conditions as “deplorable and unlivable.”
Officers conducted the welfare check Sept. 29 after Middletown City Schools reported that two 10-year-old children appeared dirty and said they had no food to eat, police said.
The children also said two cats were dead inside their home, the complaint said.
During the check, officers found holes large enough to see outside in the walls and floors. One of the couple’s four children said the holes were caused by punching when Melanie and Christopher would get angry, the complaint said.
The home also had little to no edible food inside, officers said.
According to the complaint, the floors were covered in dirty clothes, trash, animal feces, and debris. The house was also infested with bedbugs and cockroaches.
Police removed all four children from the home and placed them with other family members. Officers also removed four cats, pet fish, mice, gerbils and pet tarantulas.
The couple is facing four counts of child endangerment and several counts of animal cruelty.
Both are in custody at the Butler County Jail. They will be arraigned Thursday.
