title: Don’t eat fish downstream from Keddy Mill on Presumpscot River in Windham, EPA warns
text:
Officials are warning the public not to eat fish caught on a stretch of the Presumpscot River in Windham downstream from a former mill site that is undergoing cleanup.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is advising residents not to eat fish caught between the Little Falls Dam and Mallison Falls Dam in South Windham, downstream from the former Keddy Mill site.
The Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention first updated its seafood consumption guidelines in August to place the area under a “do not eat any fish from these waters” status, according to the EPA.
The town of Windham shared a recent EPA advisory and associated fact sheet in a Facebook post this week, which says testing found elevated levels of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) — toxic chemicals that accumulate in fish tissue.
In 2014, the Keddy Mill on Depot Street was designated as a Superfund site on the National Priorities List, a program that locates, investigates and cleans up hazardous waste sites. Nearly a decade later, the EPA proposed a plan to clean up the polluted site, to the tune of an estimated $17 million and up to four years of work.
In February, the EPA provided an update on the project, which is to be conducted in multiple phases beginning in early 2027. The first phase includes demolition of the mill complex.
The former mill, which has been dormant since the 1990s, was determined to be a source of contamination of soil, sediment, groundwater and fish in the area, according to the federal agency. That includes PCBs, heavy metals, and petroleum hydrocarbons.
The site was home to a variety of mills over the years, dating to the 1700s. Since the mid-1990s, developers, property owners, the town of Windham, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, and EPA have been evaluating the level of toxic contaminants present on the grounds.
The advisory is expected to remain in place until remediation of the site is completed.

title: Edgecomb receives $3K MMA grant for generator
text:
On Oct. 27, Edgecomb selectmen announced the town had received a $3,000 Maine Municipal Association grant to buy a stand-by generator for the town hall. Selectmen debated whether a 14-kilowatt or 20-kilowatt generator would serve their interest.
Selectmen Forrest Carver and Cara Gaffney decided the 14-kW model was the best fit. Selectmen will now seek a further recommendation from the building committee and an anonymous donor who pledged to provide additional funding.
In other action, selectmen set Tuesday, Dec. 8 at 6 p.m. for a special budget meeting for municipal departments and non-profit groups seeking municipal funding. Each group is directed to deliver a “succinct 10-year budget history” designed to establish clear historical context for developing the next fiscal year budget.
Time will strictly be enforced so there will be no time for questions from the public. Carver added there will be time for questions at a future budget meeting.
Selectmen are considering their options regarding timely municipal audits. The town is still waiting for the FY23 audit. Gaffney reported she had made four attempts at contacting the William Brewer, CPA firm without success.
Carver reported Edgecomb is one of 20 municipalities and townships which are over two years behind in the annual audits. Selectmen considered using another CPA firm for future audits. Town Clerk Claudia Coffin offered to contact the Brewer agency to discover the FY23 audit’s status.
Administrative Assistant Jessica Mague said the building committee found a suitable countertop for a new upstairs service center. The committee purchased a countertop for $300 and plans on using volunteer labor for renovations. The committee has a $6,500 project budget and Mague said the renovations would begin later this fall.
Edgecomb will receive assistance from Midcoast Energy in Damariscotta with the electrical work. Resident Karen Flynn contacted the company on the town’s behalf. Midcoast Energy is celebrating its 50th anniversary and is offering the help as part of the celebration.
Carver and Gaffney would like to establish a deputy clerk position to provide municipal services when the elected Town Clerk Claudia Coffin is not available. Selectmen asked Coffin if she could train a deputy town clerk.
“It's a goal of the selectboard to have fail-safe in mind for every duty in the town office. We don't want to be ‘up the creek without a paddle’ so we’d like to have a system in place such as during early voting or absentee voting. Is it possible to train a deputy?" Carver asked.
Coffin didn’t think it was practical to have a deputy clerk.
Selectmen and Coffin also disagreed about the need for hiring a payroll service. Selectmen thought hiring a private firm would eliminate municipal liability on payroll issues and save time. Coffin is the town's elected treasurer and said payroll is part of the job. “I don’t feel comfortable spending the taxpayer's money on something we don't need. You’re already paying a treasurer who according to state law does payroll.”
Selectmen tabled whether to hire a payroll service.
Selectmen meet next at 6 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 10 in the conference room.

title: Caregiver advocate shares 3 policies that could help family caregivers
text:
(Aging Untold) — More than 60 million Americans are family caregivers, balancing work, kids and care for an aging parent or loved one.
Jason Resendez, president and CEO of the National Alliance for Caregiving, recently testified before the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging. He joined gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck to talk through the solutions he presented.
The three policies he brought to lawmakers
Resendez said the National Alliance for Caregiving is championing changes “to address so many of the pain points that family caregivers face every day.”
1) Older Americans Act funding
He said one priority is reauthorization and funding of the Older Americans Act. Resendez said the law provides dollars for state Area Agencies on Aging to deliver services for older adults, such as Meals on Wheels and caregiver support.
“One of the only federal line items for caregiving comes through the Older Americans Act, and it’s called the National Family Caregiver Support Program,” Resendez said.
He said the program funds respite, which gives caregivers the chance to take breaks. It also funds training, education and outreach, so family caregivers have peer support and someone to turn to when navigating local resources.
The program is funded at about $200 million a year, Resendez said.
“That’s a drop in the bucket compared to the scale of the need for this kind of support,” he said.
2) National paid family and medical leave
Another priority is a national paid family and medical leave program.
“We are still one of the only industrialized nations that doesn’t have a paid family and medical leave program,” Resendez said.
He said 13 states and the District of Columbia have set up programs because of the lack of federal action. Virginia is the first southern state to do so, Resendez said.
A national program “can help people provide care while staying in the workforce and putting food on the table,” Resendez said.
3) A bigger role for Medicare
Another priority is for Medicare to do more to recognize and support family caregivers. Resendez said the group is pushing for stronger access to caregiver training services and stronger in-home health benefits through Medicare.
If only one policy passed
When asked which policy would be most beneficial if only one were to pass, Resendez pointed to Medicare.
He said changes there would bring immediate support to families and modernize a program created in 1965. He said the older adult community has changed since then.
An in-home health benefit, stronger caregiver support and parity with what Medicaid does for low-income families would “transform what it looks like to age in America today,” Resendez said.
Extending that support to families at all income levels “would revolutionize what it looks like to provide care in America today,” he said.
One step to take in the next 30 days
Cradduck asked for one concrete step that lawmakers, employers or communities could take in the next 30 days.
For Congress, Resendez said the step is to pass the Older Americans Act.
“And so that’s a no-brainer there for policymakers who want to step up for family caregivers and do it on an issue and policy that’s extremely bipartisan, is to cast that vote to reauthorize the Older Americans Act,” Resendez said.
For employers, he said the first step is asking employees whether they have caregiving responsibilities.
Employers are not systematically asking that question, he said, and without that data, they are not designing benefits for employees who are handling both work and caregiving.

title: Report: Peltola’s campaign involved in effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan for Alaska Senate race
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The Democratic campaign for Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state’s August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday’s general election.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press.
A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. The U.S. Constitution sets out only age, citizenship and residency requirements to run for the Senate.
President Donald Trump, who directed his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit last week pre-emptively contesting a Peltola win due to the presence of the second Dan Sullivan, called for legal penalties against Democrats over the situation: “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done,” Trump wrote on his social media site on Wednesday.
“Alaskans deserve the truth,” said Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan’s campaign. “Mary Peltola, her campaign and her senior advisers colluded with the DSCC, national Democrat lawyers and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse and deceive voters.”
Peltola’s campaign, in a statement Wednesday, said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan’s candidacy.
Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick.
“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan,” the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan.
Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. Department of Justice. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
“It’s a dirty campaign trick, and it’s good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot,” said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. “But now it’s in the hands of the voters, not litigation.”
It’s not the first time a candidate’s appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot.
The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week. Efforts by the AP to reach Rios were not immediately successful.
As of Monday, 46,204 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sen. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.
___
Riccardi reported from Denver.

title: How to spot fake crystals and avoid costly mistakes
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SEDONA, Ariz. (Aging Untold) — The crystal and gemstone industry is booming, fueled in part by social media, but experts warn buyers to be cautious of fake products flooding the market.
Jamie Inglett, who owns a crystal shop in Sedona, said consumers can find fake crystals in stores and at gem shows.
“As a consumer you really kind of have to do your own research,” Inglett said.
Growing popularity drives demand
The crystal craze has exploded online, with #crystals generating 20 billion views on TikTok.
Inglett has built up 215,106 Instagram followers and opened a physical storefront in Sedona after finding success online.
“You don’t have to believe in crystal healing or crystal energy to appreciate their beauty,” Inglett said.
What to know about fake crystals
Shannon Wimberly, a crystal collector for several years, said she has encountered fake crystals and now scrutinizes purchases more carefully.
“I absolutely know I’ve run into getting fake ones, so I started scrutinizing other things more and more,” Wimberly said.
Inglett said buyers could end up with lab-grown crystals sold as natural stones. She showed a lab-grown crystal purchased from a Sedona shop for more than $100 that could be found online for $5 to $20.
“You’ll see hundreds of these, depending on the store. They’ll all look about the same,” Inglett said.
Buyers could also purchase completely synthetic items made from plastic or glass.
How to identify fakes
Inglett recommends asking questions about origin and authenticity.
“Asking the shop, where is this from? And then they should at least be able to tell you the country of origin, if not the actual mine name,” Inglett said.
Physical tests can help identify fake crystals. Glass fakes sound different, don’t get cold and have unnatural dye patterns, Inglett said. Fake moldavite lacks natural grooves and textures and appears too uniform in shape, she said.
Inglett said lab-grown crystals are not an issue as long as sellers disclose what buyers are purchasing.

title: Driver dies in Windham head-on

title: South Portland City Council approves emergency ordinance restricting ICE cooperation
text:
South Portland City Council approves emergency ordinance restricting ICE cooperation
Councilors unanimously approved the ordinance and an amendment including school employees
South Portland City Council approves emergency ordinance restricting ICE cooperation
Councilors unanimously approved the ordinance and an amendment including school employees
The South Portland City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to enact an emergency ordinance restricting city cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Councilors also unanimously approved an amendment to include school employees under the ordinance following a unanimous vote by the South Portland School Board supporting their inclusion.
The ordinance prohibits city employees from voluntarily assisting federal immigration enforcement through the use of city personnel, funds, equipment, information or property, except where required by law, court order or judicial warrant.
It also restricts federal immigration agents' access to nonpublic city facilities for enforcement operations, while allowing South Portland police to respond to immigration enforcement scenes to maintain public safety and order.
Under the ordinance, city employees will also receive training on its requirements, including procedures for responding to immigration enforcement requests.
Mayor Elyse Tipton said it is important for South Portland to do everything it can to protect its residents and expressed hope that the city's action would serve as an example for other communities.
The ordinance takes effect immediately.

title: All Hallows’ Eve at the Stonington Opera House
text:
STONINGTON – Come to the Stonington Opera House for a night of Halloween music and fun from the Celtic Isles at 6 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 30.
Scottish fiddler Louise Bichan is joined by guitarist Conor Hearn, mandolinist Ethan Setiawan and cellist Brendan Hearn playing music from their brand new record “Binnorie” featuring Samhaim (Halloween) traditions, folk tales and songs of trowies, sea serpents and selkies.
Bichan is a Maine-based musician and photographer who uses both mediums to tell stories old and new. Growing up in the remote but culturally rich Orkney islands, a place where creativity abounds and playing music has been a part of the social fabric for centuries, gave Bichan a solid grounding in music. Her music is thoughtful, complex, curious and playful. She composes in response to her roots and the world around her; weaving through stories of connection to people, nature, the past and the possibility of the future.
Bichan returned to her Scottish roots to collect material for “Binnorie” stating, “I had a lot of fun pulling together a collection of music and folk tales, some I’ve grown up hearing and playing, some that I’ve written, and some which are new to me.”
Come to the Opera House for All Hallows’ Eve disguised in your best costume and bring your most frighteningly carved neep (turnip) or pumpkin to win a prize! Candles for your Jack-O-Lanterns will be available. Children are welcome, but a few songs will include dark themes, such as murder ballads.
All Hallows’ Eve is part of the Live! for $5 series, offering tickets at only $5 per person. Hancock County students attend all live performances for free. To purchase tickets or for more information call 207-367-2788 or visit operahousearts.org.

title: Federal Reserve keeps interest rates unchanged ahead of midterms despite elevated inflation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9% despite stubbornly high inflation, as Chairman Kevin Warsh suggested its policies are already showing signs of having an impact.
“Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s 2% inflation target, the statement said.
The Fed raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to cool inflation more quickly. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and reduce price increases.
Michael Reynolds, vice president of investment strategy at Glenmede, a wealth management firm, said the statement suggested the central bank will likely hike its key rate by a quarter-point at its next meeting Dec. 8-9. Wall Street investors now see the odds of an increase then at nearly 85%, according to CME Fedwatch.
“It’s likely going to take one more (hike) from the Fed to get interest rates into restrictive territory,” where they can slow inflation, he said.
The Fed’s decision comes just six days before a midterm election that has focused heavily on concerns around the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items. Warsh denied the election played a part in the Fed’s staying pat.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said at a news conference following the announcement. “I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
Warsh faces plenty of challenges in getting inflation back to target. Some of the forces pushing up prices — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — may not be easily tamed by higher interest rates.
Still, Warsh said the “overwhelming consensus” among Fed officials is what they’ve done “is starting to work some,” noting that credit conditions “tightened for some businesses and households.”
He said specifically that as large tech firms rely more on borrowing to build data centers, higher rates will have a greater ability to cool that investment.
“Do interest rates matter?” Warsh asked. “I believe they do, and I don’t think they’re divorced from the rest of the economy.”
Parts of the economy are being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans’ sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
A separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, comes out Thursday and is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month. Earlier this month, the consumer price index showed inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier.
Warsh denied that consumers would lose faith in the Fed’s ability to get inflation back to its 2% target, given its decision to forgo a rate hike.
“There is no soft inflation target,” he said.
Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. This is Cook’s first dissent since she was appointed to the board by President Joe Biden in 2022.
Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied.
President Trump has also slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank’s rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed.
The Fed’s policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada met earlier, and lifted its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. Warsh said growth in the July-September quarter likely rose above 3%. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter.

title: Cherryfield dam removal opens path for Atlantic salmon
text:
CHERRYFIELD, Maine (WABI) - Crews removed the Cherryfield Ice Dam this summer, allowing Atlantic salmon to swim farther upstream.
The Downeast Salmon Federation (DSF) partnered with the town, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on the project.
One of the key goals of the improvement project is to increase fish passage. Years ago, hundreds of fish passed through the river. In recent years, that number has dropped significantly.
Ellie Mason, habitat restoration project manager for the Downeast Salmon Federation, said the dam was known to block fish.
“There was video footage from the top of the dam where you could see salmon jumping, but they weren’t getting to the other side,” Mason said. “And so everyone knew, okay, this is something that’s blocking fish passage.”
Mason joined the federation in 2024 and oversaw the design, permitting and construction.
Cable Pool Park upgrades
The project also includes upgrades to the adjacent Cable Pool Park. Crews are finishing a play area and expanding public access.
Crews also are repurposing old concrete from the dam to build an amphitheater.
Construction is almost complete. Final improvements are set to be done next year.
Community tour
The Downeast Salmon Federation is hosting a community open tour of the project Friday, October 30 from 4 to 5:30 p.m.

The seventh-seeded Crusaders had advanced through the preliminary round but couldn't get past Calais in the quarterfinals.

title: Robbins family member will return home to Searsmont 5 months after deadly mill disaster
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A member of the Robbins family will return home to Searsmont this week, more than five months after she suffered critical burns in a silo explosion at the local lumber yard.
Lily Robbins, who has been recovering at Massachusetts General Hospital’s burn unit since May, will make her homecoming Friday, according to the town of Searsmont.
Residents are encouraged to bring snacks, desserts and homemade “Welcome Home” signs to the fire station starting at 9 a.m. Friday. The town will later release more details about the timing of Robbins’ return and her travel plans, “so everyone who wishes can come out and welcome her home!”
“Thank you to our amazing community for all the love, prayers, encouragement, and support throughout Lily’s recovery. Let’s give her the welcome home she deserves!” the town wrote in a social media post.
The fire broke out about 10:05 a.m. on May 15 at the Robbins Lumber campus off Route 131 in an area where wood shavings are packed in plastic bags and spread to a nearby silo.
At the time, the silo was about 20% filled with sawdust and wood shavings. The silo had a fire suppression system, but it failed to activate because the temperatures at the top had not become hot enough to trigger it.
Smoke could be seen coming from the base, and later an orange glow, prompting firefighters to pour water into the silo and the room at its base, which unbeknownst to them was adding oxygen and stirring up dust suspended in an “explosive mixture,” according to a federal investigation into the disaster.
Then the silo exploded without warning about 11 a.m., throwing, in a blast of pressure and fire, mill employees, firefighters and EMS providers who stood nearby.
Firefighters, many of them critically injured, rushed to pull survivors away from the inferno, as nearly 300 firefighters from 46 departments across four counties scrambled to the lumber yard to contain the blaze and tend to the wounded.
Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross, 27, died at the scene of the fire. Searsmont’s assistant fire Chief, Wayne Woodbury, succumbed to his injuries on June 14. The blaze, one of the worst industrial disasters in recent Maine history, also killed one of the company’s co-owners, Alden Robbins, who died on July 2.
At least 10 other people, including first responders, a mill employee and another of the mill’s co-owners, were injured in the fire.
Robbins Lumber is a leading supplier of eastern white pine products, with roots in Searsmont that stretch back nearly 150 years. It employs more than 100 people.
The mill resumed operations on May 26.

title: Nathan Bernard joins Central Maine Growth Council
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Central Maine Growth Council (CMGC) has named Nathan Bernard to the newly created position of Project Manager of Technology, Innovation, and Infrastructure. In this role, he will advance economic development, municipal innovation, and infrastructure modernization across central Maine and the state.
As part of CMGC’s economic development and artificial intelligence (AI) strategy, Bernard will drive technology and infrastructure projects with member municipalities and support new and existing innovation programs with business, academic, and community partners. At Dirigo Labs, CMGC’s business incubator and innovation accelerator, he will help grow the region’s startup ecosystem, supporting founders as they launch, scale, and commercialize new ideas, and expand AI and data analytics capabilities.
Bernard brings experience in both the public and private sectors. He most recently served as a community development specialist in the Waterville City Manager’s office, and before that as grants and program manager at the Alfond Youth and Community Center.
He has worked as a project manager at Code for America, a national civic tech nonprofit, where he helped bring modern digital tools to government. In New York City, he founded and built a software company that raised capital, reached hundreds of thousands of users, and was featured in Business Insider, The Boston Globe, and The Next Web.
Bernard holds a bachelor’s degree in operations, engineering, and technology management from Boston University. He is pursuing a master’s degree in public policy, planning, and management at the University of Southern Maine’s Muskie School of Public Service and serves as a Policy Research Fellow at Colby College’s Bram Public Policy Lab. His research examines how municipal governments can govern, adopt, and develop ethical AI products, policies, and practices into their operations.
“Communities and businesses across Maine are being asked to solve 21st-century challenges, from AI to aging infrastructure to a shifting economy, often with small staffs and tight budgets,” said Garvan D. Donegan, president and CEO of the Central Maine Growth Council. “Nathan brings a rare combination: he has built a technology company, delivered civic tech at the national level, and worked inside City Hall right here in Waterville. That blend of startup speed and public-sector know-how is exactly what our member municipalities and Dirigo Labs entrepreneurs need.”
“This role is a direct investment in our region’s capacity to innovate,” Donegan added. “With Nathan supporting this work, CMGC can help our communities adopt smarter tools, use data to plan for growth, support the next generation of startups, and turn good ideas into real projects that strengthen the Kennebec Valley and the State of Maine.”
“CMGC provides a unique opportunity to expand my public service work across the region and help central Maine navigate critical issues, including AI, economic resiliency, infrastructure, and affordability,” Bernard said.

title: ‘It is killing us’: Truck driver says friends had to find different jobs due to diesel costs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (KETV) – A Nebraska man who has driven a company truck for more than 25 years said rising diesel costs have him fearing for his livelihood.
“The gas prices, the fuel prices, man, it is killing us,” trucker Dave Turner said.
Americans rely on truckers to move goods every day, but drivers are concerned about the future of the industry.
“It’s astronomical and almost makes us nonexistent,” Turner said.
Diesel prices
Diesel prices reached an all-time record high of about $6.50 a gallon last month. Prices have remained in the same range since then.
Turner said rising fuel costs have already changed how drivers get from one destination to the next.
“A lot more time sitting and waiting for the company to be able to actually find decent routes for us as far as having to route us to the cheapest places to be able to get fuel,” Turner said.
Most company drivers have help finding lower prices.
Independent drivers
Asiwome Faiti, another company driver, said not all truckers are feeling the impact equally.
“You don’t have the capacity to hedge your fuel, so those are the people suffering, the mom and pop small businesses,” Faiti said.
Independent drivers are paying out of pocket to fill their tanks, and the rising cost is taking some of them out of the business.
“I have actually several of my friends, close friends that are independent truckers, and out of about 13 of them, seven of them have already had to shut down their trucks and find different jobs,” Turner said.
According to federal transportation data, trucks carried about 65% of U.S. freight by weight in 2024.
Faiti said he wants to be able to continue driving.
“All I can say is we pray that this crisis is over soon,” Faiti said.

title: Lawsuit seeks to block ICE from hiding locations of detainees with final removal orders
text:
Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration’s new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.
The policy, adopted suddenly last month to expedite deportations, interferes with immigration lawyers’ rights by making it difficult, and sometimes impossible, to locate their clients, according to the lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston. It asks a judge to issue an order blocking the “unlawful and inhumane” change.
“No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them,” said Jacquelynne Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services, one of the four groups listed as plaintiffs. “This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.”
The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts. As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.
ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, didn’t immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the lawsuit.
The agencies have not publicly confirmed the change, but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation. They have also said they are facing a “historic number of injunctions” from courts blocking their efforts. The agencies have denied that they are disappearing detainees, saying they remain free to make phone calls.
Since 2010, lawyers and family members have used the online system to track detainees as they get moved from facility to facility through ICE’s sprawling detention network.
Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal, which means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed.
Those individuals still have several options to challenge the conditions of their detention and looming deportations, including asking to reopen proceedings, seeking relief from removal to third countries and challenging violations of their rights. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.
Since the change went into effect, lawyers have been unable to find clients and potential clients and have spent “significantly more time” tracking down others, the lawsuit says. Calls to ICE, including to its Detention and Removal Information Line, “lead to long wait times on hold, sudden hang-ups, a general lack of information or no answer at all,” it says.
As a workaround, some lawyers have tried to find their clients through an ICE program that schedules legal calls, but only a small percentage of detention centers use it, the lawsuit says. The result has been delayed or missed legal filings and fewer cases taken, according to the organizations.
The lawsuit argues the change violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it was adopted without explanation and the First Amendment, which protects lawyers’ ability to advise people of their legal rights and seek prospective clients.

title: John W. Goodman
text:
John W. Goodman passed away peacefully on Aug. 30, 2026, in Saratoga, Wyoming.
John was born in Sheridan, Wyoming 1948. In 1962 the family moved to Boothbay Harbor, Maine where he spent his teenage years. John then graduated high school in Maine. He then attended Maine Maritime Academy. At the age of 21, John proudly joined the United States Navy, serving from 1969 to 1972. His time in the Navy was an important part of his life and something he carried with him throughout the years.
After leaving the Navy, John met Cathy Dighton, and together they had three children. In 1990 John and his son Kevin moved back to Wyoming where he spend the remainder of his life. Throughout his life, John worked in the oil field, a career he was passionate about and took great pride in. His work ethic and dedication were a reflection of the man he was—strong, hardworking, and committed to providing for those he loved.
John’s greatest joy, however, was his family. He spent countless hours supporting his nieces and nephews at their various sporting events, always showing up to cheer them on and be part of their lives. Family gatherings, time with friends, and simply being surrounded by the people he loved were some of his favorite moments.
After retiring, John enjoyed having more time to spend with family and friends and was able to take trips and make memories that he cherished. One of his special adventures was traveling back to Maine and to Alaska with his brother, Chuck.
John had many things he enjoyed throughout his life. He loved playing cards, fishing, golfing, poker, and cribbage. He enjoyed watching football and baseball, spending time with friends and family, and traveling. Above all, John loved his family, his friends, and his country.
John was preceded in death by his father, George E. Goodman; his mother, Guyla M. Taylor; his sister, Patricia A. Arnold; his brother, Marvin D. Goodman; his daughter, Ciji Goodman; his brother-in-law, Rob Loftice; his sister-in-law Donna Goodman and Aunt, Virginia Scanlond
He leaves behind his son, Kevin Goodman; his brother, Chuck Goodman; and his sister, Vicki Loftice.
John is also survived by his grandchildren, Ciji Goodman, Orion Goodman, and Grayson Goodman; his nephew, Robert Loftice; nieces Robin Loftice (Ken O’Leary) and Kim Loftice; Nephew Jed Goodman (Tonya Goodman); niece Jenny Goodman; great-niece Sierra Martinez; great-great-nephew Kodah Martinez; great-nephews Galloway O’Leary and Sloan O’Leary; great-niece Ashley Loftice; great-great-nephew Rhett Cruickshank; and great-nephew Charles Watts, along with extended family and many friends who will forever cherish his memory.
John will be remembered for his love of family, his hardworking spirit, his sense of adventure, and the countless memories he created with the people he loved. His presence, stories, laughter, and friendship will be missed.
Though he is no longer with us, the memories John made and the love he shared will live on in the hearts of his family and friends.
Rest peacefully, John. You will be deeply missed and forever remembered.

title: Pemetic students share thoughts on Declaration of Independence

SOUTHWEST HARBOR — Pemetic middle school students will present their thoughts on what the Declaration of Independence means to them personally and to their community in a public program at the Southwest Harbor Public Library on Monday Nov. 9, at 5:30pm. title: These Cities Have the Most Ghost Sightings in Maine
text:
These Cities Have the Most Ghost Sightings in Maine
Okay, Maine friends, I have a question. Have you ever been sitting in your house, minding your own business, when you hear a noise upstairs and suddenly decide you absolutely do NOT need to know what that was? Yeah. Same.
Well, just in time for Halloween, we've got another reason to keep the lights on.
A new ranking from search-data company Answer Socrates puts Maine at the sixth most haunted state in America per person, with a spooky score of 73 out of 100.
Maine Ranks Among the Most Haunted States in America
And apparently, we're not just making this stuff up in our heads. Maine reportedly has the most ghost sightings per person in the country, with 811 reader-submitted sightings.
We also have 2,998 cemeteries, ranking fourth per person. So, there's that.
My thoughts are that basically, we're surrounded by places where ghosts could hang out. How wonderful! And get this, do you want to know where Maine's ghost activity is supposedly happening?
Well, Sanford takes the top spot, with 27 reported sightings, followed by Auburn and Bangor.
And here's my favorite part: Maine ranks second in the country for Googling cryptids, those mysterious creatures like Bigfoot.
Even Google seems to think we're a little spooky, with searches about why Maine is so haunted pointing people toward Portland, Bangor, and Derry and yes, that the fictional town made famous by Stephen King.
Read More: Must Visit Haunted Attractions in New England
The ranking is based on reported sightings, cemeteries, spooky locations, and search trends. It doesn't prove ghosts are real, obviously… but it certainly gives us something to think about.
So tell me: Have you ever experienced something you absolutely cannot explain here in Maine? I'm listening. Just please don't tell me your story right before I go to bed, deal?

title: Commitment 2026 Election Special
text:
Maine's Total Coverage Commitment 2026 Election Special
Maine voters will head to the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, in one of the most closely watched elections in the state's history. Maine's Total Coverage hosted an hourlong election special Wednesday night, which can be watched in the YouTube video embedded below.
From governor to the U.S. Senate and U.S. House, Maine's Total Coverage reintroduced the candidates who appear on the ballot.
Maine's Total Coverage also provided a look at some of the local measures communities will be asked to weigh in on during the election.
In addition, Maine's Total Coverage shared how the candidates for governor and U.S. Senate plan on addressing the issues that matter most to Maine voters.
More information about the candidates for Maine governor, U.S. Senate and both of Maine's U.S. House seats is featured below.
Race for Maine governor
Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat, is in the final year of her second straight term, and under Maine law, no governor can serve three consecutive terms. This means the state will have a new governor in 2027.
Republican candidate Bobby Charles and Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree won their respective primary races following ranked-choice voting tabulations. State Sen. Rick Bennett qualified to appear on the ballot as an independent candidate.
There are two declared write-in candidates in the governor's race: independent Jon Glowa and Republican Randy Wilcox.
Race for U.S. Senate
Incumbent U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, is seeking her sixth term in the Senate, and she was the only candidate who qualified for the GOP primary ballot.
Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson is the Democratic candidate who is challenging Collins. Jackson, who finished third in the Democratic primary for governor, was chosen as the U.S. Senate nominee by the Maine Democratic Party during a special nominating convention held on July 25. A new Senate nominee had to be chosen because the winner of the Democratic primary, Sullivan oyster farmer Graham Platner, dropped out of the race on July 8 following allegations of sexual assault.
There are six declared write-in candidates in the Senate race: unaffiliated candidate Brent Andrews, Democrat Sigrid Ann Olson, independent Gina Oswald, Faith in Humanity candidate Joseph Steinberger, unenrolled candidate Michael Turcotte and Democrat Ashley Webb.
Race for 1st Congressional District seat
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat, is seeking her 10th term representing Maine's 1st Congressional District in the House. She was the only candidate who qualified for the Democratic primary ballot.
Ron Russell won the Republican primary, setting up a rematch of the 2024 general election that he lost to Pingree.
Maine's 1st Congressional District includes all of Cumberland, Knox, Lincoln, Sagadahoc and York counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Albion, Benton, China, Clinton, Litchfield, Pittston, Unity Township, Vassalboro, Waterville, West Gardiner, Windsor and Winslow.
Race for 2nd Congressional District seat
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat who is in his fourth term representing Maine's 2nd Congressional District, announced in November 2025 that he will not seek reelection to the House.
State Auditor Matt Dunlap won the Democratic primary following a ranked-choice voting tabulation. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage was the only candidate who qualified for the Republican primary ballot in the CD2 race and advanced to the general election.
Independent candidate Gregory Ward is the lone declared write-in candidate for this race.
Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest by area east of the Mississippi River. CD2 includes all of Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.

title: Follow the money | Editorials
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
During this election cycle, more money will have been spent in Maine to run a handful of negative attack ads in one race than on keeping the state’s neediest residents warm through the winter heating season.
Let that sink in for a minute.
According to an analysis by The Maine Monitor, more than $54 million has been spent or committed on negative ads in the U.S. Senate race, and almost all of it came from so-called super PACs outside the state.
In total, according to the reporting, “13 of the most expensive negative ads came from Democratic-aligned groups attacking Collins, and 12 came from Republican-aligned groups attacking Jackson. Republican-backed groups have spent slightly more overall than the Democrat-backed groups have on these ads, $28.7 million versus $25.8 million.”
The timing hits right in the wallet, as heating oil hit a record $6.02 a gallon last month, up about 80% over last year. The Natural Resource Council of Maine estimates an added cost of $1,262 for an average household this winter, and MaineHousing says that LIHEAP applications are up 4%. According to MaineHousing, $42 million is expected to flow into the state for heating assistance, and that number is made up of $24 million in direct assistance, $6 million for weatherization and improvements, $9.8 million to administer the program, $3.6 million set aside for emergencies, and $1 million set aside for a program that helped educate about energy self-sufficiency.
This is obviously not an apples-to-apples comparison, but it is one worth noting. Campaign spending is private money, and heating aid comes from federal appropriations. Dollars cannot move from one pot to the other. What the numbers do show are priorities and what organized money chooses to do in the last few weeks of a high-stakes campaign, while highlighting what the public system provides to individuals and families in need.
Mainers have already weighed in. In 2024, nearly 75% of voters backed a $5,000 limit on donations to super PACs, but the measure remains in the federal court system, being challenged on First Amendment grounds. However, nobody has to be silenced to fix this. Mainers can ask for more transparency, for additional disclosures and to know who is behind the messages and ultimately behind the super PACs.
Demanding transparency and accountability go a long way toward reform. Voters have the right to know who is behind the political messages and should be able to pull back the curtain and see exactly who is paying to influence their vote.

title: Senate vote is about Maine’s future generations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Troy Jackson is the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine.
I’d like to talk to you about my first grandchild.
Just a few short weeks ago, my family welcomed Willet into the world. She’s a tiny, beautiful baby girl. Just over 7 pounds, and growing every day.
And when I hold her and look at her tiny fingers, hold up her little head, hear the sounds she makes, I’m reminded of the stakes in this election.
Susan Collins and I are on the ballot for U.S. Senate, but this election isn’t really about us. It’s about the world we want to create and the life we want to leave behind for our children and our grandchildren.
I believe it’s time we have a government that works for us, not the billionaires who are trying to buy this election and our country.
When Willet came, my family got lucky. No big health complications. A hospital close by. And we could afford the medical bills. A lot of Mainers aren’t that lucky.
Today, community hospital units and birthing centers are closing. Women are afraid of pregnancy complications and not being able to get care. More than 60,000 Mainers are seeing their healthcare costs rise or could lose healthcare altogether because of Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”
Susan Collins voted to advance these cuts.
Collins claims she’s one of the most powerful senators. But when Trump wanted to cut healthcare to pay for tax breaks for billionaires, she didn’t stop it — she greenlit the cuts. And it’s not the first time.
When women across Maine begged Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, she voted to confirm him anyway. Now Roe v. Wade is gone, women across the country have lost their rights and Collins still says she doesn’t regret her vote.
She gave ICE $70 billion that they have used to target our neighbors. She enabled the Trump administration’s trade war with Canada, which drove up costs for Maine families and businesses. And she voted five times to let his war with Iran continue, which is driving up heating oil costs for all of us.
Collins has spent the last 30 years in Washington. Since Trump returned to power, she’s voted with him 96% of the time.
When Trump and the billionaires need her — for judges, tax cuts or wars — Collins is there. It doesn’t have to be this way.
I’ve spent my career trying to make life better for working families because I know what it’s like to work hard and fall behind.
In the Maine Legislature, I stood up to Big Pharma and passed bills to lower prescription drug costs. I fought to make sure every child in Maine can get free meals at school. I helped pass paid family and medical leave, so Mainers don’t have to choose between a paycheck and caring for someone they love.
When Roe was overturned, I fought like hell to protect and expand reproductive rights in Maine.
I fought for workers’ right to organize and collectively bargain. And I fought for rural communities like the one where I grew up, because your ZIP code shouldn’t determine whether you can see a doctor, afford your medicine, feed your kids or build a decent life.
That’s the same fight I’ll bring to Washington.
I’ll fight for Medicare for All, lower prescription drug costs, rural hospitals, abortion rights and working people who have watched corporations and billionaires get their way in Washington for far too long.
Because when I think about Willet growing up, I don’t think about whether Democrats or Republicans are winning some argument in Washington.
I think about whether she’ll be able to afford a home someday. Whether there will be a hospital nearby if she needs one. Whether she’ll have the same rights her mother and grandmother had. Whether she can find a good job, raise a family and build a life in Maine.
That’s what this election means to me.
And if I’m lucky enough to earn your support, I will fight for you, your children and your grandchildren just as hard as I’d fight for mine.

title: 24-year-old deputy killed in crash with coal truck while on duty, sheriff’s office says

title: InvestigateTV+: Bringing the hospital to neighborhoods
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ explores a pilot program bringing the hospital to people’s homes, delivering more than preventative care while working to expand nationwide.
Plus, we take an in-depth look at a federal initiative to recruit and retain foster homes and whether states can meet the goal of a home for every child.
Then, a story of sweet success: we go behind the scenes with a Vermont sugar maker keeping nearly century-old traditions alive.
Nurses in the neighborhood
A pilot program called Neighborhood Nursing is providing basic primary care outside the traditional clinic setting in East Baltimore, setting up in a church and visiting apartment complexes and homes to reach residents.
The program’s services are open to anyone who lives in the area. Those services are free and funded for now largely through philanthropic donations.
A home for every child
Kids sleeping in shelters, bussed between hotels, and overnights in office buildings. That’s the reality for many foster children in America.
For every 100 children in foster care, federal data shows that only 57 licenses homes are available.
In an effort to close that gap, the federal government launched a campaign in November 2025 called “A Home for Every Child.”
Traveling for hand surgery
A family traveled from Turkey to St. Louis for their daughter’s surgery to treat a rare condition affecting fewer than 100 people worldwide.
Elisa, an 18-month-old, was born with eight fingers on her left hand. She was diagnosed with Ulnar Dimelia, also known as Mirror Hand Syndrome.
The science of sugar making
During the season of sugar making at Walker’s Pure Vermont Maple Syrup in Underhill, they steam ahead with batch after batch of the sweet stuff.
The guys in the sugarhouse will be working 10 hours or more each day. Craig Walker, who’s 86, spent a lifetime making maple syrup. Now, much of his day is on the road. “That’s my job, I’ve been promoted to truck driver,” he said. “We have to have the sap first to make the syrup.”

title: Meet the volunteers who bring flowers from weddings and funerals to hospice patients
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (Aging Untold) — Inside Crescent Hill Baptist Church in Louisville, a group of volunteers gathers each week surrounded by color, creativity and collaboration.
They call themselves the Flower Buds.
From events to those in need
The Flower Buds take donated flowers from weddings, funerals, wholesalers, supermarkets, florists, galas, banquets and other community events. They cut, clean and arrange the blooms into vases, then deliver them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities and shelters.
“Amazingly gifted with so many flowers from places like Kroger who have overbought and can’t sell them, and they allow us to pick them up and then bring them here, and then we cut them, clean them and vase them. Then we take them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities,” Jodie Raible, a Flower Buds volunteer, said.
The group sends out about 100 vases every week.
“I take flowers to Up for Women and Children, it’s a day homeless shelter for women,” Stephanie Mullins, a Flower Buds volunteer, said.
Delivering to the VA
Volunteer Clem Russell is a veteran and takes particular pride in delivering flowers to the VA hospital.
“We deliver to the hospice unit there at the VA and they love seeing them come in. The families are so happy to see the flowers,” Russell said.
“When you are in the end stages of your life you want to be cheered up,” Raible said.
A growing group with a big milestone
The Flower Buds started with six to eight volunteers. The group now has 40.
Mullins has been doing it for 18 years.
“I love flowers and this is what I wanted to do when I retired, so, I’ve been doing this for 18 years now,” she said.
The group is celebrating a major milestone: since 2006, the Flower Buds have delivered more than 90,000 vases of flowers.
“All these flowers would be thrown in the garbage, so we put them to good use,” Mullins said.

title: How the One Big Beautiful Bill Act is impacting the midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Throughout the 2026 midterm election season, candidates have been speaking out about the impacts of the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
“With our Republican Congress, I signed a great, big, beautiful bill delivering the largest tax cuts in American history,” President Donald Trump said, at a midterm rally in Corpus Christi on Tuesday.
The law, that was signed by the president in July 2025, implemented several tax breaks for Americans and cut some social service programs.
Republicans have been touting the law throughout the election cycle, saying that it is helping Americans.
“Americans don’t know that there’s no tax on tips, no tax on overtime…” said Rep. Derrick Van Ordern, R-Wis, at the GOP’s midterm convention in September.
But George Washington University Professor Dr. Todd Belt said that the law is not making much of a difference for voters right now because of affordability concerns that are plaguing many people.
“That’s why affordability is the number one watchword,” he said. “Gasoline prices, grocery prices, health care, child care, all these things we’re hearing from voters who are saying that they just can’t make ends meet, whether they got a little bit of a tax cut or not. That’s just not making a dent in it.”
Democratic candidates have been highlighting other parts of the law, including its disproportionate benefits for high-income taxpayers.
In Texas, U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico has suggested repealing the law’s tax breaks for the top 1% of earners.
“...reversing the tax breaks for the top 1% in that big ugly bill, and giving that $1 trillion to the middle class in the form of a cost-of-living tax adjustment,” he said, in an interview in August. “And so these are policies that actually benefit Texans.”
The law also includes significant cuts and policy changes to Medicaid. Some voters say those changes will impact how they vote in the elections.
“It is definitely getting me to look much closer at candidates that are running,” said Amber Mader, a voter in Arkansas who relies on Medicaid and Social Security Disability.
Mader, who is disabled and paralyzed, said the programs that she relies, that provide home health care nursing and transportation services to appointments, have been reduced after the law’s passage.
“We’re not going to see a single cent in benefit from these tax cuts,” she said. “We are, however, dealing daily with severe difficulties and disruptions to basic services, things that are not optional for me because of this bill.”
Tax experts have also said that the law’s policy changes are unlikely to address cost-of-living issues.
“You know, it’s hard for tax policy to be used to directly tackle sort of immediate affordability issues,” said Elena Patel, co-director of the Urban Brookings Tax Policy Center.
Patel also said the law’s impacts will become more apparent over time.
“So some of the changes early on really benefited middle and lower class families,” Patel said. “But the longer we are into this bill, the more people will notice that it’s benefiting high income tax people.”

title: Obituary: Bruce Johnson Mott
text:
TOPSHAM – Bruce Johnson Mott, 98, died Oct. 9, 2026. He was born in Providence, RI, the son of Edgar C. (Dick) Mott and Ruth Johnson Mott.
Bruce graduated from Tufts University in 1950, where he was a member of Alpha Tau Omega fraternity. He subsequently graduated from Army Artillery Officer Candidate School at Fort Sill, Okla., and served in combat in Korea as a forward observer with the 10th Field Artillery Battalion of the Third Infantry Division. He was honorably discharged with the rank of First Lieutenant and was awarded the Bronze Star for his military service.
Following his military service, he went on to earn a vice presidency at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Boston and later served as a corporate officer of Connecticut Mutual Life Insurance Company in Hartford, Conn. He spent nearly six years as a corporate executive recruiter before retiring to Maine in 1993.
An accomplished sailor, Bruce was a veteran of the Marblehead–Halifax Ocean Race and the Manhattan Island circumnavigation race. He served as navigator or crew aboard a variety of racing boats along the East Coast and owned several sailboats throughout his life.
Bruce and his wife, Abbie, enjoyed the quiet beauty of the Maine coast. They were avid downhill skiers at Sunday River and shared a love of flying, owning and piloting a single-engine Cessna aircraft.
In addition to his professional accomplishments and many adventures, Bruce was a corporation member of Mid Coast Hospital, a member of the United Church in Brunswick, Maine, and a 32nd-degree Master Mason.
Bruce will be remembered for his distinguished military service, successful business career, love of the sea and the outdoors, and adventurous spirit. His life reflected a commitment to service, a passion for exploration, and an appreciation for the many pursuits that made his years in Maine so fulfilling.
Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.

title: A long-dry Maine town will vote on whether to allow its 1st pub at its only store
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A procession of locals stopped on the porch of Northern Bay Market in Penobscot on Monday to talk with owner Jamie MacNair, who sat in a rocking chair: a local newspaper editor, a selectman, workers on their lunch breaks.
“See, this is why we need a pub,” she said.
MacNair, who bought the market with her then-husband in 2017, has long wanted to open one in a separate building she plans to build behind it, and hopes to do so next summer.
But she can’t, unless residents vote to change local laws that make Penobscot a partially dry town, where liquor can be sold in containers — a change voters allowed just within the last decade, also for Northern Bay Market — but not served on-site.
Not everyone’s on board with the pub idea, questioning how such a change to longtime regulations would affect the rural Hancock County town’s character, at the tail end of a long, slow cultural change in Maine. For MacNair, it’s a way to provide a gathering space and bring in revenue to keep the mom-and-pop establishment going amid “astronomical” costs that challenge rural businesses.
Maine was among the states leading the charge against alcohol sales in the 19th century, restricting several times before federal prohibition in 1920; towns here kept local control over the rules after that.
Many, including Penobscot, first voted on specific liquor ordinances in a 1968 referendum. Some have remained dry because, in small communities with few local businesses, there’s simply been no reason to revisit the subject.
Numerous towns have loosened up laws in recent years, often holding votes at the requests of local businesses — though others have told the Bangor Daily News in the past that they’re happy to keep their restrictions, saying the bans suit the quiet natures of their towns.
Penobscot is one of the last incorporated towns in Hancock County with alcohol restrictions, according to state data.
MacNair pictures a cozy, English-inspired 20-by-20-foot pub with a courtyard and picnic tables. It would be open seasonally from Thursdays through Saturdays, run by her son and daughter-in-law, and may host small local gatherings like trivia events.
The store’s pizza- and lobster-centric menu would stay mostly the same, with the addition of a charcuterie board. The market would still close at 7, as would the pub.
She’s open to the idea of expanding if it’s successful, she said, but wants to keep things small and low-key — like the market itself.
“This is a mom and pop, and it’s one of the last strongholds on the peninsula,” she said. “I really want to keep that quiet, small-town feeling, so it’s authentic to Maine’s traditional general stores.”
But a group of residents are concerned about the vote, raising concerns that changing the laws means changing what makes Penobscot special.
In a letter to the editor of the online news site The Rising Tide, one said an initial vote — later rescheduled because of notice issues — on “this sensitive and divisive issue” had been rushed. The vote asks residents to remove another longtime restriction to “usher in a new modern age for our historic community,” causing her heart to ache for the protection of Penobscot’s traditional way of life.
Changing historic things that make the town unique “weakens the foundation of the community,” she said, and crosses a line that can’t be uncrossed.
“If we vote to usher in on-premise liquor service, will we be embracing with open arms a beacon to strangers far and wide to come drink their limit before driving down our quiet unpatrolled rural roads? If yes, then what will we next embrace? A Family Dollar? A cannabis dispensary?”
MacNair said the market’s record since getting its bottled liquor license can speak for itself, and highlighted that she grew up in town, chose to stay and is raising her own children there.
The 2019 vote was quieter, she said, but some people worried about the changes then, too. Most have been supportive of her current proposal, she said, and she invites anyone with concerns about losing the town’s integrity to talk with her.
She thinks those in opposition have mostly moved in from away and don’t understand the market’s history, its role as the center of town and her need to add revenue sources in order to stay in business.
“I just want people to know I’m here, and this is my community, and I would never do anything to hurt or change it in a negative way,” she said.
She views the vote as less of a change to Penobscot’s fabric and more of a way to encourage the community gathering that starts on the porch. It’s her favorite thing to do, MacNair said. She sits out there every morning she can.
“I think it’s a perfect time to expand and see how it goes. And, I would just really like the chance to see if there’s room for growth in that area here in Penobscot,” she said. “Which I think there is.”
A public hearing on allowing on-premise liquor sales will be held on Nov. 10, followed by a town vote on the 20th.

title: Mark Kelly shrugs off Susan Collins’ knocks on Troy Jackson but won’t criticize her by name
text:
BRUNSWICK, Maine — U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona on Wednesday defended Democrat Troy Jackson against one of Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ central knocks against the former Maine Senate president: that he lacks the experience and ability to get things done in Washington.
For the second campaign stop in two days alongside Jackson, Kelly steered clear of directly criticizing or naming the five-term incumbent. He bashed Republicans at large, saying the majority party had failed to check President Donald Trump. He argued Jackson represents a working-class voice that could help a Democratic majority set a new course for the country.
“We’re in a really bad spot right now,” he told reporters outside Flight Deck Brewing. “The top 1% is just getting richer and richer, and families are falling behind and can’t afford gas in the car. Young people can’t afford rent.”
The back-and-forth with Kelly, a retired Navy fighter pilot and astronaut considering a 2028 presidential run, gets at the central tension of Maine’s U.S. Senate race. Collins is asking voters to value the seniority and Appropriations Committee gavel she has used to steer federal money home, while Jackson is betting on Trump’s unpopularity.
“Republicans in the United States Congress gave a big tax cut to the top people … and it was paid for by taking healthcare away and food assistance away from people who can’t afford it,” Kelly said. “That’s what Republicans did because this president asked them to.”
The criticism didn’t acknowledge that Collins, who has highlighted breaks with Trump on the Iran war, tariffs and healthcare cuts, was one of three Republicans who voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. She did so citing an estimated $5.9 billion cuts to Maine’s Medicaid program over a decade. Jackson during debates and in ads has said Collins’ previous vote supporting a motion to bring the bill to the Senate floor still makes her responsible for the eventual cuts.
When asked about Collins and her criticism of Jackson, Kelly suggested lawmakers over time have difficulty “in how they respond to the challenges our country is facing at any moment.”
He did not respond directly to mention of the senator touting her position as appropriations chair compared to Jackson coming into the chamber with far less immediate influence. But he made the case that the Democrat’s background would serve him well on Capitol Hill.
“Troy, like me, we come from working class families,” Kelly said. “I’m the son of two cops. I didn’t go to some fancy private school or have connections or a trust fund. I understand what it’s like for folks to struggle to get by, and I know Troy does too.”
Collins has talked up her track record of bipartisan legislation and bringing $1.5 billion in federal earmarks to Maine projects over the last five years. She argues Jackson would face an uphill battle being effective in a sharply divided Senate.
In a recent debate the senator pointed to Jackson’s Augusta record. Along with 100 combined vetoes of his bills by Govs. Janet Mills and Paul LePage, more than a third of his bills over two decades in the Legislature died after being unanimously rejected in committee. Jackson countered that lawmakers hold hearings on all bills and many that are killed have parts worked into other packages.
“If you can’t find one person in your own party to vote for your bills when you were the Senate president, how do you think you’re going to get things done … as the most junior senator?” Collins said.

title: Do zinc lozenges actually work as a cold treatment?
text:
Do zinc lozenges actually work as a cold treatment?
It's sniffle season. If you have a cold that you can't kick, you may be researching tips to overcome your infection. After looking into whether vitamin C can stop cold symptoms, we wondered about another commonly promoted cure: zinc.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com's Well Informed.
Zinc is one of the body's essential minerals. It's important for immune system function, wound healing, bone growth, hormone production, and our senses of taste and smell. People generally get all the zinc they need from their diet – zinc deficiency is uncommon in the U.S. – but over-the-counter zinc lozenges and nasal sprays are often sold as cold-quashing treatments.
Does zinc really work?
A 2024 paper published by the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews looked at the results of 34 studies on zinc to prevent or treat the common cold. The review's authors found that when it comes to preventing a cold, there is little to no benefit of regularly taking zinc supplements.
But zinc shows promise in treating colds.
The Cochrane review found that zinc may reduce the average duration of a cold by around 2.4 days when compared to a placebo. But the authors didn’t give a full-throated endorsement of zinc as a cold cure: They wrote they had "little confidence" in the evidence.
Study results aren’t always consistent. Several experimental studies and meta-analyses have found similar results supporting zinc’s cold-shortening benefits, while others haven’t found a significant effect.
In order for zinc to be even a little effective as a cold treatment, it must be taken as a lozenge or a nasal spray so it can directly affect the nose and throat where respiratory infections take root. But beware — zinc nasal sprays have been linked to permanent loss of smell, leading to FDA warnings about several products.
Dr. Harri Hemilä, a Finnish researcher who has studied how zinc affects colds, told Well Informed that part of the reason study results differ may be because doses and ingredient formulations vary.
Of the 34 studies in the Cochrane review, dosages ranged from 0.044 milligrams to 296 milligrams of zinc per day, and included several types of zinc — zinc acetate, zinc gluconate, and zinc orotate — administered in different forms, such as nasal spray, lozenge, and syrup.
In a 2011 systematic review of 13 studies, Hemilä found that trials using daily doses of less than 75 milligrams had no effect on cold duration, but those with over 75 milligrams did show a benefit.
“The greatest problem with using zinc lozenges to treat colds is the difficulty in finding proper lozenges,” Hemilä said, noting the ones on the market may be too low of a dose or include ingredients like citric acid that bind to zinc and make a lozenge less effective.
Common lozenge brands like Cold-EEZE contain around 11-13 milligrams each, meaning a person would need to consume six to seven lozenges a day to surpass that 75 milligram-threshold. That may be more than what the package instructs you to take.
These zinc cold products can cause side effects, most commonly bad taste, nausea, and diarrhea — which people may decide isn’t worth it just to shave a few days off a cold. But in terms of safety, for a short cold treatment, these higher doses of zinc are unlikely to cause dangerous zinc toxicity.
"As far as we know, there are no serious risks to taking the lozenges for a few days," said Dr. Mark H. Ebell, a family medicine professor at Michigan State University.
That doesn't mean you should be taking this much zinc regularly. The recommended daily intake for adults is 8 to 11 milligrams, and you shouldn’t take more than 40 milligrams regularly, as it can cause dangerous health effects like copper deficiency.
For someone with a bad cold, it may be worth a try, but don't expect a miracle. And always talk to your doctor before adding a new supplement to your routine.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com's Well Informed.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: NFL players help build mobility ramp for veteran in need
text:
NFL players help build mobility ramp for veteran in need
NFL players and members of the Cincinnati Bengals teamed up with Operation Ramp It Up volunteers to help give one Cincinnati man a better quality of life.
Fresh off the Oct. 25 road win over the Baltimore Ravens, several players, including Bengals offensive lineman Dalton Risner, staff members and cheerleaders, joined efforts to build a mobility ramp for an 81-year-old  Navy veteran and his wife.
The NFL says it honors and helps veterans across the country live better lives through its Salute to Service program.
“We're building a ramp for a guy to be able to get in and out of his house much easier,” offensive lineman Dalton Risner said. “He's a military veteran and served our country. So, it's the least that we could do to come out here for an hour to help build a ramp.”
Risner said serving the Cincinnati community and fans like Ken is what it is all about. 
“I wouldn't be able to play the game that I love if it wasn't for people that fight for our country and serve for our country,” Risner said.
Ken Wackenthaler said the ramp will help him and his wife get around the house. Ken and his family are Bengals fans through and through.
“I've been watching them for a long time, and ... good days, bad days, but they hang in there,” Wackenthaler said.
This is the sixth year of the Bengals’ partnership with Operation Ramp It Up

title: Pres. Trump returns to South Carolina
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will hold a rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina, a Charlotte, N.C. suburb Thursday. The goal is to encourage voters to vote for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) as she faces Democrat Annie Andrews.
The latest stop on Trump’s “midterm blitz,” will be at the Rock Hill Sports and Event Center. Doors open at 9 a.m. Eastern Time, and remarks are scheduled to begin at 12:30 p.m. Eastern Time.
Tim Phillips, a VIP attending the rally, said he is happy the president is coming. He also said the visit signals something he doesn’t like.
“Candidly, it’s also sobering. This is the second trip the president will make to South Carolina for this Senate race, the Graham Senate race here. You would like to see South Carolina kind of put to bed,” Phillips said, meaning the polls showing the Republican candidate with a solid lead.
South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1998.
Trump visited Greenville, N.C. on October 20, and Clemson, S.C. October 21 as he tries to rally his base across the country. The Republican National Committee said the party is banking on voter turnout to hold Congress.
Phillips, a South Carolina native, has campaigned for Republicans across the country. He said the rallies create a sense of community in the party.
“The energy, it’s electric. Candidly, you never know what the president is going to say, you just don’t. That is part of the fun of it. It is a show. It’s like seeing old friends,” Phillips said.
Most polls indicate Republicans only have a small chance of saving the Senate. Many of the president’s visits have focused heavily on putting his name behind Senate candidates.
