title: DOJ to send election monitors to South Portland polling locations
text:
DOJ to send election monitors to South Portland polling locations in addition to Lewiston and Portland
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the U.S. Department of Justice will send observers to the city of South Portland on Election Day, which is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Bellows said the Justice Department informed her of the plan, and that no reason was given by the department.
The news comes after Bellows previously revealed that the DOJ was planning to send election observers to the cities of Lewiston and Portland on Election Day.
In an interview with C-SPAN, Bellows said DOJ observers are "not new" and she welcomes their presence because they build public confidence in elections.
Bellows said her office will ensure that the monitors follow the law and she is confident that they will do so across the country.
"We will ensure that they follow the same protocols as anyone observing the election," Bellows said during an appearance on C-SPAN's "Ceasefire" on Friday. "They cannot interact with or intimidate voters in any way. We safeguard the voting booths and the tabulators themselves."
Bellows also emphasized that federal law prohibits armed federal agents, such as ICE personnel, from being at polling locations. She said Maine is prepared to "fight back" and stop that immediately if it were to happen.
It's unclear how many federal observers are coming to Maine, but their deployment is part of a larger effort that the Justice Department has called the "biggest DOJ election observer effort in history."
President Donald Trump plans to dispatch more than 1,000 monitors on Election Day, which is hundreds more than the Biden administration deployed in 2024.
Speaking to CNN in Georgia on Saturday, Trump downplayed concerns that the monitoring efforts would disrupt polling places or prevent anyone from voting.
"They're not going to do anything other than watch," Trump said. "If they see something wrong, we want to all have honest elections. And the one thing we have to have is honest elections."
Bellows said that recent federal attempts to obtain voter information and impose limits on voting have raised concerns among voters. She said her office has trained election workers and law enforcement on how to respond to potential disruptions, including questions about federal agents at polling places.
One vocal critic of the plan has been Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson, who says federal observers could scare people away from voting.
"If there's anyone that was doing anything wrong in Lewiston, I'm sure those poll workers are going to catch it and make it stop," said Jackson to reporters after a campaign rally in Westbrook on Saturday. "We don't need people coming from Washington to make it harder or scare people from voting."

According to the Food and Drug Administration, Taylor Farms is recalling its H-E-B Backyard BBQ Chop Salad because it may contain undeclared soy and tree nuts, specifically almonds.

title: ‘She is forever my hero’: 5th-grader’s quick thinking helps save bus driver
text:
CEDAR RAPIDS, Iowa (KGAN) - An Iowa fifth grader’s quick thinking helped save a bus driver who was struggling to breathe.
And it was all caught on camera.
It started as a routine ride home from Viola Gibson Elementary School, until bus driver Christine Houston said a strong cologne scent set off a coughing fit, and her breathing kept getting worse.
“It just kept progressively getting worse, and I kept going to at least two to three stops before I realized I can’t go anymore,” Houston said.
Fifth grader Bella Scott says she knew something was wrong and decided she had to do something.
“She was wheezing. She was struggling to breathe, and obviously she needed help. You can’t just watch something like that happen,” Bella Scott said.
She jumped into action and called the one person she knew could help — her dad.
Nick Scott was nearby, and at first he thought Bella just wanted more time on her phone, until he heard the fear in her voice.
“And the third time that she called, I could hear the terror in her voice, and I knew something was wrong,” Nick Scott said.
Nick Scott got on the bus and saw Houston was struggling to breathe. He called 911, then helped the students call their families and stay calm.
“She wanted to get the kids home, which I understand, but with 20 kids or so left on the bus, we couldn’t risk something happening. So I basically told her, too bad, we’re calling 911, and then you could kind of see the relief on her face,” he said.
Houston says Bella Scott did what students learned during bus safety training: call a trusted adult.
“She called the one that she knew would answer, and that was her dad,” Houston said.
Emergency responders arrived, and the bus driver got the help she needed. Cedar Rapids Schools later recognized Bella Scott for her quick actions.
“She is forever my hero, and I’ve said this from the beginning,” Houston said. “Not all heroes wear a cape. She had a cell phone with a backpack. She called her dad. And I don’t know, I, I just, I’m totally grateful for her.”
Houston says she’s always cared deeply about the students on her route, and Bella Scott’s actions showed that care goes both ways.

University of Maine Cooperative Extension will host an online panel discussion for current and aspiring flower farmers from 6 to 7:15 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10. The discussion will focus on how to build a flower farming business that is resilient, rewarding and sustainable.

title: ‘It’s big’: Astronomers make startling discovery of a possible dwarf planet beyond Pluto
text:
‘It’s big’: Astronomers make startling discovery of a possible dwarf planet beyond Pluto
Astronomers have spotted a new dwarf planet candidate in the solar system, beyond the orbit of Pluto, which they provisionally named ED138.
See the orbital path of the new dwarf candidate in the video above
If future observations confirm the discovery, ED138 will join a group currently made up of five dwarf planets that have been recognized by the International Astronomical Union, or IAU: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris.
The finding is the result of detections made by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, a new telescope that sits atop a 2,682-meter-tall (8,800-foot-tall) mountain in Chile and houses the world’s largest digital camera. The telescope started operating in 2025 and is capable of imaging the entire sky every three days.
Matthew Holman, a Smithsonian senior astrophysicist and lecturer in astronomy at Harvard University, ran a computer program he co-developed to comb through data collected by Rubin earlier in 2026, scanning billions of detections of moving objects. When ED138 popped up, Holman said he first reacted with "excited disbelief" and immediately checked for a false positive or an error with the computer program.
To confirm the observation, Holman, who is also a Rubin Operations team member, worked with his colleague Mario Jurić, the Rubin Solar System lead scientist and a professor in the department of astronomy at the University of Washington. Jurić looked for more observations of ED138 in Rubin’s catalog and found 20 additional ones dating back to March 2026. Eventually, using other sources, the researchers were able to plot the orbit of the object as far back as 10 years.
However, Holman warns, ED138 isn’t officially a dwarf planet yet: "At this point, it’s still a candidate. We really need to know how physically big it is, and that will take a few months, probably."
ED138 unveiled
ED138’s diameter is estimated to be between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (370 and 930 miles), which would make it bigger than the smallest of the recognized dwarf planets, Ceres. It currently orbits the sun at a distance of about 46 astronomical units — with each unit representing the average distance between Earth and the sun. That means ED138 is farther away than Pluto and also a trans-Neptunian object, or TNO — a class of objects that orbit the sun at a distance greater than Neptune’s.
In the night sky, ED138 is not visible with the naked eye but "is bright enough that really capable amateurs can see it if they know where to look," according to Holman.
Part of the reason scientists hadn’t discovered ED138 before is that it’s in the southern hemisphere, and therefore very difficult to observe from the northern hemisphere, Holman noted.
"That already rules out whole sets of telescopes that might have found this, and there aren’t as many telescopes searching the sky in the southern hemisphere," he said.
Another factor that kept ED138 hidden is that it is on the same plane as our galaxy. "For the last 20 years, the object has kind of been looping its way across the Milky Way, from our point of view," Holman explained. "People don’t typically search for things in the Milky Way, because there’s so many stars that it’s really hard to find moving objects."
The new dwarf planet candidate joins the Rubin telescope’s growing list of detected objects — largely asteroids and much smaller TNOs. According to Holman, there might be "a handful" more objects the size of ED138, and Rubin should eventually find those, too.
"Rubin Observatory is just doing its job really well, inventorying the Solar System to new depths," said Megan Schwamb, a reader in astrophysics at Queen’s University Belfast and a member of the Rubin Solar System Operations team, in an email.
"I was surprised that it found such an object so early in the commissioning observations. This was not on my bingo card for this year," Schwamb added. "It shows how Rubin’s combination of speed, depth, and sky coverage is going to transform our view of the Solar System over the next decade and especially in the next few years."
'Think of it as a world'
In 2006, the IAU adopted a new definition of a planet, describing it as an object that orbits the sun, is mostly round, and is big enough that it has cleared its orbit of objects of similar size. Scientists made the controversial decision to demote Pluto because it didn’t satisfy the last requirement, and our solar system went from nine to eight planets.
At the same time, Pluto and its ilk became known as dwarf planets — nearly round objects that orbit the sun but aren’t large enough to have cleared their own orbits of debris.
If ED138 is confirmed as a new dwarf planet, astronomers will first give it a permanent number and then an actual name, although the process could take time, and the details of who exactly will get to choose the name are still unclear.
"People have already emailed me some suggestions, and some of them are already taken by other objects," Holman said. "I don’t know. It’ll be fun. Maybe I’ll get to suggest something, but I’m not going to hold my breath, because this is a big, big project."
The finding is significant for the field, said Michele Bannister, an associate professor at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, who was not involved with the discovery of ED138.
The object is "scientifically really cool because it’s a trans-Neptunian object and it’s also physically quite large, but still a lot fainter than you can see with the naked eye," said Bannister, who studies the small worlds of the solar system.
The size of the object is just within the range where we can start to think of it as a world, she added, and other telescopes will now pick up the baton to find out more about it.
"Maybe if we ever fly a spacecraft there, we’ll find it has a nitrogen glacier like Pluto," Bannister said. "That would be great to see. But at the moment, all we know is that it’s big, and the rest is going to be speculation for a little bit, about what its physical characteristics really are."

title: How to spot fake crystals and avoid costly mistakes
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SEDONA, Ariz. (Aging Untold) — The crystal and gemstone industry is booming, fueled in part by social media, but experts warn buyers to be cautious of fake products flooding the market.
Jamie Inglett, who owns a crystal shop in Sedona, said consumers can find fake crystals in stores and at gem shows.
“As a consumer you really kind of have to do your own research,” Inglett said.
Growing popularity drives demand
The crystal craze has exploded online, with #crystals generating 20 billion views on TikTok.
Inglett has built up 215,106 Instagram followers and opened a physical storefront in Sedona after finding success online.
“You don’t have to believe in crystal healing or crystal energy to appreciate their beauty,” Inglett said.
What to know about fake crystals
Shannon Wimberly, a crystal collector for several years, said she has encountered fake crystals and now scrutinizes purchases more carefully.
“I absolutely know I’ve run into getting fake ones, so I started scrutinizing other things more and more,” Wimberly said.
Inglett said buyers could end up with lab-grown crystals sold as natural stones. She showed a lab-grown crystal purchased from a Sedona shop for more than $100 that could be found online for $5 to $20.
“You’ll see hundreds of these, depending on the store. They’ll all look about the same,” Inglett said.
Buyers could also purchase completely synthetic items made from plastic or glass.
How to identify fakes
Inglett recommends asking questions about origin and authenticity.
“Asking the shop, where is this from? And then they should at least be able to tell you the country of origin, if not the actual mine name,” Inglett said.
Physical tests can help identify fake crystals. Glass fakes sound different, don’t get cold and have unnatural dye patterns, Inglett said. Fake moldavite lacks natural grooves and textures and appears too uniform in shape, she said.
Inglett said lab-grown crystals are not an issue as long as sellers disclose what buyers are purchasing.

title: How the One Big Beautiful Bill Act is impacting the midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Throughout the 2026 midterm election season, candidates have been speaking out about the impacts of the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
“With our Republican Congress, I signed a great, big, beautiful bill delivering the largest tax cuts in American history,” President Donald Trump said, at a midterm rally in Corpus Christi on Tuesday.
The law, that was signed by the president in July 2025, implemented several tax breaks for Americans and cut some social service programs.
Republicans have been touting the law throughout the election cycle, saying that it is helping Americans.
“Americans don’t know that there’s no tax on tips, no tax on overtime…” said Rep. Derrick Van Ordern, R-Wis, at the GOP’s midterm convention in September.
But George Washington University Professor Dr. Todd Belt said that the law is not making much of a difference for voters right now because of affordability concerns that are plaguing many people.
“That’s why affordability is the number one watchword,” he said. “Gasoline prices, grocery prices, health care, child care, all these things we’re hearing from voters who are saying that they just can’t make ends meet, whether they got a little bit of a tax cut or not. That’s just not making a dent in it.”
Democratic candidates have been highlighting other parts of the law, including its disproportionate benefits for high-income taxpayers.
In Texas, U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico has suggested repealing the law’s tax breaks for the top 1% of earners.
“...reversing the tax breaks for the top 1% in that big ugly bill, and giving that $1 trillion to the middle class in the form of a cost-of-living tax adjustment,” he said, in an interview in August. “And so these are policies that actually benefit Texans.”
The law also includes significant cuts and policy changes to Medicaid. Some voters say those changes will impact how they vote in the elections.
“It is definitely getting me to look much closer at candidates that are running,” said Amber Mader, a voter in Arkansas who relies on Medicaid and Social Security Disability.
Mader, who is disabled and paralyzed, said the programs that she relies, that provide home health care nursing and transportation services to appointments, have been reduced after the law’s passage.
“We’re not going to see a single cent in benefit from these tax cuts,” she said. “We are, however, dealing daily with severe difficulties and disruptions to basic services, things that are not optional for me because of this bill.”
Tax experts have also said that the law’s policy changes are unlikely to address cost-of-living issues.
“You know, it’s hard for tax policy to be used to directly tackle sort of immediate affordability issues,” said Elena Patel, co-director of the Urban Brookings Tax Policy Center.
Patel also said the law’s impacts will become more apparent over time.
“So some of the changes early on really benefited middle and lower class families,” Patel said. “But the longer we are into this bill, the more people will notice that it’s benefiting high income tax people.”

title: Statue of Liberty marks 140th birthday after 1886 dedication in New York Harbor
text:
Statue of Liberty marks 140th birthday after 1886 dedication in New York Harbor
On Oct. 28, 1886, the Statue of Liberty was dedicated in New York Harbor by President Grover Cleveland.
Video above: Crescent moon sets behind Statue of Liberty in New York
The statue was a gift from France to the United States in honor of the alliance between the two countries during the American Revolution.
The sculpture is officially titled "Liberty Enlightening the World" and was forged by Frederic-Auguste Bartholdi.
The statue alone stands 151 feet tall (305 feet and 1 inch from the ground below the base to the tip of the torch). It is made of sheets of copper, which has naturally oxidized to form the outer green coating.
It was designated a national monument in 1924. Visitors can go inside the statue and are able to climb hundreds of stairs to the top of the crown for a breathtaking view.

title: Artificial intelligence transforms the workforce, regulations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Nearly all industries have been impacted by Artificial Intelligence. Goldman Sachs estimates 300 million jobs will be impacted by the emerging technology by 2030. AI is reshaping industries by the day, resulting in jobs being transformed or erased. The changes are bringing a greater need for AI oversight.
“People need to understand that there still needs to be human involvement,” Barry Jones, a Vice President at X2X said. X2X is an AI governance company. Jones said there’s not enough oversight AI oversight right now.
“Imagine an AI assistant preparing financial reports,” Jones said. “That’s a potentially productive tool. But just imagine if that AI system provided that critical financial information outside of the company’s internal workings.”
Before Congress left Capitol Hill for the midterms, several congressmembers made clear where they stood on what role the government should play on regulation.
“Well, look, anytime you can give the federal government out of it, I think we’re better off,” Rep. Buddy Carter (R-GA) said. “We don’t want to stifle innovation. But at the same time, we got to get this right. That’s the key. We got to get a right. I can be a very useful tool, unbelievably useful tool. But there are some concerns and there are some dangers there.”
“First, the United States needs to address the very real risks created by increasingly powerful AI systems, and these decisions need to be made by the American people through their representatives,” Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) said.
Jones said big picture, self-governance isn’t enough.
“But to say that something is self-governing is like having the fox watching the henhouse,” Jones said. “You really need to have a third party, layer in some cases, even the government saying these are the things that I can do and I cannot do.”
Jones said that private oversight is creating roles that have been replaced by technology. Microsoft recently announced they offered 60,000 employees buyouts due to AI. Jones has advice for people looking for a career pivot due to AI.
“Start learning AI,” Jones said. “Understand how it applies to your profession. Also understand that judgement, experience, trust and accountability matter. The goal shouldn’t be to compete with the machine. The goal should be to become someone who knows the useful power of the technology and using it responsibly.”
Efforts to regulate Artificial Intelligence are stalled on Capitol Hill but the 120th Congress could take up the rapidly evolving technology in January.

title: Pres. Trump returns to South Carolina
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will hold a rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina, a Charlotte, N.C. suburb Thursday. The goal is to encourage voters to vote for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) as she faces Democrat Annie Andrews.
The latest stop on Trump’s “midterm blitz,” will be at the Rock Hill Sports and Event Center. Doors open at 9 a.m. Eastern Time, and remarks are scheduled to begin at 12:30 p.m. Eastern Time.
Tim Phillips, a VIP attending the rally, said he is happy the president is coming. He also said the visit signals something he doesn’t like.
“Candidly, it’s also sobering. This is the second trip the president will make to South Carolina for this Senate race, the Graham Senate race here. You would like to see South Carolina kind of put to bed,” Phillips said, meaning the polls showing the Republican candidate with a solid lead.
South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1998.
Trump visited Greenville, N.C. on October 20, and Clemson, S.C. October 21 as he tries to rally his base across the country. The Republican National Committee said the party is banking on voter turnout to hold Congress.
Phillips, a South Carolina native, has campaigned for Republicans across the country. He said the rallies create a sense of community in the party.
“The energy, it’s electric. Candidly, you never know what the president is going to say, you just don’t. That is part of the fun of it. It is a show. It’s like seeing old friends,” Phillips said.
Most polls indicate Republicans only have a small chance of saving the Senate. Many of the president’s visits have focused heavily on putting his name behind Senate candidates.

title: Judge denies federal request to segregate California ballots, says it would 'wreak havoc' on voting
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A federal judge rejected on Wednesday a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations they are likely noncitizens, warning it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.
The ruling by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state. Over 500,000 votes have already been counted.
The decision is the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections ahead of voting that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term.
The Republican administration sued election officials in the Democratic state in mid-October, accusing the officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.
The federal government’s request, Carter wrote, “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”
The administration had asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The federal government also had asked the appeals court for a quick ruling — before a district judge’s scheduled Oct. 27 hearing in the case — but that effort was rejected by the higher court.
The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn’t win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in Congress.
Carter’s order was a forceful rebuke of the federal government’s demand, arguing that segregating ballots at this time in the election would require counties to develop new methods for sorting ballots and “risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters.” In other words, Carter argued, it would have the same effect as purging voters and therefore violates the National Voting Rights Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls within 90 days of an election.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred,” Carter wrote. “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.”
Carter also rejected the Justice Department’s argument that California was impeding the federal government’s ability to enforce the law. He argued that prosecutors already demonstrated the ability to enforce election law when they arrested 28 noncitizens who had voted or registered to vote illegally.
Federal prosecutors did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment on Wednesday evening.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who argued on behalf of the federal government on Tuesday, has previously said that the federal government’s request wouldn’t impede the election. Instead, he argued that the Justice Department was trying to “safeguard the elections.”
“Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later,” he said. “It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots.”

title: What you need to know about Tremont's special deer hunt
text:
TREMONT — In less than a week, Mount Desert Island will host its first deer hunt in almost 100 years, with hunters gearing up to set blinds or deer stands under a strict, controlled plan within Tremont’s town limits to help reduce the area’s deer population.
According to Town Manager Jesse Dunbar, “The town received 99 applications, and 92 have been approved.”
Dunbar confirmed each hunter will be allotted two deer tags due to the 200 harvest limit and said, “Applicants will receive a phone call from the town office this week if they are approved, and then they must come pick up their permission slip prior to hunting, which begins Monday, Nov. 2.”
Dunbar wanted to make sure people know the hunt starts on Nov. 2, and not Oct. 31.
Once hunters receive their permission slip, they must keep it on their person at all times while hunting. After shooting a deer, hunters must present the slip at the tagging station. One tagging station will be located at Gott’s Store in Tremont.
“Gott’s Store is where they will get their tag put on the deer, and it will be recorded for the state of Maine at that point,” explained Dunbar. “Gott’s will issue tags during normal operating hours,” which, according to its website, is seven days a week, 5 a.m. to 9 p.m., although Maine law does prohibit hunting on Sundays statewide.
Hunters participating in the hunt will be limited to archery and shotguns from a fixed position.
Additionally, the Deer Management Plan on Tremont’s website states, “Stand locations must be in conformance with state laws for required setbacks from other structures and dwellings unless appropriate permissions have been obtained. Landowners must provide stand locations and any documentation to prove compliance with State laws.”
Landowner permission is required before anyone can hunt on private property. The normal implied consent laws for hunting in Maine do not apply for the special hunt in Tremont.
Residents can contact the town office and have their property listed as “yellow,” which means “use caution/restricted and permission is required or “red,” which means it is closed, hunting is not allowed/strictly prohibited and will be treated as trespassing.” In all cases, permission is required to hunt on private property.
Voters approved the deer management plan in May by a vote of 314-227.
This initiative follows the past introduction and failure of state Bill LD 1438, which sought to make deer hunting legal on Mount Desert Island. Rep. Billy Bob Faulkingham (R–Winter Harbor) proposed the legislation, but it did not make it out of committee.
The Committee on Inland Fisheries and Wildlife unanimously voted on May 7, 2025, that the bill ought not to pass, thereby halting its progress through the legislative process.
After months of debate and public hearings reviewing plan drafts, approval eventually came from the Tremont Select Board, and then from residents at the town meeting ballot.
Some residents and critics wanted to protect the deer population on Mount Desert Island, while others argued that the population needs to be thinned and deer around the island pose a safety risk due to ticks and motor vehicle accidents.
The special deer hunt, if successful, will run for three years in the month of November of 2026, 2027, and 2028. At any time, if the town feels the hunt needs to be shut down, it can.
The management plan states: “The proposed Special Hunt was created in response to voter approval for increased deer reduction measures to relieve deer-related problems. Tremont has taken a conservative approach in developing this Special Hunt and will continue to work closely with MDIFW to evaluate its effectiveness. The key to success of this initial effort is to have the process run smoothly and to gain social acceptance of the program. It is the hope of the Town of Tremont that demonstrating a well-run program will encourage additional property owners to open more land for hunting in subsequent years, and residents’ support for increased hunter participation and permits.”

title: ‘It is killing us’: Truck driver says friends had to find different jobs due to diesel costs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (KETV) – A Nebraska man who has driven a company truck for more than 25 years said rising diesel costs have him fearing for his livelihood.
“The gas prices, the fuel prices, man, it is killing us,” trucker Dave Turner said.
Americans rely on truckers to move goods every day, but drivers are concerned about the future of the industry.
“It’s astronomical and almost makes us nonexistent,” Turner said.
Diesel prices
Diesel prices reached an all-time record high of about $6.50 a gallon last month. Prices have remained in the same range since then.
Turner said rising fuel costs have already changed how drivers get from one destination to the next.
“A lot more time sitting and waiting for the company to be able to actually find decent routes for us as far as having to route us to the cheapest places to be able to get fuel,” Turner said.
Most company drivers have help finding lower prices.
Independent drivers
Asiwome Faiti, another company driver, said not all truckers are feeling the impact equally.
“You don’t have the capacity to hedge your fuel, so those are the people suffering, the mom and pop small businesses,” Faiti said.
Independent drivers are paying out of pocket to fill their tanks, and the rising cost is taking some of them out of the business.
“I have actually several of my friends, close friends that are independent truckers, and out of about 13 of them, seven of them have already had to shut down their trucks and find different jobs,” Turner said.
According to federal transportation data, trucks carried about 65% of U.S. freight by weight in 2024.
Faiti said he wants to be able to continue driving.
“All I can say is we pray that this crisis is over soon,” Faiti said.

title: She was born with eight fingers on one hand. Her family traveled to America for the surgery
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - A family traveled from Turkey to St. Louis for their daughter’s surgery to treat a rare condition affecting fewer than 100 people worldwide.
Elisa, an 18-month-old, was born with eight fingers on her left hand. She was diagnosed with Ulnar Dimelia, also known as Mirror Hand Syndrome.
“Mirror Hand is incredibly uncommon, and even surgeons like myself who take care of a great deal of kids almost never see this in their career. So, it’s really uncommon. Numbers are hard to come by, but one in a million or less is probably about right,” said Dr. Charles Goldfarb, Chief of Orthopedic Surgery at St. Louis Children’s Hospital.
The condition leaves patients without a radius bone. This means significant limitations in wrist and elbow motion and preserved shoulder movements.
“From the very beginning, he was really warm, genuine, and gave us a lot of hope. Honestly, the trust and support he gave us played a huge role in our decision to come to St. Louis,” said Emircan Buga, Elisa’s father.
Communication and care
Emircan and his wife, Gulten, only speak Turkish and used a translator. They said the language difference never got in the way of their daughter receiving care.
“Initially, I had conversations with them, from afar, but we talked on the phone and we did FaceTime, just communicating about her condition,” Goldfarb said.
“They provided us with immense support regarding every problem we might encounter or face along the way. We would like to thank them for the support they provided, both financially and psychologically,” Emircan said.
Through St. Louis Children’s International Free Care Fund, funded through the St. Louis Children’s Hospital Foundation, Elisa’s family connected with the orthopedic surgery team.
The surgery
On Jan. 30, Goldfarb led a team that completed a three-hour reconstructive surgery.
“And it’s so fun for me as a surgeon, who interacts with kids young and old, but at an early point in their life, to watch what happens after. And I do think a surgery like this is life-changing and will really help her succeed in all aspects,” Goldfarb said.
Elisa is now recovering.
“One of the things that makes me so excited in taking care of young children is seeing what they will accomplish later in life,” Goldfarb said.
Emircan said, “From now on, she will continue her life with more confidence and courage. But when we look back, we will miss that hand because that’s how the story began.”

title: Maine backs off eliminating emerald ash borer quarantine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A ban on freely transporting wood from areas of Maine infested by emerald ash borer will remain in effect after tribal governments and conservation groups protested a state plan to ease restrictions.
State Horticulturist Gary Fish said a proposal to end a quarantine aimed at slowing spread of the invasive insect attracted more than 80 public comments. Nearly all urged the state to keep the quarantine.
“So it was an easy decision for the [Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry] commissioner to just decide that we would keep the quarantine going,” Fish said.
Emerald ash borer was first discovered in Maine in 2018, and the quarantine has extended to every county except for Washington County. The insect tunnels into native ash trees, cuts off water and nutrients and can kill a host within five years, according to the forest service.
This summer, after ash borer was discovered in the Aroostook County town of Benedicta, the state said ash borer populations in northern and southern Maine had merged, and the quarantine was no longer effective.
But the move met with pushback from conservation groups, land trusts and Wabanaki Nations that rely on ash wood for traditional basketmaking.
Under the rules, it’s against the law to transport hardwood firewood from quarantine zones into areas that are not infested. Lumber companies and finished wood manufacturers also need state certification to move products between infested areas.
Fish said the forest service will continue enforcing the ban, although it will remain a challenge to stop ash borer from spreading further in the state.
“Basically, what keeps moving emerald ash borer are people moving firewood, and we have so many visitors to Maine that don’t understand that their firewood is potentially infested and spreading emerald ash borer and maybe some other forest killing pests,” Fish added.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: 83-year-old prepares for 51st NYC Marathon
text:
83-year-old prepares for 51st NYC Marathon as only runner to complete every marathon since 1976
Some running organizations estimate that less than 1% of the global population has run a marathon since the year 2000.
The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon will mark 83-year-old David Obelkevich's 116th marathon.
After growing up in an active family in Binghamton, New York, attending college at Columbia University was what brought Obelkevich to New York City in the 1960s. He ran his first marathon in 1974 on a whim when the race was run only in Central Park.
According to the New York Road Runners, he is the only person to have completed every single New York City Marathon since 1976, when the race expanded to all five boroughs.
He's completed more than 110 marathons when including other cities like Boston and Tokyo.
The former public school teacher, father and grandfather says it's the people he's met along the way that keep him running, including his wife, Lyn.
"She was coming towards me, and I was going up, so I said, 'Hi Lyn,' and she said, 'Hi Dave,'" Obelkevich told WCBS. "Fell in love with her during that date."
Obelkevich's streak has gone uninterrupted even through a blood clot in his leg in 2020. He recalls his fastest time was two hours and 40 minutes in 1982, eight years after his first marathon. Though he doubts that he'll ever meet those numbers again, his advice for first-time runners is that what matters is that you finish, no matter how slow.
"If I run a quarter of a mile, I get completely out of breath. So my walking is going to be what I do in the marathon," Obelkevich said with a laugh while walking in Central Park. "That's OK. Other people walk too ... Anyone can start it, but it takes a good person to finish."

title: Suspects in alleged school shooting plot in Georgia had floor plan, had chosen a date, warrants say
text:
Suspects in alleged school shooting plot in Georgia had floor plan, had chosen a date, warrants say
Three people arrested over an alleged plot to carry out a shooting at a Georgia high school had gotten a floor plan of the school and chosen a date to carry it out early next school year, according to arrest warrants.
Shane Keith Taylor, 17, and Michael Brandon Terry, 21, had reached an agreement with an unidentified juvenile suspect to provide weapons and had planned outfits and discussed buying body armor, video cameras and combat boots, according to arrest warrants. They chose next Aug. 20 as the date, just a couple of weeks after the first day of school on Aug. 2.
The suspects are accused of planning a shooting at Cherokee High School in Canton, about 45 miles north of Atlanta, and are charged with conspiracy to commit murder, police said. The juvenile is also accused of disrupting or interfering with the operation of public schools.
Related video above: Safety experts weigh in on additional measures schools could take to prevent or delay a shooter from gaining entry
A lawyer for Taylor, who is considered an adult under Georgia criminal law, said he had just gotten the case and did not have a comment. Online records show that he was being held without bond and has a preliminary hearing set for Nov. 13.
It was not immediately clear whether Terry, who was awaiting transfer from California to Cherokee County, had a lawyer, and The Associated Press could not immediately locate contact information for him. Police did not release the name and age of the juvenile suspect.
The FBI identified “threatening social media posts” and notified school police, who then contacted the Canton Police Department.
Police figured out the identity of the juvenile suspect, who they said lives in Canton and was connected to the threats. He was arrested Oct. 20. Taylor, who lives in Metter, Georgia, 240 miles southeast of Canton, and Terry, who lives in Chatsworth, California, were arrested on Oct. 23. It's not clear what connection, if any, Terry has to Georgia, or how the suspects might have known one another.
Investigators collected guns, ammunition and electronic devices as evidence, police said. No ongoing threat to the high school or any other school in the county was identified, and the investigation remained active, police said.
Cherokee County School District Superintendent Mary Elizabeth Davis sought in a video message posted online Tuesday to reassure parents.
“The mere thought of a school threat, let alone hearing of an alleged conspiracy to carry one out, is honestly devastating, and, like you, I have experienced the range of emotions that follow this type of news,” she said. But she added that law enforcement agencies working together had “completely disrupted” the alleged plot and said knowing that the processes in place worked the way they were supposed to was “reassuring.”

title: College professor among 2 found dead in home; suspect in custody, police say
text:

Wednesday morning, police responded to the Oberlin College Conservatory lot at 77 E. College St. to assist firefighters with a vehicle smoking and possibly on fire.
When crews arrived, they tried to find the registered vehicle owner, identified as Daniel Jones, 31, to conduct a welfare check.
When officers arrived at Jones’ home to check on his family, they found the victims dead inside the home.
Pipo Nguyen-Duy, a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College, was found dead on the first floor with an apparent gunshot wound.
A woman found dead on the second floor was not immediately identified. She also had an apparent gunshot wound.
Jones was located aat bout 10:20 a.m. and taken into custody. Charges are pending.
The investigation is ongoing.

An occupant and a pet escaped unharmed after a fire broke out at a home in Auburn Wednesday morning, according to the Auburn Fire Department.
Firefighters responded to 29 Lubear Way around 11:16 a.m. within three minutes and reported heavy fire coming from the front of the building and extending to the roof, officials said.

title: Medicare Advantage customers face fewer options, higher costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — Numerous residents covered by Medicare Advantage plans recently learned their coverage has been dropped and that alternatives are limited.
The news came through Annual Notice of Change letters arriving by mail since mid-September.
In his 51 years as an insurance broker, Carroll Harper said he’s never seen anything like the state of local Medicare Advantage options going into 2027. Harper is president of Carroll Harper and Associates Inc., a Medicare health plans agency in Southwest Harbor.
“It’s not a healthy environment for Maine seniors to be in,” Harper said. “Medicare Advantage does not have a healthy forecast. It’s problematic.”
Medicare Advantage plans, otherwise known as Part C coverage, are Medicare-approved plans through a private company that seniors can choose as an alternative to traditional Medicare. Roughly half of Americans on Medicare are covered by Medicare Advantage plans.
Harper said many residents have reached out to his office with concerns about being notified of lost coverage. For-profit conglomerates like United Healthcare, Aetna and others have drastically cut services in Hancock County, deeming coverage unprofitable, he said. Of the remaining options, some plans do not include major healthcare providers like Northern Light Health as part of their coverage networks.
“The federal government allows these for-profit carriers to pick and choose the counties they can make money in, and for 2027 they pretty much pulled out of Hancock County,” Harper said.
In addition to market factors, Harper pointed to changes at the federal level impacting the healthcare ecosystem, such as the ripple effects of the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” that President Donald Trump signed into law in 2025.
The legislation cut over $1 trillion from health programs, according to the Center for Medicare Advocacy, which estimates 10 million people will lose their health insurance coverage. These cuts primarily target Medicaid, the joint federal-state program that provides health coverage to low-income individuals and families.
“While these broad health care cuts will affect many Medicare beneficiaries indirectly, including those who are dually eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid, several provisions of the OBBB directly target Medicare beneficiaries,” according to the nonprofit law organization.
Ellsworth resident Gretchen Wilson, who was covered with a Medicare Advantage plan under United Healthcare, recently learned her coverage has been terminated.
“I made an appointment with my insurance broker to go over next year’s Medicare, and he texted me I need to bring my denial letter,” Wilson said, stating it was a total surprise. “I thought, ‘Really? I didn’t even know I got a letter.’ I did hear there were a lot of companies pulling out of small markets.”
She said she is tired of third-party interference in her healthcare. Wilson said she went months without crucial arthritis medication after her insurer denied coverage for the drug.
“Anytime I change meds, it’s an automatic denial that goes back to the physician who has to defend it,” she said. “I was an RN a long time ago. I used to do a lot of claims for an orthopedic surgeon, and it’s gotten so much worse. It’s more corporate and money-based — we never had insurance companies deciding which medication you should take then.”
Another resident showed the Islander a letter stating her current Medicare Advantage plan had been terminated, followed by a list of five alternative plans. The first did not have Northern Light within its network. Three did not include dental coverage. Two options from Mutual of Omaha Medigap would require the additional purchase of a standalone Part D prescription drug plan and did not cover a routine physical.
Most Medicare Advantage plans (Part C) include prescription drug coverage, called Medicare Part D, which is the government health insurance program’s prescription drug benefit and is used by tens of millions of older or disabled beneficiaries. In July 2026, the Trump administration announced it was ending a temporary health insurance subsidy program aimed at capping prescription drug plan premiums for seniors. With subsidies set to expire, the likely result, according to some experts, will be higher prescription costs and increased premiums. Additionally, the cap on annual out-of-pocket expenses for Medicare Part D drugs will increase to $2,400, up from $2,100 in 2026, and the standard deductible will increase from $615 to $700.
“There are only around four different drug plans left here in Maine for 2027,” Harper said. “We’ve lost a lot of choices because the bill causes carriers to potentially pay a lot more.”
So what should Mainers do if they find out their coverage is ending or they have other concerns about a Medicare Advantage plan?
Harper said if one can afford a higher premium, traditional Medicare with state Medicare supplement insurance is the best route to go.
“The safety net is with these both,” he said. “The plans are available for life; they’re not one-year contracts.”
“An individual can go anywhere they want in the U.S., to any doctor and receive care with these plans — no referrals, no networks — so the stability right now is in the original Medicare and Medicare supplement combination,” Harper continued. “It gives people the greatest freedom even if they pay more for the policy.”
But what about the dental, vision and hearing coverage often in Medicare Advantage plans?
“There’s not a plan like that included in any Medicare Advantage that’s worth the paper it’s written on,” Harper said. “They’re very limited in benefits, and most of our area’s general providers are not in the network. It’s a joke.”
He said while plan enrollment ends Dec. 7, those losing their plans technically have until January 31, 2027, to switch.
“The only thing is, if they don’t make a change before December 31, their new medical coverage won’t start until February 1. If one wants to go to Medicare supplement insurance after losing coverage instead of Medicare Advantage, they have until February 28, 2027, to make that change.”
While federal law states people have a one-year window to try out Medicare Advantage and are allowed to move to traditional Medicare with Medicare supplement insurance, no questions asked, Harper said under Maine law, it’s extended to a three-year window.
“People who are losing coverage need to understand they have a unique opportunity to switch to medical supplement insurance of their choice,” he said. “They may not have that opportunity again.”
Harper said he worries about those unable to advocate for themselves.
“Many people may fall through the cracks,” he said. “Those of us with computers nearby can find plans, but some 85-plus-year-old alone with no family support may not have the luxury of someone to help them get into the right plan. My fear is that these people will go without coverage for 2027. It’s a very sad situation.”

title: Bath Housing starts work on 47-unit apartment complex for older adults
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bath Housing last week broke ground on an income-limited apartment complex for adults age 55 and up. The development, Anchorage South, is part of a multiyear plan to add nearly 200 housing units along Congress Avenue priced for a range of incomes.
The four-story, 47-unit apartment community located at 80 Congress Ave. will replace the Anchorage, an outdated property that also serves low-income older adults.
The 33 residents currently living in the 1970s-era building will have the option to move into Anchorage South when it opens, according to Bath Housing. The housing agency plans to demolish the old Anchorage development once residents move into their new homes to make way for more housing.
Ouellet Construction is building the complex, which is expected to take about 16 months to complete, according to Bath Housing. Residents will move in around early 2028.
To make way for the project, Bath Housing demolished its administrative office, built in 1992, and moved its operations to another one of its properties at 520 Centre St.
The new apartments will be available to tenants 55-plus who earn 60% or less of the area median income.
The housing agency said Anchorage South will be more accessible, comfortable and energy efficient than the older Anchorage property.
Most of the Anchorage South units have project-based vouchers, meaning qualified tenants will pay about 30% of their income in rent. The remaining few units will go for about $1,200 per month. Those interested in renting can reach out to the Bath Housing office.
Residents of the Anchorage participated in planning and designing the new apartment complex, according to Bath Housing.
“Our goal was not simply to replace an aging property, but to provide current residents with a better housing option while allowing them to remain part of their community,” said Debora Keller, Bath Housing executive director.
In the coming years, Bath Housing is planning 84 market-rate housing units for workers at 150 Congress Ave. and a series of small house lots at the 100 Congress Ave. site of the Anchorage, once residents move into their new homes. As part of this long-term vision, Bath Housing set aside 10 acres to be conserved through the Kennebec Estuary Land Trust.

title: Maine voters are turning out in huge numbers. Will Democrats keep their edge?
text:
Early voting turnout in Maine will soon soar past recent midterm elections, the latest state data shows — and Democrats continue to dominate those numbers.
Hotly contested elections for Senate, House and governor could hinge on partisan turnout, with polls showing that relatively few voters remain undecided.
Thursday is the final day Mainers can vote early in-person or request an absentee ballot, and those ballots must be returned by 8 p.m. on Tuesday. Maine voters can track the status of their absentee ballot at absenteeballotrequest.sos.maine.gov.
Here’s how early voting is going, as of Tuesday — one week from the election.
OVERALL TURNOUT
Municipal clerks around the state had accepted nearly 222,000 ballots so far. That adds up to about one-quarter of Maine’s registered voters, using the most recent count from the Maine Department of the Secretary of State. About 48,000 voters who requested absentee ballots had yet to return them.
That means absentee turnout is up by about 32% over the most recent midterm in 2022. A week before that election, the state had accepted about 168,000 ballots.
If absentee turnout continues at the same pace as it did in that midterm election, with the biggest turnout days at the end of early voting, absentee totals would likely end up above 310,000.
Compared to this point in 2024, a presidential election year in which a record 840,000 voters cast ballots in Maine, absentee vote totals are down just 20%.
PARTIES
Democrats continue to dominate early voting, with about half of those who have cast a ballot so far being registered to that party.
This follows the conventional political wisdom, and data in other states, that Democrats vote early, while Republicans tend to vote on Election Day. About 36% of registered Democrats have cast their ballots so far, while only 18% of Republicans have.
But in the past week and a half of absentee voting, Republicans have picked up a small bit of ground. Now, about 22% of voters who have returned their absentee ballots are registered Republicans — similar to this point in 2022.
Much has changed since 2014, the last midterm election in which Republican Sen. Susan Collins was on the ballot in Maine, but Republicans have a slightly higher margin of absentee votes than they did in that election.
Unaffiliated voters make up more than a quarter of votes cast; which way these voters break could determine who wins Maine’s key races.
CONGRESSIONAL DISTRICTS
Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is expected to be much more politically competitive, but the Democratic-leaning 1st District is continuing to dominate early turnout so far.
About 61% of early votes have come from the southern Maine district, a greater share than at this point in 2022 and 2024.
The 1st District’s House member, Rep. Chellie Pingree, is running for a 10th term in Congress this year and is widely expected to ease past her opponent, Republican Ron Russell. Enthusiastic turnout in the district is likely not driven by that election, but by the two statewide races on the ballot.
In the 2nd District, where former Gov. Paul LePage is trying to mount a political comeback against Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap, early turnout doesn’t look particularly promising for Republicans.
Democratic Rep. Jared Golden won that district in a tight race two years ago. At this point in 2024, 33% of early voters in that district were Republicans. So far, just 27% of early votes have come from that party.

title: Here's which candidates came out on top in Maine's student mock election
text:

Students voted for governor, U.S. senator and their congressional representative
Maine Secretary of State's Office shares results of 2026 student mock election
Students voted for governor, U.S. senator and their congressional representative
More than 12,000 students across 115 schools participated in the mock election held by the Maine Secretary of State's Office.
As part of the mock election, students voted among candidates for Maine governor, U.S. Senate and Congress.
Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, a Democrat, won the mock election for governor with 41.8% of the vote. Republican candidate Bobby Charles, a former U.S. assistant secretary of state, finished second with 30.4% of the vote. State Sen. Rick Bennett, an independent candidate, received 24.4% of the vote. The Secretary of State's Office said 3.4% of students voted for a write-in candidate.
Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson won the mock election for U.S. Senate, as the Democratic candidate got 50.8% of the vote. Incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins finished with 45.1% of the vote, while 4.1% of students voted for a write-in candidate.
Rep. Chellie Pingree won the mock election for Maine's 1st Congressional District. The incumbent Democratic congresswoman got 57.5% of the vote, while Republican challenger Ron Russell received 39.7% of the vote and 2.9% of students voted for a write-in candidate.
In the mock election for Maine's 2nd Congressional District, Republican candidate and former Gov. Paul LePage won with 52.0% of the vote. State Auditor Matt Dunlap, the Democratic candidate, received43.2% of the vote, while 4.8% of students voted for a write-in candidate.

title: New Hampshire man charged in I-95 crash that injured Maine worker
text:
A New Hampshire man has been charged and issued a summons in connection with a crash in a construction zone on Interstate 95 in Maine that injured a worker from Westfield.
Jonathan McDonald, 22, of Laconia, New Hampshire, has been charged with an accident involving death or personal injury, driving to endanger and failing to report an accident, Maine State Police said Wednesday. He was issued a summons.
The crash occurred at about 8:15 a.m. on Oct. 14 in a construction zone on the northbound side of the highway near mile marker 150 in Pittsfield, according to Shannon Moss, spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
Moss said in a news release at the time that a light-colored pickup truck towing a black dump trailer struck a Jersey barrier on the right side of the roadway as well as an orange construction barrel, and the barrel was “propelled” into Richard Smart, 56, of Westfield.
Smart, an employee of Northeast Construction, was transported to Northern Light Sebasticook Valley Hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, Moss said. He has since been released.
Maine State Police released a photo of the suspected vehicle last week, seeking the public’s aid in identifying the driver. Police said they believe he was aware of the crash, as witnesses reported seeing him turn in their vehicle before speeding away.

title: Bangor woman raises safety concerns over trash, needles near apartment
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Laurie Savageau has lived in her Hancock Street apartment for nearly a decade and a half and says trash and safety concerns around the complex have gotten worse in recent years and months.
“As I was driving to work last winter, you can look down when the leaves are gone and you can see down to the river. And there was like piles and piles of trash,” Savageau said.
Resident describes encounters, drug use
Savageau said she loves living in Bangor but called recent instances scary.
“It’s hard because I do love it here. I love my apartment. I have great neighbors. I’m close to work. I’m close to my son and daughter-in-law and grandson. But, it’s a little scary, too, because of these instances happening,” she said.
In recent months, those instances included an encounter with non-tenants blocking the path to her apartment entrance late at night. This summer, she said she saw what she believes was open drug use on and nearby her complex’s property.
“A lot of people coming on the property that don’t live here, stashing shopping carts, trash, clothes, needles, personal hygiene wipes, fecal material in the bushes, and more drug use,” Savageau said. “It is not every homeless person, and I have nothing against the people. It’s the actions and the trash and destruction that’s left behind.”
Encampment cleanup
Last December, a homeless encampment along the railroad tracks near Savageau’s apartment was cleared. CSX, the railroad company that owns some of the land, cited public safety as the driving force behind the cleanup.
Piles of trash can still be seen along the tracks.
In a statement Wednesday, CSX said cleanup efforts from last winter continued this summer.
“At CSX, the safety of our employees and the surrounding community is our top priority. Our crews began cleanup and remediation efforts in the Bangor area last December and again this summer,” the statement said. “We have been made aware of these recent concerns and are planning additional cleanup and remediation efforts.”
CSX said railroad rights of way are active, hazardous environments and entering railroad property without permission is illegal and can result in serious or fatal injury. Members of the public may reach out to the CSX Public Safety Coordination Center at 800-232-0144 to report illegal dumping and trespassing near the railroad.
Turning to city council candidates
Savageau said she reached out to CSX multiple times, as well as to the city, but felt no one was taking her concerns seriously until she began speaking to candidates for City Council this year.
For the first time in years, Savageau said she is turning to the polls to have her voice heard.
“I feel like Bangor has so much potential. It is a beautiful spot. And it needs a different direction, I feel. And I reached out to a few different candidates and had some discussions with them. And I liked what they had to say. So, I decided this year, I am going to vote because I want change. I want Bangor to be the city that it could be,” she said.
The city has not responded to a request for comment.

title: Ballot-ready before they can vote: Bangor juniors take their oath to work Election Day
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Every other year, Bangor High School juniors raise their right hand and get sworn in — not for court, but for Election Day.
The AP Government and Politics students from Bangor High School join nearly 150 poll workers and volunteers staffing the polls on Nov. 3, learning the nuts-and-bolts of democracy from check-in tables to ballot boxes.
A decade-long tradition
For nearly 10 years, City Clerk Lisa Goodwin, now in her 35th year with the city, has partnered with the high school to turn a civics lesson into hands-on experience.
“I just think it’s important for the kids to get involved in the process so they understand what happens at the polls and that their voice matters,” Goodwin said.
Goodwin calls it a well-oiled machine — veteran wardens and clerks paired with first-time student workers eager to learn.
First time at the polls — without a ballot
For most of the 11th graders, like Asa Corui and Pink Austin, it’s their first time inside a polling place as workers — even though they can’t vote yet.
“A lot of people my age are already involved a little bit in politics, they just can’t vote yet,” said Corui.
“I think everyone’s voice matters. I see a lot of people online saying one vote doesn’t change anything, but it’s important to get your voice out there,” said Austin.
The next generation of voters
Goodwin says the goal is simple: take the mystery out of voting, ease any fears about the process, and inspire future voters — and future poll volunteers.
“The students nowadays are more in tune and they’re dialed into what is going on, and I think this class is fabulous,” Goodwin said.
Austin already plans to return:
“I know when I’m older, I’ll come back and volunteer at the polls again.”

title: Edgecomb receives $3K MMA grant for generator
text:
On Oct. 27, Edgecomb selectmen announced the town had received a $3,000 Maine Municipal Association grant to buy a stand-by generator for the town hall. Selectmen debated whether a 14-kilowatt or 20-kilowatt generator would serve their interest.
Selectmen Forrest Carver and Cara Gaffney decided the 14-kW model was the best fit. Selectmen will now seek a further recommendation from the building committee and an anonymous donor who pledged to provide additional funding.
In other action, selectmen set Tuesday, Dec. 8 at 6 p.m. for a special budget meeting for municipal departments and non-profit groups seeking municipal funding. Each group is directed to deliver a “succinct 10-year budget history” designed to establish clear historical context for developing the next fiscal year budget.
Time will strictly be enforced so there will be no time for questions from the public. Carver added there will be time for questions at a future budget meeting.
Selectmen are considering their options regarding timely municipal audits. The town is still waiting for the FY23 audit. Gaffney reported she had made four attempts at contacting the William Brewer, CPA firm without success.
Carver reported Edgecomb is one of 20 municipalities and townships which are over two years behind in the annual audits. Selectmen considered using another CPA firm for future audits. Town Clerk Claudia Coffin offered to contact the Brewer agency to discover the FY23 audit’s status.
Administrative Assistant Jessica Mague said the building committee found a suitable countertop for a new upstairs service center. The committee purchased a countertop for $300 and plans on using volunteer labor for renovations. The committee has a $6,500 project budget and Mague said the renovations would begin later this fall.
Edgecomb will receive assistance from Midcoast Energy in Damariscotta with the electrical work. Resident Karen Flynn contacted the company on the town’s behalf. Midcoast Energy is celebrating its 50th anniversary and is offering the help as part of the celebration.
Carver and Gaffney would like to establish a deputy clerk position to provide municipal services when the elected Town Clerk Claudia Coffin is not available. Selectmen asked Coffin if she could train a deputy town clerk.
“It's a goal of the selectboard to have fail-safe in mind for every duty in the town office. We don't want to be ‘up the creek without a paddle’ so we’d like to have a system in place such as during early voting or absentee voting. Is it possible to train a deputy?" Carver asked.
Coffin didn’t think it was practical to have a deputy clerk.
Selectmen and Coffin also disagreed about the need for hiring a payroll service. Selectmen thought hiring a private firm would eliminate municipal liability on payroll issues and save time. Coffin is the town's elected treasurer and said payroll is part of the job. “I don’t feel comfortable spending the taxpayer's money on something we don't need. You’re already paying a treasurer who according to state law does payroll.”
Selectmen tabled whether to hire a payroll service.
Selectmen meet next at 6 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 10 in the conference room.

UN condemns US economic embargo of Cuba though more nations sit out after Trump administration push
text:
UN condemns US economic embargo of Cuba though more nations sit out after Trump administration push
The U.N. General Assembly condemned the U.S. economic embargo of Cuba for the 34th year on Wednesday, even as Washington’s campaign to influence the outcome led to a number of countries voting against the resolution or sitting out the decision for the first time.
The vote was 130-17, with 25 abstentions — a notable decrease in support from last year, when more than 160 nations supported the measure and only 12 abstained. While such resolutions at the U.N. General Assembly are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion.
For the first time in 34 years, Western countries like Germany, Italy and Latvia were among those that refrained from voting. Bosnia, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Lithuania, Morocco, North Macedonia, Paraguay and Slovenia, were among those member states that voted no — most for the first time.
Related video above: Driving through Havana, Cuba during another blackout
It marks a stunning shift in international support at a time when the small island country weathers outages, shortages and other deepening financial troubles as the Trump administration looks to force changes to Cuba’s political system by increasing an already punishing economic campaign. President Donald Trump last week once again raised the specter of U.S. military intervention, saying American warships could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.
“A great power is attacking through economic war a member state of this organization,” Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said ahead of the vote. “Cuba is not a threat. The blockade is a threat.”
U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told member nations that “your vote today is the only thing standing between the corrupt, kleptocratic communist regime and using this body and your vote for another propaganda victory at the expense of the Cuban people.”
Tensions between Washington and Havana have spilled over into fiery public spats at the United Nations. On Tuesday, Waltz and Rodríguez got into a shouting match on the floor of the General Assembly while debating the embargo resolution.
Shortly after Waltz had begun his criticism of the socialist government, Rodríguez walked down to the podium where the U.S. envoy was addressing the hall and called him a liar while trying to get a point of order from the official presiding over the session.
“This individual needs to back away from this podium. He’s not going to intimidate me in the United States of America,” Waltz said as U.N. security and personnel tried to intervene. "You understand who you’re dealing with? This is America. Back up.”
In a post on X, Rodríguez reminded Waltz where he was making his remarks, saying he was at the U.N., not at a national security meeting at the White House.
“With his crude lies at the UN General Assembly, the U.S. government has launched another desperate attempt to justify its economic aggression against Cuba and its criminal energy blockade,” he continued.
A week earlier, a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, took place outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behavior of the island’s government.
It all reflects a clear break from the traditional diplomatic decorum expected at the U.N. and the new phase of contentiousness between the U.S. and Cuba.
The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960 after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations.
As a result, the Caribbean country has spent decades facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba.
The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that impact basic services such as water supply and internet and telephone services.

title: Here are the Maine towns weighing data center bans
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Voters in parts of Maine will decide whether they want to temporarily ban data center construction next week, joining a growing list of municipalities pre-emptively blocking the controversial projects.
At least seven towns in Maine will weigh temporary moratoriums on Nov. 3, and one, North Berwick, will vote on an outright ban on data centers. An analysis by The Maine Monitor found at least 21 municipalities have already adopted similar ordinances.
Plans to build new data centers, which power a variety of electronic functions including artificial intelligence, are facing bipartisan backlash nationally. Opponents point out that the projects are often energy and water intensive.
The Maine Legislature passed what would have been a first-in-the-nation moratorium on data center development in April. Gov. Janet Mills vetoed the bill to save a data center project in Jay, which has since stalled.
All three candidates hoping to replace Mills as governor have said they would have signed the legislation, which is likely to resurface during the next year’s legislative session. In most towns, active or proposed moratoriums could last until the spring, buying them time until the state can weigh in.
Some towns, such as Lewiston and Eastport, created data center ordinances in response to project proposals. But most towns weighing bans are trying to preempt projects that may never materialize.
Data center developers in Maine and elsewhere have kept their plans under wraps. Officials in Jay only learned of the plan to build a data center in the town’s former mill after The Bangor Daily News reported on the project.
Some towns have received advice from Maine Conservation Voters, an environmental group, when creating their ordinances. The group began offering to help municipal officials move against data centers after Mills’ veto.
That group is also working on data center regulation proposals for the next legislative session, which begins in December.
The cities and towns voting on data center bans on Nov. 3 are: Brownfield, Eliot, Freedom, North Berwick, Peru, Sabattus, Wells and Wiscasset. You can find more information about those proposals, and the measures that have already passed, by clicking on each municipality in the map below.
Maine Monitor writers Caitlin Andrews, John Forbes, Ben Hanstein, Melissa Razdrih and Stephanie McFeeters contributed reporting.
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between The Maine Monitor and the Bangor Daily News, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: She was born with eight fingers on one hand. Her family traveled to America for the surgery
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - A family traveled from Turkey to St. Louis for their daughter’s surgery to treat a rare condition affecting fewer than 100 people worldwide.
“Mirror Hand is incredibly uncommon, and even surgeons like myself who take care of a great deal of kids almost never see this in their career. So, it’s really uncommon. Numbers are hard to come by, but one in a million or less is probably about right,” said Dr. Charles Goldfarb, Chief of Orthopedic Surgery at St. Louis Children’s Hospital.
The condition leaves patients without a radius bone. This means significant limitations in wrist and elbow motion and preserved shoulder movements.
“From the very beginning, he was really warm, genuine, and gave us a lot of hope. Honestly, the trust and support he gave us played a huge role in our decision to come to St. Louis,” said Emircan Buga, Elisa’s father.
Communication and care
Emircan and his wife, Gulten, only speak Turkish and used a translator. They said the language difference never got in the way of their daughter receiving care.
“Initially, I had conversations with them, from afar, but we talked on the phone and we did FaceTime, just communicating about her condition,” Goldfarb said.
“They provided us with immense support regarding every problem we might encounter or face along the way. We would like to thank them for the support they provided, both financially and psychologically,” Emircan said.
Through St. Louis Children’s International Free Care Fund, funded through the St. Louis Children’s Hospital Foundation, Elisa’s family connected with the orthopedic surgery team.
The surgery
On Jan. 30, Goldfarb led a team that completed a three-hour reconstructive surgery.
“And it’s so fun for me as a surgeon, who interacts with kids young and old, but at an early point in their life, to watch what happens after. And I do think a surgery like this is life-changing and will really help her succeed in all aspects,” Goldfarb said.
Elisa is now recovering.
“One of the things that makes me so excited in taking care of young children is seeing what they will accomplish later in life,” Goldfarb said.
Emircan said, “From now on, she will continue her life with more confidence and courage. But when we look back, we will miss that hand because that’s how the story began.”

title: Barricaded subject in Berwick arrested after shots were fired
text:
Barricaded subject in Berwick arrested after shots were fired
A 25-year-old Berwick man faces a firearm-related charge after police say he fired multiple shots from his home early Wednesday morning
Barricaded subject in Berwick arrested after shots were fired
A 25-year-old Berwick man faces a firearm-related charge after police say he fired multiple shots from his home early Wednesday morning
A 25-year-old man was arrested Wednesday morning after police say he fired multiple shots from his home during a barricade situation that prompted a response from several law enforcement agencies and shut down Route 9 in Berwick.
According to the Berwick Police Department, officers responded to a criminal mischief complaint at 407 School Street around 12:57 a.m. Wednesday.
Police say a woman found a box on her porch with a message telling her to leave. A paint can was also thrown through the caller's window.
While an officer was speaking with the woman, police said shots were heard coming from a neighboring house.
The woman was immediately removed from the area as officers from South Berwick, North Berwick, and the York County Sheriff's Office responded and surrounded the residence at 409 School Street.
Police said they tried to communicate with the subject who was barricaded inside the home, but additional shots were fired around 2:11 a.m.
The Southern Maine Special Response Team was called to the scene and a drone from the York County Emergency Management Agency was deployed to monitor the residence.
Police say the man eventually came outside and was taken into custody.
The suspect was identified as 25-year-old Tyler Carpenter of Berwick. He was charged with reckless conduct with a firearm and is being held at York County Jail on $20,000 cash bail.
Route 9 was closed during the incident, according to police.

Maine’s Job Market Is Booming, According to New National Rankings
Maine is once again among the nation's leading states in a category that matters to every single one of us: jobs. That's the kind of news I never get tired of hearing.
WalletHub, a personal finance website, recently published its annual report of the best and worst states for jobs.
How Does Maine Stack up With the Rest of the Country for its Job Market?
Maine came in with an impressive 7th-place ranking, a very strong showing. It was also good enough to make Maine the second-highest-ranked state in New England, with only New Hampshire finishing higher, in 5th place.
Maine’s overall jobs score was 59.66. The scoring is based on a 100-point system divided into two major categories: Job Market and Economic Environment. These categories were further broken down into 34 subcategories to make the analysis as detailed as possible.
Maine ranked 29th in economic environment, likely brought down by subcategories such as commute-friendly jobs and average starting salaries, areas that aren’t necessarily the state’s strongest.
However, Maine bounced back with an incredible 4th-place ranking in the job market category, which includes factors like job opportunities, unemployment rate, and job security.
It’s great to see our state thrive in this category. It's a wonderful testament to both employers and employees. The workforce is strong, my friends. We should all be proud.
