title: Where the candidates in Maine stand on immigration
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: Where the candidates for office in Maine stand on immigration
Maine's Total Coverage asked viewers what issues they are most interested in learning more about heading into the midterm election.
After hundreds of submissions, one of the top issues on voters' minds is immigration. Maine's Total Coverage asked all the candidates for governor and congressional office about their stance on the issue.
Gubernatorial candidates
The race for the Blaine House began with two crowded primaries. Republican Bobby Charles was the winner of a seven-way ranked-choice voting primary and Democrat Hannah Pingree won in a five-way race. Independent Rick Bennett, who left the Republican Party last year, was the only independent who got the required number of signatures to get on the November ballot.
In January, the Trump administration launched "Operation Catch of the Day," during which an increase in immigration officers came to Maine to detain what the Department of Homeland Security calls "the worst of the worst" and this summer, a fatal shooting of a 25-year-old Colombian man at the hands of an ICE agent.
A new law that does not allow local law enforcement officers to work with the federal government on immigration issues is also in effect in Maine.
Bennett said he's concerned about the politicization of federal officers.
"I support meaningful guardrails around the ability for federal law enforcement to come in and command our state and local law enforcement, which is paid for with state and local tax dollars. And it shouldn't be misused for some of these operations," Bennett said.
Charles is supportive of law enforcement at all levels. He said we need to discourage illegal immigration, which is something he claims Democrats in Maine are doing. He added he does not support the new law limiting law enforcement communication.
"We need to reverse this sanctuary state status. This doesn't work when you cut off communications between local and state on one hand, and the federal government on the other hand, the federal enforcement community, you blind both of them," Charles said.
Pingree has called for the reform of ICE.
"Mainers do not appreciate ICE being in Maine. I would like to see ICE leave our state. I don't think that they have made us safer. Obviously, the killing of a 25-year-old dad on his way to work. Somebody who is here legally, it's completely unacceptable," she said.
Not only has the state passed legislation to limit local law enforcement's relationship with immigration officers, but many municipalities have as well.
Senate candidates
The midterms are high stakes for both parties. Democrats are hoping to take the majority in Congress, heading into President Donald Trump's final two years in office. Republicans, who hold the majority in both chambers, want to keep it.
The highly-anticipated Senate race has been closely watched for months. Senator Susan Collins is seeking a historic sixth term in Washington. Democrat Troy Jackson replaced Graham Platner as the party's nominee in late July after Platner dropped out following a sexual assault allegation he denies. Jackson, who finished third in the Democratic primary for Maine governor, now seeks to help Democrats flip the U.S. Senate.
The state of Maine has seen a high amount of immigration enforcement just this year alone, and both candidates for senate are weighing in on the highly-debated topic.
Jackson says he wants ICE abolished, pushing to put more funding into U.S. Customs and Border Protection instead.
He claims that ICE is tarnished and that some officers don't have proper training.
"If I had the opportunity, I would put that law enforcement in Customs and Border Patrol. They used to do, you know, sex trafficking work, drug smuggling and all that," Jackson said. "People saw them as legitimate law enforcement, but what we have now is not legitimate law enforcement, and I would cut the funding off for them."
On the contrary, Senator Collins says she wants to keep ICE running. She says the work ICE does goes far beyond deportation, including investigations into human trafficking and drug smuggling.
"I don't believe that people who are here legally and are waiting for an asylum hearing should be deported," Collins said. "I don't believe that people who are brought here as little children, they didn't make the decision to violate the law and who have known no other country. I don't believe they should be deported unless they have a criminal record."
The senator does say the agency needs to be reformed, pointing to her effort to fund body cameras for ICE agents and getting them sent to Maine.
The senator also voted to approve roughly $70 billion in funding for ICE and Customs and Border Patrol earlier this year.
Candidates for Maine's 1st Congressional District
The race for Maine's 1st Congressional District is a rematch. Army veteran Ron Russell is challenging Congresswoman Chellie Pingree for her seat in Washington.
Pingree has held the congressional seat for nearly two decades. Russell ran against her back in 2024, but lost.
Russell secured the Republican nomination back in June, defeating newcomer Joshua James Pietrowicz.
Pingree says ICE is out of control and has said it should be abolished. She has spent a large part of this past year working with families who had someone detained by ICE.
"If they are willing to deal with the reforms that many of us believe are critically important, and if we can claw back some of the excessive amount of money that they have to hire officers, meet quotas, build these detention centers, I would consider allowing them to operate," Pingree said. "But I have been saying it's time to abolish ICE because their track record is horrendous."
Russell, the Republican challenger, says he wants to keep ICE where it is. He says it doesn't make sense to get rid of the agency, adding it has done some wonderful things in the past few years.
However, Russell does say ICE needs reform. He also says local, federal and state law enforcement should work together on these issues.
"When they don't, we have things like what happened in Minneapolis and what happened in downtown Biddeford," Russell said. "Now, after the fact, we are clamoring for an investigation to be joint with local, state and federal law enforcement working together and sharing information. We should have shared information beforehand, and the incidents most likely would never have occurred."
Candidates for Maine's 2nd Congressional District
The race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District began when Congressman Jared Golden still planned to run for his seat.
Former two-time Republican Governor Paul LePage got in the race to take on Golden. LePage was uncontested in the primary. Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap filed paperwork to primary Golden.
Golden eventually left the race, and three other candidates got in to primary Dunlap.
Dunlap won in a four-way ranked-choice voting primary in June to take on LePage.
Dunlap said immigration is "a mess," adding that the immigration process is confusing to navigate.
"We need to sit down as Republicans and Democrats, independents as well, and try to figure out what immigration should look like," he said. "What does it mean to come here to study? What does it mean to come here to work? What does it mean to become an American citizen?"
LePage disagrees with the new law that limits local law enforcement's contact with federal agencies. He said the United States has strong laws, but they're not being enforced.
"Our immigration laws are antiquated. They need to be fixed, but the Democrats and Republicans don't want to work together to fix it. And it's really easy to fix. I don't have a problem with allowing people to obtain work permits, buying a house, paying taxes," LePage said.

title: Planners hold two public hearings, approve three applications
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The China Planning Board’s Oct. 13 agenda included two public hearings and approval of three applications.
The first hearing, on Kirk and Judy Sherman’s four-lot subdivision on 19.25 acres on Danforth and Pleasantview Ridge roads, with three of the lots off Danforth Road, drew questions and comments from neighbors and others.
Part of the discussion was about a graveyard where either Native Americans or early European settlers were buried. Milton Dudley, chairing the meeting in Chairman Toni Wall’s absence, said the issue was outside the board’s purview.
Kirk Sherman said the former graveyard is not inside the subdivision; and he had been assured by “the church” that all bodies had been moved.
Later in the meeting, board members found the proposed subdivision met all town ordinance criteria and approved it on a 4-0 vote.
The second hearing, lasting about five minutes, was on Shawn Hoague’s application to open a car repair garage in an existing building at 238 Dirigo Road (see the Oct. 1 issue of The Town Line, p. 3). Two neighbors spoke in favor of Hoague’s application; there were no questions or objections.
After the hearing, board members voted that the application met all ordinance criteria and unanimously approved it.
Between the two hearings, board members returned to Harmoni Towers’ application for a 195-foot-tall communications tower on Parmenter Hill (subject of a Sept. 22 public hearing that brought no testimony). They found the plan met all ordinance criteria and approved it unanimously.
Board member Bruce Fitzgerald repeated his request that China emergency services departments be allowed to put equipment on the tower, if needed.
Dudley reminded all three applicants that there is a 30-day period during which the board’s actions may be appealed.
The next regular China Planning Board is scheduled for 6 p.m., Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the town office meeting room. Codes Officer Nicholas French said another subdivision plan, for land on Dirigo Road, might be ready for review.

title: MDI Thanksgiving Baskets program returns, bringing holiday meals to families in need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — In the true spirit of the season, the MDI Thanksgiving Basket program is returning to bring warm meals to everyone’s tables on the island again this year.
SarahJoy Chaples is heading up the project for the first time this year after serving on the planning committee for four years. The project started roughly 50 years ago through the Bar Harbor Congregational Church. Now, packaging up Thanksgiving baskets has become an island-wide effort.
Each basket comes with stuffing, canned gravy, cranberry sauce, fresh potatoes and carrots donated by Galyn’s restaurant, dessert, and, of course, the all-important turkey.
Chaples said they offer extra items for larger families, and any donated items that don’t fit into the baskets are available for participants to bring home.
Anyone can apply for a Thanksgiving basket, and there are no eligibility criteria that applicants must meet.
Last year, the Thanksgiving Baskets program saw a 15% increase in participants requesting a meal, and Chaples predicts this year may have even more families in need. Thanksgiving will fall on Nov. 26, as Mainers head into winter with increased heating oil costs.
“We’re expecting to see more this year as folks are really looking at their budgets and trying to figure out, you know, how can they put on a Thanksgiving meal,” said Chaples. “One of the things that we think is really important is that people have the opportunity to gather with their families at Thanksgiving and feel connected and not have the worry of, you know, ‘can we do this this year?’”
Local organizations, faith groups, and schools are lending a hand by running food drives to collect different ingredients for the baskets.
According to Chaples, it’s the little things that can make these baskets even more accessible to families in need. Instead of plain canned pumpkin, they ask for donations of pre-spiced pumpkin so there is one less ingredient to worry about when putting together a pumpkin pie.
The application to request a Thanksgiving basket is now open and the deadline to apply is Nov. 19. There is an online application that can be found on the Bar Harbor Congregational Church’s website: barharborucc.org. Paper applications are available at the Bar Harbor Food Pantry and Bar Harbor Congregational Church.
Participants can also list any allergens on their application.
Volunteers are also available to assist people with their application at the Bar Harbor Food Pantry and over the phone at 207-812-0725. If an applicant lives in a housing authority, there are staff available to assist with applications.
Baskets will be ready for pickup or delivery on Nov. 22 and 23.
The program is still in search of volunteers for organizing, packing, and delivering baskets, which will take place Nov. 20-24. Anyone interested in volunteering can reach out to Chaples via email at 29turkeybaskets@gmail.com.
The First, Machias Savings Bank and Bar Harbor Bank and Trust in Bar Harbor will have donation boxes starting now through Nov. 18, where anyone can drop off items for the baskets. Food items can also be dropped off at the Bar Harbor Congregational Church.
The Thanksgiving Baskets program is still seeking stuffing and canned goods, including spiced pumpkin pie filling, gravy, cranberry sauce, green vegetables and non-green vegetables. Those interested in donating money can send a designated check to the Bar Harbor Congregational Church.
Deliveries will be made to the following properties, and applicants can request that their basket be delivered on MDI or the outer islands.
Beech Cliff, Southwest Harbor; Birchwood Apartment, Tremont; Eden, Prospect Avenue Bar Harbor; Eden, Woodbury, Bar Harbor; Harbor Hill Estates, Bar Harbor; Malvern Belmont, Bar Harbor; Maple Lane, Northeast Harbor; Norwood Cove, Southwest Harbor; Roddick Lorraine, Bar Harbor; Ridge Apartments, Village Greenway, Southwest Harbor; and Union River Estates, Ellsworth.
The program is volunteer-run, and Chaples says the community response is large when they seek volunteers and donations. “Whenever I reach out to whoever and ask ‘can you help with this?’ they’re always like ‘yes I’ll help with that and what else can I do?’ and it, you know, it’s really just this amazing effort that spreads across the island,” said Chaples. “This is a many, many, many hands make light work.”
Chaples emphasized that the program is judgement-free and focused on bringing the holiday to more homes. “So, we want to make sure folks have a chance to enjoy a Thanksgiving meal but also have that sense of connectedness to their family.”

title: Federal judge releases six defendants in MaineCare fraud case with conditions; all plead not guilty
text:
Federal judge releases six defendants in MaineCare fraud case with conditions; all plead not guilty
A judge released all six people charged in a federal MaineCare fraud case with conditions after they pleaded not guilty in a Bangor courtroom, according to court filings.
Federal judge releases six defendants in MaineCare fraud case with conditions; all plead not guilty
A judge released all six people charged in a federal MaineCare fraud case with conditions after they pleaded not guilty in a Bangor courtroom, according to court filings.
Prosecutors had filed motions asking the court to detain the defendants, citing "serious risks" of obstruction and the defendants fleeing before trial.
A judge disagreed and released all six on Tuesday "on conditions." The court docket does not include a full release order or specify what those conditions are.
The defendants are 37-year-old Noora Abd, 51-year-old Faysal Kalayaf Manahe, 47-year-old Adel Al Rashid, 47-year-old Sura Almohammed, 46-year-old Ethar Alyaseen and 41-year-old Mohammed Alkhalaf.
Abd is cited as the owner and operator of Community Home Health Care in South Portland, which was also named in the now unsealed federal grand jury indictment. It alleges that she and her five employees conspired to defraud MaineCare by submitting electronic visit-verification records for personal care services that were not provided. According to the U.S. Attorney's Office, Community Home Health Care and Abd allegedly submitted more than $600,000 in claims since 2020 for services purportedly provided to one client.
Abd and her husband Manahe are also charged with obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation; prosecutors allege they pressured someone who knew about the alleged fraud scheme not to speak to investigators. Alkhalaf is charged with making false statements.
According to a filing opposing detention, Abd's attorneys argued that the government's motion sought detention based on flight risk, did not claim Abd was a danger to anyone and did not qualify for a statutory presumption of detention.
Abd's attorneys also pointed to the government's timeline. They said the indictment was returned Oct. 22, but Abd was not arrested until Oct. 27, and that the conduct attributed to her in the indictment ended in August. Attorneys argued those delays undercut the government's claims that she posed a serious flight or obstruction risk. In the filing, attorneys wrote that Abd knew she was the subject of a federal fraud investigation since June, but in the four months since, she did not leave her home in Maine.
"A defendant who presents a serious risk of flight is not left in her home for five days after a grand jury returns a sealed indictment against her," wrote attorney Michael J. Conley in submitted court documents. "A defendant who presents a serious risk of obstruction is not left alone for two months after the government says her conduct stopped."
Abd's attorneys also argued that prosecutors had not shown that release conditions could not address there concerns. They said that Abd would accept any conditions that the court deems necessary, including the surrender of her passport, travel restrictions, living at an approved address, location monitoring and no-contact provisions.
Community Home Health Care was previously cited by Maine's Department of Health and Human Services over more than $49,000 in alleged overpayments for services billed between 2016 and 2019. The company repaid the amount in August.
If the defendants are convicted of healthcare fraud conspiracy, they face up to 10 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000 or twice the total loss due to fraudulent claims, and up to three years of supervised release. The charges of obstructing a healthcare fraud investigation and making false statements each carry a maximum of five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release.

title: ‘She was screaming for her life’: Terrifying attempted kidnapping caught on video
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) — A terrifying kidnapping attempt in the middle of the afternoon on the Diamond Head Gold Coast in Honolulu was caught on video.
Authorities said they were called to Kainalu condominiums on Coconut Avenue around noon on Monday about the reported kidnapping.
Surveillance video from the area showed a truck parked outside the condominium complex that afternoon before a man was seen going inside the garage, appearing to confront two women and chasing one of them.
A 77-year-old condo resident, who asked not to be identified, said the man picked up her 24-year-old friend.
Police said the suspect elbowed the 77-year-old woman in the face.
“He shoved me away from my friend and he picked her up,” she said. “He looked like a monster. He just had so much hatred and craziness in his eyes.”
The woman added, “I was yelling, ‘Help! Help!’ and she was yelling, too. She was saying, ‘You don’t want to do this. Don’t do this.’”
The 77-year-old said her friend was trying to fend off the kidnapper while she was hoping others would hear their screams for help.
Neighbor and witness Beverly Louis said she could see the man bear-hugging the woman and dragging her to the back of his truck.
“I just started screaming, ‘Drop her! Drop her! Drop her!’” Louis said. “She was screaming for her life. She was terrified.”
Neighbor and fellow witness Mike Finkelstein said he also yelled at the man to let the woman go.
“Let her go. I’ve called the police. I’m coming down there after you,” Finkelstein recalled yelling.
Several neighbors then intervened after seeing and hearing the commotion, helping the 24-year-old break free.
Witnesses said the man in question got into his truck and sped off. Police were able to take him into custody a few hours later after police said a suspicious man matching his description was seen running naked in a nearby neighborhood.
The 77-year-old woman thanked her fellow residents for their help but said she and her friend were continuing to have nightmares as the neighborhood remained on edge.

title: Bangor council approves $100,000 for warming shelter funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor city councilors voted Monday to direct a total of $100,000 to local nonprofits to support two city warming shelters.
$10,000 will go to The Well Warming Center, a daytime shelter that councilors said served roughly 70 to 80 people a day last winter.
Up to $90,000 will go to the Together Place Peer Run Recovery Center for its as-needed nighttime warming shelter.
The two shelters were selected because of the services they provided last winter.
The funding comes from money the city already had for heating assistance, general assistance and a community development block grant.
Together Place board President Shea Mullaney said at Monday’s meeting that the allocation is a maximum expenditure for services as delivered. He said that means the organization will not receive the money upfront.
Mullaney said the funds will help support operations at the state average of $44 a bed per night. He said the funds will also allow Together Place to pay its staff.
The city’s advisory committee on homelessness will develop requirements and policies for the shelters’ operations.
The funding passed unanimously, though Councilor Wayne Mallar was reluctant in his approval. Councilor Michael Beck recused himself from the vote because of a conflict of interest. Councilor Daniel Carson was not present for the meeting.

title: Illegal moonshine distillery explodes, catches fire in mountains, officials say
text:
WILKES COUNTY, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - An explosion at an illegal moonshine distillery sparked a fire in the North Carolina mountains on Monday, according to authorities.
Special agents from North Carolina’s Alcohol Law Enforcement Division were called to investigate the explosion in Wilkes County, North Carolina.
Agents found an active 200-gallon illegal distillery. They seized about 1,800 gallons of mash, which is used to make moonshine, and 161 gallons of illegal moonshine.
North Carolina officials shared photos showing the charred inside of a metal building. Distilling equipment was also damaged.
Billy Ray Anderson, 69, was arrested and charged with manufacturing a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession for sale of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of distillery equipment, possession of distillery ingredients and allowing property to be used for the manufacture of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage.
Moonshine is believed to have originated in North Carolina and was once an important source of income, particularly for rural residents.

title: Death toll from train collision in central Spain rises to 64, authorities say
text:
URDA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks Wednesday in Spain, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies.
The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January.
“Today all of Spain is grieving,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” said Sánchez, who faces an election on Nov. 29.
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the central province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading south in the same direction from Madrid to Seville.
A train operated by the state-owned RENFE company struck the rear of another train operated by private company IRYO that was stopped. The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the IRYO train and the front of the RENFE train.
Samy Paul, a British tourist, described the shock of the impact to The Associated Press after being rescued from the RENFE train.
“Suddenly, everything started falling apart. Bang! We fell down,” he said. “We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over.”
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working nearby when he heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
“People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived,” he said. “As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg.”
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Transport minister says crash was due to ‘inexplicable’ decision
Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a “stop signal” active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
“I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts,” Puente said.
Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
“We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact,” he said. “The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.”
Authorities said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help.
Spain’s King Felipe VI also visited the crash site.
“We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected,” Spain’s royals said in a statement.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “My heart goes out to the victims’ families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you.”
Spain’s soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.
Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when an IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
Before this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992.
Spain is a leader in high-speed rail
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country’s railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.
Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. The Italian-owned IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”
___
Wilson reported from Barcelona, Spain. Teresa Medrano in Madrid and Iain Sullivan in Urda contributed to this report.

title: Driver hurt after car strikes camper, goes vertical in Sidney
text:
SIDNEY, Maine (WABI) - One man was hurt after a crash left his car standing on its front end in Sidney Wednesday morning.
It happened around 6:40 a.m. on West River Road near Ferry Road.
The Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office says an 18-year-old Augusta woman tried to pass a 48-year-old Sidney man on a curve, but an oncoming car forced the two together.
The man’s car went off the road, hit a culvert, tore through a camper parked on a lawn and came to rest vertical.
Crews cut him out. He was taken to the hospital with minor injuries. The woman was not hurt.
No charges have been filed.

title: Grandmother not indicted in baby’s death after police say she left her in hot car for 8 hours while she worked
text:
MADISONVILLE, Ky. (WFIE/Gray News) — A Kentucky doctor who accidentally left her grandchild unattended in a hot car for about eight hours will not be indicted for the baby’s death.
Madisonville police said 10-month-old Scottie Crowell died in August.
On Tuesday, a grand jury found there was insufficient probable cause for an indictment.
Police said Scottie’s grandmother picked her up in the morning of Aug. 13 and was supposed to take her to daycare.
She forgot the child was in the car and went to work, police said.
She arrived at Owensboro Health Multi-Care, where she works as a doctor, around 8 a.m.
The baby’s father called his wife after trying to pick up Scottie from daycare, but the child was not there.
The baby’s mother called the grandmother at work, and the grandmother ran outside and saw Scottie was still in the vehicle around 4 p.m., police said.
After 911 was called, first responders tried to administer lifesaving measures, but the baby died.
“I would ask that you keep the infant’s parents and family in your thoughts and prayers as they continue to grieve and process this unimaginable loss,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Hannah Kington-Jarvis.

title: Susan Collins pushes her seniority while campaigning to Maine shipbuilders
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BATH, Maine — U.S. Sen. Susan Collins on Wednesday sought to counter Democrat Troy Jackson’s argument that the billions in federal dollars she’s helped bring to Maine were not enough to make up for steep cuts to healthcare and more under the second Trump administration.
The senator pointed to her push for the Navy to build more destroyers at Bath Iron Works, where she and supporters greeted workers changing shifts. After lobbying from Collins and the rest of the Maine congressional delegation, the Pentagon earlier this month cleared a path for another destroyer to be built at the critical facility. The Trump administration’s 2027 budget request had only called for one, with officials citing capacity concerns.
“You could ask a lot of the workers at BIW,” Collins said. “I worked very hard in previous years to make sure the funding was there to build another destroyer, to be built by the best shipbuilders in the world.”
Hours earlier less than 6 miles away in Brunswick, Jackson campaigned alongside Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, a potential 2028 presidential contender in a two-day swing supporting Maine Democrats. Jackson said what Collins brought to Maine amounted to “a pittance” compared to what’s been lost in funding for healthcare, veterans care and food assistance. He also cited Mississippi’s Ingalls Shipbuilding, which builds a wider variety of ships, having a larger backlog of ship orders.
The back-and-forth between the candidates, in a contentious toss-up that could decide which party controls the Senate, marked one of the final arguments for voters headed to the polls in just six days. Collins has touted her experience, bipartisan wins and a powerful position as chair of the Appropriations Committee. Jackson and his allies say she’s failed Mainers and too often sided with President Donald Trump.
Both were asked Wednesday what their final message was to voters, especially the small number of undecided Mainers. Jackson cited higher fuel prices, an unprovoked war in Iran, and punishing healthcare cuts.
“What I would say to people,” he said, “is ‘Do you think the government’s working for you?’”
The five-term incumbent stuck with the theme of her experience in Washington. Undecided voters, she said, should consider “who can do more for the people of Maine.”
“Someone who is the chair of the Appropriations Committee … or someone who is at the bottom for seniority?” she said, noting that she’s returning to BIW to meet workers during Wednesday’s night shift.

title: Parents say students were forced to get off school bus and walk 3 miles home on dangerous roads
text:
GUNTOWN, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) — Parents in Mississippi are demanding answers after they said their 11-year-old daughter’s school bus driver told her to get off the bus and walk miles home.
James and Ann Lofton said their child and several other kids were forced to walk three miles to get home, though it’s unclear why.
“You put your children out to catch the bus, you expect them to be safe on the bus,” Ann Lofton said. “You expect them to get to school safely, you expect them to get home safely, and then you get a phone call [saying] they’re walking down the side of the road. How is that keeping them safe?”
The parents said they reported the incident to the Lee County School District. The Loftons said Superintendent Coke Magee suspended the driver for five days after the complaint.
“We are aware of this, and it is being handled as a personnel issue,” the Lee County School District said in a statement.
James Lofton said he wants everyone involved to lose their jobs.
“That’s bull. It is bull crap. I think all their jobs, the superintendent, the one over the buses. I think they all need to be fired,” James Lofton said. “Because they’re hired to keep our kids safe. Instead, they put them out on the side of the road.”
James Lofton took his concerns to law enforcement. Lee County Sheriff Jim Johnson said investigators have not found evidence to support criminal charges against the driver.
The Loftons are now seeking a lawyer as they consider their options.
“I’m not only protecting my kids by doing this. I’m protecting your kid, the neighbor’s kid, and the kid down the street,” James Lofton said. “What happens when one of these kids gets killed? I will take action, as in the court of law. Because it’s not just my kid. It’s the community’s kids.”

title: VASSALBORO: Group talks about why grants were denied
text:
Four Vassalboro Conservation Commission members spent most of their Oct. 21 meeting talking about the grant they didn’t get and how to make approval of future grants more likely.
They also wondered whether some of the grant opportunities they foresee are outside their jurisdiction; perhaps some other town board, existing or to be created, should make the applications.
Commission Chairman Holly Weidner said the group learned in September their application for a Community Action Grant (CAG) through the Kennebec Valley Council of Governments’ (KVCOG) Community Resilience Partnership (CRP) was not approved.
They decided their document had failed to meet some of the criteria and to provide enough information to help those reviewing applications make a decision.
They further decided to discuss with select board members whether Vassalboro needs a grant-writing committee.
Commission members had for review a 28-page Vulnerability Assessment, part of the CRP. The introduction explains: “The purpose of this assessment is to identify climate-related hazards, community vulnerabilities, and priority areas for resilience investment in order to inform future planning, capital improvements, and eligibility for Community Action Grant funding.”
The study makes three recommendations for Vassalboro: strengthen transportation and stormwater infrastructure; protect local water resources; and strengthen emergency preparedness.
Weidner said Olivia Kunesh, at KVCOG, did most of the work for the assessment; she and commission member Mary Schwanke helped. She questioned whether this project is under the commission’s jurisdiction.
She said Kunesh is scheduled to present the study at the Oct. 28 select board meeting. Commission members plan to attend to talk about the failed CAG grant.
The Oct. 21 meeting was preceded by a field trip to find and mark trees bought with Project Canopy money. In more than an hour, commission members and volunteer Bob Milano located 23 trees, in part of East Vassalboro.
With the time about to change so it will be dark earlier, members did not schedule another pre-meeting trip. Member Steve Jones listed from memory another dozen Project Canopy trees in other parts of town, from North Vassalboro to Riverside.
The next regular Conservation Commission meeting is set for 6:30 p.m., Wednesday, Nov. 18, in the Vassalboro town office meeting room.

title: Up and Down the Kennebec Valley: Medical history in central Kennebec Valley
text:
Readers who have been following this series on doctors who practiced in selected central Maine towns have likely noticed two glaring omissions.
One is that very few sources explained why a man with a medical degree, whether brand-new or a bit worn, whether from Bowdoin or Dartmouth or Bellevue, should decide that a small town in the Kennebec Valley was the place he wanted to establish his practice.
Occasionally, someone wrote that he knew another doctor there or was otherwise connected; mostly, we are left to guess.
The second and more significant omission is the absence of information on what kind of medicine these men practiced. What training and resources did they have? What diseases did they recognize? What could they do to deal with injuries and diseases?
For these second questions, your writer found partial answers from various sources. Some of the information below applies specifically to one doctor; some seems to apply to most doctors of the period.
And some, of course, wanders off to other topics your writer found interesting.
* * * * * *
In his introduction to the chapter on medicine in Rev. Edwin Carey Whittemore’s Waterville centennial history, Dr. Frederick C. Thayer wrote that “scientific medicine” owed more to 19th century discoveries than to everything accomplished before then. Whether any of the Waterville doctors played any part in developing or using new discoveries, he did not say.
Henry Kingsbury mentioned one in his 1892 Kennebec County history: Robert J. Martin, son of Pittsfield native Dr. George W. Martin (born in 1834), got his degree in 1887 from the University of New York’s medical department and in 1890 “went to Germany…to study the Koch method of lung treatment, and was the first to practice it in Maine.”
(Wikipedia explains that German physician Dr. Robert Koch [1843 – 1910] discovered, among other things, the cause of tuberculosis. In 1890, he discovered tuberculin; he thought it would cure tuberculosis, a belief that turned out to be wrong.)
By 1890, Dr. George Martin had been in practice in Augusta since 1867; whether his son joined him, Kingsbury did not say, and your writer found no other sources of information about either father or son.
Ernest Marriner, in his Kennebec Yesterdays, agreed with Thayer on the lack of scientific medicine before the 20th century. His medical chapter started in the 1800s, when, he said, a doctor had a hard enough life, called out at all hours to drive his horse and buggy through rain or snow to a patient who had already waited hours for him, and in a maternity case might keep everyone waiting hours more.
But, Marriner wrote, doctors in the 1700s had even more demanding jobs.
“Not only did they lack buggies; often they didn’t even have a road,” he said. Or a bridge; he (and midwife Martha Ballard, in her famous diary) wrote they crossed open rivers by wading, frozen ones on the ice.
“When they amputated a patient’s limb,” Marriner continued, “they had to call in the neighbors to hold him down, for they had no anesthetics.”
“They bled patients to death; they deprived folks of fresh air instead of prescribing it; they never heard of sterilizing an instrument. In fact they did a lot of crude, unscientific things, but they did the best they could in their day. And that best was a lot.”
* * * * * *
The majority of 18th and 19th century doctors in the Kennebec Valley seem to have been in general practice. There were a few exceptions.
In his chapter in Whittemore’s Waterville history, Thayer described most of the men he profiled as practicing “medicine.”
He named a few who specialized in ear, eye, nose and throat care, including his partner, Dr. James Frederick Hill. Dr. Hill (1854 – May 1941) got his medical degree in 1885, left Waterville for post-graduate work in New York in 1895-1897, and afterwards “devoted himself to special work of the eye, ear, nose and throat.”
Dr. Louis King Austin (1869 – October 1952) came to Waterville in 1902, and “devotes his attention entirely to diseases of the eye, ear, nose and throat.”
Definitions
An on-line source says a capital surgical case was a major operation, with the patient’s life at risk.
A 2003 book on British medicine titled For Fear of Pain, by Peter Stanley, excerpted on line, says early in the 19th century these operations included “trepan, amputation, hernia and lithotomy”; excision and ovariotomy were added later.
“Tepan” presumably means trepanning, drilling a hole into the skull – Wikipedia calls it “one of the oldest known surgical procedures.”
“Amputation,” the “removal of a limb or other body part,” is also an ancient medical method.
“Hernia” presumably means the repair of a hernia.
“Lithotomy” means the surgical removal of kidney, bladder or gallbladder stones.
“Excision” means removing body tissue, usually because of cancer.
“Ovariotomy” means the surgical removal of one or both of a woman’s ovaries.
Any of these operations would require sharp tools and knowledge of human anatomy.
Thayer listed several men as surgeons (mostly as military titles).
Dr. James Fanning Noyes (1817 – February 1896) “performed many capital surgical operations,” he wrote.
In Rev. Whittemore’s profile of Thayer, he, too, was credited with “skill and success in capital surgical cases.” (See box.)
Another surgeon who was apparently known to Kingsbury, and who received detailed attention in the medical chapter in his history, was Leander J. Crooker, born in Nova Scotia Feb. 24, 1837, to an Edgecomb-born doctor father.
Young Crooker “early evinced a natural aptitude for anatomical investigation,” and did his “first surgical operation” – removing a tooth – when he was 12 years old. Six years later he removed a tumor from a woman’s axillary cavity, “an operation which the surgeons of the town had refused to undertake.”
(An on-line medical reference defines the axillary cavity: “a pyramid-shaped space located beneath the shoulder joint that acts as a major passageway for blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics traveling between the neck/thorax and the upper limb.”)
He studied medicine with his father, and at 21 opened “an irregular practice in Vassalboro and Belgrade.”
(Kingsbury does not explain this move. Deborah Noblesmith, in her continuation of Crooker’s story in the September-October 2025 issue of Kennebec Current, the Kennebec Historical Society newsletter, wrote that “in his early teens” he had spent “most of a year” with a married sister in Somerville. An older brother, Aaron, was a doctor in Belgrade by 1857, she wrote).
Despite his minimal training, Crooker did so well that he postponed taking a medical degree. “It seemed as if he were impelled by some unseen power to operate,” Kingsbury wrote.
In addition, he was mechanically skilled, designing and making at a blacksmith’s shop his own surgical tools.
Kingsbury described the “difficulties” of Crooker’s “first operation for strangulated hernia.” (Strangulated hernia is described on line from a medical source as “a life-threatening medical emergency that happens when a piece of intestine or fatty tissue gets trapped in an abdominal wall defect and its blood supply is completely cut off.” Symptoms include severe pain, an immovable lump, nausea and vomiting.)
Crooker was then 22; it was winter and the snow was so deep he had to abandon his horse and walk several miles, reaching his patient well after dark. “By the light of two tallow candles and the assistance of a neighbor, it was cut down upon and the bowel returned. Ether was not used…for the very good reason that he had none with him.”
Older brother Aaron died in 1863, Noblesmith said, and Crooker took over the Belgrade practice
A short time later Crooker finally decided he needed a medical degree. He moved to Boston and attended lectures at Harvard Medical School; and married for the second time, his first wife having died, and fathered his only child, a son who also became a doctor.
“In 1870 he moved to Augusta and allowed himself the time to attend the final course of lectures and the examinations at Dartmouth College. He was awarded his Doctor of Medicine degree after 13 years of an active practice of medicine and surgery,” Noblesmith wrote.
In 1872, Kingsbury and Noblesmith said, Crooker invented an important surgical instrument that Kingsbury said was famous as Crooker’s Spiral Spring Ligater (Ligater or ligator is a surgical tool used to put a rubber or other band around the base of a bit of tissue to cut off the blood supply and kill it.)
Noblesmith summarized: “He was considered a thoughtful and caring family doctor as well, often staying with a seriously ill patient for days until the worst had passed. One published account in the Daily Kennebec Journal in 1873 describes a father giving Crooker a gift of $1,000 as a token of gratitude for saving his child’s life by his days-long ministrations.”
In 1892, Kingsbury said, Crooker, age 55, was practicing in Augusta and consulting widely, “especially in surgery.”
Kingsbury added that Crooker approved of antiseptics and especially believed in “perfect cleanliness in all surgical operations.” Only six of his patients had died as a result of his operations, and those, Kingsbury said, were considered incurable and operated on “as a forlorn hope.”
The latter part of Noblesmith’s article focused on Crooker’s real estate interests, especially Ocean Point in Boothday, and his political activism. Dr. Crooker died of stomach cancer on Oct. 9, 1917, “having been in continuous practice for 61 years.”
* * * * * *
Few, if any, 19th-century doctors made their living exclusively by practicing medicine.
Frederick Thayer said Waterville’s Dr. John McKechnie was “an active civil engineer and business man,” who jobs including surveying land in much of the Kennebec River Valley as it was settled in the late 1700s and early 1800s. Marriner agreed, saying McKechnie’s “fame…rests not on his practice of medicine, but on his surveys for the Plymouth Company.”
Thayer praised a later Waterville doctor, Nathan Goldsmith Howard Pulsifer (1824 – December 1893), for his “judgment of financial affairs,” and said he was president of the People’s National Bank for years prior to his death.
A contemporary of Dr. Pulsifer’s, Dr. Henry Hancock Campbell (1820 – January 1895) “was largely interested in real estate, having large holdings at the time of his death.”
Thayer himself, according to editor Whittemore, tended to “his large business interests” between professional and civic duties.
Marriner wrote: “Asa Quimby [1792 – May 1829] of Albion operated in lumber more than he did on patients. Daniel Stevens [1782 – August 1841], China’s first doctor, delivered more wheat to the mill than he did babies to nervously expectant fathers. Stephen Barton [1740 – October 1804) who came to Vassalboro with a bag of medicines in 1774, ran a ferry; at least he owned it, though his wife and boys probably attended to most of its trips across the [Kennebec, presumably] river.”
(Dr. Barton was the subject of this subseries in the Oct. 1 issue of The Town Line.)
Kingsbury added that Albion’s Dr. Asa Quimby opened the town’s first store around 1800, “with a shrewd eye to increasing the scanty income derived from his practice.”
Kingsbury noted that Waterville’s Dr. Nathaniel Boutelle (1821 – December 1890) bred “Jersey cattle and Southdown sheep” on his Waterville farm. He was also a banker, a director of the Ticonic National Bank in 1875 and its president from 1884 until his death.
(Dr. Boutelle was profiled in an article on Jefferson Medical College graduates in the Nov. 24, 2022, issue of The Town Line. Your writer found little information about what kind of medicine he practiced.)
Another Waterville doctor was apparently in the real estate business. Kingsbury wrote that Dr. John L. Fortier graduated from Brunswick Medical School in 1883 and opened a practice in Waterville. “In 1889 he opened a drug store on Main street, and in 1891 opened another on Water street, in the block which he built in 1890.”
Main sources
Kingsbury, Henry D., ed., Illustrated History of Kennebec County Maine 1625-1892 (1892)
Marriner, Ernest, Kennebec Yesterdays (1954)
Whittemore, Rev. Edwin Carey, Centennial History of Waterville 1802 – 1902 (1902)
Websites, miscellaneous.

title: Did You Know Sugarland Was Originally a Trio?
text:
Did You Know Sugarland Was Originally a Trio?
The country group behind hits like “Baby Girl” and “Stuck Like Glue” started out as a trio before becoming the duo fans know today.
👇 KEEP READING: 68 Artists Not in the Country Music Hall of Fame 👇
Sugarland formed in the Atlanta area in 2002 as a trio featuring Jennifer Nettles, Kristian Bush and Kristen Hall.
Hall played guitar, sang harmony and helped write songs for the group’s 2004 debut album, “Twice the Speed of Life,” which included the hits “Baby Girl” and “Something More.”
She left in late 2005, and Nettles and Bush announced her departure in January 2006, saying she wanted to stay home and focus on songwriting.
Nettles and Bush continued together, releasing their second album, “Enjoy the Ride,” later that year.
Sugarland is celebrating the 20th anniversary of “Enjoy the Ride” with the 2026 Ride or Die Tour, featuring hits and fan favorites from the duo’s catalog.
The tour will stop at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor on Nov. 11, with special guest Payton Sullivan.
And there you have it! Sugarland’s familiar two-person lineup took shape just before the release of one of the group’s best-known albums.

title: Finding Our Voices provides $540,000 in aid to Maine domestic abuse survivors
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Finding Our Voices, the grassroots nonprofit supporting Maine women survivors of domestic abuse and their children, has distributed $540,000 in direct financial assistance to more than 1,000 low-income survivors across all 16 Maine counties through its Get Out Stay Out Fund.
Launched in 2021, shortly after the group became a nonprofit, the fund provides low-barrier microgrants for essential needs that can make the difference between remaining in danger, constraint, and misery, and building a safe, independent life. Assistance includes security deposits, car repairs, gas and grocery cards, overdue utility bills, legal expenses, and other critical costs.
According to Finding Our Voices CEO+Founder Patrisha McLean, financial abuse with the resulting lack of available funds is the number one factor trapping women in domestic abuse.
The program began with a $50,000 grant from Doris Buffett’s Sunshine Lady Foundation. Finding Our Voices is entirely donor-funded and does not accept government funding, a model that allows the organization to respond quickly and flexibly to survivors’ urgent needs, according to McLean.
“Finding Our Voices kept my electricity on and gas in my car," one funding recipient said, after I had been physically, emotionally, & financially abused by my ex-boyfriend and isolated 2000 miles away from my family and friends. They helped me when nobody else could, or would.”
Demand for emergency assistance is growing
Finding Our Voices is experiencing a surge in requests for help that they attribute to rising costs of housing, fuel, and groceries and cutbacks to the social safety net. McLean said the survivor-led nonprofit, working out of a home office in Camden and with a staff of three plus a brigade of volunteers spanning the state, now receives an average of eight reach-outs a day from referral partners and survivors, increasingly involving women who are homeless or living in cars with their children.
“We are immensely grateful to our donors for allowing us to provide lifelines to the most vulnerable women and children in our communities,” McLean said.
The assistance is often immediate and practical: a security deposit that makes a hard-to-find apartment accessible; a gas card that allows a survivor to flee the state when a dangerous former partner is released early from prison; a car repair that enables a woman to keep her job; or storage fees that preserve treasured belongings, including children’s artwork and, in one case, a mother’s ashes.
McLean described a growing gap between survivors’ urgent needs and the help available through other systems. One woman reported spending more than eight hours on hold with social service agencies. Another single mother was told she needed to take a day off from her new job to apply for assistance in person. In early October, a woman was told the next available appointment to apply for heating assistance was in January.
Helping survivors stay out and rebuild their lives
The “Stay Out” component of the fund recognizes that leaving an abusive relationship is only the beginning of a survivor’s journey. Rebuilding financial stability, navigating legal proceedings, addressing trauma, and supporting children can create significant challenges long after a woman has gotten herself and her children physically safe.
“I left my abuser 17 months ago,” one recipient wrote to Finding Our Voices. “But no one ever tells you how hard the next part is. I felt like I was drowning—in legal fees, in the ongoing divorce being weaponized against me, mounting therapy fees for PTSD, and still trying to earn an income without a car to drive.”
The survivor described the support she received from Finding Our Voices as more than financial: “I felt like I was hanging off a cliff by my fingernails. The help I received from you guys was not only a lifeline, but a tsunami of relief that gave me the strength to keep going.”
The fund’s impact is reflected in its recent growth. According to McLean, assistance has doubled since 2024. In the first 10 months of 2026 alone, Finding Our Voices distributed $120,000 to 245 survivors and their 95 children. That amount represents more than one-third of the organization’s annual budget.
The fund has also established separate Children’s and Pet Funds, recognizing the impact of domestic abuse on children and the importance of pets in the healing journey. Recent Children’s Fund payments have included $350 for art camp, an $80 weighted stuffed animal, and $750 for driving lessons for a teenager who had just finished testifying in a domestic violence trial involving her father.
Pet Fund assistance has included a muzzle and flea treatment needed for a dog to accompany its owner into emergency shelter, as well as $750 for a life-saving operation for a beloved furbaby named Daisy.
A network of community support
Finding Our Voices works with an expanding network of referral partners throughout Maine, including health care and social service agency caseworkers, therapists, and state workers and officials who connect survivors with assistance through Finding Our Voices that they cannot find anywhere else.
After Finding Our Voices paid a client’s $1,000 overdue electric bill, Nancy Cormier, a caseworker with the mental health clinic Spurwink, praised the nonprofit.
“I had a response by email and phone within an hour of submitting the contact form,” Cormier said. “This is a life-changing organization. The amount of kindness shown has blown me away.”
Finding Our Voices provided another survivor with a $500 grocery card after her food assistance benefits were suspended, and a $500 gas card to allow her to escape terrifying stalking of her ex by staying with family in Texas.
“Finding our Voices was a light in the middle of a lot of darkness for my client,” her caseworker said. “They were genuinely interested in my client’s needs, and were quick to respond and provide tangible and practical help.”
“They are actually helping victims of domestic violence. They are active and proactive. They are using their funds well and wisely and helping survivors break through.”
Funding comes from a mix of grants, individual donations, and creative community fundraising campaigns. Grants this year include $20,000 from the John T. Gorman Foundation exclusively for security deposits.
Finding Our Voices’ largest fundraising initiative is its annual Into the Light! Yellow Festival, with 100 percent of proceeds going to the Get Out Stay Out Fund. During July, businesses promote, and donate proceeds from, yellow-themed menu or retail items, with participation this year from 126 businesses from Damariscotta to Stonington. Proceeds are significantly boosted with corporate sponsorships including lead sponsors Camden National Bank and First National Bank.
Additional fundraising efforts include register round-ups this year at Aubuchon Hardware locations in Buxton and Belfast, both locations of Morning Glory Natural Foods in Brunswick, and Lois’ Natural Marketplace in Scarborough. Christine Buckley has raised a total of $7,000 for the Get Out Stay Out Fund through art sales at Christine’s Framing Gallery and “yellow dot” sales at her second business, Camden Curated.
Beyond financial assistance
Finding Our Voices also supports survivors through Finding Our Smiles, which connects women with donated dental care from 40 volunteer dental providers across Maine; Healing Together workshops and retreats; and a weekly online support group.
The nonprofit’s public education efforts include its Teen Healthy Relationship program, with classroom visits in 2026 to 18 schools from Sanford to Baileyville.
For the domestic abuse survivors running Finding Our Voices including McLean, the group's COO Mary Kamradt, and dozens of devoted volunteers, these services and the financial assistance are part of a broader effort to empower their sisters to cross over to the bright side of safety and freedom, as they managed to do.
A recent donation captured that journey in the donor’s own words:
“I’m on the other side of a rough 15 years. I’ll always be grateful for your work. It wasn’t until I read one of your posters in Belfast that it truly hit me how mentally abusive my ex was. My life now is peaceful, purposeful & full of good friends. Thank you for helping others get through the dark and into the light.”
As requests for assistance continues to rise, Finding Our Voices invites donations from the public, which can be designated for the Get Out Stay Out Fund, its children or pet offshoots, or any other of its programs.
About Finding Our Voices
Finding Our Voices is the Maine-based, grassroots nonprofit and sisterhood supporting women survivors of domestic abuse and their children. Its programs include the Get Out Stay Out Fund, Children’s Fund, Pet Fund, Finding Our Smiles donated dental care initiative, Healing Togetherworkshops and retreats, a weekly online support group, and public education campaigns promoting awareness of domestic abuse and teen dating abuse.
The group is hosting a free Financial Health workshop in Camden on Tuesday November 10 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
For more information about Finding Our Voices, its programs, or ways to support its work, visit the organization’s official website https://findingourvoices.net or contact McLean directly at hello@findingourvoices.net

title: The Latest: Trump pushing to keep red-state Senate seats in GOP hands
text:
President Donald Trump told Texans they’d better accept data centers in their communities and floated making Venezuela the 51st state as he stumped for Republican Ken Paxton, while Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico said a “corruption crisis” plagues U.S. politics.
Social media videos believed to be produced with artificial intelligence and linked to Russia are misusing real people’s names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in the final stretch of midterm voting.
And Republicans have spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats as Americans go to vote, betting that struggling GOP candidates can leverage the divisive cultural issue to overcome concerns about Trump’s leadership and the state of the economy.
Here’s the Latest:
Trump has made the midterms all about himself. Will it work?
President Donald Trump likes to play make-believe with his supporters: “Just close your eyes,” he tells them, “and pretend I’m on the ballot.”
It’s a typically self-involved appeal as Trump finishes the midterms with a cross-country blitz of campaign rallies that allow him to bask in applause.
Outside the venues, he’s profoundly unpopular. While Republicans still love Trump, his overall approval ratings are low enough to potentially sink his party.
And with voters concerned about the war with Iran, artificial intelligence, redistricting fights, high energy prices and the cost of living, Trump’s approach might be the election cycle’s biggest gamble.
“I don’t think there’s anybody that wants Donald Trump out there at these rallies more than Democratic candidates,” said Jessica Mackler, president of EMILY’s List, which focuses on electing Democratic women who support abortion rights. Every time there’s another Trump event, she said, “we look at that as a win.”
Buttigieg campaigns in Mississippi with Democratic Senate hopeful
The former Transportation Secretary joined Democrat Scott Colom in Biloxi on Tuesday, where he said it’s time to end “the name calling” and “viciousness” of today’s politics.
“It is time for a politics that recognizes that the U.S. flag isn’t planted on one side or the other of a political aisle, because all of us are loyal to the Republic for which it stands,” said Buttigieg, a potential 2028 presidential candidate who has been campaigning with Democrats in Republican-leaning areas like Mississippi.
Colom is running against GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. On Monday, Trump visited the state to hold a rally for the Republican senator.
Buttigieg spoke about the high price of diesel and Trump’s decision to go to war in Iran, telling voters, “We can do better than that under new management.”
Who should be believed? Trump’s social media post on golf course leads lawyers back to court
Trump’s social media posts on the renovation of a historic golf course in the nation’s capital are putting Justice Department lawyers in the uncomfortable position of explaining whether the president of the United States should be believed or not.
U.S. Judge Ana Reyes said Tuesday that the department should clarify “whether any plan exists to close East Potomac Golf Course on or around November 15, 2026.” She ordered Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. to appear in court Friday or Monday for a status hearing.
Tuesday’s order came in response to Trump’s social media post late Monday criticizing Reyes’ temporary injunction stopping work at East Potomac Park.
That injunction, issued Monday, was in large part due to previous Trump announcements — via social media — that plans had been completed for the golf course and construction would begin next month. Trump said the facility would be closed for 15 months. The following day, he set the timetable to “immediately.”
Republicans emphasize transgender ads, putting cultural issues over voters’ economic anxiety
Republicans have spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats in the final phase of this year’s midterm elections, betting that struggling GOP candidates can leverage the divisive cultural issue to overcome voters’ concerns about Trump’s leadership and the state of the economy.
The massive investment through Oct. 25 produced about 217,000 TV spots nationwide and exceeds the amount Republicans spent on similar ads in 2024, a presidential election year, at the same point before Election Day, according to tallies provided to The Associated Press by data firm AdImpact.
The spending campaign matched messaging from other Republicans on the campaign trail, led by Trump, who has played down surging gasoline prices and other rising costs, but highlighted what he described as an urgent threat to America’s children from Democratic policies.
The Republican emphasis on transgender issues offers a consequential test of whether a theme that had worked in past elections — and especially in deep red states — can still be potent when voters consistently say high prices are their chief concern.
Disinformation videos, likely from Russia, are exploiting real people to malign Senate candidates
Social media videos believed to be produced with artificial intelligence and linked to Russia are misusing real people’s names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in the final stretch of midterm voting.
One of the targets is Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio. The video, which appears to include some AI manipulation, depicts a newscast and includes pictures of Haya Akbik, who interned for Brown several years ago, and other former staff members.
It was appalling to Akbik, who told The Associated Press that any claims attributed to her in the clip are “completely made up.”
“It’s my name, it’s my reputation, making this allegation, and it’s just completely false,” she said. “And it harms the senator, someone else, in the process. So, it’s just messed up.”
The videos demonstrate how foreign adversaries continue to use a familiar playbook to try to influence American voters who are deciding which party controls Congress next year. The threat could be magnified with AI, a powerful tool for fabricating damaging information that can sometimes appear very real.
Talarico vows to ‘take back Texas’ as Trump makes last-minute push to keep the state in GOP hands
Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico on Tuesday decried a “corruption crisis” he says is plaguing the U.S. political system, competing for the spotlight with President Donald Trump in deeply conservative West Texas ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
Trump was in Texas for the third time in a month in a last-minute push to back Republican Ken Paxton and block Democrats from notching their first statewide election victory in more than three decades.
Talarico took the stage in Lubbock an hour after Trump wrapped up his own speech across town. A seminarian and a former teacher, Talarico reached for metaphors from both the Bible and a famous Texas pastime — Friday night football — to cast himself as an underdog against powerful forces including Trump and Elon Musk, who is bankrolling attack ads against Talarico on Paxton’s behalf.
“We’re going to shock the nation and shock the world when we beat the billionaires and take back Texas,” Talarico said.
Moments earlier, Trump leaned into cultural issues to portray Talarico as too liberal for Texas.

title: No one can find sewer contract with Winslow
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Vassalboro’s sewage goes via Winslow’s pipes to the Waterville treatment plant, and Winslow’s charge for the use of its pipes is part of the costs the Vassalboro Sanitary District (VSD) bills to its customers in North and East Vassalboro.
When Lauchlin Titus, chairman of the VSD board of trustees, looked for the contract between the two towns that allows Winslow to set and increase fees, he found only a 2016 memo of understanding that says the two towns will work together.
Titus asked Watershed Maine, the VSD’s financial assistant; no one there could find a contract, either. He told the rest of the VSD board at their Oct. 22 meeting that his next step is to check the file cabinets in the VSD headquarters building for a paper copy.
Charles “Chuck” Applebee, of Wiscasset-based Water Quality and Compliance, the company running the Vassalboro sewer system, said he will check their files, too.
After the meeting, Daphne Paulette, of Watershed Maine, said VSD is still paying Winslow the same rates as in 2016: $1,212.19 per quarter plus $6.66 for each 100 cubic feet of sewage sent.
Based on figures from the first three quarters of 2026, Paulette wrote, “As of September 30, 2026, the Town of Winslow’s sewer bill represents 34.06 percent of the District’s operating expenses and 18.81 percent of its total expenses.”
In other business at the Oct. 22 meeting, board members unanimously adopted a public comment policy that Titus adapted from the town’s. (The town policy is part of the select board rules of order, found on the town website, Vassalboro.net, under Ordnances and Policies, which are under Documents on the main page.)
Trustees briefly discussed financial and operating reports and found nothing alarming.
Treasurer Donald Robbins planned to attend a late-October meeting at which Kennebec Water District officials and representatives of towns KWD serves are to discuss changing billing from quarterly to monthly. Titus explained after the meeting that KWD (and the East Vassalboro Water Company) provides VSD with water usage information that the sewer district uses to bill its customers.
If KWD changes to monthly billing, Paulette advised VSD trustees not to follow. Postage is too expensive, she said.
The next two VSD trustees’ meetings are scheduled for 3 p.m., an hour earlier than in recent months, on Thursday, Nov. 19, and Thursday, Dec. 17, in the Vassalboro town office meeting room.

title: Troy Jackson wins Maine’s student mock election
text:
Maine students voted for Democratic candidate Troy Jackson in the U.S. Senate race by almost 6 percentage points over Republican incumbent Susan Collins in a statewide mock election Tuesday.
Students also chose Democrat Hannah Pingree for governor, with 41.8% of the vote, over Republican Bobby Charles at 30.4% and independent Rick Bennett not far behind with 24.4%.
The mock election, hosted each year by the Maine Department of the Secretary of State for students in elementary, middle and high schools around the state, has shown an exceptional capacity for predicting the state’s real election outcomes. Maine’s students have voted for the successful presidential candidate in every election since 2008, although they diverged in the matchup between Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon in 2020, when students chose Gideon.
In the state’s northern 2nd Congressional District, the students chose Paul LePage, the Republican nominee and former governor, by nearly 10 percentage points over Matt Dunlap, the Democrat.
And students in the southern 1st Congressional District chose Democrat Chellie Pingree, who garnered 57.5% of the vote, over Republican Ronald Russell, who received 39.7%.
Last year, students voted for the first time on statewide referendums, where they successfully predicted the passage of a red flag law and the failure of a voter ID proposal.
This year, more than 12,000 students from 115 schools participated in the mock elections.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows visited Maranacook Community High School in Readfield on Tuesday morning to meet with students as they cast their ballots.
“We think that this a great way for students to get introduced to the idea of voting, and to recognize that it’s pretty easy, that it doesn’t take a lot of time, that it’s not terribly complicated,” Bellows told reporters from the front lobby at the Regional School Unit 38 high school. “It demystifies voting for young people, so they’re more likely to vote in the future.”
Isabelle Gannett, a senior from Manchester who was working the school’s mock polls, said turnout among her peers was strong.
Maine had one of the highest youth turnout rates in the country during the 2022 midterms.
Staff Photographer Joe Phelan contributed to this story.

title: Azteca Mexican Restaurant opens in South Portland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The owners of Tacos La Poblanita in the Maine Mall recently opened a Mexican restaurant in South Portland.
Azteca Mexican Restaurant launched at 1422 Broadway last Thursday. The 36-seat space had formerly been the Jamaican restaurant Caribbean Taste.
Co-owners Jamie Rodriguez and Karina Contreras previously owned a brick-and-mortar version of Tacos La Poblanita in Westbrook, though it closed last year. Rodriguez said it was their dream to open a full restaurant again.

title: Widow searches for lost wedding ring when husband dies 3 days after getting married in Las Vegas
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) — A South Dakota woman is asking for help finding the wedding ring her husband lost in Las Vegas the night they married.
Tammy Bishop and Will Mulroy were married Oct. 20 at the Viva Las Vegas Chapel.
Bishop said they celebrated on a party bus and toured the Strip. At a bar, though, she says Mulroy looked down and realized his ring was gone.
“We got to a bar. He looked down and his band was gone. He lost it. He started crying,” Bishop said.
According to Bishop, he told her the ring was two sizes too big because he had lost weight.
She said the ring may have slid off on the bus or while he moved into his wheelchair. It may also have come off while he rolled down the Strip.
“We backtracked our steps. We told the bus driver. We had everyone looking. We couldn’t find it,” she said.
The next day, she joked with him: “You didn’t even have your ring on for 24 hours and you lost it.”
Everyone laughed, she said.
“I said it’s not a big deal; we will buy you a new one, but now that he is gone it is a big deal to me,” Bishop said.
Sadly, Bishop said Mulroy died just three days after their wedding.
She said he was in a lot of pain on the way home and mentioned going to the ER as soon as they returned to South Dakota.
The next morning, he was so congested that she told him not to go to work.
Bishop said she couldn’t wake him and called 911. She said doctors declared him brain dead at the hospital. He was on life support for 24 hours. His heart stopped three times in the ER.
“It just doesn’t make sense. When we started dating, that’s when the accident happened, then we got married, and it’s hard,” Bishop said.
Bishop and Mulroy met in July 2023 and began officially dating in March 2024.
However, a week later, Mulroy was in a motorcycle accident and became paralyzed.
“There was a lot of anger at first,” Bishop said.
Mulroy kept asking her to marry him. And this summer, she said yes.
On her Oct. 4 birthday, Bishop said he told her he had planned a Vegas wedding, everything was booked, and her friends were going.
“It was a perfect day,” Bishop said. “He was on cloud nine,” she said.
The groom’s party and bride’s party got ready separately. Mulroy first saw Bishop in her dress when she walked out to the party bus.
“It was pretty cool,” she said.
Bishop remembers Mulroy as a hands-on guy.
“He was very savvy, very mechanically inclined, could fix things, just that guy,” she said. “He didn’t have to call other guys to get stuff done.”
He worked at Fleet Farm and had worked with party buses in the past. The couple had decided to start their own party bus business.
Now, Bishop hopes a stranger finds the ring.
“It would mean a lot. The rings were blessed, and that was our wedding ring, and that was him and how much it meant to him. That’s why it means so much to me,” she said.
