title: Artificial intelligence transforms the workforce, regulations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Nearly all industries have been impacted by Artificial Intelligence. Goldman Sachs estimates 300 million jobs will be impacted by the emerging technology by 2030. AI is reshaping industries by the day, resulting in jobs being transformed or erased. The changes are bringing a greater need for AI oversight.
“People need to understand that there still needs to be human involvement,” Barry Jones, a Vice President at X2X said. X2X is an AI governance company. Jones said there’s not enough oversight AI oversight right now.
“Imagine an AI assistant preparing financial reports,” Jones said. “That’s a potentially productive tool. But just imagine if that AI system provided that critical financial information outside of the company’s internal workings.”
Before Congress left Capitol Hill for the midterms, several congressmembers made clear where they stood on what role the government should play on regulation.
“Well, look, anytime you can give the federal government out of it, I think we’re better off,” Rep. Buddy Carter (R-GA) said. “We don’t want to stifle innovation. But at the same time, we got to get this right. That’s the key. We got to get a right. I can be a very useful tool, unbelievably useful tool. But there are some concerns and there are some dangers there.”
“First, the United States needs to address the very real risks created by increasingly powerful AI systems, and these decisions need to be made by the American people through their representatives,” Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) said.
Jones said big picture, self-governance isn’t enough.
“But to say that something is self-governing is like having the fox watching the henhouse,” Jones said. “You really need to have a third party, layer in some cases, even the government saying these are the things that I can do and I cannot do.”
Jones said that private oversight is creating roles that have been replaced by technology. Microsoft recently announced they offered 60,000 employees buyouts due to AI. Jones has advice for people looking for a career pivot due to AI.
“Start learning AI,” Jones said. “Understand how it applies to your profession. Also understand that judgement, experience, trust and accountability matter. The goal shouldn’t be to compete with the machine. The goal should be to become someone who knows the useful power of the technology and using it responsibly.”
Efforts to regulate Artificial Intelligence are stalled on Capitol Hill but the 120th Congress could take up the rapidly evolving technology in January.

title: Riverton housing complex clears final legal hurdle as judge again sides with city, developer
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Superior Court judge has ruled in favor of the city of Portland and the developer behind the Belfort Landing housing complex, this time over the neighbors’ claim that the property was improperly rezoned.
The ruling issued Tuesday marks the final legal hurdle for the 50-unit project after a group of Riverton neighbors and the owners of Moran’s Market on Forest Avenue filed a seven-count civil complaint challenging the city’s decision to approve the development.
All other counts were previously decided or dismissed, allowing construction to proceed on the parcel between Belfort Street and Talbot Community School.
The project has been seen as a bellwether for new housing projects approved under the city’s 2024 ReCode effort and has even divided the candidates for City Council in District 5.
Alex Coupe, the developer with Acre Properties, said Wednesday that the ruling shows that the neighbors “had no legal merit all along,” adding that “baseless lawsuits” throughout the state continue to stall new housing from being built.
Construction on the two buildings has continued even as the court battle played out. Coupe said one building is framed and mechanicals are being installed, while framing for the second building will be complete in November.
Coupe purchased the land in 2022 from the Larsen family, which owns Moran’s Market. In 2024, a portion was rezoned to allow multifamily housing as part of Portland’s ReCode effort.
The neighbors’ claim argued that, during the ReCode process, the city made an “eleventh-hour decision to spot-zone the property” at the owner’s request, and without proper resident notification.
In the ruling issued Tuesday, Justice Thomas McKeon said Coupe lobbied city officials for the 1.5-acre parcel to be rezoned through ReCode, because city staff were not originally planning to rezone the land. After communication from officials, including Councilor Kate Sykes, the parcel was reclassified ahead of the final ReCode vote, the ruling states.
While McKeon acknowledged that the city “changed its mind” regarding the rezone, he said law court precedent is clear that “the court must refrain from meddling in the city’s legislative process and is limited to comparison of the project to the comprehensive plan.”
McKeon said Belfort Landing was consistent with the city’s comprehensive plan because it advances the city’s goals for developing “complete neighborhoods” and providing additional housing to Portland. The location along Forest Avenue is identified as a primary growth area in the plan and has access to public transportation.
“(The) parcel is located next to a school, local market and community center, all of which are components of a complete neighborhood,” McKeon wrote.
He also said that the city’s “deficiencies” in properly noticing public meetings “do not provide a basis for invalidating the rezoning.”
In response to the neighbors’ claim that the chosen zoning was out of character with the surrounding neighborhood, McKeon acknowledged that the chosen zoning “departs from the plan’s description of areas of recommended for higher-density housing.”
But, the judge said, “that contradiction does not render (the) zoning inconsistent with the plan as a whole.”
A representative from the neighborhood group could not immediately be reached for comment Wednesday.

title: South Portland detectives arrest N.Y. man accused in $125,000 phone scam
text:
A New York man was arrested Tuesday and charged with theft by deception in relation to a scam in which a South Portland resident lost more than $125,000.
South Portland Police Department detectives arrested Jian Chen, 49, of Brooklyn, New York, after “a ruse” transaction with the victim, the department said in a news release Wednesday.
Detectives met with a resident on Monday who believed they had been “defrauded” of more than $125,000 in a phone scam involving someone impersonating a U.S. Marshals Service agent, the department said.
The victim was told that his Social Security number was compromised and that purchases were being made under his name.
“The alleged agent told the victim that the only way to stop the crimes and keep his finances safe was to provide undercover federal agents with cash payments,” the department stated. “The victim was convinced this was a legitimate investigation, and proceeded with the requests.”
The victim told police he met with someone, whom he believed was an undercover agent, twice in order to pay them in cash and received receipts for the payments, the department said. The victim met with a different person each time.
The scammers continued to request more money from the victim, the department said, and they worked with the victim to “set up a ruse and help organize another cash payment” on Tuesday.
A different person — Chen — arrived to meet the victim at the Lowe’s parking lot in Scarborough, where nearby detectives watched the interaction. The department said Chen was apprehended without incident and taken to the Cumberland County Jail.
Police say they believe Chen “is part of a large-scale fraud ring” and they are continuing to investigate other suspected participants.
“There appears to be a recent uptick in these types of scams in our area lately,” and multiple people have reported losing tens and even hundreds of thousands of dollars, the department said.
The department directs community members who believe they are being targeted by a phone scam to hang up and report the issue to local police.
The department noted that no law enforcement agency will demand cash payments via call, text or email, or ask someone to pay fines with gift cards. They also advised that law enforcement agencies don’t request financial information over the phone.

title: US cruise ship suspends global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, passengers stranded
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
US cruise ship suspends global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, passengers stranded
A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
Related video: How are President Trump's tariff policies affecting businesses?
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said.
However, a blogger who has been on the cruise, Randy Cassingham, wrote online that “the company has done absolutely nothing to help: we couldn’t even walk out of the port, so there were shuttle buses that dropped us in the middle of town, Sihanoukville, Cambodia."
“They didn’t even give us a list of hotels, let alone help us get there or pay for them," Cassingham said on his website. The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 were American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.
——-
Associated Press writers Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Grant Peck in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: Disinformation videos, likely from Russia, are exploiting real people to malign Senate candidates
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Social media videos believed to be produced with artificial intelligence and linked to Russia are misusing real people’s names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in the final stretch of midterm voting.
One of the targets is Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio. The video, which appears to include some AI manipulation, depicts a newscast and includes pictures of Haya Akbik, who interned for Brown several years ago, and other former staff members.
It was appalling to Akbik, who told The Associated Press that any claims attributed to her in the clip are “completely made up.”
“It’s my name, it’s my reputation, making this allegation, and it’s just completely false,” she said. “And it harms the senator, someone else, in the process. So, it’s just messed up.”
The videos demonstrate how foreign adversaries continue to use a familiar playbook to try to influence American voters who are deciding which party controls Congress next year. The threat could be magnified with AI, a powerful tool for fabricating damaging information that can sometimes appear very real.
Another target is James Talarico, who is running against Republican Ken Paxton for a Senate seat in Texas. The video, also believed to include some AI manipulation, is framed as a direct-to-camera confessional from a former student of Talarico.
“The most powerful people in the world know they can’t beat James Talarico with the truth, so they’re slandering him with AI deepfakes, foreign bots, and conspiracy theories to protect their broken, corrupt political system,” Talarico spokesperson JT Ennis said in a statement.
The social media company X has taken down the initial posts that shared the videos and suspended the users for violating the platform’s rules. However, copies could still be found online Tuesday — some with hundreds of shares — demonstrating how difficult it can be to contain disinformation that can proliferate in the final days of an election.
Experts see a resemblance to Russian clips from 2024
The videos resemble clips from a Russian network known as Storm-1516 that targeted former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris and her running mate, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, two years ago.
The new ones bear similar hallmarks and are likely products of the same network, according to Clemson University professor and media forensics expert Darren Linvill. He found that the accounts that shared recent material had also shared former content from Storm-1516.
The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the past, it has denied interfering in U.S. elections.
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has publicly identified some videos as Russian disinformation in past election cycles, also didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Hany Farid, a Dartmouth College professor who studies artificial intelligence deepfakes, said his analyses showed that videos targeting Brown and Talarico were likely either generated or manipulated using the technology.
He noted the video targeting Brown is a “fairly low-tech fake.” The other one, targeting Talarico, is likely generated by AI and “it is consistent with previous disinformation campaigns released close to Election Day,” Farid said.
Akbik said the video featuring her shows the importance of Congress regulating “AI slop on the internet.”
“This is so damaging,” she said.

title: No, Lockheed Martin donations are not unique to Susan Collins
text:
Nicholas Jacobs is the Goldfarb Family Distinguished Chair in American Government at Colby College, where he also serves as the inaugural director of the Bram Public Policy Lab.
There is nothing particularly surprising about defense contractors contributing to politicians who oversee defense spending.
Whether those contributions purchase political favors is another matter, and one that deserves serious investigation. Unfortunately, a recent article from The Intercept, republished by this newspaper on Oct. 15, substituted insinuation for precisely that kind of scrutiny (“Lockheed Martin showered Susan Collins with cash as F-35 program hit turbulence”).
The article reports that Lockheed Martin employees and executives gave Sen. Susan Collins $59,500 in May and June 2023. In July, Collins voted for a defense bill funding 83 F-35 aircraft. “The effort appeared to pay off for Lockheed,” the article declares.
Except President Joe Biden had requested exactly 83 F-35 jets in March, before those donations and before the critical Government Accountability Office report that supposedly set events in motion. The Senate Appropriations Committee subsequently advanced the defense bill 27–1. Apparently, Lockheed bought almost the entire committee, Democrats included, into supporting precisely what a Democratic president had already proposed.
Neither fact appears in the story. Nor did the GAO recommend cancelling aircraft purchases, as the report insinuates by leading with its criticism of the program. It called for better accounting and oversight, concerns Congress subsequently addressed and which Collins voted for. Without those facts, readers are left with a story that looks rather different from what actually happened.
I did what the editors should have done, which is check the Federal Election Commission records myself. Yes, Lockheed executives concentrated contributions on Collins. But they have repeatedly done the same for powerful congressional defense gatekeepers, Republicans and Democrats alike.
The same Lockheed executives who gave Collins donations gave Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, $28,000 in a single two-week stretch of 2024. They did the same for Speaker Mike Johnson and for Ken Calvert, the Republican who chairs House defense appropriations. The same names, the same $1,000 checks, the same six-week bursts. The Intercept had these records in front of it. They are in the same database, a click away from the Collins figures. It chose not to report them.
Go back a cycle and the pattern repeats again. I also disagree with this form of influence, but there is nothing in the data to support that it is tied to a damning GAO report.
In the 2020 election cycle, my review identified 125 individual contributions of at least $1,000, totaling approximately $176,000, to Republican Kay Granger, a senior appropriator whose district included Lockheed’s F-35 factory.
Democratic House Armed Services Chairman Adam Smith received 43 comparable contributions; Democratic Sen. Jack Reed received 39. In the 2026 cycle to date, Democratic Sen. Chris Coons, the ranking Democrat on Senate Defense Appropriations, has received 30.
Lockheed’s attempt to influence key appropriators is worthy of public scrutiny, but instead Mainers were treated to “data” that turned a longstanding, bipartisan fundraising practice into the appearance of a scandal unique to Collins.
The Intercept neglects the obvious comparison involving individual donors. Why?
Instead, it imports ProPublica’s separate investigation into allegations involving another contractor, Navatek, and a convicted fraudster’s account of political favors. Again, critical context is missing; the FBI said an earlier inquiry found nothing implicating Collins or her campaign. A later inquiry remained unresolved. Neither establishes anything about Lockheed’s 2023 contributions. Guilt by association is not corroboration. In my classroom, passing it off as evidence earns a failing grade.
I’ve come to know many journalists at the Maine Trust for Local News, and I deeply respect their work. They ask probing questions, pursue difficult stories and take seriously their responsibility to readers. This was not their reporting, and it does not reflect the standards I have come to admire.
Instead, it reflects the work of an unapologetically progressive publication that describes journalism as an “instrument of civic action” and declares, “We’re here to change the world, not just describe it.” It even operates a platform organizing political petitions. Its ideological commitments are hardly concealed.
No wonder the article reads more like opposition research dressed up as investigation — a far cry from the Trust’s own ethics policy that emphasizes context, verification and fairness. I would think, however, that those obligations matter just as much when publishing outside reporting.
The Intercept is entitled to its editorial commitments, but Maine readers are entitled to the facts necessary to make their own judgments.
It took me one morning with public records to uncover what the article left out. I hope Maine readers and the Maine Trust for Local News will take another look, too.

title: Long-term care costs rose about 50% in five years, report finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The cost of long-term care jumped nearly 50% in five years, while income for older households rose just 22%, according to a new AARP report.
The report found long-term services and supports are becoming even less affordable for middle-class Americans. Alan Weil, senior vice president for public policy at AARP, said the gap is the most important finding.
“Between 2019 and 2024, a five-year period, the cost of most long-term care services went up about 50%, but the incomes for older households only went up by about 22%,” Weil said. “So the gap between what people can afford and what it costs has grown.”
The AARP also looked at what different types of care cost. Weil said the more skilled the service, the higher the price.
“If you need someone to come in and help you prepare food, that’s less expensive than if you need someone to come in and provide nursing-level care,” Weil said. “Although I’ll also say that we’ve learned that a lot of caregivers are being forced to provide nursing care that they can’t afford to pay someone else to do, even though they’ve never been trained in nursing. So that’s where the burden falls back on the family.”
The financial burden often extends beyond the person who needs care. Weil said many families are part of what he called the sandwich generation.
“If you’re paying for care that your parents need, you’re not saving for your kids’ college,” Weil said. “So this is a squeeze coming from both directions.”
Weil said the best way to prepare is to plan ahead and look into assistance programs that might fit a family’s needs.
“Some people will be qualified for Medicaid, a state and federal program,” Weil said. “The rules differ by state, and at AARP we fight really, really hard to make sure that these services are as available for people as possible.”
Weil said families in the sandwich generation should not assume they are stuck paying out of pocket. He recommends asking a state Medicaid office about eligibility and checking AARP.org for help finding assistance programs in your area.

title: Grand opening of the Franklin County Children’s Task Force Family Resource Center
MAINE-LY GARDENING: Thinking of spring
text:
As the world around us becomes a little less colorful each day, and strong yellows, oranges, reds, and ambers fading, it’s time to think ahead to the colors of spring, with its softer yellows, pinks and blues accented by clear whites and pops of bright red. It’s time to plant bulbs for spring color. There are more and more choices every year as the offerings in catalogs, garden centers, even hardware and grocery stores, reveal.
Daffodils deserve their popularity. They are especially hardy, living and multiplying for decades. Their cheerful yellows are complimented by bright whites. There are tiny ones, and tall ones, some with the familiar simple shapes we see in the oldest gardens and still popping up in the dooryards of abandoned farms. Other varieties are “double” with extra petals. There are multicolored blossoms, too, with center trumpets that contrast with the background white or yellow petals.
Daffodils are toxic to animals so there are no worries about deer gobbling up your display. Some curious squirrels may dig up a few, if the bulbs are closer to the surface than they should have been planted, before realizing that’s a waste of their time, so it’s a good idea to look around for those and replant them. Like other spring bulbs, daffodils are happy enough with most soils, though a little bone meal, or bulb fertilizer will be appreciated.
Most daffodils aren’t very fragrant, but their colorful blossoms make up for that. You can find varieties known for delightful fragrance and plant them where they’ll be noticed. If you want “a host of golden daffodils” inspired by Wordsworth’s poem, you can save money by buying a collection of somewhat smaller bulbs made for landscaping. They won’t be as large as some of the “giant” types at first but will continue to grow for years and produce offset bulbs to form nice clumps. As time goes on, you can divide the clumps for more and more spring blooms for free.
Collections made up of different varieties are available if you can’t decide among your favorites. Some are all one color, but differing shapes; others are mixed. Some collections of daffodils are made up of types that bloom earlier, mid-season, and late to provide a longer season of enjoyment.
If you love tulips, be aware that deer share your admiration, but they want to feast on them. It may require a little experimentation to determine if the local deer have discovered this treat. Tulips don’t live as long as other spring bulbs but make up for that with their wide range of color from the whitest whites through every imaginable shade of pink and red to almost black. And there are the flashy parrot tulips, whose wild color combinations are caused by a virus, and have been sought after for hundreds of years. The Tulip Mania of the mid 1600s in Holland has been shown by economists to be an exaggeration but is still cited as a warning to folks looking for a get rich quick scheme.
For more spring color, consider some crocuses, dwarf irises, snowdrops, hyacinths, grape hyacinths, camasses, fritillaria, flowering alliums! Scilla, another small spring flower bulb, is now on the invasive plant list in some states as these pretty little blue or white star-sheds flowers can spread wildly, crowding out our native trilliums, blood root, other spring flowers that we often ignore.
If the lack of color in the next few months makes you sad, prepare now for a spring garden that will be even more appreciated when winter comes to an end
© Judith Chute Hsiang
Jude Hsiang is a retired University Extension Master Gardener Program instructor and a member of the China Community Garden.

title: For politics, what is an October surprise?
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - An October surprise is an event that could shake up an election, but does it often make the difference?
Matt Dallek, a professor of political management at George Washington University, described it as “an event that, at least in theory, has the potential to shake up an election, something that people did not foresee coming that upends the debate.”
He said the term dates back to around the 1980 election, when President Jimmy Carter failed to secure the release of American hostages being held in Iran before November 4, 1980, election day. Carter lost to Republican rival Ronald Reagan.
Several surprises have occurred in the years since.
Surprises can be driven by a campaign or by news events. Examples include Iran-Contra-related indictments in 1992 and the global financial collapse in 2008.
Dallek said those surprises likely did not change the outcome of the election that November.
“There’s no evidence that they flip a dynamic that was already in place,” Dallek said. “What’s more typical is that an event occurs, it dominates the news cycle and the trend line starts to move further toward the candidate who was already doing well, who was already likely to prevail.”
One exception was the Comey letter. In 2016, less than two weeks before the election, then-FBI Director James Comey wrote a letter informing Congress the FBI had received new information concerning the email investigation into Hillary Clinton.
Days before Election Day, Comey wrote another letter saying the new information did not change previous conclusions in the investigation.
“It became a big news story,” Dallek said. “And it rekindled the impression, at least for some voters, it cemented this idea that she was corrupt. She was hiding something. It reminded people of her email scandal.”
Dallek said the closest thing to an October surprise this year may be the much-talked-about ad in the Ohio governor’s race. Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy tracked down his rival’s estranged mother. The ad uses the mother of his opponent, Amy Acton (D), to attack her.
The full impact of that ad will not be known until the votes are counted.

title: Citgo plans to reduce emissions at South Portland tanks
text:
Citgo Petroleum Corporation on Wednesday announced a plan to reduce emissions for its South Portland Terminal and fund expanded air monitoring.
The move came a day after many South Portland residents urged the city to take action to protect public health at a packed City Council meeting, and more than a month after a report from the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention found that residents living near the more than 100 petroleum tanks in the city could be at higher risk of cancer and other chronic health issues as a result of long-term exposure to carcinogenic emissions, based on six years of ambient air monitoring.
In the announcement, the company said it would invest in more advanced detection and monitoring technologies, speed up infrastructure improvement plans and review its operating practices to identify more ways to reduce emissions.
“We hear the community’s concerns about the study findings and we take those concerns seriously,” said Karl Schmidt, vice president of supply and marketing at Citgo. “We are not waiting for additional monitoring to take action. We are moving forward with emissions-reduction measures, investing in expanded community monitoring and working with the city and Maine DEP as this effort progresses.”
The petroleum company operates three refineries, 43 active terminals and three pipelines across the country.
“We want these corporations to behave like good neighbors,” said James LaPlante, a South Portland resident. “A good neighbor doesn’t poison you.”
The South Portland City Council plans to host a workshop on Dec. 1 to discuss available avenues to reduce toxic air emissions from the petroleum tanks that speckle the city, such as licensing fees for oil companies, mandating better emissions control technology and collaborating with state legislators on statewide policy.
Representatives from the CDC and the DEP presented findings from the report to the council and a high school auditorium of more than 100 concerned residents on Tuesday night.
Monitors along the fenceline of some of the tanks, including the ones at Citgo’s South Portland Terminal, regularly logged long-term average benzene concentrations in ambient air that exceeded state guidelines, according to fenceline data collected by the DEP over a year and a half.
Benzene is a known carcinogen, and acute exposure can cause fatigue, dizziness, irregular heartbeat and headaches. High long-term exposure can cause cancers, including leukemia.
“This is a very South Portland problem,” said Chelsea Byun, a resident and former Portland Press Herald editor.
The tanks are visible from backyards, schools and the Greenbelt pathway that snakes through the city. Other petroleum storage facilities in the state aren’t close to residential neighborhoods like these are, according to Stacy Knapp, division director of air quality assessment with the DEP.
Many residents are concerned about the air quality and the implications for their health.
“It’s been a long time,” said resident Cathy Chapman. “I’m tired of coming up here and talking about air.”
Chapman has lived in the city for about 15 years, and thinks she’s developed asthma, which does not run in her family, from continued exposure.
“It’s time we do something,” she said.
Julia Edwards was nearly brought to tears during her public comment.
“I want my kids to be at a preschool where they’re not smelling the tanks almost daily,” she said.
Edwards grew up in South Portland and worked at the Dairy Queen at Cash Corner for about 10 years. She was disheartened but not surprised by the results of the report.
She said she smells the pungent odor of oil emissions in her house multiple times a week, even thought the tanks aren’t visible from her house. Her family members get headaches and regularly feel dizzy.
“I would invite anyone doing fenceline testing to come to my home,” she said.
The DEP recommended another year of data collection to understand how quickly the benzene concentrations dissipate further from the fenceline, which wasn’t included in the six-year report.
However, some councilors say more data collection isn’t enough.
“Testing in the absence of further action is not acceptable for our community,” said Mayor Elyse Tipton.
The Maine DEP is the agency that has oversight of the petroleum tank farms. It issues air quality emissions licenses and is responsible for evaluating compliance with all state and federal air-quality regulations. It’s also the entity responsible for enforcing federal regulations.
Some residents don’t trust the DEP to take enough action on its own.
“The agency hasn’t taken this as seriously as the residents who have to live next to these tank farms do,” Byun said.
For instance, the state agency didn’t take action against Global Partners LP nearly 10 years ago because officials didn’t think it had violated emissions limits for volatile organic compounds based on the data the company submitted.
The U. S. Environmental Protection Agency used a different methodology, and sent the petroleum company violation notices for years. The agency sued the corporation over ongoing compliance issues, and Global ultimately settled with a $40,000 fine, which many thought was an inadequate response. The EPA sued Sprague Operating Resources LLC the next year.
Maine DEP officials later admitted that it was wrong to fight the federal enforcement.

title: Homestretch: Will Trump's trips to ruby red states and swing districts sway voters?
text:
Homestretch: Will President Trump's trips to ruby red states and swing districts sway voters?
President Donald Trump is in the final stretch to rally support for Republican candidates in key races as Election Day nears.
Homestretch: Will President Trump's trips to ruby red states and swing districts sway voters?
President Donald Trump is in the final stretch to rally support for Republican candidates in key races as Election Day nears.
President Donald Trump is making campaign stops in Texas and Ohio less than a week before Election Day to support Republican candidates in critical races.
The president has been traveling to Republican strongholds like Texas, where he campaigned for Ken Paxton, who is running against Democrat James Talarico.
"So on election night, Texas is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate it. America belongs to those who love it, and the only choice for proud patriots of Texas is the greatest attorney general in the history of your state," Trump said.
Trump is also focusing on battleground states like Ohio, where he is heading today to boost Republicans in competitive races. Recent polls indicate the Senate race between former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown and Republican Sen. Jon Husted is tightening.
The governor's race in Ohio is also contentious, with Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy drawing criticism for an ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton's estranged mother. Acton's mother lost custody of her children after her husband was indicted for raping Acton when she was a child.
Last week, Trump was questioned about the ad where he told Ramaswamy to "ride with it."
"Amy Acton's mother said horrible things about Amy Acton" and "she's fair game," Trump said.
In Acton's first one-on-one interview with WLWT since the controversy began, she said the last time she saw her mother was when she was 12 years old.
"Obviously it's a very sad situation to see my mother. Last time I saw her, I was 12 years old in a courthouse where she and her husband were indicted before they skipped town as fugitives from the law with a warrant against their arrest. And it didn't surprise me because I know there's no low that my opponent won't go to. He knows his campaign is struggling," Acton said.
A recent Associated Press analysis shows voter turnout is soaring compared to the last midterm election in many states that could determine control of the Senate. The question remains whether enough voters will head to the polls on Nov. 3 or stay home.
Keep watching for the latest from the Washington News Bureau:

title: Caregiver advocate shares 3 policies that could help family caregivers
text:
(Aging Untold) — More than 60 million Americans are family caregivers, balancing work, kids and care for an aging parent or loved one.
Jason Resendez, president and CEO of the National Alliance for Caregiving, recently testified before the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging. He joined gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck to talk through the solutions he presented.
The three policies he brought to lawmakers
Resendez said the National Alliance for Caregiving is championing changes “to address so many of the pain points that family caregivers face every day.”
1) Older Americans Act funding
He said one priority is reauthorization and funding of the Older Americans Act. Resendez said the law provides dollars for state Area Agencies on Aging to deliver services for older adults, such as Meals on Wheels and caregiver support.
“One of the only federal line items for caregiving comes through the Older Americans Act, and it’s called the National Family Caregiver Support Program,” Resendez said.
He said the program funds respite, which gives caregivers the chance to take breaks. It also funds training, education and outreach, so family caregivers have peer support and someone to turn to when navigating local resources.
The program is funded at about $200 million a year, Resendez said.
“That’s a drop in the bucket compared to the scale of the need for this kind of support,” he said.
2) National paid family and medical leave
Another priority is a national paid family and medical leave program.
“We are still one of the only industrialized nations that doesn’t have a paid family and medical leave program,” Resendez said.
He said 13 states and the District of Columbia have set up programs because of the lack of federal action. Virginia is the first southern state to do so, Resendez said.
A national program “can help people provide care while staying in the workforce and putting food on the table,” Resendez said.
3) A bigger role for Medicare
Another priority is for Medicare to do more to recognize and support family caregivers. Resendez said the group is pushing for stronger access to caregiver training services and stronger in-home health benefits through Medicare.
He said the three policies together “represent a stronger foundation to help family caregivers provide care sustainably, with dignity and with equity over time.”
If only one policy passed
When asked which policy would be most beneficial if only one were to pass, Resendez pointed to Medicare.
He said changes there would bring immediate support to families and modernize a program created in 1965. He said the older adult community has changed since then.
An in-home health benefit, stronger caregiver support and parity with what Medicaid does for low-income families would “transform what it looks like to age in America today,” Resendez said.
Extending that support to families at all income levels “would revolutionize what it looks like to provide care in America today,” he said.
One step to take in the next 30 days
Cradduck asked for one concrete step that lawmakers, employers or communities could take in the next 30 days.
For Congress, Resendez said the step is to pass the Older Americans Act.
“And so that’s a no-brainer there for policymakers who want to step up for family caregivers and do it on an issue and policy that’s extremely bipartisan, is to cast that vote to reauthorize the Older Americans Act,” Resendez said.
For employers, he said the first step is asking employees whether they have caregiving responsibilities.
Employers are not systematically asking that question, he said, and without that data, they are not designing benefits for employees who are handling both work and caregiving.

title: Bangor family buys international Coffee News publication
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Walk into a grocery store, doctor’s office waiting room or bagel shop in Bangor and you’re likely to spot a stack of Coffee News papers with fun facts, trivia questions, local ads and smiling, round-faced illustrations.
The free, single-sheet publication is part of an international franchise system, and its ownership transferred from one Bangor family to another this fall when Ben and Malorie Sprague purchased the company from Bill and Sue-Ann Buckley.
The new owners see Coffee News as a Bangor success story as the franchise system has been based in the city for years, maintaining the same model and similar content throughout rapid shifts in the media industry.
“In this day and age when people are so overwhelmed by online stimulation and AI slop and just bombarded with constant interruptions, the printed, tangible page still has a really key importance to us,” Ben Sprague, who has worked in banking in the city for years and is also a member of the School Committee, told the Bangor Daily News.
The weekly publication was founded in Canada nearly 40 years ago, and there are now more than 300 Coffee News franchises in the U.S., Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The type of content in its pages has remained mostly consistent over time: feel-good stories, jokes, trivia, horoscopes and local events.
“It’s all written by actual human beings,” Sprague said, noting that all of the content is penned by writers in Maine and Canada and provided to the franchises through the headquarters in Bangor, although each franchise has its own section with events in its area.
Bill Buckley, also a Bangor resident, brought Coffee News to the U.S. in the 1990s and later acquired the entire franchise system. The Spragues bought the Bangor-area franchises two years ago and still plan to operate those editions while they oversee the international network.
Sprague grew up reading Coffee News in the Bangor area with his parents and grandparents and was excited to go all in on the publication, in part, because he believes strongly in print media. He noted a family history that includes one grandfather who worked as a linotype operator at the BDN and another who sold magazine subscriptions.
“Coffee News is a really special thing because it has been so consistent over time,” Sprague said. “We feel like we’re an emotional tether for people, that they can see Coffee News and get a very predictable experience out of it, and hopefully a heartwarming one that makes them feel good.”
He pointed out how Coffee News is “almost part of the visual infrastructure of the community,” adding that it feels familiar because it pops up in so many locations.
“I love to go to Bagel Central and see parents and their kids, or grandparents and their kids, doing the jokes and the trivia together, and I think Coffee News brings people together,” Sprague said.
He and Malorie Sprague, his wife and co-owner, plan to modernize Coffee News and make it more relevant to a younger audience, while still “keeping everything exactly the same as it’s always been.”
Correction: An earlier version of this report misstated who Ben and Malorie Sprague purchased Coffee News from. They purchased it from both Bill and Sue-Ann Buckley.

title: Collins ad featuring retired broadcaster draws criticism in Maine Senate race
text:
MAINE (WABI) - Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson have released new ads in the final days of Maine’s U.S. Senate race, and the Collins campaign’s latest ad is making national headlines.
What the ad says
The Collins ad, “Cord of Wood,” features retired broadcaster Bill Green. Collins credited Green as being instrumental in her 2020 win over Sara Gideon.
In the ad, Green calls Collins one of the most decent and honest people he knows. He then references Jackson’s logging background, saying he knows both Collins and Jackson.
“We’re not talking about a cord of wood here, we’re talking about the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective,” Green says in the ad.
Critics say the ad talks down to Maine’s working class.
Political analyst weighs in
WABI asked UMaine’s Political Science Chair Mark Brewer if he thinks this could make a difference in the final days of the race.
“It certainly can have an impact in the race, and anytime you’re dealing with a race this close, any kind of an impact, even an impact say at the margins, could be enough to move the race in one direction or the other and help determine the outcome. I don’t know that this ad is that in this race. And I know that we’ll know until after the fact,” said Brewer.
Candidates respond
Jackson said, “This is about a cord of wood — and about Mainers struggling to afford to heat their homes this winter.”
The Collins campaign responded to a request for comment.
“Susan Collins would never talk down to any Mainer. And she wouldn’t tell anyone to shut up, like Troy Jackson said to her — or say that she kisses someone’s *** like Troy said. Troy spends all his time attacking Susan Collins, but never describes his plans for the future — because his whole campaign is based on trying to tear her down. The point of the ad is quite simple — Susan Collins is the most qualified person to represent Maine in the United States Senate,” the campaign said.

title: Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader and feminist, dies at 96
text:
Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation’s fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase “Sí, se puede!” that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta’s family said she died Wednesday at home.
“We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy,” they said in a statement shared by her foundation.
Huerta kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women’s rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.
Huerta’s resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to “Yes, it can be done” — was grounded in the belief that people who take action can affect change.
Her work over the decades earned her accolades including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. When President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and noted that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.
In 2021, Huerta wrote an open letter expressing support for an effort to unionize employees at Bates College in Lewiston, where she had been awarded an honorary degree two years earlier.
“Forming a union is about having a voice,” Huerta wrote at the time. “It is part of creating a balance of power at work and building democracy in our society.”
This year, Huerta sent shock waves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement’s co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she had kept for 60 years, long after he died.
From the early 1970s on, Huerta’s life partner was Richard Chavez, César’s brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.
Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared coming forward would compromise her life’s work and unravel all the progress made for workers.
When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: “It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I’ll say it that way.”
Homegrown activism
Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who won a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.
Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.
Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the agricultural San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students’ poor living conditions.
“I couldn’t stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes,” she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. “I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children.”
Huerta’s early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.
She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year “Delano Grape Strike.” With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers.
Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.
On the campaign trail
She met Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and volunteered with his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her, moments before he was shot.
The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing. Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating.
In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush’s opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco.
Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer’s baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims.
After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus and hit the road to campaign for women’s rights and encourage Latinas to run for office.
She also campaigned for Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden. California Gov. Gavin Newsom considered her a close friend.
Fueled by courage
Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores’ 13 children, said during an interview that his mother’s courage drove her life’s work.
“To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farmworkers, to take on agriculture, which to this day is still a powerhouse. … That took a lot of guts,” he said.
Huerta learned the art of lobbying politicians, securing financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farmworkers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and campaigned against federal guest worker programs.
By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass the first state law recognizing farmworkers’ right to collective bargaining.
Among her many accolades, she was the first Latina inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame, and she received nine honorary doctorates from U.S. universities. Schools are named in her honor in California, Texas and Colorado. Her image graces many murals, and streets bear her name.
But she didn’t always win favor with more liberal activists.
In 2016 when she endorsed Hillary Rodham Clinton instead of Sen. Bernie Sanders in the presidential Democratic primary, actor Rosario Dawson — a Sanders supporter who played Huerta in a 2014 movie about César Chavez — said Huerta had become “an instrument of the establishment.”
Dawson and Huerta eventually reconciled.
Guitarist Carlos Santana later oversaw a documentary based on Huerta’s life after the pair had a late-night conversation about music while in Hawaii. Santana, a Miles Davis fan, discovered Huerta was a huge fan of bebop legend Charlie Parker.
“I even met Charlie Parker. That’s my claim to fame,” Huerta joked during an interview with The Associated Press when she was 87.
Huerta’s work as a labor movement leader reverberated through the U.S. and beyond, making her name synonymous with civil rights. In the 2025 documentary “Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta,” she recounted her decades-long activism, and said the inspiration she drew from the women’s movement during the 1970s provided the validation she needed to take the stage with other labor leaders.
“I hope that my legacy will be one of an organizer that organized to fight injustice,” she said in the film. “We want to give our children an inheritance of justice, right, not jewels or property or money because they’ll just fight over it. So the main thing to do is to give them this love for justice — and that is the greatest gift I think that any of us can have.”

title: Trump could seek vengeance on Collins, Maine
text:
On Jan. 11, 2021, Susan Collins said that President Trump had “incited” the Jan. 6 riots. On Feb. 13, 2021, Collins voted to convict Trump, stating that Trump had “incited an insurrection.”
Has Sen. Collins forgotten just how unfit she believes Trump is for office?
The problem is this: Trump has not forgotten Collins’ remarks or her impeachment vote. If Collins retains her seat and the GOP keeps the U.S. Senate, past experience tells us that Trump will seek revenge against Collins and could push for her removal as chair of the Appropriations Committee, ignore Collins’ appropriations opinions or punish Collins and, by extension, Maine by cutting federally controlled funds, contracts and jobs — or all three.
If Collins wins, she will lose the political power she now claims. Maine will become the target of another of Trump’s well-known vengeance campaigns.
Terry Duddy
Falmouth

title: Cornell faculty to begin voting on no-confidence resolution over handling of fraternity gang rape
text:
Cornell University faculty will meet Wednesday to conclude debate and begin voting on a proposed no-confidence resolution in the university’s administration following widespread frustration over its response to a woman who reported she was gang raped at a campus fraternity house in 2024.
The meeting comes after an Oct. 14 Faculty Senate meeting at which angry faculty members confronted Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff about the university’s handling of the allegations.
The meeting was closed to the media, but in an audio recording obtained by The Associated Press, Kotlikoff acknowledged some missteps, defended his leadership and asked for more time to implement reforms and push for cultural changes in student social life. He urged faculty to have confidence in his leadership, pointing to an independent investigation into the university’s handling of the case that he said could lead to meaningful reforms.
A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All seven men have denied her allegations.
The criminal investigation by Cornell’s police department stalled after the local district attorney declined to pursue charges. But in an interview with The New York Times, Kotlikoff said he never followed up to learn what had happened to the woman or the criminal investigation.
Asked by a faculty member whether he read the Cornell Police Department’s report on the rape allegations, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he had not, but said that was because the police investigation was confidential and university policy is that top administrators shouldn’t have a role in criminal investigations.
“I really reject the idea that I had no interest in it or was not concerned about it,” Kotlikoff said.
He insisted experienced leadership was necessary to confront problems. Replacing a president would harm Cornell’s reputation, Kotlikoff said.
Faculty also questioned Cornell’s handling of a disciplined student’s return to campus, including his assignment to a shared dorm room with a roommate unaware of his disciplinary history.
After Kotlikoff departed, a string of faculty speakers said they had lost confidence in the administration’s ability to combat sexual assault on campus. Some Faculty Senate members warned that a hasty no-confidence vote would do little to address the underlying problems.
Wednesday’s meeting is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. and will be closed to the public and media. Electronic voting will open afterward and remain open through Nov. 6. Individual votes will be anonymous.
A no-confidence vote by the faculty would be largely symbolic, but could send a message to the university’s trustees, who ultimately decide who leads it.
Kotlikoff became the university’s interim president in July 2024 and took the job permanently last year.
He’s faced challenges including a dining and custodial workers strike, ire over his decision last year to pay $60 million to settle Trump administration civil rights investigations, and accusations from activists that his administration stifled campus protests.

title: How Trump’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ is playing in Maine’s US Senate race
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Hospital and birthing center closures. Healthcare workforce shortages. Rising insurance premiums. As Mainers grapple with increasing health-related costs and dwindling access to care, those issues have become a focal point of the U.S. Senate race.
Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson have sparred over healthcare during debates and on the airwaves. The candidates differ in their overarching approaches to healthcare — Jackson, a proponent of Medicare for All, and Collins, a critic of a “big government” healthcare takeover.
At the center of many of their arguments over healthcare is President Donald Trump’s signature spending package, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which is expected to slash Medicaid funding in Maine and across the country.
Jackson, like many Democrats across the country, has tried to pin the healthcare cuts on Collins. Collins, who voted for a procedural motion to advance the bill but against the final package, has in turn touted the rural healthcare fund she secured in the bill during negotiations.
The Rural Health Transformation Program could mitigate but will not fully offset the larger cuts in the law, said Zachary Levinson, project director of the KFF project on hospital costs.
Maine was awarded $190 million in initial program funding in fiscal year 2026, which has all been committed as of this fall for a range of projects such as hospital financial sustainability, workforce recruitment and training, and technology improvements.
While the program was established in part to address concerns about the impact of Trump’s spending law on rural hospitals, the funding is being used for broader purposes than that and has restrictions that limit its ability to address urgent needs, Levinson said.
The votes
Ads from Jackson’s campaign and supportive super PACs claim Collins cast the deciding vote on the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
In late June 2025, Collins voted to advance the bill, a 51-49 vote. Throughout the negotiation process, Maine’s senior senator expressed concern about the impact the bill would have on rural hospitals and on some Medicaid recipients, though she supported adding work requirements to the low-income healthcare program. Days later, Collins voted against the final package, which narrowly passed in the Senate with Vice President JD Vance casting the tie-breaking vote.
Collins has repeatedly justified her vote to advance the bill, arguing that she otherwise would not have been able to include the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program that she authored in the package.
Collins has also highlighted the program in a campaign ad, which touts the funding without mentioning the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
Jackson equated Collins’ approach to “an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out” during a debate on Oct. 6. He has also pointed out that her Republican colleagues had called her a “team player” for advancing the legislation.
At the time, Sen. John Hoeven, a Republican from North Dakota, told the Boston Globe that Republicans knew that when it came to the final vote, Collins likely “couldn’t get there just because of her state.”
Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York weighed into the matter during her visit to Portland last week.
“There’s a lot of procedural votes that say, ‘You can go ahead, you can go ahead.’ It doesn’t just show up on the floor one day,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “At every single moment, you have an opportunity to stand up and say no.”
Snags
Maine applied for $200 million through the program last November and was awarded $190 million at the end of December.
In late March, Collins claimed that the funding had been in jeopardy because “the state missed milestones and provided inadequate information to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.” Collins said she spoke with CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz and that CMS worked with the state to bring it into compliance.
However, according to Lindsay Hammes, press secretary for the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, at no point had CMS indicated to Gov. Janet Mills’ administration that Maine’s responses were untimely, inadequate, or that the funds were potentially at risk. Hammes said the department submitted a fully allocated budget for the program to CMS that was approved in March.
On Oct. 15, CMS confirmed that the totality of Maine’s grant award was obligated, meaning the state has legally committed its allocated funds. The program uses a cost-reimbursement model, so funds will be drawn down as expenses are accrued.
CMS did not respond to questions about whether Maine’s funding had ever been at risk. Instead, an unnamed spokesperson said in an email that it is standard procedure for CMS to request states amend budgets and adjust initiatives during grantmaking. CMS maintains ongoing oversight through reporting, monitoring, and annual progress assessments, the spokesperson said.
Maine and several states had to change their initial plans to fit CMS guidelines.
For instance, Maine initially proposed using some funding for uncompensated care payments and provider payments for essential health services to people who are uninsured. However, those plans were removed from the final budget.
While not included in the text of the law, CMS guidance says the funds are not intended “to be used for perpetual operating expenses, rather for investments… that will have sustainable impact beyond the end of the program.”
Also, payments to providers for services have a number of limits. They cannot exceed 15% of a state award in a given budget period, be used for short-term relief, or supplement existing funding sources, including Medicaid.
CMS is viewing the rural healthcare fund as an “opportunity to transform how healthcare is delivered in rural parts of the country,” Levinson said. “But the trade-off is that they’re really not focused on providing short-term, immediate relief to rural hospitals or other providers, and that means this fund is less targeted towards these more immediate concerns about rural hospitals closing their doors or eliminating certain service lines.”
Nearly half of Maine’s 24 rural hospitals are considered “at risk” of closing, according to an analysis by the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform. Labor and delivery units are often the first to go. Since 2015, 12 birthing centers in the state have closed.
Impact
The “One Big Beautiful Bill” is projected to slash Medicaid funding nationally by $911 billion and by nearly $3 billion in Maine over the next decade. Considering only rural areas, the law is estimated to cut $137 billion nationally.
That means the rural healthcare program could offset about 5% of the total estimated cuts to federal Medicaid spending and 37% of the estimated cuts in rural areas, according to a KFF analysis of the Congressional Budget Office’s estimates released shortly after the law’s enactment.
“It’s also worth noting that the reductions in Medicaid spending will become much more significant in later years after the rural health fund has started to dry up, and many of those cuts are permanent,” Levinson said. The rural healthcare program is primarily being distributed over a five-year period.
In Maine, $66 million of the state’s $190 million will go toward improving hospitals’ financial sustainability, such as $35 million for the Rural Hospital Efficiency Fund and regional planning activities, and $29 million for helping providers transition to alternative payment models.
The next largest share of the funding, $53 million, will go toward technology, including telehealth hubs and services, cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence. The Hallowell-based MCD Global Health is leading this work.
Community care is another component of Maine’s approved plan, with $34 million going toward things like evidence-based practices, nutrition education, and school-based care. Another component is workforce recruitment and training, with $31.5 million obligated for rural clinical training, simulation equipment and workforce transportation, among other efforts.
With this work just beginning, Jeffrey Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association, said it is too early to speak to actual impacts of the rural healthcare program. As for the overall effect of the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” Austin said, “We certainly have some concerns in the short-term that some cuts will absolutely materialize, but decades-long projections are something I avoid.”
Austin said there are “plenty of ways the federal government could help in the future,” including “no additional cuts.”

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Mary Raye Heathcote passed into the arms of her savior Oct. 26, 2026 after a battle with Alzheimer’s at her home in Union. She was born in Eastport on June 21, 1946, the first daughter of Alexander Hardie and Mary-Helen Hardie (Raye).
Mary grew up in Union, went to Union schools where she played in the band, was a State Science Fair winner, was a member of the National Thespian Society and the National Honor Society and was co-salutatorian, graduating with honors. She went on to the University of Maine, graduating Phi Beta Kappa with a degree in economics.
After some time in Georgia while her husband served in the military, she returned to Maine and settled in Nobleboro for 37 years and went to work for Mr. Reny, working her career path to become vice president of human resources. While living in Nobleboro she accepted Jesus as her lord and master and attended Nobleboro Baptist Church, teaching children in Sunday school for years.
Upon retirement she moved to Union, attended Appleton Baptist Church where she served as church secretary for several years until the disease overtook her.
Mary always had a great love for cats which led to Sam, a large gray tiger who came to live with her as a kitten, the Mr. Moto, who developed diabetes and had to be given insulin shots every day, and finally Cedar and Flint, names given because of their color.
Mary leaves her husband, Wally, of 58 years; a sister, Carol, of Charlotte, N.C.; a brother-in-law, Arthur (wife Kate), of Oceanside, Calif.; brother-in-law, Stephen (wife Debbie), of Orrington; several nieces and nephews; plus old friends from Renys.
A time of visitation will be held at Hall Funeral Home, at 949 Main St. in Waldoboro on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026 from 5-7 p.m. A funeral service will be held at South Hope Community Church, at 142 Main St. in Hope on Nov. 7, 2026 at 11 a.m. Burial will follow the service at the Dunbar Cemetery in Nobleboro.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home of Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a story with the Heathcote family, please visit Mary’s book of memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Florida police called to remove family from 3-year-old's soccer game after dispute
text:
Florida police called to remove parents from 3-year-old's soccer game after dispute
Florida officers were called to a soccer game after a dispute broke out between league officials and a player's parents, according to the Winter Park Police Department.
League officials from the i9 Sports program contacted police for help with a disturbance involving the family and their 3-year-old son, who was playing in a game.
'The kid is good, he's great, really good'
The police department released body-camera video on Monday showing separate interactions with the family and soccer league officials.
Upon arrival, police met with someone from the soccer league who made the call to police requesting that the family be asked to leave the area in which the soccer games were being played.
The man can be heard on the video saying, "The kid is good, he's great, really good, so what happened is he is very advanced compared to the other ones."
But he said the 3-year-old was allegedly pushing other players, so he told the child and the parents that no pushing was allowed.
The man said the child's parents became irritated and caused a "big scene, arguing with the other parents," according to the body-camera video.
"I just want them out, immediately," he said.
Police said that because the games were being played in a public park, they could not be forced to leave, but that they would meet with the family to figure out what was going on.
The league official said that the mother was live-streaming their interactions, and that's why he walked away from the family. The officers made their way to the other side of the field where the family was.
When officers made contact with the family, the mother said they were just confused and didn't understand why her child was being removed from the soccer games and why they were being asked to leave the park.
She went on to say that the game was over, and they were going to leave the park anyway, but they would like to organize a way to get their refund. Otherwise, they'd take the soccer league to court.
i9 Sports program officials shared the following statement:
"We are aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously. The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us. We have reached out to the family and have begun a review that includes speaking with those involved. While we work to understand the circumstances, we will not speculate or share unverified information. We appreciate everyone who has brought their concerns to our attention."

title: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family land in Miami after leaving Brazil
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family arrived in Miami on Wednesday after he refused to concede the election to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and fled the country.
In a circuitous journey, Bolsonaro left for Argentina on Tuesday with his wife and two daughters, then traveled to Ecuador, according to Argentina officials and flight data. The 45-year-old senator, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, visited the White House in May, and the Trump administration approved U.S. visas for him and his family this week.
Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later.
Flávio Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court, accused of corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. The court had ordered him to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.
Bolsonaro lands in Miami
Dressed casually in a dark polo shirt and flanked by his wife and two daughters, Bolsonaro stepped out of the plane shortly after it landed in Miami about 9:30 a.m. EDT. Florida is home to the largest population of Brazilians in the U.S.
The family fled Brazil late Tuesday, entered Argentina via a border checkpoint and quickly boarded a private charter plane, Argentinian immigration officials said.
Flightradar24 showed the plane believed to be carrying Bolsonaro landed in Guayaquil, Ecuador, about 4 a.m. local time, then took off minutes later for Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport.
Before the family landed in Florida, Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, spoke to dozens of supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia.
Bolsonaro’s route through Argentina could deepen diplomatic tensions between Lula’s government and Argentine President Javier Milei, another Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to assist in Bolsonaro’s campaign.
Representatives of Brazil’s government didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump questions Brazilian election results
Trump has said Bolsonaro is welcome in the U.S., calling him and his family “fine people.”
“The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on Tuesday. Earlier, Trump also said, without evidence, that the election was “rigged.”
Leaders around the world and the Organization of American States have endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round.
The U.S. has imposed double-digit sanctions on Brazil, which boasts Latin America’s largest economy. Lula has championed Brazil’s long tradition of nonalignment, cultivating ties with competing powers. His government has deepened trade ties with China and sought greater global influence through BRICS, a group of emerging economies.
Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving Brazil
Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered the defeated candidate to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received the order outside the home where his father is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for his attempted coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.
A Brazilian diplomat who was not authorized to speak about the matter publicly told The Associated Press that Bolsonaro used an Italian passport to enter Argentina and that Brazilians leaving the country via a land border are not scrutinized by Brazilian authorities.
The diplomat said Brazil’s federal police were not monitoring Bolsonaro when he left his home in Brasilia because the Supreme Court had not issued a warrant for his arrest.
Flávio Bolsonaro said in a video Monday that he was attempting to organize opposition to the election results among his congressional colleagues. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027.
Brazil’s Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker. Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing.
___
Mauricio Savarese reported from Sao Paulo.

title: Long-term care costs rose about 50% in five years, report finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The cost of long-term care jumped nearly 50% in five years, while income for older households rose just 22%, according to a new AARP report.
The report found long-term services and supports are becoming even less affordable for middle-class Americans. Alan Weil, senior vice president for public policy at AARP, said the gap is the most important finding.
“Between 2019 and 2024, a five-year period, the cost of most long-term care services went up about 50%, but the incomes for older households only went up by about 22%,” Weil said. “So the gap between what people can afford and what it costs has grown.”
The AARP also looked at what different types of care cost. Weil said the more skilled the service, the higher the price.
“If you need someone to come in and help you prepare food, that’s less expensive than if you need someone to come in and provide nursing-level care,” Weil said. “Although I’ll also say that we’ve learned that a lot of caregivers are being forced to provide nursing care that they can’t afford to pay someone else to do, even though they’ve never been trained in nursing. So that’s where the burden falls back on the family.”
The financial burden often extends beyond the person who needs care. Weil said many families are part of what he called the sandwich generation.
“If you’re paying for care that your parents need, you’re not saving for your kids’ college,” Weil said. “So this is a squeeze coming from both directions.”
Weil said the best way to prepare is to plan ahead and look into assistance programs that might fit a family’s needs.
“Some people will be qualified for Medicaid, a state and federal program,” Weil said. “The rules differ by state, and at AARP we fight really, really hard to make sure that these services are as available for people as possible.”
Weil said families in the sandwich generation should not assume they are stuck paying out of pocket. He recommends asking a state Medicaid office about eligibility and checking AARP.org for help finding assistance programs in your area.
