title: Death toll from train collision in central Spain rises to 64, authorities say
text:
URDA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks Wednesday in Spain, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies.
The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January.
“Today all of Spain is grieving,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” said Sánchez, who faces an election on Nov. 29.
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the central province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading south in the same direction from Madrid to Seville.
A train operated by the state-owned RENFE company struck the rear of another train operated by private company IRYO that was stopped. The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the IRYO train and the front of the RENFE train.
Samy Paul, a British tourist, described the shock of the impact to The Associated Press after being rescued from the RENFE train.
“Suddenly, everything started falling apart. Bang! We fell down,” he said. “We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over.”
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working nearby when he heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
“People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived,” he said. “As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg.”
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Transport minister says crash was due to ‘inexplicable’ decision
Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a “stop signal” active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
“I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts,” Puente said.
Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
“We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact,” he said. “The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.”
Authorities said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help.
Spain’s King Felipe VI also visited the crash site.
“We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected,” Spain’s royals said in a statement.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “My heart goes out to the victims’ families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you.”
Spain’s soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.
Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when an IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
Before this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992.
Spain is a leader in high-speed rail
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country’s railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.
Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. The Italian-owned IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”
___
Wilson reported from Barcelona, Spain. Teresa Medrano in Madrid and Iain Sullivan in Urda contributed to this report.

title: MaineHealth offers free CNA apprenticeship training

text:
MaineHealth is offering a certified nursing assistant (CNA) apprenticeship training program, providing a paid pathway for individuals interested in beginning a health care career.
The upcoming session of the six-week program begins Jan. 11, 2027 and will be held at the MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital Education Center in Damariscotta. Training takes place four to five days per week and includes classroom instruction, hands-on skills labs and clinical experience at local hospitals and long-term care facilities.
The CNA apprenticeship program is a collaborative effort between Maine Adult Education and MaineHealth. Participants are hired as CNA apprentices at either MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital or MaineHealth Pen Bay Hospital and paid during training. They are also eligible for benefits, provided they agree to a one-year work commitment following successful completion of the program.
To be considered, applicants must attend a required virtual information session via Microsoft Teams. Sessions will be held:
• Oct. 29, 6-7 p.m.
• Nov. 12, 10-11 a.m.
• Dec. 10, 10-11 a.m.
During the information sessions, attendees will learn about the application process, program requirements and next steps. They can also complete their registration for the program.
Following the session, candidates will be contacted to schedule the Comprehensive Adult Student Assessment Systems (CASAS) exam, which must be passed at a 9th-grade reading level.
To apply, candidates should visit careersatmainehealth.org and search for “CNA Apprentice” and the Damariscotta location.

title: Your Choice, Your Voice: Mainers on immigration
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: Maine residents on immigration
Domingo, a Guatemalan man living in Maine, said he was wrongfully deported from a bus stop in Maine.
"I wasn't doing anything wrong," Domingo said.
He came to Portland in December 2022 from his home country of Guatemala. He works in a restaurant as a dishwasher and came to the United States because he could make more money here and could send it back to help support his wife and kids.
He was detained and deported to Guatemala during the Department of Homeland Security's "Operation Catch of the Day."
"I was on my way home from work and standing at the bus stop, I was apprehended by ICE agents. They took me, placed me in the back of their pickup truck, and began asking for my residency documents—for papers showing my legal status here. I don't have any such documents; the only identification I carry is my Guatemalan passport," he told Maine's Total Coverage in Spanish. The conversation has been translated to English.
Domingo said he was in detention for about a week in both Massachusetts and Louisiana before being deported to Guatemala. He was back in his home country for seven months.
His boss at the restaurant wanted to help him get back to Portland.
"He said, 'If you want to come back this week, I'll help you out; I'll even send a plane to bring you back,'" Domingo said, recalling a conversation with his boss. "I told him I needed to think about it first—maybe later—and that I'd get back to him if anything changed."
"They told me, "You're lucky. Not everyone is lucky, especially given how difficult the current situation is," he said telling a story about when he was coming back to Maine. "They said, "you're lucky to have been able to come back."
Domingo said he doesn't resent the officers who detained him, but he does resent the federal government.
He is now back working in Portland and is going to his immigration appointments, trying to gain legal status.
While many people in Maine are supportive of immigrants, some people in Maine have concerns. Including John Morin who said interpreters were cheating on immigrant driver permit tests.
"Just reading the question and the three possible answers to himself. And and then just saying A, B or C and nothing about that. And then the applicant would click on whatever letter they said," Morin said.
He used to administer these tests at different Bureau of Motor Vehicles branches across the state.
He said he would see the same interpreters over and over again and he would see a 100% pass rate.
"That is statistically impossible when the statewide fail rate on those tests is about 30%," Morin said.
Last summer, there were two fatal pedestrian crashes on back-to-back days. According to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, both drivers were undocumented immigrants and have been detained by ICE.
Morin said interpreters sign a paper that says they understand that if they help someone cheat, it's a crime.
He said the rules surrounding interpreters have changed since he went to the legislature's Government Oversight Committee.
The Secretary of State's Office said that the BMV modified the interpreter program to maximize the number of written language exams available, while minimizing risks inherent with allowing customers to provide their own interpreters.

title: Election: Tabulating and tallying
text:
Part 4: Conclusion
Maine state law, Title 21-A, §626, states that opening time for the polls are flexible. The polls must be opened no earlier than 6 a.m. and no later than 8 a.m. on election day, except that in municipalities with a population of fewer than 500, the polls must be opened no later than 10 a.m. The municipal officers of each municipality shall determine the time of opening the polls within these limits.
The polls must be closed at 8 p.m. on election day, except in municipalities of population fewer than 100 which may close the polls after all registered voters have voted.
The warden shall give all voters present at the voting place at closing time the opportunity to vote. Any person who arrives at the voting place after the time for closing the polls has passed may not vote. The municipal clerk shall state the times of opening and closing the polls in the notice of the election.
Once the polls close, the process of tallying the votes begins. This is done in open session, where members of the community are permitted to observe the tallying. They are allowed to remain behind the guard rail and not attempt to interfere with the tallying.
Depending on the model each tabulator sits on a large ballot box on wheels. The ballot box has a large compartment to collect the fully counted ballots. It has no moving parts or electrical components. The tabulator is not connected to the internet. It stands alone. The ballot box has a lock to affix the tabulator in place. The front of the ballot box has a small opening called the auxiliary box, where ballots can be placed that the machine will not accept. These ballots are hand counted at the end of the evening.
On tallying forms provided by the Secretary of State, tallying teams of two – usually one from each major political party – begin the process of transferring results from the tapes generated by the tabulators on to the forms. Hand counted ballots are then added to the totals. Totals are then entered on a spread sheet that will be matched with the number of cast ballots, where the number of ballots cast and the results must be reconciled so all ballots are accounted.
The tabulators are sometimes questioned by voters. Time and again, hand recounts of races using tabulators on election day have upheld the results. These are simple machines that do their job very well.
Once tallying is complete, all ballots cast are sealed in metal, tamper proof boxes, locked and sealed. The lock numbers and seal numbers are recorded on a form, verified and signed by the warden. This prevents the seals from being removed, ballots tampered with and the boxes resealed with other seals, which do not have the same number assigned to them. The boxes are then transported, usually by police or other secured methods, and placed in a vault. The computer sticks from the tabulators are also secured.
Within 72 hours following an election, official results are transferred to the Secretary of State by the municipal clerk.
In the event of a recount, all election materials are picked up and transported to the Secretary of State’s office, in Augusta, by state police.
Roland Hallee has 40 years experience in conducting elections, the last 25 years as warden in Waterville.

It is also expensive!

title: South Portland added to list of Maine cities where Justice Department will send election monitors
text:
South Portland has been notified by the U.S. Department of Justice that federal election monitors will be present at polling locations on Election Day, according to Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows.
In a written statement Wednesday, Bellows said three Maine cities have received such notices. The DOJ announced plans last week to send monitors to Portland and Lewiston.
“It’s important to note that DOJ has sent monitors to observe elections for decades,” Bellows said “Any monitors are subject to the same laws and rules as any other observer at the poll, they can observe what’s taking place, but they may not interact with voters, handle ballots or equipment, or disrupt voting in any way.
“We will monitor their activities to ensure that they follow state and federal law and that every voter is able to cast their ballot free from interference or intimidation.”
It’s not yet clear which of South Portland’s five polling locations the observers would visit, said Jana Spaulding, a spokesperson for the secretary of state. Portland and Lewiston voters can expect observers to float between all of those two cities’ polling places throughout the day, Spaulding said.
Recent reports of possible voter intimidation in Lewiston have prompted a nonprofit coalition of military veterans to launch its own poll-watching program; their intention is to make sure federal agents or other groups aren’t intimidating voters. However, that prompted Bellows to issue a warning.
“While well meaning, the presence of large groups at polling locations may actually have the opposite effect (and discourage) some voters from voting,” Bellows said, adding that her office “will be working closely with local clerks and the Office of the Attorney General to safeguard the right to vote for every Maine citizen.”

title: As AI in politics becomes more common, here's how voters can stay vigilant
text:
As AI in politics becomes more common, here's how voters can stay vigilant
Experts say voters cannot rely on visual clues alone to spot fake election content.
As AI in politics becomes more common, here's how voters can stay vigilant
Experts say voters cannot rely on visual clues alone to spot fake election content.
Political content made with artificial intelligence is becoming more common and more sophisticated.
Experts say voters need to stay on guard this election season, given the lax regulations governing the use of this rapidly evolving technology.
The Associated Press reported on Wednesday that social media videos believed to be made with AI and linked to Russia are misusing real people’s names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in close races: Sherrod Brown in Ohio and James Talarico in Texas.
Ari Lightman, a digital media and marketing professor at Carnegie Mellon University, said foreign adversaries are using increasingly advanced tools to power a familiar playbook.
"In order to achieve a purpose, which is really to create greater levels of polarization and lead to some sort of political outcome that's favorable to them," Lightman said.
Political groups in the United States are also increasingly leveraging AI in campaign ads.
The Wesleyan Media Project has tracked 220 midterm election ads that were generated — at least in part — using AI tools. The analysis described the total released earlier this month as "almost certainly an undercount."
The ads were put out by stakeholders in both parties, but most stemmed from Republican candidates and organizations.
The analysis also identified a surge of spending on AI-generated ads. The price tag had exceeded $137 million as of earlier this month.
“For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, in a press release. “Much of the AI use is not disclosed through any type of disclaimer.”
According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 31 states have enacted laws regulating the use of deepfakes in political messaging, though some have been challenged in court on free speech grounds. There are still no disclosure requirements at the federal level.
Meanwhile, it's getting increasingly difficult to spot visual clues as AI improves.
How voters can remain vigilant
While there may be giveaways in some cases, like misshapen hands, impossibly smooth skin, or misaligned shadows, experts say voters cannot rely on these tells alone.
"These have all gotten so sophisticated. It's really hard for the layperson to tell whether the information that's being sent to them is real or completely fabricated," Lightman said.
Lightman said voters should look into credentials and context behind potential AI content, and verify information through independent sources.
Voters should also be skeptical of content that seems designed to evoke an immediate emotional response and think twice before sharing on social media.
Are AI models taking action?
OpenAI confirmed on Wednesday that it's launching an Election Operations Center this week. It will run until all votes are counted to identify the spread of misinformation and combat the potential abuse of tools like ChatGPT. The plans were first reported by Politico.
A new Brennan Center report found that OpenAI was the only company that significantly improved protections against generating fake election content since the center ran tests on six of the most popular models earlier this year.

title: I promise I’ll stand with the people of Maine every time
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Troy Jackson is the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. He lives in Allagash.
I’m a dad, a grandpa, and a fifth-generation logger from Allagash. And as much as Susan Collins and her billionaire backers want you to think I’m the bogeyman, I’m not. I’m just a working guy who’s tired of working Mainers being ignored.
I made my living in the woods working 80-hour weeks. I know what it feels like to work harder and harder and still fall behind.
For me, it started in 1998 when billionaire landowners in Maine tried to cut our wages.
We asked Sen. Susan Collins for help. She did nothing.
So we organized. We blocked the border. We made people listen.
That’s why I got into politics. Working people aren’t powerless. We’re made to feel powerless when we stand alone.
Nearly three decades later, I’m running for the U.S. Senate because it’s about damn time working people have a say in this country, and that’s exactly why I think Collins and the billionaires are trying to take us down.
The truth is, we’ve all been lied to — and not just in the ads on TV. I always believed that government should work for people who work hard and play by the rules, but that’s not how it is.
I’ve met Mainers working two or three jobs who still can’t afford gas, groceries, or heating oil.
And where’s our senator? She hasn’t had a town hall in 25 years. She’s voting for policies that are making things worse.
Collins’ donors appear to get access and handouts. Working Mainers get left behind. Families struggling to afford groceries, medicine and heating oil shouldn’t have to write a campaign check to get their senator’s attention.
And the money she’s brought back to Maine amount to pennies compared to what we’ve lost from the policies she’s rubber-stamped.
Just last year, Collins voted to advance President Donald Trump’s budget bill, which cut Medicaid and delivered tax breaks to the wealthiest Americans. Now, 60,000 Mainers are expected to see their healthcare costs rise or could lose healthcare altogether, while Elon Musk gets a fat tax cut.
That’s a choice about whose lives matter in Washington. So was Collins’ vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v. Wade. A vote she says she doesn’t regret.
I’m running for the U.S. Senate, but this isn’t about me. It’s about Maine people rising up and demanding the government they deserve.
Look at the ads, look at the attacks. I think the billionaires are terrified that they’ll lose their power.
Collins and her ultra-rich donors appear to be saying and doing anything they can to hold onto their power — even if it means lying about me and my family.
Their ads don’t talk about the cost of prescription drugs or heating oil. They don’t defend her votes to support ICE, or to allow Trump’s illegal war in Iran, or to endanger women’s reproductive rights.
I think she’s let us down. But I still believe that working people can have a government that works as hard as they do.
In the Maine Legislature, I fought to lower prescription drug prices, passed universal school meals, protected union jobs, expanded rural healthcare, delivered property tax relief and helped pass some of the strongest reproductive health protections in America. That’s what it looks like when you have representatives that don’t owe billionaires a thing.
I didn’t win every fight. But nobody had to wonder whose side I was on.
In the Senate, I’ll fight to lower costs, protect Social Security and Medicare, defend abortion rights, and make the wealthy pay their fair share.
I think this campaign boils down to Susan Collins and the billionaires versus the people of Maine. Collins has spent the last 30 years in Washington. I think she’s been there too long and she’s become part of the problem.
I promise you this: I’ll stand with the people of Maine every time. I don’t owe Trump or the billionaires anything. I owe the people of Maine everything.

title: Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at his rape and sex assault trial
text:
Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at his rape and sex assault trial
Actor-comedian Russell Brand said “today is the day for truth and justice” as he arrived at a London court Wednesday to deny charges of rape and sexual assault.
Brand spoke briefly to reporters as he entered Southwark Crown Court alongside his wife, Laura Gallacher.
Brand, 51, stood in the witness box and took the oath, then gave his full name: Russell Edward Brand. He answered “no” to each of the charges: three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Related video: 'You deserve to be safe': bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
Questioned by his lawyer, Ian Winter, Brand said the allegations had a “devastating” impact.
“My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations,” he said.
Over the past two weeks of the trial, prosecutors have set out their case and the jury heard from six women who accuse Brand of sexual misconduct between 1999 and 2009.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors that Brand was “ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution says, he was a sexual predator.”
Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

title: Portland mulls moving 5th grade to middle school, or closing a school
text:
Portland’s school board was presented Tuesday night with two options to resolve issues at its middle schools: close one of the three schools or move fifth graders from its elementary schools.
The district’s middle schools have struggled with declining enrollment, underutilization of buildings and significant facilities issues. A coalition tasked with studying the problem said this week that maintaining all three buildings as is would not be sustainable.
Tuesday’s presentation at the board’s Casco Bay High School meeting was the culmination of a seven-month study. The board passed a resolution in March asking the superintendent to review the possible reorganization of the schools.
But parents and students shouldn’t expect to see major changes anytime soon. Despite its initial goal of making a decision in time for implementation at the start of next school year, presenters suggested that timeline be pushed back based on the scale of work that is needed.
Board members first considered reducing from three schools to two, but the latest proposal seeks an alternative plan.
The status of Lincoln Middle School — the oldest of the three, built in 1897 — has colored the conversations since the beginning. Last month, a facilities study found that Lincoln had nearly $20 million in obsolete infrastructure that should already have been replaced, significantly more than the other two buildings. It’s also the least-utilized building, with space for more than 200 additional students.
The coalition that conducted the study is recommending keeping all three schools and adding fifth graders, but said that will likely be the more costly option.
“There is no option that doesn’t come without significant trade-offs,” said Damon Yakovleff, a district parent and member of the coalition. “And there is no option that does not come without significant expense.”
Yakovleff told the board Tuesday that moving fifth grade to middle school will improve opportunities for those students, and allow the elementary schools to better serve early childhood needs. At most of the district’s primary schools, fifth graders already change classes on their own, one of the biggest adjustments between elementary and middle school.
However, the cost to repair all three buildings is over $64 million.
If the board is interested in closing a school, Yakovleff said the coalition didn’t specify which one, but the group did model the impact of closing Lincoln.
If it did so, the district would still need to spend about $36 million on repairs at King and Lyman Moore, the other middle schools, and would need to build additional space, since the remaining schools would then exceed their capacity by about 115 students.
On top of that, Yakovleff said, even if the district did consolidate, there would still be costs associated with operating the third building if it were repurposed.
Board members are expected to come to the Nov. 10 meeting prepared to say which option they prefer.
The presentation followed months of community and student engagement sessions and multiple surveys. In addition to the question of facilities, the coalition addressed programmatic changes to the middle schools, including offering more rigorous academic courses to prepare students for high school, and creating smaller organizational structures within schools so that all students are well known.
The district looked at three new possible academic models — expeditionary learning, International Baccalaureate and community schools — and told the board they could pursue choosing one model for all middle schools, or allowing each school to pick a format.
Emery Grant, the student representative to the board from Portland High School, said there was a lot of support for moving fifth grade to middle school among her peers. She also said many students come to high school unprepared for the academic rigor, and would invite a more preparatory academic model for middle school.
Board members asked for more specific cost figures in advance of their next meeting to make their decision.
Board Chair Sarah Lentz said the district is approaching a daunting amount of necessary facility repairs. Board members discussed a recently uncovered mold issue beneath the tiles at Reiche Community School, for example.
Some of these issues have stemmed from the district not acting quickly enough to address problems as they arise, Lentz said.
“Over the course of the last three or four years, the district has done a real good job at saying, “Hold on, let’s see what the big picture is here in the district,”‘ she said.
At the same meeting, the board unanimously approved submitting its final application for a state grant that would allow Portland to consolidate its three high schools on one campus, along with technical and higher education programs and workforce partnerships.
There are eight groups of high schools vying for funding from the state program — most of which are in more rural parts of the state — and final applications are due by the end of October.

title: Two arrested, pound of cocaine seized during drug bust at a Waterville motel
text:
A pound of cocaine seized during drug bust at Maine motel
Two people are facing charges after police say they seized about a pound of crack cocaine during a bust at a motel in Waterville.
The Waterville Police Department says officers responded to the Budget Host Airport Inn on Kennedy Memorial Drive at about 10:30 p.m. on Sunday to investigate the alleged sale of illegal drugs.
During the investigation, officers seized the drugs as well as several thousand dollars in suspected drug money.
Police arrested Joshua Baez, 25, of Waterville, and charged him with aggravated trafficking of scheduled drugs, violating conditions of release, and a probation hold. Tahj Haynes, 26, of the Bronx, New York, was charged with aggravated trafficking of scheduled drugs and a probation hold. Both men were held without bail and are due in court in December.
Police said more charges are possible as their investigation continues.

title: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has emerged as the critical sticking point between the U.S. and China. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition.
Trump said while campaigning for president that tariffs would form the crux of the bilateral relationship. The U.S. and China, the world’s two largest economies, have been engaged in a trade war during both of Trump’s terms.
Speaking Sept. 13 in Ireland, Trump said the U.S. is leading China in AI.
“We’re leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said.
During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“And it’s to me an honor. We’ve had a fantastic relationship. We’ve gotten along. When they were difficulties, we worked it out,” Trump said.
Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September for a state visit. He touted what he called “the tremendous strides” he and Xi had already made on national security, trade and technology.
At the summit, the U.S. and China agreed to extend a trade truce until January. No agreement was reached on implementing safeguards for AI.
Trump and Xi are set to meet again in China next month.

title: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family land in Miami after leaving Brazil
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family arrived in Miami on Wednesday after he refused to concede the election to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and fled the country.
In a circuitous journey, Bolsonaro left for Argentina on Tuesday with his wife and two daughters, then traveled to Ecuador, according to Argentina officials and flight data. The 45-year-old senator, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, visited the White House in May, and the Trump administration approved U.S. visas for him and his family this week.
Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later.
Flávio Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court, accused of corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. The court had ordered him to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.
Bolsonaro lands in Miami
Dressed casually in a dark polo shirt and flanked by his wife and two daughters, Bolsonaro stepped out of the plane shortly after it landed in Miami about 9:30 a.m. EDT. Florida is home to the largest population of Brazilians in the U.S.
The family fled Brazil late Tuesday, entered Argentina via a border checkpoint and quickly boarded a private charter plane, Argentinian immigration officials said.
Flightradar24 showed the plane believed to be carrying Bolsonaro landed in Guayaquil, Ecuador, about 4 a.m. local time, then took off minutes later for Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport.
Before the family landed in Florida, Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, spoke to dozens of supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia.
“I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true,” Lula said. “This act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”
Bolsonaro’s route through Argentina could deepen diplomatic tensions between Lula’s government and Argentine President Javier Milei, another Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to assist in Bolsonaro’s campaign.
Representatives of Brazil’s government didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump questions Brazilian election results
Trump has said Bolsonaro is welcome in the U.S., calling him and his family “fine people.”
“The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on Tuesday. Earlier, Trump also said, without evidence, that the election was “rigged.”
Leaders around the world and the Organization of American States have endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round.
The U.S. has imposed double-digit sanctions on Brazil, which boasts Latin America’s largest economy. Lula has championed Brazil’s long tradition of nonalignment, cultivating ties with competing powers. His government has deepened trade ties with China and sought greater global influence through BRICS, a group of emerging economies.
Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving Brazil
Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered the defeated candidate to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received the order outside the home where his father is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for his attempted coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.
A Brazilian diplomat who was not authorized to speak about the matter publicly told The Associated Press that Bolsonaro used an Italian passport to enter Argentina and that Brazilians leaving the country via a land border are not scrutinized by Brazilian authorities.
The diplomat said Brazil’s federal police were not monitoring Bolsonaro when he left his home in Brasilia because the Supreme Court had not issued a warrant for his arrest.
Flávio Bolsonaro said in a video Monday that he was attempting to organize opposition to the election results among his congressional colleagues. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027.
Brazil’s Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker. Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing.
___
Mauricio Savarese reported from Sao Paulo.

title: Aging Untold: Fat-free doesn’t always mean healthy
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we separate facts from fiction on “fat-free” foods to help you protect your heart and make healthier grocery choices.
Then, National Alliance for Caregiving CEO Jason Resendez joins us to discuss the mounting pressures facing the sandwich generation and policy solutions offering caregiver relief.
Plus, we meet the “Flower Buds,” an inspiring volunteer group in Kentucky that rescues discarded blooms to deliver hope and comfort across its community.
The “fat-free” option at the grocery store is not always the healthy option.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the label can be misleading.
“So if they’re removing the fat, they had to replace it with something else. So you have to look at the ingredients and look at the packaging,” she said.
Rogers said she used to find all the fat categories confusing, so she created a simple way to sort them.
The National Alliance for Caregiving is championing changes “to address so many of the pain points that family caregivers face every day,” President and CEO Jason Resendez said.
He recently testified before the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging and brought three policies to lawmakers: funding for the Older Americans Act, national paid family and medical leave and a bigger role for Medicare.
He said the three policies together “represent a stronger foundation to help family caregivers provide care sustainably, with dignity and with equity over time.”
The crystal and gemstone industry is booming, but experts warn buyers to be cautious of fake products flooding the market.
Jamie Inglett, who owns a crystal shop in Sedona, said consumers can find fake crystals in stores and at gem shows. She said buyers could end up with lab-grown crystals being sold as natural stones.
Volunteers who call themselves the Flower Buds are giving flowers from weddings, funerals and other community events a new life.
They bring the donated flowers to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities and shelters.
The group is celebrating a major milestone: since 2006, the Flower Buds have delivered more than 90,000 vases of flowers.

title: Obituary: Joyce Stratton Blossom
text:
PORTLAND – Joyce Stratton Blossom, born on Oct. 16, 1943, passed away peacefully surrounded by close family on Oct. 1, 2026.
Born in West Chester, Pa., she graduated from high school in York, Pa. in 1961 and Juniata College in Huntingdon, Pa. in 1965 with a bachelor’s degree in biology. After a year working as a social worker in Baltimore, Md., she moved to New York City to attend New York Medical College where she received her master’s degree in nursing in 1969. She obtained a second master’s degree in psychology from the New School for Social Research in 1975. She taught psychiatric nursing at the Helene Fuld School of Nurses in New York City for five years while studying to become a psychotherapist of the Blanton-Peale Institute for Religion and Health earning her certification in 1982. She continued a private practice until she retired in 2008.
A lifelong love of nature along with a deep commitment to Quaker values informed every endeavor she engaged in and every personal relationship she nurtured. The lucky who enjoyed this bounty are her first husband, Arthur and their daughter Joanna (and her husband Sinan); her second husband, William and his son Jackson (and his wife Barbara) along with Joyce and William’s children Megan and Hannah , their husbands Brady and Benedikt; her grandchildren Mara, Nathaniel, Mateo, Daphne, Marigold, Kurt and Lola; her brother Lewis (and wife Helen), sister Ann Dean (and husband William); many cousins; nieces and nephews; and countless friends.
Joyce deeply valued creative expression and the arts. She quietly and diligently honed her artistic skills as a painter, and leaves behind a body of work that reflects her deep connection to the natural world. She enjoyed many happy years of William’s performances with the New York Philharmonic. Her greatest joy came from her role as a mother, witnessing her own children growing up and then raising children of their own.
Beginning in the summer of 1985, and almost every summer since, she and her family spent a couple of glorious weeks in Maine which included Deer Isle, Lake Sebec, and Peaks Island. When it came time for William to retire, they chose to move to Portland, Maine where they could be closer to children and grandchildren.
A memorial service and celebration of life for Joyce will be held on Sunday, Nov. 15 at 1:30 p.m. at the Portland Friends Meeting where Joyce was an active member; 1837 Forest Ave, Portland, Maine.
To read more about Joyce’s life story and share memories, please visit legacy.com and search for her name.
At Joyce’s request, donations can be made to: the American Civil Liberties Union (https://action.aclu.org/give/now) or the American Friends Service Committee (https://afsc.org/give) in lieu of flowers

title: Fort Kent firefighters and police stage a battle on the court to help families
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A friendly rivalry battled out on the basketball court will benefit Aroostook families this winter.
Fort Kent’s ninth annual Badges vs. Blazes charity game will pit law enforcement against firefighters on Saturday, Nov. 14, to raise funds for a program that helps local kids who need a boost.
For the organizers, it’s a chance to have some fun away from jobs that can be harsh while also pulling the community together. But more than that, as inflation and heating costs soar all over Maine, the donated prizes — including 100 gallons of heating oil — and the funds they raise will make things a little easier for some of the region’s most vulnerable.
“It’s nice to see this whole community and local businesses come together, especially in the hard times that we’re living in now, to contribute to this event,” said organizer Bob St. Germain, Eagle Lake Fire and Rescue chief, who started the games with Fort Kent Police Chief Michael DeLena. “Everybody is just one big family. That’s what it feels like.”
This year, all proceeds will benefit the Shop with a First Responder effort, which not only helps kids buy holiday gifts for loved ones, but pays for family movie nights at the local cinema and an Easter activity.
It all started with a Facebook post. St. Germain had read about a charity game where first responders played a high school team, and mentioned starting something similar in the St. John Valley region. DeLena contacted him right away, he said.
They decided to focus on different local charities. The first year, they made enough to donate $2,000 to help Fort Kent Community High School install outdoor soccer lights. In the past they’ve helped the Hope & Justice Project, a brain injury support group, local scholarships and a substance use rehab facility, among others.
Last year’s basketball game raised more than $2,000 for the Ethan Townsend Memorial Scholarship Fund. Townsend, 12, died in 2022 as a result of a skiing accident in Fort Kent.
Firefighters have enjoyed getting together with law enforcement partners to socialize outside of their regular jobs, which aren’t always pleasant, St. Germain said.
The games — and Shop with a First Responder — also embody “community policing for kids,” as DeLena put it, giving kids a chance to see first responders in a different light, so when they see them around town or in school they appreciate them on a personal level.
“It’s absolutely fascinating as far as the smiles that we see,” DeLena said. “When we say we do this for the kids, this is what we love: the smiles, the hugs that we get, the fist bumps and the appreciation that we get from the families.”
The Fort Kent area school district identifies elementary-age students who may struggle financially with holiday gift-giving and help them make out wish lists, he said. Then, police, firefighters and emergency medical personnel take them shopping at Fort Kent businesses.
Other agencies, including the Maine State Police, Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office, Customs and Border Protection and Forest Service, also pitch in, DeLena said.
After shopping, it’s back to the town office conference room to wrap all the gifts and enjoy a pizza party and a visit with Santa.
DeLena expects the high costs of food and fuel will affect more families this winter.
“We grow every year,” DeLena said. “We had 17 [kids] last year and I’m sure we’ll have more this year.”
The game will take place at 6:30 p.m. in the Fort Kent Community High School gym.
DeLena and St. Germain want to see the place filled so the event can help as many people as possible. They have a few new surprises in store.
In a bid to involve the audience more, they’re gathering prizes from donors and businesses to raffle off. The grand prize is a three-day, two-night trip to a Boston Celtics game with seats near courtside. Second prize is 100 gallons of heating fuel, appropriate with oil prices at record highs. More prizes are forthcoming.
Raffle tickets are available at the Fort Kent Police Department or can be purchased at the event. Game admission is $10 for adults, $5 for children 6-12 and free for ages 5 and under.
People look forward to the game each year, and so do the teams. There is a trophy involved, which travels either to the firefighters or police. It’s been with the firefighters for the past three years.
“It’s a great time and, of course, it gets a little competitive,” St. Germain said.
Will the firefighters win again?
“Oh, of course we will,” he said.

title: Houlton, Fort Fairfield and Wisdom Girls Move On to Semifinals
text:
The County Scoreboard: Houlton, Fort Fairfield and Wisdom Girls Advance to Regional Soccer Semifinals
Three more Aroostook County girls soccer teams are moving on after convincing victories in Tuesday's regional quarterfinals.
Houlton scored seven goals against Central, Fort Fairfield shut out Washburn, and Wisdom put six goals on the board against George Stevens Academy.
All three teams earned their places in the regional semifinals, setting up some interesting matchups later this week.
Here's how Tuesday's girls tournament games played out.
Class C North: Houlton Rolls Past Central
(4) Houlton 7, (5) Central 2
Houlton's girls are headed to the Class C North semifinals after a 7-2 victory over Central on Tuesday.
Ava Ezell and Raina Ezell led the way for the Shires, each recording a hat trick in the win.
The two combined for six of Houlton's seven goals, helping the fourth-seeded Shires pull away from fifth-seeded Central. Gwen Ramsay also had 16 saves for the Shires.
The victory sets up a County showdown in Friday afternoon's semifinals, when Houlton travels to take on top-seeded Fort Kent.
With a trip to the regional championship on the line, it'll be another big matchup between two County programs.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield Shuts Out Washburn
(2) Fort Fairfield 4, (7) Washburn 0
Fort Fairfield's girls are also moving on after a 4-0 quarterfinal victory over Washburn.
Chloe White scored twice for the second-seeded Tigers.
Kendall Ainsworth and Madison Parks also found the back of the net, while Addison Cole recorded the shutout in goal.
Fort Fairfield now awaits the winner of Wednesday's matchup between third-seeded Central Aroostook and sixth-seeded Van Buren.
That semifinal will determine which team moves on to play for the Class D North championship.
Eight-Person Girls: Wisdom Scores Six Against George Stevens Academy
(2) Wisdom 6, (10) George Stevens Academy 1
Wisdom's girls put together another strong offensive performance Tuesday, defeating George Stevens Academy 6-1 to advance to the eight-person regional semifinals.
Ellie Cyr led the Lady Pioneers with a hat trick and an assist.
Blake Pelletier and Peyton Roy each added a goal and an assist, while Madisyn Cyr rounded out Wisdom's scoring.
Chloe Schildreth scored the lone goal for George Stevens Academy.
The second-seeded Pioneers move on to the semifinals, where they'll look to take another step toward a regional championship.

title: Judge orders 30-year prison sentence for key figure in Minnesota food fraud
text:
Judge orders 30-year prison sentence for key figure in Minnesota food fraud
A man who played a major role in defrauding a federal food program in Minnesota was sentenced Wednesday to 30 years in prison, the latest punishment in a sprawling scheme to collect millions of dollars during the COVID-19 pandemic by claiming to have fed needy children.
Video above: Trump announces $25 million whistleblower program for alleged government fraud
The depth of fraud in Minnesota — dozens of people have been convicted — has repeatedly drawn the attention of President Donald Trump, who ridiculed the Democratic governor for failing to stop it and partly cited it as grounds for a massive immigration crackdown in the state's largest cities.
Salim Said operated Safari Restaurant in Minneapolis, which specialized in dishes from Somalia. He was accused of vastly overstating the number of meals when seeking payment for providing food. The government said he was responsible for $44 million in fraud, some of which was committed by others he recruited.
“You took more than taxpayers' dollars to enrich yourself. You took the reputation of our state down with you,” U.S. District Judge Nancy Brasel said.
Said was claiming a “ridiculous daily distribution of 6,000 meals” while FBI cameras showed 40 people a day collecting food, prosecutors said in a court filing.
“The defendant and his sites did not serve thousands of children; he served a calculated, lucrative lie,” prosecutors said.
Said, a native of Somalia, denied the allegations while testifying at the trial in 2025, saying many meals were delivered off-site. But at his sentencing Wednesday, he changed course and expressed remorse. Defense attorney Barry Zone, who had asked for a 12-year prison sentence, disputed that Said was the “architect” as the government alleged.
COVID-19 brought changes to a federal program that typically fed children through schools. Restaurants could participate, and food distribution was extended to places outside schools.
“For 21 consecutive months, Said made thousands of fraudulent reimbursement claims, day after day, month after month,” prosecutors said. “Each submission represented meals purportedly provided to underprivileged children, yet the listed children themselves were entirely fictitious.”
The government said Said hit the jackpot: He bought a $1.2 million home, commercial real estate and an $87,000 pickup truck.
Said was convicted of a raft of charges in 2025, along with Aimee Bock, the leader of a Minnesota nonprofit, Feeding Our Future. She is serving a 42-year prison sentence for devising the overall plan to recruit Said and others to join the federal food program during the pandemic.
State auditors found that the Minnesota Department of Education received numerous complaints about Feeding Our Future, but often told the group to police itself. In January, Gov. Tim Walz said he would not run for reelection after being pounded by Trump about theft in programs that rely on federal cash.

title: Sheriff candidates field questions at forum
text:
BLUE HILL — Roles for mental health professionals in police departments, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations locally and relations between the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office and other public safety entities were among the topics of questions that panelists posed to candidates seeking election to serve as the next sheriff.
Ellsworth Det. Corey Bagley, a Republican, and Hancock County Sheriff’s Lt. Dakota Dupuis, a Democrat, seek the position of Hancock County Sheriff, and both attended a standing-room-only forum at the Blue Hill Library Oct. 21.
Library Director Rich Boulet estimated the crowd at 140 people.
Whoever wins on Nov. 3 will replace Sheriff Scott Kane on Jan. 1. Kane has served three terms and is not seeking re-election.
Neither candidate thinks the position of sheriff should be partisan.
“When I go to a complaint, I don’t ask anyone what their political views are,” said Bagley. “I think it’s important to be impartial. I think it’s important to base your decision on the law.”
Dupuis replied, “There’s no room for politics. Laws should be applied and enforced equally. That’s our obligation at the sheriff’s office.”
Blue Hill Select Board member Amanda Woog moderated the forum.
The three panelists asking questions included Faith DeAmbrose, managing editor of the Mount Desert Islander; Andy Webster, deputy editor of Penobscot Bay Press; and Jon Epstein, a freelance reporter representing Rising Tide Media.
Both candidates were asked, “How do you plan on repairing relations with other law enforcement departments in the county?”
“I do talk to the other law enforcement agencies,” Bagley said. “I don’t think the relationship is very good right now. If I were elected sheriff, that’s one of the first things I’d be working on.”
Bagley said he would work to strengthen relationships with fire departments, EMS and “the other agencies that are so crucial for us to do our job,” including The Next Step Domestic Violence Project and Healthy Acadia. “We can’t do this job alone. It’s so important our partners in law enforcement, fire and EMS understand we need their help as well.”
“I do have good relationships with personnel and administration with other agencies,” countered Dupuis. “I would make the effort to mend those where there is damage. I would say it’s important to build on those to ultimately make our community safer. That’s what we’re here to do.”
Both were asked about what a deputy would do if the officer stopped a person of Hispanic descent for a motor vehicle infraction and the individual was found not to be a legal resident.
“We’re following state law, which means we’re not contacting anybody,” Bagley said. “We’re handling what the issue is. If they don’t have a license, that’s what we handle. We aren’t in the immigration enforcement business. Our job is to handle state laws.”
Similarly, Dupuis said, “It’s not our job to enforce immigration status. Our priority is the communities we serve and the complaints. And to prioritize the calls for service we receive. If someone wants to come here and better themselves, I’m not against that.”
Both candidates were asked what sets each apart.
“Why should voters choose you?” given that their responses to many questions were similar.
Bagley said experience is the biggest difference. “I have 34 years of experience, both as a patrolman and in leadership roles. I devoted my life to law enforcement in Hancock County as well as community service. I’ve been involved in youth sports for over 30 years.”
In turn, Dupuis talked about modern policing, setting him apart.
“Law enforcement has changed significantly over the past 10 to 12 years,” Dupuis said. “I recognize that and realize the sheriff’s office needs to evolve with the times. I recognize that change needs to occur and put that into motion.”
Bagley was allowed a rebuttal.
“Law enforcement has changed,” said Bagley. “But the basics are still there. It’s talking and dealing with people.”
Both were asked about whether patrol officers had quotas to fill.
“I put out an expectation that deputies will have 30 contacts a month,” Dupuis said. “It’s about promoting positive community engagement. It’s a standard pretty common in most law enforcement agencies.”
“No, there’s no quotas, but community policing is so important,” Bagley said. “That’s something I would encourage while they’re out on patrol.”
“I would encourage my employees to be someone who’s going to be involved,” said Bagley. “Stopping at town offices, talking to people at the stores and people on the street. Build community trust, and they’re more likely to reach out to you before a tragedy happens. There would be no quotas in my administration.”
This is the first contested race for sheriff in recent years.
Kane, a Republican, had been challenged in the 2014 primary by the late Alan Brown of Hancock, who also had sought the Republican nomination. However, there was no Democratic nominee, so Kane ran unopposed in the general election for the position.
And Kane continued unopposed for two additional terms: 2018 and 2022.
Kane replaced Bill Clark, a Republican who had been sheriff for 34 years and is now a Hancock County Commissioner.
Clark ran unopposed for much of his career with the exception of 1984, when he was challenged by Harold Johnson. Then in 2002 and 2006, Clark was challenged by Terry B. Cole, an Ellsworth Democrat.
Bagley is currently a detective with the Ellsworth Police Department and has worked in law enforcement in Hancock County for over three decades. He was a patrol deputy with the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office for 12 years, then 13 years with the Maine Drug Enforcement Agency, before returning to duty as a patrol deputy, followed by patrol lieutenant. Bagley was chief deputy from 2022-23, before joining the Ellsworth Police Department.
Dupuis is currently a lieutenant with the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office. He first began as a patrol officer for the Orono Police Department, and in 2018, he became a patrol deputy for the Hancock County Sheriff’s Department. From 2022-23, he worked with the Maine Drug Enforcement Agency, and then he was promoted to lieutenant with the sheriff’s department in 2024.

title: ‘Genocide’ can hurt. I will still vote for Maine Democrats.
text:
Dr. Peter J. Stein of Sandy River Plantation is a scientist and engineer and the founder and current president of Scientific Solutions.
I get a laugh these days when I point out the fact that what Jesus Christ and Bernie Sanders have most in common is that they were both raised Jewish.
I, too, was raised Jewish. I am incredibly proud of my Jewish heritage — it shaped who I am and anchored the values that guide my life today.
In those critical early years, I was taught that the word Shalom means hello, goodbye and peace. I was taught Tikkun Olam, a fundamental tenet of Judaism that translates to “repair the world.” My upbringing instilled in me the belief that we are not on this planet just to serve ourselves; our individual lives are but a whisper, and we bear a collective responsibility to serve others and the generations that follow.
We Jews are taught relentlessly from a young age to value education, to seek knowledge and to do something meaningful with the fleeting time we have been given.
Driven by these cultural imperatives, Jewish people frequently pursue advanced degrees and high-paying fields, often achieving significant wealth and influence. Though we make up just 0.2% of the world’s population, we Jews represent 22% of all Nobel laureates. This foundational respect for education naturally led me to a career rooted in science, data and objective facts. As a 67-year-old scientist and engineer, I look at the world through a lens of empirical reality.
Science proves that all human beings share essentially the same genetic makeup; the unequal realities of our world are largely a matter of the environments we are born into. Above all, my scientific background and my Jewish upbringing converge on a single truth: every person on this planet wants, needs and deserves to live a peaceful and healthy existence.
I can promise you that if every country works together, we possess the required technology to responsibly solve all the world’s major problems. As Bernie Sanders says, “We are all in this together.”
It is this exact intersection of my Jewish values and scientific outlook that has led me — like the majority of American Jews — to a progressive political philosophy. In fact, I agree with just about everything the progressive left of the Democratic Party stands for.
Conversely, Donald Trump will go down as the worst president in U.S. history, and the
Republican Party that enabled his trampling of the Constitution for political and personnel gains must be removed from power until it can meaningfully reform. So much of our society is broken, and there is so much to fix that can be fixed.
I laid this all out in my July 25 op-ed about checking our egos at the door. We need a new progressive era — the next evolution of American democracy. We, the people, need to take back control of our country through a political revolution.
Yet, what deeply pains me right now as a progressive Jewish Democrat entrenched in politics is how the current division over Gaza threatens to fracture this necessary revolution. I hear the pain from all sides of our party. There are those among us who look at the devastation and call it a genocide, strictly adhering to the U.N. definition. Given the horrific imagery coming out of Gaza, it is easy to understand why they use that word.
Yet, there are others who hear “genocide” and instantly think of systematic extermination — the historical trauma of thousands upon thousands loaded into railroad cars and sent to gas chambers. For them, after the Holocaust and the horrors of Oct. 7, accusing Israel of an intent to commit genocide feels like an impossible slander.
We all want the killing to stop. The atrocities of Oct. 7 cannot be swept aside, but neither can the severe overreaction of Benjamin Netanyahu’s extremist government. Israel may believe it is defending itself, and its core intent may not be the total extermination of the Palestinian people, but bombing innocent children and forcing a population into starvation is no path to peace. Neither is the continued expansion of settlements in the West Bank.
While nearly all of us view a two-state or multi-state solution as the only viable path forward, others see a single-state reality as the only option. To bridge this divide, we across the entire Democratic spectrum — from the far-left progressives to the most conservative Democrats — must step up and talk about the Arab-Israeli conflict. We cannot allow those who want to halt our political revolution to divide us as we enter the 2028 election cycle.
The oligarchy has largely co-opted organizations like AIPAC, weaponizing the word “genocide” and pouring massive amounts of money into efforts to stop “our revolution.” They are actively fomenting antisemitism to keep us divided, and we cannot let them get away with it. We must talk, we must debate and we must solidify the American Democratic Party’s stance as a definitive force for peace.
Ultimately, now is not the time for American Jews to become single-issue voters over Israel. Nor for those that are dedicated to the Palestinian cause. We cannot help anyone abroad if we do not maintain a functioning, democratic United States government at home.
As a Jew, I understand why the word “genocide” hurts, but I am still proudly voting for Troy Jackson and the entire Democratic ticket. My urgent plea is that everyone who truly cares about the future of the United States, Israel and the Palestinian people does the same, here in Maine and beyond.

title: International fugitive sentenced for one of the largest health care fraud schemes in U.S. history
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - A man whom federal prosecutors called the architect of one of the largest health care fraud schemes in U.S. history was sentenced Monday.
Herbert Kimble was sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment with three years of court-ordered supervision. He was also ordered to pay more than $199 million in restitution to Medicare and forfeit more than $195 million in what prosecutors described as “ill-gotten gains.”
Kimble pleaded guilty in 2019 to conspiring to commit health care fraud, violate the anti-kickback statute, and defraud the United States in connection with a telemedicine and durable medical equipment scheme involving back, shoulder, wrist, and knee braces.
Prosecutors say Kimble ran offshore call centers that recruited elderly Medicare beneficiaries, paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies for signed prescriptions, then sold those orders to medical equipment companies that billed Medicare. Court filings put the intended loss at more than $400 million, with Kimble personally gaining more than $195 million.
Kimble cooperated with investigators in what became Operation Brace Yourself, but failed to appear for three court dates in fall 2024 and fled to the Philippines, where he remained a fugitive for nearly two years.
In June, the FBI named Kimble to its Most Wanted Fraudsters list. Days later, he was apprehended in the Philippines and returned to the United States. He later pleaded guilty to three counts of failure to appear as part of the 2026 National Health Care Fraud Takedown.
Bryan Stirling, U.S. attorney for the District of South Carolina, said Kimble’s sentence matches the seriousness of his crimes.
“Kimble orchestrated one of the largest international healthcare fraud schemes in our nation’s history,” Stirling said. “Today’s sentence underscores the seriousness of his crimes and reinforces the Department of Justice’s commitment to investigate and prosecute those who steal from American taxpayers.”
Kimble is not eligible for parole.

title: Inmate's escape is just the latest problem for Tennessee's troubled prison system
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — The weekend escape of a Tennessee inmate who was convicted of murdering a co-worker was just the latest black eye for the state’s troubled prison system, coming only weeks after the failed execution of Christa Pike.
Jacob Morley was last known to have been in Marion, Illinois, on Tuesday. Authorities say he stole a truck from a nearby farm after escaping late Sunday from the Northwest Correctional Complex near Tiptonville, Tennessee, and abandoned it Tuesday behind a strip mall in Marion, which is about 120 miles (193 kilometers) north of the lockup.
Police have been trying to determine where Morley went after ditching the truck.
Authorities haven’t received any credible tips that Morley remained in the Marion area or reports of other vehicles that have gone missing in the city since Tuesday, Marion Police Chief David Fitts said Wednesday.
Escape is latest problem at Tennessee prisons
Morley’s escape is the latest blemish for Tennessee’s prison system.
After the failed execution of Pike last month, Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada announced his resignation after less than three years on the job.
State Sen. Tom Hatcher said the resignation couldn’t come soon enough.
“We need new leadership,” the Republican from Blount County said. “We’re doing oversight work behind the scenes about several of our prisons. We’re just waiting to see who our next governor will be and who is the next commissioner.”
Lack of staff is a big problem
Understaffing is a big problem at Tennessee’s prisons, said Hatcher, who is the chairman of a legislative subcommittee looking into the prison system. He noted that Strada didn’t show up for the last oversight meeting, which happened days before Pike’s execution date.
During a subcommittee hearing, prison officials said they had 470 open jobs among their 6,000-person workforce. They also warned that a 2022 law requiring inmates to serve more of their sentences was increasing prison populations and could lead to overcrowding.
Prison leadership also isn’t transparent about problems and doesn’t accept oversight well, even though the problems repeat themselves, Hatcher said.
“Until we get someone who wants to look at all of this, we’re going to keep having problems,” he said.
A prison spokesperson said the agency was not commenting at this time.
The prison where the escape happened can be violent
The prison Morley escaped from has had several violent attacks between inmates and by employees in recent years.
District Attorney Danny H. Goodman Jr. is overseeing the prosecution of 19 cases stemming from indictments this summer at the Northwest Correctional Complex.
The cases include five inmates killed behind bars and assaults against staff and inmates. Former prison employees charged with aggravated assault are among the people named in 50 indictments.
Goodman said there is no evidence that Morley was involved in any of those attacks.
Staffing at the isolated prison, which is about 90 miles (145 kilometers) from Memphis, Tennessee, has been a major problem, Goodman said, noting that although he suspects that understaffing could have contributed to the escape or the violence, he doesn’t have any proof.
“There is a huge shortage of staff there,” Goodman said. “The ones that are there, they have to work so much. It’s not unusual for them to have to work double shifts.”
No sign anyone helped Morley escape
There’s no evidence yet that anyone helped Morley escape, but the investigation is ongoing, Goodman said.
Authorities said Morley, 28, slipped through a fence in his prison clothes late Sunday night before walking to the nearby farm and stealing the truck. He is white, 5 feet 11 inches (1.8 meters) tall and weighs 240 pounds (109 kilograms). He has brown hair and green eyes.
Morley is serving a life sentence for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s home after he had been missing for a few weeks. The two lived in Carter County, in eastern Tennessee.
___
Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina.

title: Conservative activists O'Keefe, Higby charged with unlawful voting in Minnesota
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Conservative activists James O’Keefe and Cam Higby were charged Wednesday with unlawful voting and identity theft after a Minnesota prosecutor said they gave false names to poll workers during the state’s primary election. The men recorded the exchanges for a video to expose what they say are vulnerabilities in the state’s voting laws.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the felony charges at a news conference. She said O’Keefe, 42, of West Palm Beach, Florida, and Higby, 26, of Covington, Washington, wore costumes and used the names of registered state voters while starting the “vouching” process in the Aug. 11 primary. The process provides a way for unregistered voters who lack proof of their current address to register and vote after signing an oath of eligibility.
Poll workers were suspicious and reported their behavior. Moriarty said the situation shows that “the system for identifying misconduct and responding to it functioned well during the primary.”
O’Keefe, who founded and later was ousted as leader of Project Veritas, came to notoriety by publishing undercover sting-style videos like the one made at the Minnesota polling places. He was not immediately available for comment, and court records do not name an attorney to comment on his behalf.
Higby did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment and did not have an attorney in court records. Neither of them has had an opportunity to enter a plea.
Minnesota allows registered voters to “vouch” for another voter in the same precinct by signing an oath attesting to the second person’s identity and that they live in the precinct. The person being vouched for also must sign an oath attesting to their identity and eligibility to vote, and must also provide their Minnesota driver’s license or identification card number or the last four digits of their Social Security number.
The process is rarely used but is most commonly done by older adults who have not updated their address on a driver’s license because they no longer drive. In the November 2024 election, fewer than 0.6% of votes cast used the process, according to the Minnesota Secretary of State’s office website.
Workers flag ‘strange behavior’
In their video that was posted to YouTube on Aug. 13, O’Keefe, Higby and others dressed in costumes similar to attire worn by some Muslims and used fake accents while asking about the vouching process at multiple Minneapolis voting sites. Higby’s face was covered, and when talking to poll workers, O’Keefe referred to him as his wife.
Moriarty said both men “identified themselves using names of registered voters in the precinct without those voters’ knowledge or permission.”
The poll workers noticed the “strange behavior” and flagged it to election officials, Moriarty said, who asked police to investigate. The men stopped short of signing the oath required for vouching, but Moriarty said that giving false names and starting the process was enough to justify the felony charges.
“Free and fair elections are the bedrock of democracy, and their protection is one of our highest priorities,” Moriarty said.
O’Keefe’s organization, O’Keefe Media Group, posted a statement and the video on its website and said the men presented “an intentionally extreme scenario to expose what they see as the lunacy of the state’s ‘vouching’ system.”
“The team wanted to determine how election workers would respond, what safeguards they would describe, and how far they would allow the vouching process to proceed,” the statement said. “Not every election worker reacted the same way. While several workers explained how the undercover team could proceed under the vouching rules, others became suspicious of the group and took issue with the investigation. Some workers communicated concerns about the team over their radios.”
David Becker, a former Justice Department official and the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said he wasn’t aware of any examples of vouching leading to organized or widespread fraud. But he said there have been more efforts recently by those pushing voter fraud claims to commit questionable acts themselves.
“Impersonating another voter is a very serious crime,” Becker said.
Voter ID laws vary
Voter identification laws vary from state to state. Thirty-six states have laws requesting or requiring voters to show some form of identification at the polls, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, but that identification can range from a photo ID to things like a utility bill or bank statement.
In the remaining 14 states and Washington, D.C., voters can cast a ballot without showing ID. They must verify their identity in various other ways, like signing an affidavit or providing personal information like birth date, name or address.
Some states, like Minnesota, allow election officials or other registered voters to vouch for people without a current ID. Alaska and New Hampshire, for instance, allow officials like a clerk or a supervisor to verify a voter’s identity if they know the voter personally. North Dakota allows people who lack identification cards because of a disability to have an attester certify that they are a qualified voter. West Virginia allows an adult who has known a voter for at least six months to sign a sworn statement verifying the voter’s identity.
___ Boone reported from Boise, Idaho. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson contributed.

title: Driver hurt after car strikes camper, goes vertical in Sidney
text:
SIDNEY, Maine (WABI) - One man was hurt after a crash left his car standing on its front end in Sidney Wednesday morning.
It happened around 6:40 a.m. on West River Road near Ferry Road.
The Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office says an 18-year-old Augusta woman tried to pass a 48-year-old Sidney man on a curve, but an oncoming car forced the two together.
The man’s car went off the road, hit a culvert, tore through a camper parked on a lawn and came to rest vertical.
Crews cut him out. He was taken to the hospital with minor injuries. The woman was not hurt.
No charges have been filed.
