title: ‘I miss her like crazy’: Loved ones remembering post office worker hit and killed by car
text:
FORT THOMAS, Ky. (WXIX/Gray News) - Loved ones and a Kentucky community are mourning a post office worker who was hit and killed by a car while walking earlier this month.
Marchelle Bertram worked at the front desk of the Fort Thomas Post Office for years, helping people who came in. Sadly, she lost her life in a collision in Bellevue on Oct. 15.
Her daughter, Whitney Bertram, said she is remembering her mother while seeing a large amount of support from the community following her death.
“There are so many people I don’t know whose lives she’s touched and affected,” Whitney Bertram said.
The crash occurred while Marchelle Bertram was walking on Memorial Parkway near her home. Her daughter said she rushed to the hospital after learning her mother had been hit by a vehicle.
“Given the grave amount of injuries she sustained, there was no way she was going to survive,” she said.
Marchelle Bertram died at the hospital. Whitney Bertram said the driver stayed at the scene and believes the crash was an accident.
“I miss her like crazy; I try not to think about it too hard because I’ll break down,” she said.
According to Whitney Bertram, there has been an outpouring of support telling her that her mother was kind and well-known in the area.
Additionally, a woman at the post office began crying when she learned of Marchelle Bertram’s death.
“If she could come back for a moment just to see what a reaction has come about because she’s no longer with us, I think she’d be stunned,” Whitney said.
Whitney Bertram said those who would visit the post office would call her mother “the nice lady at the post office,” and knowing the good she put into the world is helping her get through the loss.
“You’re never truly gone until you’re forgotten about. It’s good to hear other people reaching out and expressing how much they miss her, too,” Whitney Bertram said.

title: 100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County Maine selects CHiP as major donation recipient
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Oct. 6, more than 200 local women gathered at Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens to socialize, network and share joy. During the meeting, names for three nominated nonprofits were drawn at random: CHiP, Mainely Memory Foundation, and Healthy Lincoln County. After hearing brief presentations about each organization, members voted to award the quarterly “Impact Donation” to CHiP (Community Housing Improvement Project), an organization dedicated to “neighbors helping neighbors stay safe, warm and dry” by assisting with seasonal fuel and firewood assistance, urgent home repairs, wheelchair and accessibility ramps—all while lifting spirits and giving neighbors hope.
The meeting netted an initial contribution to CHiP of $18,011, and the total will grow until the next quarterly meeting in January. Project Manager Brittany Gill of CHiP stated, “This is coming just in time for heating season and I already have 40 people who are really eager to get help so it’s really nice to get finances to help us go into this season confidently. We really appreciate the women who come out and want to support their community because this is such a community-based effort. We can’t do this alone; we have to do this together.”
Mainely Memory Foundation and Healthy Lincoln County went home with just over $1,000 each thanks to funds raised from the raffle. The meeting also provided an opportunity to present Lincoln County Dental with a check for $18,294 resulting from the July meeting. Director of Development Holly Stover addressed the crowd regarding the impact the donation will make toward sustaining and improving oral health for so many in our community.
The local chapter of 100+ Women Who Care operates exclusively on a donation basis led by the volunteer leadership team comprised of Leah Bauer, Kate Elmes, Shannon Parker, Alyssa Allen, Ali Stevenson and Jessica Tindal. Together, the team gathers support from local businesses to host quarterly meetings, food and raffles. October’s meeting would not have been possible without the donation of space from Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens (CMBG), with special thanks to Gretchen Ostherr, president and CEO of the gardens for her imaginative and eager support. After one year in existence, membership in 100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County stands strong with over 400 women.
Financial support for “100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County Maine” has arrived from local businesses including Tindal & Callahan Real Estate; Bangor Savings Bank; Jordan Construction; Damariscotta Region Chamber of Commerce; The Cheney Financial Group; First National Wealth Management; Mid-Maine Millwork; Social Graze Charcuterie, Coastal Maine Popcorn and a handful of anonymous donors. Raffle items have raised over $6,000 for local non-profits and include donations by Fiction Bookshop in Wiscasset; Veggies to Table in Nobleboro; The Tipsy Butler Inn in Newcastle; Moose Crossing in Waldoboro; Frances Perkins Center in Newcastle; The Waldo Theatre in Waldoboro; Creative art by Deb Arter, Shannon Parker, Felicity Myers and Alistair McCallum; Skidhompha Public Library; Du Jardin, and Waterstruck Wellness in Newcastle; Adrienne Zahner with Sotheby's; Local Batch Kitchen in Damariscotta; Ocean Blue Fitness in Damariscotta, and Morning Dew Farm in Newcastle.
Lincoln County’s 100+ Women chapter has set a target of raising $100,000 by the end of 2026 and are currently within a few thousand of reaching that benchmark. Readers are encouraged to inquire about how to contribute to help our community reach this impactful goal.
Want to participate in “100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County Maine”? Membership forms and nomination forms are available on the organization’s website at WomenWhoCareLincolnCountyMaine.org.
The next quarterly meeting is scheduled for Tuesday, Jan. 5 from 5 to 7 p.m. at Bigelow Laboratory in East Boothbay. As with all meetings, attendees can expect light bites, refreshing drinks and inspiring company. The organization hopes you’ll join “100+ Women Who Care Lincoln County Maine” for vibrant and diverse gatherings that prove there’s strength in numbers. Because together we are a wave of change.

title: Pennsylvania woman scammed out of $60,000 aids FBI in catching suspect
text:
Pennsylvania woman scammed out of $60,000 aids FBI in catching suspect
A Pennsylvania woman who was scammed out of $60,000 worked with authorities to catch a suspect accused of posing as a courier in the scheme, according to court documents.
The scam began with a pop-up message on the victim's phone, which falsely claimed she had purchased child pornography and needed to contact the FBI, according to the criminal complaint.
Changsong Huang faces multiple felony charges for allegedly serving as a courier in the scam.
According to the criminal complaint, the victim was told her identity had been stolen and her IP address compromised. The suspects, who claimed to be federal officials, convinced her to purchase gift cards to verify her account and withdraw cash to help investigate the alleged identity theft.
On Oct. 8, the victim withdrew $25,000 from a home equity loan and delivered it to a man at a Sheetz on Perry Highway in McCandless, Pennsylvania.
McCandless is roughly 12 miles outside of Pittsburgh.
Three days later, she withdrew another $35,000 and delivered it to a man at a Dollar General location in the area.
After the second delivery, the victim began to suspect she had been scammed and reported it to police. She then agreed to help investigators set a trap.
The victim worked with police to arrange a third pickup at a local ice cream and frozen yogurt shop, using $30,000 in imitation currency provided by the FBI.
According to court documents, FBI agents observed a man approach her vehicle, take the box, and drive away. Police stopped the vehicle at a gas station and identified the driver as Huang. He was then taken into custody.
Local police charged Huang with felony counts of theft by unlawful taking, theft by deception, and conspiracy.
The criminal complaint states investigators learned Huang was having an immigration hearing and could be facing deportation. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was contacted, and Huang remains in ICE custody in Cambria County, Pennsylvania.

title: Letter: Supporting Bobby Charles and local control of education
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
As a longtime Maine school administrator, special education advocate, and parent of a son with disabilities, I have spent years working alongside teachers and families navigating our educational system. I have seen firsthand the dedication of Maine educators and the commitment parents make every day.
I have also watched schools struggle under an increasing number of regulations and administrative mandates. While education spending rises, too much funding is consumed by bureaucracy instead of reaching classrooms and the students who need support most. Schools face significant challenges recruiting and retaining qualified teachers, particularly in special education. Students depend on critical services like speech therapy, occupational therapy, and specialized instruction. Every dollar diverted to unnecessary administrative requirements is a dollar not used to help children learn.
That is why I am supporting Bobby Charles for governor. I appreciate his belief that parents, teachers, principals, and locally elected school boards should have the strongest voice in educational decisionmaking. The people closest to students understand their needs far better than state bureaucracies.
Bobby Charles has pledged to reduce unnecessary administrative spending, eliminate burdensome regulations, and direct more funding into classrooms. I believe this election is about restoring local control and ensuring taxpayer dollars are spent where they make the greatest difference for children. Maine’s children deserve an education system that prioritizes academic excellence, fiscal responsibility, and local decisionmaking.
Beth Anne Lorigan
Brewer

title: MDI volleyball sweeps Wells, returns to Class C final
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUGUSTA — It’s a return to the Class C final for the Mt. Desert Island volleyball team.
The Trojans rolled to a 3-0 victory over Wells on Wednesday in the Class C divisional championship game at Cony High School. MDI (9-7), the defending state champion and No. 3 seed in the tournament, will play in the state title game at 1 p.m. Saturday at Husson University in Bangor.
“It’s a relief because there was so much pressure to get back (to states),” said senior libero Grace Sinclair.
The Trojans won each set (25-17, 25-16, 25-16) by eight points or more and have won all of their six sets in the playoffs.
“We’re excited (for states), we’re ready to go,” said MDI coach Whitney Walls.
Wells, the No. 7 seed, finished 5-11. Down 24-12, the Warriors won four straight points before MDI clinched it on a hit by senior outside hitter Janiece Anderson.
Here are some other takeaways from Wednesday’s game:
Trojans are on a roll
With the exception of a 3-2 loss to Washington Academy – one of the top programs in the state – on Oct. 15, MDI has won five of its last six matches. That includes a 3-2 victory over Class D standout Narraguagus and a 3-1 win over rival Ellsworth.
“They’re confident,” said Walls. “We’ve been training all year for this, and they’ve been fired up and ready to go.”
Aside from its preparedness, Walls has been impressed with its ability to stay cool under pressure.
“This team has fun. Everything they do, they have fun,” Walls said. “They keep it silly, they keep it loose. I think they play better when they’re having fun, and they do that as a team.”
Wells stays up for the challenge
The Warriors, who edged Medomak Valley 3-2 to reach the divisional final, competed throughout and kept their composure, even as MDI pulled further ahead.
Wells kept a good back-and-forth pace with the Trojans into the middle of each set, before MDI would find a rhythm and run away in points.
MDI boasts two wins over Wells, also beating the Warriors 3-0 in the season opener Sept. 4.
A championship edge
The Trojans won their first state championship last year with a 3-1 victory over Gardiner. Having that championship-game experience gives the Trojans added confidence entering Saturday’s state final.
“I think it gives us a lot of confidence knowing that we’ve done it before and we can definitely do it again,” Anderson said. “We beat Gardiner last year and we split Ellsworth (in the regular season) … Either way, I’m confident in (what we can do).”
Statistical leaders
MDI: Cora VanDongen (11 kills, 9 digs); Janiece Anderson (7 kills, 5 digs); Grace Sinclair (10 digs, 4 aces).

title: South Portland boys soccer finishes its home season with quarterfinal win
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SOUTH PORTLAND — Lamed Khelendende is normally the person setting up goals for South Portland.
Wednesday night, the senior co-captain was the finisher. Khelendende scored his first two goals of the season in a 2-0 Class A South quarterfinal win against Deering at Geroge E. Martin Field.
“I’m so happy. But I’m also sad. This is our last home game and I’m a senior. I love this school,” Khelendende said.
No. 4 South Portland (10-3-2), which has gone 8-0-2 since a 2-3 start, will be at No. 1 Thornton Academy (12-1-2) for Friday’s regional semifinal. Thornton won the regular-season match, 2-1.
No. 5 Deering, which started 6-0-1, finished 10-4-2.
FINISHING CHANCES
Khelendende’s first goal came off a long throw-in by Oliver Jenkins. The natural grass field at South Portland is quite narrow and Jenkins was able to throw the ball well into the box. After a couple of misfires by South Portland, Khelendende was on the spot to kick it home.
South Portland scored one goal in its three early-season setbacks. It has scored at least two goals in each of its last five games.
“The hard work we’re doing every day in practice and the focus to get better every day. I think it’s paying off right now and that’s why we’re here,” Khelendende said.
Khelendende’s second goal came on a strong header when he jumped high to meet a long cross by Anthony Nielsen, another of South Portland’s four senior captains.
Nielsen, a winger adept enough to play on both sides, won a ball near the South Portland bench and heard head coach Jeremey Longchamp shout, “run at him.”
Nielsen did just that, getting past the first defender and advancing the ball all the way to the right corner. With another slick dribbling move, Nielsen found space just inside the corner flag and spotted Khelendende.
“Coach trusts us with the ball at our feet. He wants us to get creative in the final third. And I guess that’s what we did,” Nielsen said. “We got creative. I took some chances, got the ball over to Lahmed for a beautiful finish. It was a team effort, like they always are.”
DEERING MISSES
Overall, South Portland controlled the game and deserved the win. But the Rams did have some good looks, particularly in the first 10 to 15 minutes of the match. South Portland goalie Jude Charltray was alert to come out quickly and cover or kick away some long through balls. After that, South Portland’s back line, featuring center backs and captains Isaac Arey and Gil Ingram, were able to clear away any near-dangerous situations.
“We had more momentum the first opening few minutes, a couple of opportunities to score, quality chances,” said Deering coach Joel Costigan. “Definitely deflated after that first goal. Not the type of goal we ever want to concede, considering it was a (loose) ball in the box.”
STATISTICS
Deering: Linden McAuliffe, 4 saves; Team, 6 shots (4 on goal), 4 corner kicks.
South Portland: Lahmed Khelendendre 2 goals, Anthony Nielsen 1 assist; Jude Charltray, 4 saves; Team, 9 shots (6 on goal), 9 corner kicks.

title: Cornell faculty to begin voting on no-confidence measure over handling of sexual assault allegations
text:
(AP) - Cornell University faculty will meet Wednesday to conclude debate and begin voting on a proposed no-confidence resolution in the university’s administration following widespread frustration over its response to a woman who reported she was gang raped at a campus fraternity house in 2024.
The meeting comes after an Oct. 14 Faculty Senate meeting at which angry members confronted Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff about the university’s handling of the allegations.
The meeting was closed to the media, but in an audio recording obtained by The Associated Press, Kotlikoff acknowledged some missteps, defended his leadership and asked for more time to push for cultural changes in student social life and make reforms. He urged faculty to have confidence in his leadership, pointing to an independent investigation into the university’s handling of the case that he said could lead to meaningful reforms.
A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All seven men have denied her allegations.
The criminal investigation by Cornell’s police department stalled after the district attorney declined to pursue charges. In a New York Times interview, Kotlikoff said he never followed up to learn what had happened to the woman or the investigation.
Asked by a faculty member whether he read the Cornell Police Department’s report on the rape allegations, Kotlikoff acknowledged he had not, but said that was because the police investigation was confidential and university policy is that top administrators shouldn’t have a role in criminal investigations.
“I really reject the idea that I had no interest in it or was not concerned about it,” Kotlikoff said.
He insisted experienced leadership was necessary to confront problems. Replacing a president would harm Cornell’s reputation, Kotlikoff said.
Faculty also questioned Cornell’s handling of a disciplined student’s return to campus, including his assignment to a shared dorm room with a roommate unaware of his disciplinary history.
After Kotlikoff left the Oct. 14 meeting, a string of faculty speakers said they had lost confidence in the administration’s ability to combat sexual assault on campus. Some Faculty Senate members warned that a hasty no-confidence vote would do little to address the underlying problems.
Wednesday’s meeting is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. and will be closed to the public and media. Electronic voting will open afterward and remain open through Nov. 6. Individual votes will be anonymous.
A no-confidence vote by the faculty would be largely symbolic, but could send a message to the university’s trustees, who ultimately decide who leads it.
Kotlikoff became the university’s interim president in July 2024 and took the job permanently last year.
He’s faced challenges including a dining and custodial workers strike, ire over his decision last year to pay $60 million to resolve Trump administration civil rights investigations, and accusations from activists that his administration stifled campus protests.

title: Letter to the Editor: Troy Jackson for Seniors
Judge orders 30-year prison sentence for key figure in Minnesota food fraud
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — A man who played a major role in defrauding a federal food program in Minnesota was sentenced Wednesday to 30 years in prison, the latest punishment in a sprawling scheme to collect millions of dollars during the COVID-19 pandemic by claiming to have fed needy children.
The depth of fraud in Minnesota — dozens of people have been convicted — has repeatedly drawn the attention of President Donald Trump, who ridiculed the Democratic governor for failing to stop it and partly cited it as grounds for an extraordinary immigration crackdown in the state’s largest cities.
Salim Said operated Safari Restaurant in Minneapolis, which specialized in dishes from Somalia. He was accused of vastly overstating the number of meals when seeking payment for providing food. The government said he was responsible for $44 million in fraud, some of which was committed by others he recruited.
“You took more than taxpayers’ dollars to enrich yourself. You took the reputation of our state down with you,” U.S. District Judge Nancy Brasel said.
Said was claiming a “ridiculous daily distribution of 6,000 meals” while FBI cameras showed 40 people a day collecting food, prosecutors said in a court filing.
“The defendant and his sites did not serve thousands of children; he served a calculated, lucrative lie,” prosecutors said.
Said, a native of Somalia, denied the allegations while testifying at the trial in 2025, saying many meals were delivered off site. But at his sentencing Wednesday, he changed course and expressed remorse. Defense attorney Barry Zone, who had asked for a 12-year prison sentence, disputed that Said was the “architect” as the government alleged.
COVID-19 brought changes to a federal program that typically fed children through schools. Restaurants could participate, and food distribution was extended to places outside schools.
“For 21 consecutive months, Said made thousands of fraudulent reimbursement claims, day after day, month after month,” prosecutors said. “Each submission represented meals purportedly provided to underprivileged children, yet the listed children themselves were entirely fictitious.”
The government said Said hit the jackpot: He bought a $1.2 million home, commercial real estate and an $87,000 pickup truck.
Said was convicted of a raft of charges in 2025, along with Aimee Bock, the leader of a Minnesota nonprofit, Feeding Our Future. She is serving a 42-year prison sentence for devising the overall plan to recruit Said and others to join the federal food program during the pandemic. A judge ordered her to repay $242 million.
State auditors found that the Minnesota Department of Education received numerous complaints about Feeding Our Future, but often told the group to police itself. In January, Gov. Tim Walz said he would not run for reelection after being pounded by Trump about theft in programs that rely on federal cash.

title: An Unexpected Matchup: Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream Battle for 2026 WNBA Championship
text:
The 2026 WNBA playoffs have been marked by unexpected moments, stunning upsets, and hard-fought battles that have had fans and the sports community at the edge of their seats.
After a competitive post season, the championship matchup features the Atlanta Dream, making their first finals appearance since 2013, and the Golden State Valkyries, one the league’s newest franchises, competing for their first WNBA championship.
Entering the playoffs, the Minnesota Lynx held the No.1 seed for the second consecutive year after finishing the regular season with an impressive 33-11 record. No.2 2026 draft pick Olivia Miles proved herself to be an imperative addition to the Lynx’s roster, and because of her strong performance in the regular season, she was named 2026 Rookie-of-the-Year.
However despite their success in the regular season, the Lynx had an unanticipated early first round exit after being upset by the No.8 New York Liberty who swept them in a two game series. Despite advancing to the second round, the Liberty’s success was short-lived after being shut out by the Dream.
After being named the league’s Most Valuable Player for the fifth time and becoming the first player in league history to win the honor three consecutive times, A’ja Wilson entered the post season alongside the Aces looking to secure back-to-back championships.
The Aces advanced to the second round after winning the first series against the Indiana Fever 2-1. However, the Valkyries prevented the defending champions from advancing to the final round after overcoming a thirteen point deficit in Game 3 that resulted in a 3-0 series shutout.
The Dream and the Valkyries proved to be forces in the league as they reached the postseason in 2025. The Valkyries were the first WNBA expansion team to do so in their inaugural season. Both teams had an impressive regular season, with the Valkyries clinching the No.2 seed and the Dream finishing at the No.4 making them deserving contenders for a championship.
Even though they both faced early first-round exits, the front offices made key roster moves ahead of the 2026 season that helped set the stage for their finals appearances. The Valkyries added forward Gabby Williams after earning WNBA All-Defensive First Team honors in 2025, and the Dream made an imperative trade with the Chicago Sky for Angel Reese, who recently secured the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year award.
The series has gone back and forth, with the teams tied at 2-2, as they head into Game 5. The intensity has extended beyond action on the court where Reese commented that she reads the Valkyries’ facial expressions and enjoys the mental game alongside the physicality.
“I can take their confidence and try to do whatever to mess it up,” Reese said.
Both teams are known for their suffocating defense and minimizing scoring opportunities for their opponents. The Valkyries finished the regular season with No.1 defensive rating and were able to take Game 4 holding Angel Reese to eight points on 2-12 shooting.
However, the Dream finished right behind them, ranked No.2 in the league for their extreme physicality, quickness, and ability to force turnovers. The Dream’s pressure had rattled the Valkyries prime ball handlers, and in Game 3, the Dream forced 17 turnovers which they converted to 22 transition points.
In Game 5, both teams were stagnant offensively, recording the lowest scoring half in WNBA finals history. However, the Valkyrie’s X-factor fanbase and home court advantage propelled them to take the series 3-2, and are only one win away from their first championship.
Game 6 will take place in Atlanta’s State Farm Arena on Thursday, Oct. 29th, at 12:30 p.m. The game was moved up from its originally scheduled 8 p.m. start to avoid a scheduling conflict with the Atlanta Hawks’ regular-season matchup against the Cleveland Cavaliers.
With both teams capable of disrupting their opponents and finding ways to capitalize on scoring opportunities, the series has become a test of mental toughness and physicality. One of these two deserving teams will claim the 2026 title and establish themselves as a new powerhouse in the WNBA.

title: Son indicted in mother’s death; medical staff say she had feces, insects in hair
text:
TUSCALOOSA COUNTY, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - A man has been indicted on charges related to the death of his mother in Alabama.
Jonathan Chad Simmons faces one count of manslaughter and one count of second-degree elder abuse in the death of his mother, according to Tuscaloosa County court documents obtained by WBRC.
The court documents referred to the victim as Jonathan Chad Simmons’ mother, Brenda Hallman Simmons.
Deputies found woman unresponsive
Tuscaloosa County deputies and medical personnel were called to the 13000 block of Alabama Highway 216 on May 16. Law enforcement found Brenda Hallman Simmons, 76, alive but unresponsive.
Brenda Simmons died several days later while receiving medical care. The autopsy revealed she died from sepsis due to complications from multiple open bedsores.
Joint investigation begins
The Tuscaloosa Violent Crimes Unit and the state medical examiner’s office began a joint investigation after the family and health personnel suspected neglect.
According to medical staff at the hospital, Simmons had multiple open wounds and sores on her body and showed signs of not being bathed. She had feces and insects in her hair.
When investigators executed a search warrant at the residence Simmons shared with her adult son, Jonathan Simmons, they found it “excessively dirty and unsanitary.”
Son’s statements to investigators
Jonathan Simmons told investigators he was the custodian and caretaker of his mother. He admitted to being aware of her medical issues, including open wounds and bedsores.
“He stated that he had not taken her to a doctor in over a year,” Jack Kennedy, with the Tuscaloosa Violent Crimes Unit, said.
Charges outlined in indictment
The indictment accuses Jonathan Simmons of recklessly causing his mother’s death by abusing and neglecting an elderly person. It also alleges the abuse or neglect caused his mother serious physical injury.
Jonathan Simmons is being held in the Tuscaloosa County Jail with a $30,000 bond.

title: Bates Women’s Golf Achieves Highest National Ranking in Four Years: Fall Season Recap
text:
The Bates women’s golf team wrapped up the fall season at the New England Intercollegiate Golf Association (NEIGA) Championship. The tournament was held on Saturday, October 17th and Sunday, October 18th at The Captains Golf Course in Brewster, Massachusetts.
Last season, the Bobcats won the event by an impressive 81 strokes. Tory Adams ‘27 took home the individual title following rounds of 75 (+3) and 73 (+1). This season the Bobcats increased their margin of victory to 118 strokes. Isabelle Meltzer ‘28 came out victorious after firing off a 77 (+5) in rainy conditions on Saturday, October 17th and an 80 (+8) on Sunday, October 18th.
Meltzer’s performance earned her the distinction of Bobcat of the Week, an award given to two students on a weekly basis by the Bates College athletics department for exemplary achievement at the varsity level. When asked to provide a comment on her game, Meltzer said, “I think that I’m in a good spot coming off a win to stay motivated throughout the off season. The ball striking feels good. I just really need to focus on my distance control and short game.”
Other distinct accomplishments from Meltzer this season include scores of 76 (+3) and 80 (+7) at the Bowdoin Invitational, securing her a T-36th finish. In addition, Meltzer put up a 76 (+5) on Day 2 of the Wesleyan Invitational, which significantly helped the team score and allowed her to cement a T-22nd standing on the leaderboard.
Rebecca Kriegsman ‘30 was another key contributor to the team this fall. She too received the Bobcat of the Week designation after the Williams Fall Invitational. Kriegsman led the field of 73 competitors with an even par 71 on Saturday. On Sunday, she went out and shot a 78 (+7) resulting in a 5th place finish for the talented first year.
“Overall, the experience has been amazing,” Kriegsman said. “I have loved all my time with my coach and my teammates. Everyone has been so supportive and caring, it’s like having a second family.”
“As a senior captain, I am incredibly proud of the discipline we brought to the golf course every day and even more importantly, the positive culture we built on the team,” Adams said.
Adams also played well at Williams where she finished T-14th. Her rounds of 75 (+4) and 79 (+8) were a personal highlight.
“On a personal note, my rounds of 75-79 in the Williams Fall Invitational were a highlight for me, “I’m thrilled I could show strong performance to match the high standards we have set for this program,” Adams said.
Co-captain Mehar Nijjer ‘27 had a consistent season and was a reliable scorer for the Bobcats. Nijjer shot rounds of 76 (+3) and 82 (+9) as an individual at Bowdoin, which resulted in a T-49th finish. The results aligned with Niijer’s previous performances at the event during her Bates’ golf career.
“My last fall season on the team was super exciting,” Nijjer said. “It came with its ups and downs, but there’s no better way to wrap it up than with a top five individual finish, and, of course, a team championship.”
Nijjer emphasized that she’s very proud of the team for working hard, playing well, and having a great time. Though Nijjer is sad the season is over, she’s very excited for the spring. Adams and Liv Sheen ‘30 tied for 3rd place with Nijjer at the NEIGA Championship.
The Bates women’s golf team is heading into the off-season with a No. 49 national ranking, successfully moving them up 18 spots since their 2025/2026 campaign came to a close. The Bobcats are looking forward to making their mark this spring, especially at the NESCAC Tournament, which is being hosted by Trinity College. Competition will span from Friday, April 30 to Sunday, May 2, and all competing golfers will play 54 holes during the three-day event.

title: Police department closes its investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - The Greenville Police Department said it has officially closed its investigation into the death of Hayden Panettiere.
Police said Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental based on the medical examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation.
Panettiere, 36, died from an accidental overdose involving multiple prescription medications and fentanyl, according to findings previously released by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office.
Toxicology testing determined the cause of death to be the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. An autopsy showed no signs of contributing trauma.
On Aug. 16, Panettiere was found unresponsive inside an apartment in Greenville, where she had been temporarily staying. Dispatchers received a 911 call reporting a woman in cardiac arrest at approximately 1:51 p.m. She was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m.
Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the apartment where she died.
The coroner’s office had previously closed its case after the cause and manner were established. Police said at the time their independent investigation remained open while detectives continued to follow leads.
Panettiere was best known for her roles in the TV shows “Heroes” and “Nashville” as well as films such as “Ice Princess” and the “Scream” franchise.
Panettiere published a memoir in May called “This Is Me: A Reckoning.” In the book, she detailed her childhood, time in the limelight and struggles with alcohol, opioids and postpartum depression.

title: ‘Pretty low individual’: Man scammed by fake life insurance agent shortly after sister’s death
text:
CORINTH, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) — A Mississippi man says he was scammed shortly after the death of his sister.
According to Tim Williams, he was called by a woman who identified herself as the life insurance agent for his sister, Stephanie Jeanine Williams Machado.
The woman gave him account numbers and policy numbers, and requested $1,375 for the insurance company to release payment to the Corinthian Funeral Home.
Williams said he entered a three-way phone call with the woman and the funeral home, and that it all seemed to be legitimate.
All the money he had available at the time was $620, and the woman told him to send it.
When Williams asked how the woman would like the funds sent, she said to get it to her however was easiest, either by going to the insurance office or via the Cash App.
Williams said he sent the money to his nephew, who then sent it through the app.
However, Williams said the funeral home told him it never received payment, so he looked up the number and found that it belonged to a man who lived in Alabama.
The number did not belong to the woman who spoke to him or match the name on the Cash App account.
“When you’re already in a bad time in your life ... losing your loved one. Then for somebody to do this on top of that takes a pretty low individual to go to that extent,” Williams said.
Williams said that anyone who suddenly loses a loved one should make sure to double-check and triple-check that everything is real.

title: Scarborough volleyball storms into Class A final
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SANFORD — The Scarborough volleyball team last season had to go through the agony of seeing championship hopes as a top seed go up in smoke.
On Wednesday, the Red Storm got to experience the feeling from the other side.
Led by a hitting attack anchored by dominant senior Caleb Atwood and an airtight defense, No. 4 Scarborough took down top-seeded Cheverus/Waynflete, 3-0, in a Class A semifinal at Sanford High School. The Red Storm swept the sets by scores of 25-21, 25-20 and 25-12.
Scarborough lost in the semifinals as the top seed to Thornton Academy last year, which coach Nicole Petherbridge called a “crappy feeling.” She was all smiles after watching her team play a sparkling all-around game to return to the state final for the first time since 2023.
“We executed on a lot of the things we’ve been working on all season,” she said. “We moved the ball around really well. Everyone was involved in that win. … It came together really nicely.”
HARD HITTERS
• The Red Storm came in armed with one of the state’s most powerful hitters in Atwood, and she was in peerless form. She had seven kills in the first set, including the clinching point, and she added five more in both the second and third sets.
With Atwood composed, the Stags struggled to find an answer.
“I just like to take a deep (breath) after each point, especially a long rally, and think it’s not really as deep as it really is,” she said. “I felt really good about this match. I felt like I was playing at my best.”
• Scarborough’s attack went beyond Atwood, however, as Calli Juhring and Lexi Cowie each added 10 kills. As the Red Storm closed in on the win, the attack, set up by Natale Philibert and Glorya Esposito-Dalton, only sharpened.
“At the end of the second and third sets, we started running the middles a lot, which I think was a good idea,” Juhring said. “All throughout our season, we haven’t been able to do that much. (And) our defense was just so good, to the point where we could run all of our offense and we could put all of our balls down.”
UNSUNG HERO
A key to Scarborough’s success was defensive specialist Suzann Link, who kept Cheverus hits off the floor while also facilitating on offense and picking up a pair of aces.
“Suzann is one of our consummate team players,” Petherbridge said. “She’s staying calm under pressure, she picks up balls that other people wouldn’t imagine getting to. … It makes our offense able to run.”
SETBACK, BUT STEP FORWARD
Cheverus coach Gary Powers said his team had trouble shaking nerves throughout the match.
“We started playing safe and playing scared,” he said. “You can’t do that. You have to play to win.”
Powers acknowledged the progress the program has made, despite the defeat.
“This is the best we’ve ever done,” he said. “The program keeps moving up. That was my goal.”
INJURY
Scarborough’s Elena Pijunovic (three kills) went down while making a hit late in the third set and did not return. Petherbridge said she had no update on the injury or Pijunovic’s status for Saturday’s final.
STAT LEADERS
• Scarborough: Caleb Atwood (17 kills), Calli Juhring (10 kills), Lexi Cowie (10 kills)
• Cheverus: Frida Gray (seven kills), Dylan Walker (five kills)

title: Watch: Greely volleyball is Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches, fans and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Ten years. In a world where time flies, perhaps that doesn’t seem like much. After all, 2016 probably doesn’t feel like all that long ago to you, right?
Think about it, though, in the context of Greely volleyball. This is one of the state’s blue-blood programs, one with a record nine state titles, in a sport that wasn’t officially sanctioned in Maine until 1997. To go a decade without a state final berth is, indeed, a long time.
“There’s definitely a little bit of pressure that comes with that, but it’s also just really exciting that now it’s been a decade and that our program is able to make a difference and get to this point,” said Greely senior Anabelle Talley. “It will be really exciting if we can get to that stage again.”
Talley’s comments were prior to Greely’s Class B semifinal Wednesday night against Messalonskee. The Rangers, the No. 1 seed in Class B and ranked No. 2 statewide in the Varsity Maine poll, capped their regular season last Monday with a 3-2 win over York, then extended their winning streak to 13 matches by sweeping Hampden Academy in the quarterfinals on Saturday. For that, Greely is our choice for Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week.
Since losing its second match of the season to Varsity Maine No. 1 Cheverus, Greely (14-1) has dropped only six sets. The Rangers’ streak includes wins over three other teams in the Varsity Maine Top 10: defending state champion Washington Academy (No. 2), Gardiner (No. 8) and York (No. 7).
In Talley, an outside hitter who is a two-time Varsity Maine All-State selection, Greely has one of the state’s best players. Avery Enos and Alena Tierney are key setters for the Rangers. Fellow sophomore Ellie Desorbo and freshman Lilah Rosenfeld can excel as both liberos and defensive specialists.
Greely has been knocking on the door in recent years. The Rangers went 12-5 and reached the Class B semifinals in 2023. They were 11-5 in 2024, with a quarterfinal appearance, before returning to the semis and finishing with the same record last season.
Reaching at least the semifinals was one of the team’s goals, said coach Autumn Vargo.
“They started out fast; they just gelled together so quickly that we haven’t had to focus on that,” Vargo said. “They just work so well together as a team that it’s just been a fun season — a fun year to coach.”

title: College professor among 2 found dead in home; suspect in custody, police say
text:
LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio. (WOIO/Gray News) - An Ohio college professor and a woman were found shot to death in a home, and a suspect is in custody, according to authorities.
Wednesday morning, police responded to the Oberlin College Conservatory lot at 77 E. College St. to assist firefighters with a vehicle smoking and possibly on fire.
When crews arrived, they tried to find the registered vehicle owner, identified as Daniel Jones, 31, to conduct a welfare check.
When officers arrived at Jones’ home to check on his family, they found the victims dead inside the home.
Pipo Nguyen-Duy, a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College, was found dead on the first floor with an apparent gunshot wound.
A woman found dead on the second floor was not immediately identified. She also had an apparent gunshot wound.
Jones was located aat bout 10:20 a.m. and taken into custody. Charges are pending.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: EVENTS: East Vassalboro native returns to his roots for an exhibition
text:
After some 50 years of exploring creative possibilities beyond his hometown, artist and designer Denim Kent Eaton returns to East Vassalboro with Creative Comes Home, an exhibition at East Vassalboro Grange No. 322. The public is invited to meet the artist at a reception on Friday, October 30, 2026, from 4 to 6 p.m., at the Grange, on Route 32 (Main Street).
A self-described Renaissance man, Eaton has worked across architectural design, music, visual art, fashion, and craftsmanship. His career as a residential and commercial architectural designer helped support a lifelong appetite for creative ventures that do not always fit conventional categories. The exhibition offers a glimpse of that journey – and of the place where his imagination first took shape.
An unexpected connection helped bring the exhibition about. During the winter of 2025-26, Eaton was commissioned to design and build archival shelving for Gregory’s extensive artwork. Gregory spent much of his creative life on Vinalhaven Island and became part of a prominent East Vassalboro family whose lives had run alongside Eaton’s during his formative years. A practical woodworking commission thus became a new chapter in an old community connection.
For Eaton, the title Creative Comes Home speaks to more than a return address. It suggests that the landscapes and relationships of youth can continue to resonate across decades – and that the impulse to create may eventually find its way back to where it began.
Artist reception: Friday, October 30, 2026, 4 – 6 p.m., East Vassalboro Grange No. 322, Route 32 (Main Street), East Vassalboro, Maine.

title: Troy Jackson’s logger brand rests on a woods career that ended years ago
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Robert McBreairty Jr. has spent some 60 years harvesting timber in Maine’s northern woods. Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson worked for him more than a decade ago.
But when Jackson calls himself a logger in his campaign ads, it rankles the 82-year-old Fort Kent contractor, who said he could never vote for Jackson.
“Oh, it pisses me off,” McBreairty said. “He was not a logger. No. A logger, back when we called loggers, loggers, they took a chainsaw and went in the woods and cut down trees and lived it.”
The woods are the core of Jackson’s pitch against U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, the Republican seeking a sixth term in next week’s election. But Jackson, who lives in Allagash, has not reported income from logging since 2012 and has spent the past decade earning money from labor unions and political organizing, records show.
His campaign said he has kept logging “intermittently.” Ethics filings showing his sources of income and past BDN coverage illustrate how he moved in and out of the woods over more than two decades, much of it in lean years for his family and for logging in northern Maine.
The hardest stretch came in the fall of 1998. As he and his father were giving up a $300,000 delimbing machine they could no longer find work for, Jackson helped lead loggers in a blockade at the Canadian border, protesting landowners who hired bonded Canadian crews over Mainers and launching himself into politics.
His father, Joe Jackson, told the BDN that November that his log truck had sat parked since February for lack of work. He and his son had been paying $6,700 a month on the delimber before selling it.
The protest came as the industry in northern Maine was being remade. In 1994, paper and other forest-products companies owned 59% of the land held by Maine’s major timberland owners, according to a 2005 study by the Manomet Center for Conservation Sciences. By 2005, their share was just over 15%, while financial investors grew from 3% to nearly 33%.
The work also changed. Crews of chainsaw cutters and skidder drivers gave way to contractors running machines that could cost $500,000 apiece. By the early 2000s, machines handled 90% or more of production on Maine’s large timberlands, a 2004 legislative study found.
Loggers on those jobs competed with Canadian crews brought in under a federal program for temporary foreign workers. Canadians could often work for less because of the exchange rate. As late as 2009, logging companies typically sought about 600 of those waivers a year.
When he first ran for the Legislature in 2000 as a Republican, a BDN profile described the 32-year-old as a “former logger” who had moved from Allagash to attend the University of Maine at Fort Kent. He lost that race but won a House seat two years later as an independent.
From 2006 through 2012, while he was a state lawmaker, he listed northern Maine logging contractors as employers on his annual state ethics filings, including McBreairty. In 2012, he wrote in a candidate questionnaire that he still ran a delimber, a machine that strips felled trees, when the Legislature was out of session.
Writing as Senate president in a 2019 BDN column, Jackson said the blockade was what drove him, “a fifth-generation logger, to run for office.” In the same column, he wrote that “those of us who work in the woods” knew what the industry needed. He championed a law letting loggers and wood haulers bargain collectively. The next year, he filed a federal labor complaint accusing the government of failing to protect Maine loggers from Canadian competition.
By then, he had not reported logging income for eight years. His 2013 filing lists only the Legislature, and logging never shows up again. Lawmakers only have to disclose income sources worth at least $2,000, so smaller jobs would not appear.
McBreairty said both Jackson and his father ran a delimber for him. That is a far stretch from holding a chainsaw, he said. Jackson told the BDN in September that some people don’t consider him a true logger because he ran machinery.
Hilton Hafford, an Allagash logger who joined the blockade and has known Jackson since he was a kid, said the line between running a machine and wielding a chainsaw disappeared from the industry long ago, and that the critics are holding Jackson to a definition nobody else in the woods is held to.
“Troy Jackson realized that the only way to change anything in any industry was to change it within,” Hafford said. “And to change it within, you had to be part of the political world.”
Jackson’s campaign said calling himself a logger “speaks to his background and identity,” and the candidate does not claim to be currently employed as one.
“Taking on other work doesn’t erase that history or the lessons he carries with him,” campaign spokesperson David Farmer said.
After Jackson lost the 2014 Democratic primary in the 2nd Congressional District, his work largely turned to labor and political organizing, working for Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign before organizing for the International Association of Machinists from 2018 to 2020 and working for the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades from 2020 to 2024.
His association with the machinists got attention in 2020 after Jackson co-authored a letter to Bath Iron Works, whose workers the union represents, saying lawmakers could reconsider a tax break over hiring practices they disagreed with. At that time, he said his job was organizing loggers but that none had unionized.
From 2021 to early 2025, he also worked part time raising money for Food and Medicine, a progressive, labor-aligned Brewer nonprofit group that grew out of a wave of mill closures in the early 2000s. He beat its goals for an annual Thanksgiving meal drive, Jack McKay, the group’s executive director, said.
Jackson’s U.S. Senate financial disclosure filed earlier this month shows he made $85,000 from labor groups in 2025 and $58,000 so far this year, nearly all of it consulting fees from the machinists and the painters’ union. The rest of last year’s total, $5,100, came from the Eastern Maine Labor Council, which McKay also leads.
The machinists paid him through August, weeks after he entered the Senate race. The campaign said he no longer consults for either union. Neither his campaign nor the two unions responded to specific questions about his work for them.
Some of that money ran through Jackson Associates, a company Jackson incorporated in June 2021 while saying it was for construction and land management. On his state ethics filings, it was called a logging and forestry business. His campaign said the company was set up to manage Jackson’s own land but has made no money doing that.
Jackson’s credentials have become a target in the campaign’s final week. A new Collins ad features retired sportscaster Bill Green saying “we’re not talking about buying a cord of wood” in the election, and “Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective.”
He filmed a response Tuesday calling the ad “out of touch” given high heating costs. Last week while casting an absentee ballot in Portland, he flipped a reporter’s question about why the race was so close onto Collins.
“I guess I’m wondering why she’s not beating me by more,” he said. “Why is this logger from Allagash being competitive with you? I think that says a lot more about her record than it does about mine.”
BDN writer Elizabeth Walztoni contributed to this report.

title: Report: Peltola’s campaign involved in effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan for Alaska Senate race
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The Democratic campaign for Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state’s August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday’s general election.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press.
A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. The U.S. Constitution sets out only age, citizenship and residency requirements to run for the Senate.
President Donald Trump, who directed his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit last week pre-emptively contesting a Peltola win due to the presence of the second Dan Sullivan, called for legal penalties against Democrats over the situation: “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done,” Trump wrote on his social media site on Wednesday.
“Alaskans deserve the truth,” said Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan’s campaign. “Mary Peltola, her campaign and her senior advisers colluded with the DSCC, national Democrat lawyers and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse and deceive voters.”
Peltola’s campaign, in a statement Wednesday, said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan’s candidacy.
Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick.
“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan,” the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan.
Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. Department of Justice. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
“It’s a dirty campaign trick, and it’s good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot,” said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. “But now it’s in the hands of the voters, not litigation.”
It’s not the first time a candidate’s appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot.
The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week. Efforts by the AP to reach Rios were not immediately successful.
As of Monday, 46,204 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sen. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.
___
Riccardi reported from Denver.

title: Maine children's museum gets $100K to support school field trips
text:
The Children’s Museum & Theatre of Maine, located on Thompson’s Point in Portland, has received a $100,000 grant from the John T. Gorman Foundation to help schools bring students to the museum despite shrinking budgets for field trips.
“Historically, it was quite common for schools to have funds in their budgets for field trips,” said Julie Butcher Pezzino, the museum’s executive director. “That’s simply not the case anymore.”
Pezzino said schools are increasingly facing funding constraints that limit off-site educational trips. The museum’s school visit program directly subsidizes admission costs for participating schools.
The recent grant from foundation will help the museum offer tiered, needs-based admission charges, including free entry for qualifying schools, ensuring that financial constraints don’t limit learning experiences at the museum for Maine students.
“The Children’s Museum and Theatre of Maine provides valuable opportunities for children to play, learn and connect — experiences that support resilience and healthy development,” said Nicole Witherbee, president and CEO of the John T. Gorman Foundation.
“All Maine children should have the chance to benefit from these exhibits and programs,” Witherbee added. “The John T. Gorman Foundation is proud to support the Museum’s efforts to welcome students from across Maine who may not be able to visit otherwise.”
During the 2025-26 fiscal year, the museum welcomed close to 8,900 students, teachers and chaperones from 187 school groups — a 25% increase over the previous year.
The museum’s standard group rate is $9 per person. In fiscal 2026, 48% of school groups utilized reduced admission rates of $5 or less. The museum subsidized $140,141 in school visits during the fiscal year.
In the most recent Mainebiz Giving Guide, the John T. Gorman Foundation is listed as having annual revenue of $13.6 million, while the Children’s Museum & Theater of Maine has annual revenue of $4.2 million. The figures are from GuideStar by Candid.

title: 3 charged with conspiracy to commit murder in alleged Georgia school shooting plot
text:
3 charged with conspiracy to commit murder in alleged Georgia school shooting plot
Three people have been arrested in connection with an alleged plot to carry out a shooting at a Georgia high school, police announced Tuesday.
The investigation centers on Cherokee High School in Canton, which is in metro Atlanta, and comes less than two weeks after a 16-year-old boy killed three children and a teacher in a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in central Oregon.
Investigators collected firearms, ammunition and electronic devices during the investigation, police said. Authorities said they have identified no known ongoing threat to the school or any other Cherokee County school.
Related video above: Safety experts weigh in on additional measures schools could take to prevent or delay a shooter from gaining entry
Social media threats prompted investigation
The investigation began after the FBI identified threatening social media posts and alerted Cherokee County School District Police. School district officers contacted Canton police Oct. 19, prompting detectives to investigate.
Detectives linked the threats to a juvenile who lives in Canton, police said. The juvenile was arrested Oct. 20 and charged with conspiracy to commit murder and disruption or interference with the operation of public schools. Authorities have not released the juvenile’s name.
Investigators later identified two additional suspects and obtained arrest warrants Oct. 22.
Arrests in Georgia and California
Shane Keith Taylor, 17, of Metter, was arrested in his hometown Oct. 23 by Canton detectives with help from federal and state authorities and the Candler County Sheriff’s Office. He was charged with conspiracy to commit murder and taken to the Cherokee County Adult Detention Center.
Michael Brandon Terry, 21, of Chatsworth, California, was arrested the same day in California by the FBI and the Los Angeles Police Department. He was also charged with conspiracy to commit murder and was awaiting transport to the Cherokee County jail, according to the release.
Police did not detail how the three suspects were connected or what roles they allegedly played in the plot.
“The safety of our students and school staff is a top priority, and we take every threat seriously,” Canton Police Chief Marty Ferrell said. “I appreciate the quick action of our law enforcement partners and the dedication of our detectives in identifying and arresting the suspects.”
Police urge families to report threats
The investigation remains active. Police said they are withholding some details, including information about the evidence and the juvenile’s identity, to protect the investigation and comply with legal requirements.
The department urged parents to talk with their children about reporting threats and encouraged anyone who learns of a threat to contact law enforcement.
Anyone with information about the case can call Canton police at 770-720-4883 or submit a tip through the FBI’s online tip portal. Call 911 in an immediate emergency.
___
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Brunswick interfaith council to host community sing
text:
The Brunswick Area Interfaith Council will host “We the People Sing: All Voices Matter – A Pre-election Community Sing” on Sunday, Nov. 1, at 3:30 p.m. at the Gazebo on the Brunswick Mall.
Songs and readings will highlight the promise of our democracy and of the multifaith nation — that everyone participates and that all are valued. Participants are invited to bring a light (candle, lantern) to use as darkness falls on the first day of daylight saving time.
Familiar and some new easy to learn songs will be shared by a diverse group of song leaders, and lyric sheets will be provided. These are songs for all voices and designed to connect, inspire and unite us in the days just before the election.
One of the song leaders, The Rev. Kharma Amos of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Brunswick, shared in a preapared release, “As we approach the election, we gather in community because we need one another — all of us. Singing together helps us connect with our bodies and with the ever-richer harmonies that emerge when we each simply sing our part. This gathering is not designed for professional voices, nor is it intended to be a polished performance; rather, it is an invitation to be real and rooted in the knowledge that every voice in our democracy matters. Our songs of love and unity testify to a reality many of our spiritual traditions still believe is possible, and we make it more so when we work for it together.”
Participants are also invited to bring a chair if needed for this free gathering, and hot chocolate will be served.
The Brunswick Area Interfaith Council is a non-sectarian, nonprofit organization committed to fostering understanding, respect and cooperation among diverse faith traditions in the Brunswick area. Through collaborative efforts, BAIC promotes the spiritual, moral and social welfare of the larger Brunswick area community.
For more information, contact [email protected] or 207-240-0874.

title: Elvis tribute artist brings ‘Heartbreak Hotel’ to Bucksport Senior Center
text:
BUCKSPORT, Maine (WABI) - The Bucksport Senior Center turned into “Heartbreak Hotel” when Elvis tribute artist Jessi Mallory took the stage to perform Wednesday morning.
Mallory, who has performed as the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll for 17 years, brought the show to town through a partnership with beauty pageant Elana Kirby, known by her stage name “Miss Bucksport.”
The community event was meant to lift seniors’ spirits — and this crowd just can’t help falling in love with this performance.
“Elvis has been the universal language I have found because everybody has an Elvis story and everybody knows all the Elvis songs,” Mallory said. “It brings people together and that’s why I like to do this, because everybody gets along for the hour that I’m performing.”
Kirby said the idea sparked after seeing Mallory perform at another venue.
“I really like to get active in my community,” Kirby said. “I met Jessi while she was doing another gig at a different location, and I knew right away that this is something that we could definitely build on.”
When it comes to personal favorites from the King’s catalog, Mallory points to “Trying to Get to You,” while Kirby’s top pick is “Hound Dog.”
Kirby says she will be running for the title of “Ms. Maine for America Strong” this April.

title: Some packaged salads recalled for undeclared allergens
text:
(Gray News) - Packaged salads produced by Taylor Farms have been recalled due to an undeclared allergen.
According to the Food and Drug Administration, Taylor Farms is recalling its H-E-B Backyard BBQ Chop Salad because it may contain undeclared soy and tree nuts, specifically almonds.
“People who have sensitivity or allergy to soy and tree nuts (almonds) may be at risk of a serious adverse reaction if they consume this product,” an FDA press release said.
So far there have not been any illnesses or “adverse reactions” reported in connection with the recall.
The salads were sold in H-E-B stores across Texas. They can be identified by their UPC code, 041220300457, and their best-by date, Oct. 30, 2026.
Customers are asked not to eat the recalled salads and to throw them away or return them to the store for a refund.

title: 200 passengers stranded after US cruise ship suspends yearslong global voyage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia (AP) — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said.
Those on the ship had hoped to sail for years to come
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said. “We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement.”
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
For some, the venture was a risk worth taking
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn’t outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
“I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it’s a dream to live on the ship and I don’t want it to end,” Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn’t need to use a cane to walk anymore. “You come to this ship to live … it’s just sad that it’s all over.”
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship’s woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn’t regret her investment.
“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.
The cruise began in Northern Ireland in 2024
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship’s operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia’s then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.
