title: Democrats behind effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan for Alaska Senate race, new report confirms
text:
Democrats behind effort to recruit second Dan Sullivan for Alaska Senate race, new report confirms
The Democratic campaign for Alaska's U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state's August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday's general election.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press.
A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. The U.S. Constitution sets out only age, citizenship and residency requirements to run for the Senate.
President Donald Trump, who directed his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit last week pre-emptively contesting a Peltola win due to the presence of the second Dan Sullivan, called for legal penalties against Democrats over the situation: “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done,” Trump wrote on his social media site on Wednesday.
“Alaskans deserve the truth,” said Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan’s campaign. “Mary Peltola, her campaign and her senior advisers colluded with the DSCC, national Democrat lawyers and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse and deceive voters.”
Peltola's campaign, in a statement Wednesday, said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan's candidacy.
Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick.
“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan," the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan.
Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. Department of Justice. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
“It’s a dirty campaign trick, and it’s good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot,” said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. “But now it’s in the hands of the voters, not litigation.”
It's not the first time a candidate's appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot.
The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week.
As of Monday, 46,204 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sen. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.

title: DOJ expands push to halt counting of ballots cast by suspected noncitizens
text:
DOJ expands push to halt counting of ballots cast by suspected noncitizens
Critics say the Justice Department's effort risks disenfranchising legitimate voters.
DOJ expands push to halt counting of ballots cast by suspected noncitizens
Critics say the Justice Department's effort risks disenfranchising legitimate voters.
A federal judge heard arguments on Tuesday in the Trump administration's push to stop ballots cast by 20,000 suspected noncitizens from being counted in California, as critics warn the last-minute effort risks disenfranchising legitimate voters and delaying the certification of results.
As the legal battle escalates, the Justice Department separately urged Washington state this week to sequester ballots from more than 400 potential noncitizens.
“Eligible citizens are not affected. We asked counties to set aside these ballots, not cancel them, until citizenship is confirmed," said DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels.
California officials have argued that the demand comes too close to Election Day. They have also raised serious doubts about the accuracy of the federal government's list.
"There's ample reason to doubt the accuracy of that list," echoed Stephen Richer, a legal fellow at the Cato Institute. "Just because somebody's not a confirmed citizen in those federal databases does not mean by any stretch of the imagination that the person is not a citizen."
Richer said that previous audits and investigations have found that noncitizen voting is uncommon, but not nonexistent.
The DOJ said Tuesday that it has charged 133 noncitizens across 21 states with illegal voting and registration offenses in the past eight weeks. Since the beginning of the second Trump administration, 177 people have been charged with voting fraud-related offenses.
Richer said those cases are not widespread enough to sway the outcome of an election.
"That number represents a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of the number of registered voters," Richer said. "That's against over 150 million Americans voting in just the November 2020 election alone."
California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said that the Trump administration's emphasis on the issue is designed to undermine confidence in the election results.
"They are preparing for a blue wave and a shellacking in the midterms, and they're planning their post-election loss excuses by planting seeds across the country to sow distrust," Bonta told CNN on Monday.
Pels, the DOJ's spokesperson, responded to that concern in an email, saying, "What undermines confidence is non citizens voting."
President Donald Trump told reporters on Tuesday that he will accept the election results "if they are honest."

title: Illegal moonshine distillery explodes, catches fire in mountains, officials say
text:
WILKES COUNTY, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - An explosion at an illegal moonshine distillery sparked a fire in the North Carolina mountains on Monday, according to authorities.
Special agents from North Carolina’s Alcohol Law Enforcement Division were called to investigate the explosion in Wilkes County, North Carolina.
Agents found an active 200-gallon illegal distillery. They seized about 1,800 gallons of mash, which is used to make moonshine, and 161 gallons of illegal moonshine.
North Carolina officials shared photos showing the charred inside of a metal building. Distilling equipment was also damaged.
Billy Ray Anderson, 69, was arrested and charged with manufacturing a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession for sale of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of distillery equipment, possession of distillery ingredients and allowing property to be used for the manufacture of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage.
Moonshine is believed to have originated in North Carolina and was once an important source of income, particularly for rural residents.

title: REVIEW POTPOURRI: Beniamino Gigli and the golden age of opera
text:
Beniamino Gigli
Italian tenor Beniamino Gigli (1890 – 1957) recorded prolifically for Victor Red Seal since he first emerged as a major contender in the early 1920s.
I recently listened to a ten-inch acoustic shellac (Victrola Red Seal 1025) featuring two selections – Song of the Swan, which is a reworking for tenor of Camille Saint-Saens’s The Swan usually played by the cello; and Paquita, a Spanish Serenade.
In 1996, a CD label Romophone issued three sets, titled The Complete Victor Recordings. I played Volume 2 encompassing Gigli’s records from 1926 to ’28 on two discs covering 37 sides originally released as 78s (Romophone 82004-2).
The acoustic shellac had Gigli doing his very youthful best with two items of, for me, minor musical interest whereas the CDs had his glorious arias from Puccini’s Boheme and Tosca, Donizetti’s Lucia di Lammermoor, and Mascagni’s Cavalleria – the Tosca Recondita Armonia tenor solo in Act 1 as sung by Gigli as the doomed Mario never fails to give me goosebumps.
Other gems include the Rigoletto Quartet with soprano Amelita Galli-Curci, contralto Louise Homer and baritone Giuseppe de Luca and the Lucia Sextet and Tomb Scene classic duet with Enzio Pinza along with alternate takes of the same selections.
There’s a generous helping of Neapolitan Songs which Gigli, Caruso, Mario Lanza and Luciano Pavarotti had the beauty and artistry to render convincingly, in small doses, whereas other less talented tenors poured on too much maple syrup.
My first exposure to Gigli’s singing came during June 1964 when Mother and we four kids attended the annual Quaker Yearly Meeting, at Pembroke College, in Providence, Rhode Island, my first experience being in any state besides Maine and New Hampshire. To make this already long story a little less long, my first item of agenda was seeking out, and quickly finding, a big city record store, just two blocks from the dormitory where we were staying, the very well stocked Lyons Record Shop.
My 13th birthday was the very day we arrived and my late Aunt Margaret Cates (1913-2002) gifted me $2. I espied a one dollar anthology, Great Voices of the Century, featuring ten legendary singers in as many selections – Feodor Chaliapin, John McCormack, Maggie Teyte, Tito Schipa, Claudia Muzio, Lauritz Melchior, Lotte Lehmann, Elizabeth Schumann and Gigli, whose late 30s performance of Vesti la Giubba from Leoncavallo’s Pagliacci (Folks might recognize the music, often used in television shows, commercials and movies) began side one.
I found Gigli’s voice powerful yet the music didn’t particularly move me. Thirty years later, I procured a batch of Red Seal 78s which included a 1926 disc of Gigli singing Celeste Aida from Verdi’s opera Aida accompanied by the very underrated Maestro Walter Goehr (1903-1960) then only 23 but already showing enough gifts to be hired as a full time house conductor for dozens of recording sessions by England’s EMI, the same label that signed the Beatles almost 40 years later.
I have played that Victor disc numerous times and still consider it one of the finest recordings of anything from Gigli, Walter Goehr and Giuseppe Verdi.
Gigli had a voice more richly expressive than even Pavarotti and his two buddies, the very overrated Placido Domingo and the otherwise very captivating Jose Carreras.
YouTubes of Gigli abound and I would recommend hearing his recordings of Cavalleria with the composer conducting at La Scala and the Tosca, Boheme and Madame Butterfly.
My live opera experiences in Maine:
In 1966, I saw a staged production of Verdi’s Rigoletto at August’s former Cony High School auditorium, courtesy of a touring Metropolitan Opera cast.
In 1970, the Portland Symphony under its music director staged its own production of Mozart’s Cosi Fan Tutte, at Merrill Auditorium.
In 1980, the music department of the University of Maine at Orono presented Johann Strauss’s Die Fledermaus on a smaller stage than those in Augusta and Portland.
Those involved in all three operas did very good work.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Aging Untold: Fat-free doesn’t always mean healthy
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we separate facts from fiction on “fat-free” foods to help you protect your heart and make healthier grocery choices.
Then, National Alliance for Caregiving CEO Jason Resendez joins us to discuss the mounting pressures facing the sandwich generation and policy solutions offering caregiver relief.
Plus, we meet the “Flower Buds,” an inspiring volunteer group in Kentucky that rescues discarded blooms to deliver hope and comfort across its community.
The “fat-free” option at the grocery store is not always the healthy option.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the label can be misleading.
“So if they’re removing the fat, they had to replace it with something else. So you have to look at the ingredients and look at the packaging,” she said.
Rogers said she used to find all the fat categories confusing, so she created a simple way to sort them.
The National Alliance for Caregiving is championing changes “to address so many of the pain points that family caregivers face every day,” President and CEO Jason Resendez said.
He recently testified before the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging and brought three policies to lawmakers: funding for the Older Americans Act, national paid family and medical leave and a bigger role for Medicare.
He said the three policies together “represent a stronger foundation to help family caregivers provide care sustainably, with dignity and with equity over time.”
The crystal and gemstone industry is booming, but experts warn buyers to be cautious of fake products flooding the market.
Jamie Inglett, who owns a crystal shop in Sedona, said consumers can find fake crystals in stores and at gem shows. She said buyers could end up with lab-grown crystals being sold as natural stones.
Volunteers who call themselves the Flower Buds are giving flowers from weddings, funerals and other community events a new life.
They bring the donated flowers to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities and shelters.
The group is celebrating a major milestone: since 2006, the Flower Buds have delivered more than 90,000 vases of flowers.

title: They’re back: Gorham volleyball returns to Class A final
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SANFORD — Emma Tirrell didn’t try to hide it: She still gets nervous at playoff time.
Her Gorham volleyball team? Apparently, not so much.
The second-seeded Rams returned to the Class A final for the fifth straight season Wednesday, and will play for a fourth straight state title after defeating No. 3 Thornton Academy, 3-1, in the semifinals at Sanford High School.
Gorham (13-3) won the first two sets 25-23 and 25-17, dropped the third 25-14, then clinched the match with a 25-9 win in the fourth.
“I can’t tell you how nervous I get for every single playoff game for all of my 10 years. I was probably more nervous today than I have been any day,” said Tirrell, the Rams’ coach. “And then the girls come out, they squash my nerves and they show me why we’re here.”
The Golden Trojans (12-4) saw their season end with a loss to the Rams for the second straight season. Thornton fell in last year’s Class A final.
“This team is amazing. I have nothing bad to say about them,” coach Kayla Arthers said. “(Gorham) obviously (has) been in a situation like this for the past four years. And for some of us, yes, we’ve only been here for two years, for others it’s their first time.
“It is difficult in a big setting like this … (to) go against a team people want to knock down.”
PLAYOFF POISE
The experience factor seemed to pay off right away for Gorham, which needed five sets to beat Thornton in one match this year, then trailed in every set of a four-set victory in another.
On Wednesday, however, the Rams were in charge quickly. They finished the first set on an 8-5 run to gain the upper hand, never trailed in the second, and rebounded from a lopsided third set defeat with an even more one-sided win in the fourth.
“They had sort of an off night, and we just took advantage of that,” said senior setter Liana Edwards. “It’s an amazing feeling all of us have had, playing in front of big crowds and big gyms, and playing against amazing teams. I feel like we’re used to all the pressure.”
SWEET SETUP
The Rams were never better than when Edwards, the two-time reigning Gatorade Player of the Year, was setting up middle hitter Abbie Stevens by the net for a connection that often seemed unstoppable. Stevens had 18 kills — five apiece in each of Gorham’s wins — with 12 coming off assists from Edwards.
“It’s my favorite thing in the world,” Tirrell said.
Stevens said the connection is the product of repetition.
“We spend a lot of time together, because we’re on the same club team. We’ve had a lot of practice with the connection and certain plays,” she said. “Just that time, and trusting each other too. We know we can both put the ball away.”
MAKING ADJUSTMENTS
Tirrell said the Rams made a midseason switch from a 6-2 to a 5-1, giving Edwards a chance to set more exclusively. It paid off Wednesday, as Gorham had its most commanding win of three victories over the Trojans.
“We weren’t executing the way we needed to,” Tirrell said. “Changing that offense is a big thing for us, but I also think discipline and their want for it (made a difference).”
UNSUNG HERO
Kasey Plaud helped lead Gorham to the first-set victory with a pair of aces, and then had three of her five kills in the final set to help the Rams clinch the match.
STAT LEADERS
• Gorham: Liana Edwards (31 assists, nine kills, five aces), Abbie Stevens (18 kills, two aces), Sophie MacIsaac (seven kills), Kasey Plaud (five kills, three aces), Luna Button, Lindsay Farquhar (five kills each).
• Thornton Academy: Addie Petit (20 assists), Ece Eruygun (11 assists), Sophie von Meyer (11 kills), Sarah Berg (eight kills), Lotus Porter (seven kills).

title: Trump’s desperation is on display
text:
President Trump personifies desperation right now, worried that he will lose his power. He has wielded this power at will. Loyalty is an absolute in his relationship with everyone. Abuse of power is one of his defining characteristics.
Ironically, his loyalty extends to Putin. Putin is a perfect example of a person who abuses power in his need to have control. Trump’s move to release the sanctions on Russian diesel was a move to curry Putin’s favor, and a reminder of Putin’s power over our nation and our elections.
Desperation is a curious driver, and Trump relishes power and is abusing it as he faces the prospect of no longer having the autonomy that he has enjoyed. His willingness to comprise and degrade democracy is despicable.
David Hyde
Pownal

Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main challenger in Israel’s elections?
text:
Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main challenger in Israel’s elections?
Hawkish, reserved and unpolished, Israel's former military chief has a viable chance of unseating Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
His name is Gadi Eisenkot. And while the votes from Tuesday's election are still being counted, his centrist party, Yashar, along with other opposition allies, has the clearest path to power if they can join forces with Arab-led parties, though pulling it off may prove difficult.
It has been a remarkable climb for the 66-year-old, who was raised by Moroccan-Jewish immigrants, and whose son died fighting in the latest war in Gaza. But it's also a major challenge for a man relatively untested in Israel's hardscrabble tradition of coalition building.
The commander of some of Israel's most difficult wartime battles, he is now up against Netanyahu, who has shown, time and time again, an almost uncanny ability to survive the cutthroat world of Israeli politics.
Nevertheless, Eisenkot was ecstatic and determined late Tuesday as initial exit polls suggested a big loss for Netanyahu.
“We have made history!" he bellowed from a podium in Tel Aviv.
“Millions of Israelis have had enough of the culture of lies, of failure, of division and incitement," Eisenkot said. "Tonight marks the beginning of a path that must lead to the formation of a Zionist government.”
Preliminary results from Israel’s elections commission on Wednesday have since shown the prime minister’s party pulling ahead, but without a clear majority. Eisenkot's coalition — a mix of center-right and more liberal figures — is a close second but would need to partner with Arab-led parties for an outright majority.
Eisenkot could form a majority coalition but it wouldn't be easy
In Israeli politics, where higher vote counts don’t automatically translate into political victories, the ability to amass a coalition is key.
Emerging results indicated that neither Netanyahu’s nor Eisenkot’s coalition blocs would reach the 61 seats needed for a majority; local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties, and 19 for Arab-led parties.
While Netanyahu and many members of his party, Likud, have ruled out working with minority Arab parties, Eisenkot has not.
The parties, composed mainly of Palestinian Muslims and Christians, made a historic showing at the polls in Tuesday's election. If Eisenkot can convince them to join his coalition, he could gain enough seats to form a majority in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament.
Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List of Arab parties, is calling for a “true and equal” Jewish-Arab partnership to help oust Netanyahu’s government after a strong showing by Arab-led parties.
Eisenkot is up against the clock
By partnering with Arab parties, Eisenkot could lose the support of more right-wing members of his coalition, endangering his bloc from the opposite flank.
In a bid to prevent such defections, his party has asked Israel’s Arab parties to publicly profess certain principles: that Israel is a Jewish and democratic state, guided by the Israeli declaration of independence; that Hamas is a terrorist organization that should be disarmed and demolished; and that ultra-Orthodox Jews and Palestinian citizens of Israel must no longer be exempt from Israel’s mandatory military draft.
“There is currently no ultra-Orthodox or Arab party that supports these four principles,” Yashar candidate Lian Polak-David said to The Associated Press on Tuesday night.
They must reach an agreement soon or risk going to another round of elections. Thousands of citizens who flew into Israel to vote in the first round might be unable to return for a second, and Arab parties would likely suffer from lower turnout, too.
“We must act swiftly. This is the imperative of the hour, and uniting our people is essential," Eisenkot said Tuesday night in Tel Aviv.
Eisenkot is seen as an antidote to Netanyahu's Israel
Eisenkot has halting English and comes from a working-class family. He spent four decades in Israel’s military. His 25-year-old son, Gal Meir Eisenkot, was killed in combat in Gaza.
Netanyahu is a U.S.-educated elite, marred by corruption scandals. The International Criminal Court seeks his arrest. Netanyahu’s son, Yair Netanyahu, is a podcaster who lives part time in Florida and has used the legal name “Yonatan Hun,” according to Israel’s Haaretz newspaper.
After the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Eisenkot took on a role as an observer in Netanyahu’s war Cabinet. That day, the militants killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage. Israel then launched a war in Gaza that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians, according to the territory’s health ministry, which doesn’t distinguish between civilians and combatants in its count.
In June 2024, Eisenkot followed a colleague out of the Cabinet, writing in his resignation letter that Netanyahu was letting politics influence decision-making, harming Israel’s ability to achieve its war goals.
Eisenkot’s two nephews who were deployed to combat were also killed fighting in Gaza.
The personal losses raised Eisenkot’s profile among Israelis and gave him credibility as someone who, having paid the ultimate price, wouldn’t needlessly sacrifice soldiers.
Eisenkot's platform: Probe Oct. 7, widen the draft and strengthen security
Eisenkot, like others in the opposition, says Netanyahu should be held accountable for Oct. 7 and the failure to turn battlefield victories into diplomatic achievements. They support launching a state inquiry into the failures that led to the Hamas attacks that day — a probe Netanyahu has long refused.
When it comes to the country’s ultra-Orthodox population, Eisenkot has said he will not compromise on legislation mandating they also serve in the military.
Eisenkot is no dove. Like nearly all the prime minister’s rivals, Eisenkot has supported Israeli military operations in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
He says he wants to dial tensions down with the Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and follow U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan for Gaza.
He supports settlements but says he would evacuate unauthorized settler outposts, which rights groups say are the primary drivers of violence against Palestinians.
While at times he has emphasized diplomacy to address Israel’s security challenges, he also is credited with formulating Israel’s so‑called Dahiyeh Doctrine, named after the area in Beirut’s southern suburbs where the Hezbollah militant group has a stronghold. It's a military strategy advocating the use of disproportionate power against any entity that fires on Israel, no matter how small or insignificant.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: A Few Clouds Possible Wednesday, with Mild Temperatures Likely for Thursday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Wednesday. We had a decent day across the region today with plenty of sunshine, as high pressure took control off the region sitting off to our west. Skies remain clear overnight tonight, combined with light winds will result in some of our coldest readings so far this season. Sunshine is expected again tomorrow, helping temperatures rebound back closer to average heading into the midday and afternoon hours. Thursday also looks to feature sunshine, but a change in wind direction results in high temperatures well above average for this time of year.
With the rest of tonight remaining mostly clear. Temperatures will have no problem continuing to cool off overnight into tomorrow morning. Low temperatures tonight for most locations look to plumet back into the mid to upper teens. Light northwesterly winds will also be a driving factor in allowing colder air to settle into the region.
Plenty of sunshine is expected again tomorrow. The primary difference between tomorrow and today will be increased cloud coverage during the afternoon hours. I don’t expect this to ruin the day by any means, but it will result in one of the differences to tomorrow’s forecast compared to today. High temperatures tomorrow will have no problem rebounding into the lower to mid 40s after the bitter cold start to the day. Winds are still expected to remain light during the day tomorrow, but coming from a westerly direction means there won’t be as much of a temperature influence tomorrow.
Our next chance at more active weather arrives Thursday night in the form of a cold front. Expect showers over northern and western locations Thursday evening into Thursday night, with central and southern portions of Aroostook County seeing shower activity arrive during the early morning hours of Friday. I’m not expecting any sort of substantial rainfall from this cold front. Ultimately I think we’ll be lucky to see a few tenths of an inch of rainfall, before sunshine returns to the region heading into the upcoming weekend.
Temperatures are likely to peak this week during the daytime hours of Thursday, with highs by the afternoon hours reaching the lower to even mid 60s for some lucky towns. The end of the work week looks to be cooler, with mid 50 degree readings expected Friday, before falling back into the mid to upper 40s for the start of the new weekend. Temperatures are likely back above average the second half of the weekend into the new work week.

title: Dolores Huerta, pioneering labor organizer and civil rights icon, dies at 96
text:
(AP) - Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation’s fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase “Sí, se puede!” that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta’s family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.
Huerta was born in New Mexico and raised by a single mother in California’s San Joaquin Valley, where she worked as a school teacher and then helped found a local chapter of a grassroots organization that fought segregation and police brutality.
She quickly turned her interests to farm laborers and co-founded with César Chavez what eventually became the United Farm Workers of America.
Huerta’s resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to “Yes, it can be done” — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.
Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.
This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community and activist circles when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died.
From the early 1970s on, Huerta’s life partner was Richard Chavez, César’s brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.
Huerta said she stayed silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life’s work and unravel all the progress made for workers.
In the wake of the revelation, she urged people to stand firm in fighting for their rights.
Even into her mid-90s, Huerta marched and spoke in cities nationwide on race, poverty and women’s rights on behalf of her California-based Dolores Huerta Foundation.

title: Ben and Malorie Sprague become new franchise owners of Coffee News
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A nearly 40-year-old staple found in more than 300 diners and coffee shops around the globe is entering a new chapter.
Ben Sprague says he and his wife Malorie, who already operated the local Bangor edition, have acquired the worldwide franchise business.
“It’s kind of one of these secret hidden gem businesses, and we’re honored to have acquired the Coffee News franchise business,” said Sprague.
Coffee News is a free one-page, hyper-local publication known for trivia, jokes, horoscopes and community events. And its reach has gone far beyond Bangor.
“If you’re on vacation in Auckland, New Zealand, you might see a Coffee News and it would be pretty similar to how it is in Bangor,”
On why they wanted ownership, Sprague said: “I kind of feel the world needs Coffee News. It’s positive content. It makes people smile. It brings people together,” said Sprague. “We say we deliver smiles weekly to people,” Sprague added.
The ownership change happened about six months ago after what Sprague called a “quiet phase” and “honeymoon quiet phase” with the previous local owners to ensure a smooth transition.
He says the familiar look, largely unchanged for almost 40 years, will stay,
“That brand, the familiarity and the nostalgia. We’re going to keep all of that in place. But we are going to try to make some tweaks to modernize and to make sure Coffee News is relevant to the next generation of readers. That could be just adjusting the content a little bit. So say the trivia questions has a question about Harry Potter or Toy Story or Sabrina Carpenter,” said Sprague.
And if you’re wondering about what’s going to happen to the paper’s iconic character.
“It will stay Little Bill. We’re not trying to change too much and Little Bill is one of the most beloved things about Coffee News,” Sprague said.

title: ADHD linked to higher risk of late-life cognitive impairment and dementia in new study
text:
ADHD linked to higher risk of late-life cognitive impairment and dementia in new study
Research and discussion of ADHD have historically centered on kids, but the disorder affects people across the whole lifespan, including in old age. Now, scientists are probing how ADHD relates to brain health during that life stage.
A new study that examined more than 180,000 older adults linked ADHD with a higher risk of cognitive impairment and dementia. Importantly, this research doesn’t mean that attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder causes dementia, but it underscores the importance of awareness and the need for more research.
The study, published earlier this month in JAMA Psychiatry, found ADHD was associated with roughly four times the hazard of cognitive impairment or dementia in the older adults studied. Researchers also found that for people who did develop cognitive impairment, those with ADHD reported poorer mental health and social satisfaction and had more medical visits.
This study builds on growing evidence of such a link from past research in other countries.
What the study looked at
For the study, researchers from several countries analyzed health records from 187,341 U.S. adults over age 50. They found that 6.7% of study participants with ADHD developed dementia or mild cognitive impairment, compared with 3.4% of those not diagnosed with ADHD. When they controlled for factors that could affect the association, like race, gender and some other health conditions, that association remained: Participants with ADHD had a "markedly increased" risk of developing cognitive impairment.
Mild cognitive impairment includes problems with memory, thinking, or other cognitive abilities that exceed what's expected for a person's age but don't prevent someone from independently handling their everyday activities.
Because some people with ADHD also have other psychiatric conditions, like depression and anxiety, the researchers also tested whether the link held when they controlled for those variables. Indeed, ADHD was still associated with more than three times the hazard ratio for cognitive impairment or dementia in the study.
Results don't mean ADHD causes dementia
Guilherme Bauer-Negrini, a researcher in biomedical data science at the University of Pittsburgh and co-first author of the paper, said he was struck by how solid the association was.
"Despite every correction that we did — statistical model, or taking into account other factors, such as comorbidities, health access, smoking habits, any of the other things that could partially explain this association — the association with ADHD was still there and was still strong," Bauer-Negrini said, even taking into account neuropsychiatric factors that are "hugely associated with dementia."
Importantly, the study only found an association. It did not show or attempt to prove that ADHD itself causes cognitive impairment or dementia. This also doesn't mean that having ADHD necessarily means you’ll develop dementia: Though the percentage of people who did in this study was higher among those with ADHD, it was still small.
"Most people with ADHD in our study did not develop cognitive impairment," Dr. Douglas Teixeira Leffa, a psychiatrist who was co-first author of the study, emphasized.
"We should be attentive to these cognitive changes as people with ADHD age, while continuing to investigate why this association exists and whether there are interventions that could ultimately reduce the risk," Leffa said.
Study took a new angle by looking at participants' genes, not just medical records
There's thought to be a strong genetic component to ADHD. So in addition to using ADHD diagnoses to study the association, the researchers also looked at a measure of ADHD risk calculated from participants’ genes. For people who didn’t have a noted ADHD diagnosis but had a greater genetic risk of ADHD, there was a link between higher risk and cognitive impairment. Those in the highest genetic risk category had a 35% higher chance of impairment than those in the lowest risk category when statistically adjusted — a smaller jump, but still a notable one.
To their knowledge, these researchers were the first to use genetic information within one population to study this specific link.
"The genetic data sort of gives us another idea that maybe there's something that we still don't know — what it is about ADHD that might directly be associated with cognitive decline," Leffa said.
In addition to strengthening existing evidence, these researchers also brought a new finding to the field — namely, that people who had ADHD and ended up developing cognitive impairment or dementia saw some poorer health outcomes. They reported going to the doctor more, having worse mental health and being less satisfied socially.
The people studied were participants in the All of Us Research Program, an effort from a coalition of scientists to collect and study data from one million or more people in the U.S.
Future research could probe explanations and treatment
This study focused on risk and building evidence of a link between ADHD and cognitive decline, but it wasn’t aimed at determining why such a link exists. The scientific community isn't yet sure why there is a connection, and Leffa said future research is needed to investigate that.
To explore whether the disorder actually causes dementia, a study would need to follow up participants over the course of their lifespan. But that kind of long-term data isn’t available yet for ADHD.
“One question that people usually are very interested is, what is the role of treatment?” Leffa said. Could treating ADHD be beneficial in preventing the development of cognitive impairment, or is there evidence that it could somehow be harmful?
“The not-so-nice answer, but the clearest one, is that we still don't; there's not enough evidence out there to give us a good indication on either of those hypotheses,” Leffa said. “And that's because we still don't have good data to kind of explore this question.”
Sandra Kooij, a psychiatrist who’s an expert on ADHD in adults and a professor of psychiatry at the Amsterdam University Medical Center in the Netherlands, said it’s not a completely new finding that there is a relationship between ADHD and cognitive decline.
Kooij, who was not involved in this study, said future research is needed to help researchers understand what drives the link.
Every study concerning cognitive decline "increases the pressure" to address prevention, she said, emphasizing that it’s important to integrate mental and physical healthcare.
What people with ADHD and healthcare providers should know
Bauer-Negrini said he hopes research around this link provides “an opportunity for monitoring, prevention and research” and will help “provide better care for people with ADHD in late life.”
The study suggests that clinicians “should be attentive to these cognitive changes as people with ADHD age,” Leffa said, paying particular attention to what symptoms are typical of a particular patient.
“The way we understand ADHD is that those symptoms, even though they can fluctuate over time, they are relatively stable for most folks. So if you feel like something is definitely getting worse, different than how it was … you might benefit from another, from an assessment for that,” he said.
Leffa said he thinks everyone should be mindful of their cognitive health and take protective actions as they get older.
“I would suggest that individuals with or without a diagnosis of ADHD take precautions that we know can be effective to promote cognitive or brain health as they get old, like doing physical exercise, being cognitively and socially active, also being mindful about their diet, taking care of their cardiovascular risk factors,” Leffa said. “All of that contributes to brain health and decreases, potentially decreases, chances of developing cognitive decline.”

title: Grandmother not indicted in baby’s death after police say she left her in hot car for 8 hours while she worked
text:
MADISONVILLE, Ky. (WFIE/Gray News) — A Kentucky doctor who accidentally left her grandchild unattended in a hot car for about eight hours will not be indicted for the baby’s death.
Madisonville police said 10-month-old Scottie Crowell died in August.
On Tuesday, a grand jury found there was insufficient probable cause for an indictment.
Police said Scottie’s grandmother picked her up in the morning of Aug. 13 and was supposed to take her to daycare.
She forgot the child was in the car and went to work, police said.
She arrived at Owensboro Health Multi-Care, where she works as a doctor, around 8 a.m.
The baby’s father called his wife after trying to pick up Scottie from daycare, but the child was not there.
The baby’s mother called the grandmother at work, and the grandmother ran outside and saw Scottie was still in the vehicle around 4 p.m., police said.
After 911 was called, first responders tried to administer lifesaving measures, but the baby died.
“I would ask that you keep the infant’s parents and family in your thoughts and prayers as they continue to grieve and process this unimaginable loss,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Hannah Kington-Jarvis.

title: Maine agency hosts event to help veterans who are in need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Bureau of Veterans' Services hosts event to help vets who are in need
Other organizations were also on hand for the "Homeless Veterans Stand Down"
Maine Bureau of Veterans' Services hosts event to help vets who are in need
Other organizations were also on hand for the "Homeless Veterans Stand Down"
As political candidates talk about helping Maine veterans, community organizations did something about it Wednesday.
In a parking lot on the former Brunswick Naval Air Station, the Maine Bureau of Veterans' Services hosted a "Homeless Veterans Stand Down."
"They're an effort to do outreach in our communities, to make sure that we are reaching out to any homeless veteran or at-risk veteran, get them connected with benefits, housing, cold weather gear, food, whatever resources they may need for their specific situation," said Matthew Kennedy, Maine's deputy supervisor of veterans' services.
Along with the Maine Bureau of Veterans' Services, there were other organizations on hand offering information to help those in need.
Anthony Ward, 68, an Army veteran who was injured during a training exercise in the Mojave Desert in 1980, said he is getting evicted from his home.
"I got to be out November 30," Ward said. "They're trying to help me find a home. I have six cats," Ward said.
There was a food truck at Wednesday's event, as well as two employees of SportClips who were offering free haircuts.
Ward, who has shoulder-length hair, said he was passing on the free trim.
"I told my daughter that I'm not cutting my hair until I'm dead. She goes, 'Daddy, on your deathbed, I'll cut your hair,'" Ward said with a laugh.
Ward was put in touch with people who can help find him a new place to live, and for that, he said he was thankful.
"I just thank God for them. If it wasn't for the veterans, I'd probably be dead right now," Ward said.
The Maine Bureau of Veterans' Services has hosted nine of these events across the state this year. If you or someone you know would like more information, you can visit maine.gov/veterans.

title: South Portland man charged with sexual assault of a teen in Oxford County
text:
An Oxford County sheriff’s deputy conducting a welfare check Tuesday in Buckfield discovered a South Portland man who was wanted for alleged sexual assault of a girl under age 15 and furnishing liquor to her and another teenager.
The deputy was checking on a report of a possible unresponsive man at the intersection of Darnit Road and Brock School Road, Maj. Dana Thompson wrote in a news release.
The deputy determined the man, Diego Ramirez, 29, had been indicted earlier this month by an Oxford County grand jury on 12 counts, including sexual assault, sexual abuse of a minor, endangering the welfare of a child, furnishing alcohol to a minor and allowing a minor to consume alcohol, Thompson said.
Ramirez was arrested and was being held on $25,000 cash bail with a number of conditions, including no contact with the victims, Thompson wrote.
A second man in the case, Nkialuzitu Mayingi, 31, of Gorham, was also indicted earlier this month and is being held at the Oxford County Jail in South Paris. He is charged with five counts of sexual assault, several counts of sexual abuse of a minor, endangering the welfare of a child and furnishing drugs and alcohol to minors, including another girl under age 15.

title: This Maine man dresses ‘The Masked Singer’
text:
Luke D’Alessandro first became fascinated with the art and magic of creating a live show while acting in youth theater and school plays in Biddeford.
His passion and curiosity led him to a performing arts high school in Michigan, college in Australia, summer theater jobs in Italy and TV sets in Hollywood. The Biddeford native is now working on the the Fox reality show “The Masked Singer.” He won his first Emmy this fall, for his work on the show’s outrageous costumes.
“I hope that young people in Maine see that there are opportunities everywhere, you just gotta go for it and follow your dreams,” said D’Alessandro, 30. “That’s kind of what I did.”
D’Alessandro shares the Emmy with five others who help create costumes for “The Masked Singer.” The show is focused on celebrity guests who sing for a panel of judges while wearing disguises that have some elements of props or set pieces. Some of last season’s costumes included singer/actor Jack Wagner as a giant purple eggplant, actor Taraji P. Henson in a glittering costume inspired by a scarab, and former Boston Red Sox slugger David Ortiz as a fuzzy red monster with googly eyes.
Ideas for the characters come from the producers, sometimes inspired by the real identity of the person the costume is meant to disguise, D’Alessandro said. Then the costumes are built, head to toe. As head designer, D’Alessandro is involved in all the costumes. The work is more like that of a production designer, he says.
“These aren’t just garments, jeans and T-shirts, they have some elements that are soft and sculptural and some that are hard plastics or weird material,” D’Alessandro said. “They have to blend somewhere in the middle.”
D’Alessandro and five other people won the Emmy for “The Masked Singer” costumes in early September. The category was outstanding costumes for a variety, nonfiction or reality program. In a video posted after the award was presented, D’Alessandro can be seen holding the Emmy, standing on stage in the middle of the group. He thanked the Television Academy, Fox studios, a few specific people and “the entire team that makes our costumes come to life.”
The show’s most recent season ended in April. It has been renewed for another season but no specific dates have yet been announced. The show had been filmed in Hollywood but is now being filmed New Jersey, close to New York City.
MAINE STAGES
Performing arts run deep in D’Alessandro’s family. His grandfather, Eugene D’Alessandro Sr., founded the legendary Geno’s Rock Club in Portland in the 1980s. D’Alessandro’s father also ran the club. He remembers spending time there on mornings when his father had errands to run, with his twin brother, Dominic. They played songs on the jukebox, danced around and drank Shirley Temples.
As a kid, he was always diving into the costume box at home. By the time he was in Biddeford Middle School, he was acting in plays and involved in various theater programs, including theater camps. He was particularly inspired by his experience at the Academy of Developing Artists of Maine (ADAM), run by Ronda Verges in Biddeford. It was then he started to explore some of the other jobs and skills needed to put on a show, besides acting.
“I remember Ronda saying ‘OK, if you’re going to be an actor you need to have some other skills. You need to learn something about costumes, lighting, sound,” said D’Alessandro. “That sort of opened up my eyes to the backstage part of it. “
By high school he realized he had a knack for design, for helping to created characters and worlds, and wanted to focus on that rather than acting. He applied to a performing arts high school in Michigan, Interlochen Arts Academy, without telling his parents. He was accepted, and his parents were immediately supportive.
At first, the family wasn’t sure how they’d pay the tuition. But then D’Alessandro got financial aid that covered most of it, and he packed his bags and headed for Michigan. After his junior year at Interlochen, he got the opportunity to travel to Italy with some of the teachers who had summer jobs working on operas. He worked as a prop master, making hand props and painting scenery, among other things.
An Interlochen graduate who was working as a set designer on Broadway suggested to D’Alessandro that he consider attending college at the National Institute of Dramatic Art in Sydney, Australia. He applied there and to a school in London. He ended up going to NIDA, where he earned a bachelor’s degree in Properties and Objects in 2018 and a master’s degree in Design for Performance in 2020.
He began working professionally in Australia, including on Australian versions of “The Masked Singer” and “Dancing with the Stars.” He started in the workroom, sewing, dying fabric, putting on rhinestones, before working his way to costume design.
After working a couple seasons on the Australian version of “The Masked Singer,” he got a chance to work on the American version, in Hollywood. He’s been head designer for the past four seasons of the show.
When not working on “The Masked Singer,” D’Alessandro lives in Utrecht, in the Netherlands, after nearly a dozen years of living in Australia. When he talks, a slight Aussie accent can be detected.
In between seasons of “The Masked Singer,” D’Alessandro has done freelance theater design, working on sets and costumes, and as a freelance prop maker and painter. He’s also done costume work for films, including a couple of Marvel superhero films: “Thor: Love and Thunder,” starring Chris Hemsworth; and “Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings,” starring Simu Liu and Awkwafina.
D’Alessandro says what he likes most about his work is collaborating with performers to tell a larger story. He likes the challenge of creating a stretched-out sweater for a character who is portrayed as nervous or an outfit that allows an active performer to do splits or cartwheels.
“When the singer or performer joins the process, they bring to life the piece you designed on paper,” he said. “The minute the actor or performer gets involved, it really elevates the ideas.”

title: Thousands have received paid family leave under Maine’s new program
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Andrew Thompson said he wouldn’t have been able to take much time off from work after the birth of his daughter had it not been for Maine’s new paid family and medical leave law.
Thompson, a baker at Scratch Bakery in South Portland, said his wife, Katherine, gave birth to Lucy, their first child, in January. She received paid leave through her work as an elementary school teacher, but Thompson said the bakery didn’t have its own program, so he received paid time through the state program.
Maine’s paid leave law was approved by lawmakers in 2023, and was fully implemented this year. Maine residents could begin applying for their paid leave benefits in March, and start receiving them in May.
“Having it be paid leave was absolutely necessary,” said Thompson, of Bath. “I have a steady gig with reliable hours, but it’s not the most robust pay for either of us. We live pretty frugally. Had it not been paid for three months, we would have had to figure out a pretty different scenario.”
According to a report released this month by the Maine Department of Labor, 4,720 claims were approved between March 30 and June 30 under the new law. Pregnancy or bonding with a child amounted to 45.6% of claims, 42.4% were for medical leave other than pregnancy and 11.6% were to care for a family member with a health condition.
The average weekly benefit was about $816.
The law provides up to 90% of pay for 12 weeks of time off for leave that includes caring for a newborn or an ill family member, or the worker’s own medical condition.
Thompson said his wife took her leave when Lucy was born, and he took off May, June and July. He said he hasn’t added it all up, but he was able to earn thousands per month, plus avoid monthly daycare costs.
“It gave us that extra time to learn those new skills, what the child needs in the moment,” Thompson said. “I got to bond with Lucy. It can take fathers longer to bond with their kids if they have to immediately go back to work.”
State Sen. Mattie Daughtry, D-Brunswick, one of the lawmakers who spearheaded the law, said she’s heard anecdotally that paid leave is incentivizing families to raise their children in Maine.
“We are seeing folks be able to afford raising kids here, where they may not have before,” Daughtry said.
Daughtry said another benefit for people is it gives them time to recover from a major surgery, rather than rushing back to work.
Luke Monahan, director of paid family and medical leave with the Maine Department of Labor, said he expects the new law will improve workforce participation, based on what’s occurred in the other 12 states, plus the District of Columbia, that already have paid leave laws. Among the New England states, Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island also have paid leave programs.
“People who were on the sidelines now may be able to come back into the workforce,” Monahan said.
The Institute for Women’s Policy Research released a study in 2020 that showed paid leave boosted workforce participation for women in New Jersey and California, when comparing rates before and after those states implemented their programs.
In Maine, the benefits are paid for through a 1% payroll tax, split evenly between the employer and employee.
Monahan said the Department of Labor expects participation will increase in 2027 and then plateau because, by then, the public will have a greater awareness of the program.
Destie Hohman Sprague, executive director of the Maine Women’s Lobby advocacy group, said she’s pleased to see people receiving their benefits, but would like to see the denial rate decrease.
The state rejected 1,772 of 6,492 claims for a variety of reasons, including failure to send in documentation needed to support the claim, being ineligible under the minimum income requirements, and the state being unable to verify the identity of the person applying, according to the claims report.
“It’s a big complicated program,” Sprague said. “Everybody seeking these benefits right now is the first person in their family to do this. We know it’s going to be a big learning curve from the administration side and the worker side.”
Monahan said people considering applying for benefits should first determine if their employer offers paid leave.
Thompson said because his wife is a teacher, several weeks of his paid leave time in June and July overlapped with her time off.
“There was laundry everywhere, but at the end of the day we knew we were in it together,” Thompson said. “It just made the experience of having a baby that much more special.”

title: Boothbay Harbor native pens final novel in his ‘Red at Night’ series
text:
Jerry Farnham’s father was a lobsterman and a shrimp picker. Born in Boothbay Harbor, Farnham joined the Navy and now works as a marine diesel mechanic. Life on the water has been as intuitive as it is devotional for him. To no surprise, the world of his books and the characters in them take to the water too.
“Last Light,” the finale of the four-book “Red at Night” series, charts the ebbs and flows of Jack Finn — a Boothbay Harbor lobsterman — and his family through the gravitas of romance and the suspense of lurking international terrorism in equal measure.
Retired actress and Jack’s wife, Melissa Andrews, gets called back to set for a local production when an up-and-coming production threatens to overshadow her whole career. With Jack at sea in a storm and Melissa adrift in her own life, navigating marriage, parenthood and family secrets is made more complicated by the presence of the paparazzi, a production company and a darker villain suddenly lurking everywhere in Boothbay Harbor.
Boothbay Harbor plays a big role in this novel and your series. How does Boothbay Harbor play into your psyche or way of thinking about yourself as a writer?
I knew I could generate a space that people could relate to. Other people in Boothbay know those places. It’s a vacation spot, so even people from elsewhere knew some of the places I mentioned. It also hopefully sparks some curiosity. People who have never been to Boothbay want to come here. In some ways, it was a way for me to take the easy road — I don’t have to world-build too much because I already know this place. But at the same time, it was a way to celebrate where I came from.
I always wanted to write. I started the first book in the series, “Red at Night,” when I was 16 years old. But I had a fifth-grade teacher call me stupid, and I had a freshman teacher say I wasn’t getting anywhere. I let that manifest enough that I wouldn’t move. I wouldn’t go forward with it. I had all this self-doubt. Then years later, here I am, the father of a daughter who was born with no fingers on her left hand, and I’m telling her, “You can’t use that as an excuse. You have to push forward. You have to get over this stuff.” And I think, “Wow, you’re a bit of a hypocrite there, Jerry, because you’re letting all this stuff hold you back.” So I finally started writing the book, and I just didn’t stop.
‘Last Light’ is the finale in a four-book series. Did you know when you were writing the first one that this would be a series? When you live with characters this long, how do you start thinking of a grand finale?
In the first novel, Jack is a lobsterman who encounters the famous actress and singer, Melissa Andrews, escaping the limelight in Boothbay Harbor. In this novel, Melissa is retiring. She’s becoming a school teacher. She’s getting out of the Hollywood life, but then someone gives her a call saying, “Hey, look, I’m thinking about directing a movie in your area, and I need you there.” Melissa is trying to prove that she could still do it, and accepting the fact that there are up-and-coming stars that are going to outshine her, but at the same time, she’s the force that drives some of these people to aspire to that level.
To get the feel of what it was like, I watched a lot of footage of Hollywood actresses and actors dealing with the media and paparazzi. I watched fans popping up and raiding their personal space to see how they handled it, and how they balanced being a good star, but at the same time, having their own personal boundaries. It seemed really hard to do that.
How has your experience growing up on the water helped you see yourself as a writer?
It helped me a lot. From the detail of hauling traps and and the motions that the characters go through, to even the thoughts and the monologues when characters are just staring out onto the water. You’re having that peaceful moment by yourself, smelling the salt air. I was able to deliver that to my readers just because I’ve been there.
You’ve proclaimed yourself as Maine’s blue collar author. How do you own that for yourself now?
I came up with it. Self-promoting has been the biggest bear I’ve tackled because I’m not one to preach about myself. It’s just not me. I’ve had to really develop that skill. I needed some type of tagline that would bring readers in. A lot of the people I work with, when they hear “author,” they’re thinking of a smoking jacket, a pipe and sipping tea. And I’m like, “No, you can be a roughneck like the rest of us, and still write a book.” It started as a tagline just to help promote the books, but I also want it to inspire people who might be sitting at a workbench or building something to not hesitate and write it down.
What do you think it is about Maine that makes it so ripe for the thriller genre?
People perceive Maine as very innocent — and for the most part, it is. We don’t have the crime rate most states have, but there is some violence, and there’s some stuff here that’s not always rainbows and puppies. There’s a bit of a shock value when you bring crime into the books. Nobody suspects anything’s going to happen to Maine. Maine in its own little innocent nature makes it a great place to have a crime novel because you don’t expect it.
Do your kids love the water too?
Yes, they do. Unfortunately, my father had a stroke, so he’s no longer lobstering, so my son hasn’t been able to go, but my daughter did go lobstering with me and my dad once, and she loved it. Both of them loved the water and loved hearing the stories of me being on the water. It’s a different time. I used to disappear in my skiff out on the Atlantic Ocean for eight hours at a time and my parents had no clue where I was. I’d get lunch at the co-op and take off and go longer. And then I’d come back.
Lisa Hiton is a writer living in Brooklyn, N.Y. She is the author of the poetry collection “Afterfeast,” and her work has been featured or is forthcoming in the Kenyon Review, The Slowdown, NPR, New South and elsewhere.

text:

title: Letter: Why not tariff relief for all Mainers?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Last week, Sen. Susan Collins announced and took credit for securing Canadian tariff (tax) relief on several products used by Maine’s agricultural industry, such as blueberry, potato and apple growers and some wood products companies. The timing of the relief by the Trump Administration was to boost Susan Collins re-election.
In announcing the temporary tariff relief, Collins stated the relief is vital for Maine farmers and small businesses. As a Maine voter I think it is important to ask ourselves: If these tariffs are hurting our farmers and small businesses, why do we seemingly only get tariff relief during Collins reelection campaign? There are many other equally deserving small businesses that are also being harmed economically by President Donald Trump’s Canadian tariffs. Why were those small businesses excluded from tariff relief?
The fact that it apparently took the heat of a tight reelection campaign for Collins to convince the Trump administration to give some tariff relief, after she essentially let Trump have the congressional power to impose the tariffs in the first place, demonstrates their motives. I believe the late election tariff relief Collins announced benefits her and Trump far more than it benefits us.
We need a senator that will advocate on behalf of the working people of Maine all the time, not just at election time.
Jonathan Stolley
Ellsworth

Clock tower above Rumford town hall hit by gunfire
text:
The clock tower above Rumford’s historic town hall was hit by gunfire this month.
The municipal building is home to the police department, an Oxford County Sheriff’s Office substation, judicial and government offices.
Officers heard gunfire, and something hitting the municipal building, about 8:42 p.m. on Oct. 10, according to the Rumford Police Department.
As officers investigated, more gunfire was reported near the intersection of Waldo Street and Rumford Avenue. More gunfire was reported in that neighborhood the next day and again on Oct. 14.
Police executed a search warrant at a Waldo Street residence on Oct. 20 as part of an investigation into drug and gun crimes. Two people were stabbed near that residence Sunday.
As of Wednesday, three people have been arrested in connection with the criminal activity in the Waldo Street neighborhood.
Police on Wednesday used a crane to inspect the apparent gunfire damage to the clock tower and to allow for repairs to prevent additional damage to the historic building.
The crimes remain under investigation.
“Let me be clear: Enough is enough,” Police Chief Tony Milligan, a lifelong Rumford resident, said in a Wednesday statement. “We will not allow the reckless and dangerous actions of a few individuals to define our community or undermine the quality of life our residents deserve. Rumford is a good community filled with good people, and we intend to do everything within our lawful authority to keep it that way.”

title: ‘Let’s make it the 51st state’: Trump suggests Venezuela could join US
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump took to the stage Tuesday at a venue in Corpus Christi, Texas, and said to the crowd, “See that little ship out there? It’s got 1 million barrels of oil on it from Venezuela.”

title: Ernie Johnson announces this will be his final season on ‘Inside The NBA’
text:
(Gray News) - Ernie Johnson announced he will be stepping down as host of “Inside the NBA” at the end of the season.
The Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer took to social media on Wednesday to explain his decision to step away, saying, “It’s just time.”
Johnson, 70, stated that he would not be retiring, but cutting back.
“This is by no means the end. It’s just a turning of the page,” Johnson said. “And I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with ‘Inside the NBA.’”
Johnson said he plans to continue to work, including covering the NCAA men’s basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports.
The six-time Sports Emmy Award winner acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years, but that isn’t the reason he’s stepping away from the show.
“I just want to slow down a bit,” he added in his social media post.
Johnson joined Turner Sports in 1989 and has hosted “Inside the NBA” since 1990. He thanked his TNT Sports and ESPN crews for their support over the years, as well as the viewers.
“I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support. And on this day, for your understanding,” Johnson said.

title: Maine report projects robust growth in healthcare jobs over the next decade
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new state workforce report projects thousands of annual job openings in the healthcare sector over the next decade as it continues to be one of the fastest growing industries in Maine.
The Maine Department of Labor report finds healthcare is making up an increasingly large share of the state’s labor market, accounting for 17% of all nonfarm jobs as of last year.
The report’s authors estimate that there will be around 7,500 job openings annually in Maine through 2034, as the state’s aging population continues driving demand for health services.
The openings are expected to be concentrated in roles that don’t require college degrees, such as home health aides and nursing assistants.
The report also projects robust demand for registered nurses at about a thousand job openings each year.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Washington Academy volleyball beats York in Class B semifinals
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
LEWISTON — Washington Academy’s volleyball team has played in enough semifinal and championship matches over the last few years to be more than prepared to execute when it matters most.
And after dropping the first set against York in a Class B semifinal match Wednesday, that’s exactly what it did. The Raiders (15-1) took the next three sets to defeat the Wildcats 3-1, clinching their third straight trip to the state final.
“Right in that huddle, (coach Kalyn Stevens) said, ‘this is amazing but we’re not done. That (win) means nothing because we’re going for the big Gold Ball,’” Jaylyn Warren said.
HOW IT HAPPENED
All four sets were competitive, as expected in a match between teams ranked No. 2 and No. 7, respectively, in the latest Varsity Maine volleyball poll. Washington Academy’s ability to close out sets, however, proved the difference.
After taking the first set 25-22, York (11-5) appeared ready to knock off the Raiders, but momentum quickly shifted. Washington Academy won the second set 25-16, then never looked back.
The Raiders took the third set 25-20 and the fourth 25-18 to close out the match.
UNSUNG HERO
Washington Academy’s Riley Shimabukuro had a couple late aces that helped the Raiders prevail in the fourth set. The sophomore finished with five aces.
HEARD IT HERE
• “It’s super exciting. I think this program is really special and so it’s just exciting to be a part of it. I’m really looking forward to (the state championship).” — Washington Academy coach Kalyn Stevens
• “We came out super strong and super motivated. I think the second, third and fourth games for York, we just made more errors on our side than we wanted to. But I’m super proud of these girls. They worked so hard.” — York coach Deanna Martin
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Washington Academy: Aubrey Faulkingham (16 kills, 11 digs), Jaylyn Warren (nine kills, three aces), Riley Shimabukuro (five aces, 12 digs)
• York: Sophie Coite (two aces)

title: Waterville technical center hosts ‘Guard Days’ for more than 500 students
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) -A Waterville technical center gave more than 500 students a hands-on look at possible military paths Wednesday.
The Mid-Maine Technical Center worked with the Maine Army National Guard to host Guard Days. The event gave students a chance to learn about career opportunities that combine military service with their civilian aspirations.
Students see military equipment
Students handled military equipment, including a Black Hawk helicopter, a mobile kitchen trailer and medical vehicles.
Max Wyman, a junior at the center, said the event gave him a chance to learn more about a future he is already considering.
“I’m personally enlisting after I graduate, and I think that this is a very useful outlet and it’s very proactive for kids who want to enlist,” Wyman said.
Guard jobs tied to technical skills
Staff Sgt. Travis Terrell of the Maine Army National Guard said many National Guard jobs connect directly to skills students are learning at technical centers.
“We’re just trying to showcase the opportunities that the Maine Army National Guard offers. These tech programs here in the state of Maine, they relate out to the real world,” Terrell said.
Culinary student Jamison Delisle explored the Guard’s mobile kitchen trailer.
“I like to see how they make their food, what the process looks like, what kind of equipment that they get to work with,” Delisle said.
Organizers focus on information
Victor Esposito, workforce development coordinator at the Mid-Maine Technical Center, helped organize the event over the past several months.
“I think part of it is getting kids to see the military in a different way. It’s more of a career opportunity and the jobs that are out there, especially with National Guard,” Esposito said.
Organizers said Guard Days was not about pressuring students to enlist, but about giving them information so they can make their own decisions.
“Don’t write it off. Explore it. Be informed before you make a final decision about military service,” said Lt. Col. Adam Davis of the Maine Army National Guard.
