title: Meet Bandit, our Adoptable Pet of the Week
text:
Meet Bandit, our Adoptable Pet of the Week in Greater Portland
This week's featured adoptable pet from the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland is Bandit, a dog who thrives on affection and loves being around people.
Bandit is almost 8 years old, but don't let his age fool you. He has a big personality and the energy to match it.
Matt Blanchard of the Animal Refuge League said Bandit is sure to be the life of the party wherever he goes. Although you would not know it based on his demeanor, Bandit had a rough start to his life.
"He didn't get trained. He didn't get socialized, and he didn't get outside very much. So as a result of that, he never learned some of the things that a lot of 8-year-old dogs know. For instance, house training," Blanchard said. "We want his adopters to know that at 8, he is still going to require some training and he is going to require a bit of a transition period when he goes into a home."
Blanchard said Bandit enjoys being around other dogs, but the Animal Refuge League is not sure about his attitude toward cats. Blanchard said he thinks Bandit would enjoy meeting kids.
More information about Bandit is available on the Animal Refuge League's website, as long as he is still looking for his forever home.
Anyone who is interested in meeting Bandit or other adoptable pets can visit the Animal Refuge League's shelter at 217 Landing Road in Westbrook between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., except on Wednesdays, when the shelter is closed for adoptions.
The Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland does adoptions on a first-come, first-served basis. On the days the shelter is open, sign-in sheets will be placed on the front door at 9 a.m. to track the order of arrival of adopters who show up early. People who arrive early are asked to remain on the campus once they sign in.
Dog owners who are interested in adopting dogs that are older than 6 months, including Bandit, are required to have their dogs meet the adoptable pet before a new pet can be brought home.

title: ﻿2 Colorado college students remain missing after hike, search continues
text:
'This is a gut punch': 2 Colorado college students found dead after planned hike, officials say
Officials said two Colorado college students have been found dead days after they went missing during a planned hike.
In an updated post on Facebook, the Chaffee County Sheriff's Office said Kaden Matsuda, 19, and 20-year-old Jackson Donlon were located in a basin of the West Apostle Mountain around 3:30 p.m. on Oct. 28.
The sheriff's office said both men were found near each other and pronounced dead on the scene.
“Our heart aches for Kaden and Jackson’s family and friends. We are very proud of our team’s efforts to find them before this weekend’s coming storm," Sheriff Andy Rohrich said in the post. "Although this is a gut punch, our prayers were answered that we would find Kaden and Jackson, allowing some closure for the family. We ask that everyone give time and distance to family members and friends as they mourn their loss.”
Authorities said foul play is not suspected, and no additional details or "theories as to what may have happened" will be released until an autopsy can be completed.
Matsuda, from Ridgway, Colorado, and Jackson Donlon, 20, from New York, were both students at Colorado Mountain College's Leadville Campus.
The sheriff's office said in a previous post that Kaden was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Jackson was studying to be a mountain guide, "Mountainair."
This story has been updated. Read the original story below.
Two college students in Colorado remain missing after authorities said they left for a planned hike and never returned.
The Chaffee County Sheriff's Office said on Oct. 26, they received a call from staff at Colorado Mountain College's Leadville Campus explaining that two of their students left campus on Friday, Oct. 23, to go on a hike and never returned.
The students were identified as Kaden Matsuda, 19, from Ridgway, Colorado, and 20-year-old Jackson Donlon, from New York.
Authorities learned from friends and family that the pair planned on hiking Ice Mountain on the far north end of Chaffee County, Colorado. Officials said hikers usually plan to drive near Winfield County Road 390 and access the Mount Huron trailhead.
Related: Video shows Mount Dukono erupting as hikers make their way down the mountain
Matsuda's vehicle was later located in the area.
Friends told authorities that both planned on returning from the hike on Saturday if they felt unsafe. Otherwise, they would return on Sunday.
Family and friends explained that both men are experienced hikers and should have appropriate clothing. Both had also sent their friends a text with a map plot showing their planned destinations.
The sheriff's office said the area in which Matsuda and Donlon were hiking received on-and-off rain showers "for multiple days," further saying there was a brief window of snow.
Officials said eight inches of snow was on the ground underneath Matsuda's vehicle.
"Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow. In some areas of Ice Mountain there are three or four feet of snow because of sluffing and drifting," the Chaffee County Sheriff's Office said. "Because it was only the first big snow, avalanche possibilities were not a huge concern. The mountain, hence, the name, is also now incased in ice from the rain/snow. To access the mountain teams would have to cross boulder fields that are now covered in all the snow, making it extremely dangerous and virtually impossible on foot. There is also nowhere on the mountain a helicopter could land to bring staff in."
Search and rescue teams were deployed to the area, the post continued, where no human tracks were found.
The area of Ice Mountain and other peaks were searched by "aircraft, including multiple drones, helicopters and the multi-mission aircraft with infrared technology, but Kaden and Jackson were not located."
It was also learned that both of their cellphones had not been used in the last 48 hours, with service in the area being almost "nonexistent." Officials said both students may have turned off their phones to conserve battery, making the last two days "less concerning."
The next day on Oct. 27, authorities said search teams located an object near Lake Ann.
A search team was sent in on foot to the area and discovered that the object was the hiker’s tent that had collapsed under the weight of the snow. The sheriff's office said there was no snow under the tent and there were no visible footprints in the snow, which suggested this was all in place before the snow came in.
Their sleeping bags, a stove and some clothing were inside the tent, but both students were not found.
"It is unimaginable what they must be going through. We are still optimistic Kaden and Jackson are hunkered down somewhere waiting to be rescued," authorities said. "Our window of opportunity is closing as poor weather is expected again later this week, so we are putting all our available resources in the field."
Officials continued, saying, "They are both strong, young men. Kaden is studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Jackson is studying to be a mountain guide, 'Mountainair', so hope is not lost. Please keep the families in your thoughts as we continue to search."

title: Woman charged after Facebook post threatening to shoot Trump at college football game
text:
Woman charged after Facebook post threatening to shoot Trump at Georgia-Alabama football game
A woman is facing federal charges after she threatened in a Facebook post to shoot President Donald Trump during his planned attendance at a college football game, according to authorities.
Related video above: Will President Trump's trips to ruby-red states and swing districts sway voters?
Megan Lorraine Utz, 36, of Alabama, was charged in a two-count indictment with threatening the president and transmitting a threatening communication across state lines, the U.S. attorney’s office for the Northern District of Alabama announced last week.
The alleged threat centered on Trump’s appearance at the Oct. 10 matchup in Tuscaloosa between The University of Alabama and The University of Georgia, according to court documents cited by prosecutors.
Trump later canceled his appearance due to expected impacts from Hurricane Isaias.
Facebook post led to investigation
According to the indictment and criminal complaint, Utz posted the threat on Oct. 5 while discussing Trump’s attendance at the Alabama-Georgia game.
“I’ll put a bullet through him if he dares,” the post stated, according to prosecutors.
FBI agents, Secret Service agents and Florence police located Utz in Florence, Alabama, the following day. Local police arrested her on an outstanding misdemeanor warrant for harassing communications issued by the Guin Police Department.
Utz was also arrested on a federal complaint involving the alleged threat against Trump before the indictment was returned, prosecutors said.
Federal officials stress seriousness of threats
“Threats of violence, whether made online or in person, are taken seriously,” said David R. Fitzgibbons, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Birmingham office.
“People have every right to express their views, but when that expression turns into a threat against the President of the United States, it becomes a priority matter,” he said.

title: Mainers tell the stories that bring us home in ‘Mythic Migrations’
text:
“Nevertheless I long—I pine, all my days—to travel home and see the dawn of my return. And if a god will wreck me yet again on the wine-dark sea, I can bear that too, with a spirit tempered to endure.”
— Homer, “The Odyssey”
I knew my great-grandmother. In 1913, at the age of 13, she hid among bales of hay on a cargo ship traveling from Odessa, Ukraine, to the United States.
I’ve often wondered what that journey was like for her. What did it feel like to cross the ocean, hidden in the hay? What did she imagine awaited her on the other side? What did those first steps in a new land feel like? What did her imaginary “promised land” look like? I’d give anything to hear her tell that story, in all its detail, broken English, Russian accent, and all.
Stories are the heart and soul of a new kind of performance project happening at the Chocolate Church Arts Center this November. “Mythic Migrations,” an original storytelling performance co-directed by acclaimed writer and translator Ilan Stavans and me, will take place on the Main Stage on Friday, Nov. 20, at 7 p.m. The performance is the culmination of a weeklong storytelling workshop with local participants whose lives and family histories span the globe.
Our storytellers include new Mainers whose journeys have brought them from Somalia, Palestine, China, Puerto Rico, Iraq, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, alongside longtime Maine residents, including one participant whose family has lived in Bath for more than seven generations. My own older son, Nicolás, who was born in Chile, will also be taking part.
These are stories that, like my great-grandmother’s, I think of as both personal and mythic — spanning generations, geographies, and vastly different experiences, yet connected by something deeply human.
Throughout the week, participants will draw upon oral history, personal memory, and family stories to develop autobiographical monologues. Together, we’ll explore three essential chapters of the human journey: leaving home, the journey itself, and making a new home.
Stavans, who was born in Mexico City, is an internationally recognized essayist, scholar, translator, and poet. Getting to collaborate with him on this project is something of a dream for me, and I’m excited for our community to encounter him both through “Mythic Migrations” and at a special public talk about his new book of poems and essays, Fictional Translations, on Monday, Nov. 16, at 6:30 p.m., in the Chocolate Church Annex.
As for what the performance will look and feel like, we’re imagining something of a mosaic. Rather than a succession of individual monologues, Stavans and I will weave these stories together into a collectively shaped theatrical work performed by each participant. Music, objects, and projections will contribute to the staging, but the performance will remain rooted in the simplicity and intimacy of storytelling, allowing the voices and lived experiences of the participants to take center stage. None of our storytellers are professional actors, and that’s part of what makes this project so exciting.
After all, each of our lives is an epic of sorts, shaped by generations of people seeking, leaving, losing, remembering, and making home. We are all travelers, whether our families have lived in one place for centuries or have only recently arrived.
“Mythic Migrations” is about these journeys, and about the stories we carry with us, sometimes across oceans, sometimes across generations. Stories that connect us to the places we’ve left, the places we’ve come to call home, and to one another.
Matthew Glassman is executive and artistic director of the Chocolate Church Arts Center in Bath.
